add_constant_offset.name: add_constant_offset
add_constant_offset.code:
# Custom Mutation: add_constant_offset
# =====================================
# This mutation selects a random subtree and wraps it with an addition
# of a random constant: `subtree` -> `subtree + c`
#
# This is different from built-in mutations:
# - mutate_constant: only perturbs EXISTING constants
# - add_node: adds operators at LEAF nodes only
# - insert_node: inserts operator but uses random leaves, not the subtree
#
# This mutation introduces a new constant offset to any part of the tree,
# which can help discover formulas with additive terms.

# Note: This file is `include`d into CustomMutationsModule, so it has access
# to: AbstractExpressionNode, NodeSampler, constructorof, set_node!, etc.

"""
    add_constant_offset(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

Wrap a random subtree with addition of a random constant.
`subtree` becomes `subtree + c` where `c` is sampled from normal distribution.

`dataset` is accepted for signature compatibility with data-aware mutations
but is unused here.
"""
function add_constant_offset(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Find the + operator index (binary operators are indexed by their position)
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), options.operators.binops)

    if plus_idx === nothing
        # No + operator available, return tree unchanged
        return tree
    end

    # Sample a random node to wrap
    node = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))

    # Create a random constant
    constant_value = randn(rng, T)  # Sample from normal distribution
    constant_node = constructorof(N)(T; val=constant_value)

    # Create new node: node + constant
    # Randomly decide if constant goes on left or right
    if rand(rng, Bool)
        new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(copy(node), constant_node))
    else
        new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(constant_node, copy(node)))
    end

    # Replace the selected node with the wrapped version
    set_node!(node, new_node)

    return tree
end

age_regularized_survival.name: age_regularized_survival
age_regularized_survival.code:
# Custom Survival: age_regularized_survival
# ==========================================
# Default survival strategy: replace the oldest population member, mirroring
# the age-regularized evolution strategy from the original SymbolicRegression.jl.
# Behavior is identical to `default_survival` in CustomSurvival.jl; exposed here
# as a named custom operator so the meta-evolution loop has a concrete parent
# to refine from.

function age_regularized_survival(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)
    births = [(i in exclude_indices) ? typemax(BT) : pop.members[i].birth
              for i in 1:(pop.n)]
    return argmin_fast(births)
end

tournament_selection.name: tournament_selection
tournament_selection.code:
# Custom Selection: tournament_selection
# =======================================
# Default selection strategy: tournament selection with adaptive parsimony,
# mirroring `default_selection` in CustomSelection.jl (which is itself a
# self-contained reimplementation of `best_of_sample` from Population.jl).
# Exposed here as a named custom operator so the meta-evolution loop has a
# concrete parent to refine from.

function tournament_selection(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, options.tournament_selection_n; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)
    p = options.tournament_selection_p

    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
        adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
        for i in 1:n
            member = sample[i]
            size = compute_complexity(member, options)
            frequency = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        end
    else
        for i in 1:n
            adjusted_costs[i] = sample[i].cost
        end
    end

    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(adjusted_costs)
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        if tournament_winner == 1
            argmin_fast(adjusted_costs)
        else
            bottomk_fast(adjusted_costs, tournament_winner)[2][end]
        end
    end
    return copy(sample[chosen_idx])
end

affine_continuation_loss_init_8.name: affine_continuation_loss_init_8
affine_continuation_loss_init_8.code:
"""
    affine_continuation_loss_init_8(tree, dataset, options)

Evaluate an expression using an adaptive combination of raw normalized error and an
affine-calibrated structural error. A single numerically stable Welford pass computes
the raw residual sum of squares and the moments needed to estimate the best affine
mapping `a * prediction + b` analytically. The two errors are variance-normalized and
compressed with `log1p`.

When raw error is large, up to 75% of the loss comes from the affine-calibrated error,
rewarding expressions that have the correct functional shape before their constants
are tuned. This scaffold fades continuously as raw error approaches zero, so only the
actual target predictions attain zero loss. Nearly constant targets disable the
affine scaffold, and variance floors avoid unstable calibration of constant
predictions. No expression-complexity penalty is included.
"""
function affine_continuation_loss_init_8(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)

    # Online means and centered sums avoid the cancellation of raw power sums.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    mean_d = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    m2_d = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        d = p - y

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y) && isfinite(d))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        k = L(i)

        delta_p = p - mean_p
        mean_p += delta_p / k

        delta_y = y - mean_y
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        # This covariance update uses the newly updated target mean.
        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)

        delta_d = d - mean_d
        mean_d += delta_d / k
        m2_d += delta_d * (d - mean_d)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) && isfinite(mean_d) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(m2_d) &&
         isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Centered sums can become microscopically negative from roundoff.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)
    m2_d = max(m2_d, zero_l)

    n_l = L(n)
    raw_sse = m2_d + n_l * mean_d * mean_d
    if !isfinite(raw_sse)
        return L(Inf)
    elseif raw_sse == zero_l
        return zero_l
    end

    # Relative floors suppress unstable affine fits to numerically constant data.
    y_reference = max(one_l, abs(mean_y))
    p_reference = max(one_l, abs(mean_p))
    scale_floor = n_l * eps(L) * y_reference * y_reference
    prediction_floor = n_l * eps(L) * p_reference * p_reference

    if !(isfinite(scale_floor) && isfinite(prediction_floor))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    scale_sse = max(m2_y, scale_floor)
    target_is_variable = m2_y > scale_floor

    affine_sse = raw_sse
    if target_is_variable
        if m2_p > prediction_floor
            # For least-squares a*p+b, explained SSE is cov(p,y)^2 / var(p).
            normalized_covariance = cov_py / sqrt(m2_p)
            explained_sse = normalized_covariance * normalized_covariance
            if !isfinite(explained_sse)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            affine_sse = clamp(m2_y - explained_sse, zero_l, m2_y)
        else
            # A constant prediction can only fit the target intercept.
            affine_sse = m2_y
        end
    end

    raw_nmse = raw_sse / scale_sse
    affine_nmse = affine_sse / scale_sse
    if !(isfinite(raw_nmse) && isfinite(affine_nmse))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    raw_term = log1p(max(raw_nmse, zero_l))
    affine_term = log1p(max(affine_nmse, zero_l))

    # Structural guidance is strong far from the target and vanishes near a fit.
    scaffold_strength = L(3) / L(4)
    blend = scaffold_strength * raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse)
    loss_value = (one_l - blend) * raw_term + blend * affine_term

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_0.name: algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_0
algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_0.code:
"""
    algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_0(tree, options, nfeatures, rng)

A *semantics-preserving* structural mutation: it rewrites the expression tree using
elementary algebraic identities (factoring, common-denominator collection, cancellation,
division folding, and distribution) instead of perturbing the expression randomly.

The motivation is that PySR's built-in mutations are *local* edits (change one operator,
one constant, insert/delete one node), so two algebraically identical but structurally
distant forms — e.g. `x1*x2 + x1*x3` and `x1*(x2 + x3)` — are separated by many
individually-deleterious steps. Ground-truth expressions in SRBench/Feynman-style
benchmarks are usually written in a *factored / low-complexity* canonical form, so a
population that has found the right semantics in an expanded form is stuck on a
complexity plateau: it scores well on loss but is penalized on parsimony and cannot
reach the compact form gradually. This mutation performs the algebraic "jump" in one
move. Because loss is (nearly) unchanged, the move is essentially free from the
selection point of view, while the complexity often drops — so it acts as a neutral
drift / simplification operator that both compresses good expressions and re-shapes
them so that subsequent local mutations explore a different neighborhood.

Implementation: it first locates `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` in the operator set (if none of
`*`/`/` exist, it exits). It then traverses the whole tree once, and for every binary
node it checks a catalogue of rewrite patterns, building the replacement subtree
(from *copies* of the relevant grandchildren, so no aliasing occurs):
(1) exact sum cancellation `(a+b)-b -> a`, `(a-b)+b -> a`;
(2) factoring a shared multiplicative term out of a sum `a*b ± a*c -> a*(b±c)`
    (any of the four factor orderings, using structural subtree equality);
(3) common denominator collection `a/c ± b/c -> (a±b)/c`;
(4)/(5) multiplicative cancellation `(a*b)/a -> b`, `(a/b)*b -> a`;
(6) folding nested divisions `(a/b)/c -> a/(b*c)`;
(7) lifting an inner division `a/(b/c) -> (a*c)/b`;
(8) distribution `a*(b±c) -> a*b ± a*c`, allowed only when the duplicated factor `a`
    has at most 3 nodes and the result still fits inside `options.maxsize`.
All candidate sites are collected and one is chosen by weighted sampling that strongly
prefers size-reducing rewrites (weight 4), then factoring/folding (3/2), and only rarely
expansion (1) — expansion is kept because it is sometimes the precursor that lets a
later factoring find a *different* common factor. Cancellation rules (4)–(7) assume the
cancelled subtree is non-zero, which is the usual generic-position assumption; if no
pattern matches, the tree is returned unchanged.
"""
function algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_0(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    tree.degree == 0 && return tree

    binops = options.operators.binops
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), binops)
    minus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (-), binops)
    times_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (*), binops)
    div_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (/), binops)

    # Without any multiplicative operator none of the identities below apply.
    (times_idx === nothing && div_idx === nothing) && return tree

    # ---- structural (syntactic) equality of two subtrees ----
    function trees_equal(a::N, b::N)
        a.degree == b.degree || return false
        if a.degree == 0
            a.constant == b.constant || return false
            return a.constant ? (a.val == b.val) : (a.feature == b.feature)
        end
        a.op == b.op || return false
        for i in 1:(a.degree)
            trees_equal(get_child(a, i), get_child(b, i)) || return false
        end
        return true
    end

    # ---- cheap operator-identity predicates ----
    is_plus(t) = t.degree == 2 && plus_idx !== nothing && t.op == plus_idx
    is_minus(t) = t.degree == 2 && minus_idx !== nothing && t.op == minus_idx
    is_sum(t) = is_plus(t) || is_minus(t)
    is_times(t) = t.degree == 2 && times_idx !== nothing && t.op == times_idx
    is_div(t) = t.degree == 2 && div_idx !== nothing && t.op == div_idx

    # Candidate rewrites: (node to overwrite, replacement subtree) plus a sampling weight.
    sites = Tuple{N,N}[]
    weights = Float64[]
    add_site!(node, repl, w) = (push!(sites, (node, repl)); push!(weights, w); nothing)

    # Build a fresh binary node.
    bin(op, a, b) = constructorof(N)(; op=op, children=(a, b))

    total = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : 30

    # Full traversal: `any` visits every node as long as we keep returning `false`.
    any(tree) do t
        if t.degree == 2
            c1 = get_child(t, 1)
            c2 = get_child(t, 2)

            # (1) exact cancellation inside sums: (a+b)-b, (a+b)-a, (a-b)+b, b+(a-b)
            if is_minus(t) && is_plus(c1)
                if trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0)
                elseif trees_equal(get_child(c1, 1), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), 4.0)
                end
            elseif is_plus(t) && is_minus(c1) && trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0)
            elseif is_plus(t) && is_minus(c2) && trees_equal(get_child(c2, 2), c1)
                add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c2, 1)), 4.0)
            end

            # (2) factor a shared multiplicative term: a*b ± a*c -> a*(b±c)
            if is_sum(t) && is_times(c1) && is_times(c2)
                for i in 1:2, j in 1:2
                    if trees_equal(get_child(c1, i), get_child(c2, j))
                        common = copy(get_child(c1, i))
                        rest1 = copy(get_child(c1, 3 - i))   # the *other* factor of c1
                        rest2 = copy(get_child(c2, 3 - j))   # the *other* factor of c2
                        add_site!(t, bin(times_idx, common, bin(t.op, rest1, rest2)), 3.0)
                        break  # one factoring per node is enough
                    end
                end
            end

            # (3) common denominator: a/c ± b/c -> (a±b)/c
            if is_sum(t) &&
                is_div(c1) &&
                is_div(c2) &&
                trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), get_child(c2, 2))
                add_site!(
                    t,
                    bin(
                        div_idx,
                        bin(t.op, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), copy(get_child(c2, 1))),
                        copy(get_child(c1, 2)),
                    ),
                    3.0,
                )
            end

            # (4) multiplicative cancellation: (a*b)/a -> b  and  (a*b)/b -> a
            if is_div(t) && is_times(c1)
                if trees_equal(get_child(c1, 1), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), 4.0)
                elseif trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0)
                end
            end

            # (5) multiplicative cancellation: (a/b)*b -> a  and  b*(a/b) -> a
            if is_times(t)
                if is_div(c1) && trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0)
                elseif is_div(c2) && trees_equal(get_child(c2, 2), c1)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c2, 1)), 4.0)
                end
            end

            # (6) fold nested divisions: (a/b)/c -> a/(b*c)
            if is_div(t) && is_div(c1) && times_idx !== nothing
                add_site!(
                    t,
                    bin(
                        div_idx,
                        copy(get_child(c1, 1)),
                        bin(times_idx, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), copy(c2)),
                    ),
                    2.0,
                )
            end

            # (7) lift an inner division: a/(b/c) -> (a*c)/b
            if is_div(t) && is_div(c2) && times_idx !== nothing
                add_site!(
                    t,
                    bin(
                        div_idx,
                        bin(times_idx, copy(c1), copy(get_child(c2, 2))),
                        copy(get_child(c2, 1)),
                    ),
                    2.0,
                )
            end

            # (8) distribution (the only size-increasing rewrite): a*(b±c) -> a*b ± a*c
            if is_times(t)
                for k in 1:2
                    s = get_child(t, k)          # candidate sum
                    m = get_child(t, 3 - k)      # multiplier that gets duplicated
                    if is_sum(s)
                        nm = count_nodes(m)
                        # keep the duplicated factor tiny and respect the size budget
                        if nm <= 3 && total + nm + 1 <= maxsize
                            add_site!(
                                t,
                                bin(
                                    s.op,
                                    bin(times_idx, copy(m), copy(get_child(s, 1))),
                                    bin(times_idx, copy(m), copy(get_child(s, 2))),
                                ),
                                1.0,
                            )
                        end
                    end
                end
            end
        end
        return false  # never short-circuit: we want a complete traversal
    end

    isempty(sites) && return tree  # no identity applies -> leave the tree untouched

    # Weighted sampling: simplifications are much more likely than expansion.
    r = rand(rng) * sum(weights)
    idx = length(weights)
    acc = 0.0
    for (i, w) in enumerate(weights)
        acc += w
        if r <= acc
            idx = i
            break
        end
    end

    node, repl = sites[idx]
    # `repl` was built exclusively from copies, so in-place overwrite is safe
    # (this also works when `node === tree`, so the root never needs special handling).
    set_node!(node, repl)
    return tree
end

mse_loss.name: mse_loss
mse_loss.code:
# Custom Loss: mse_loss
# =====================
# Default loss: per-sample mean squared error. Behavior matches the built-in
# `_eval_loss` path on unweighted, unitless datasets, exposed as a named
# operator so the meta-evolution loop has a concrete parent to refine.
#
# For weighted datasets or unit-bearing data, the in-module `default_loss`
# (used when no operator is loaded) handles `dataset.weights` and
# `dimensional_regularization` via `_eval_loss`. This baseline assumes
# unweighted, unitless data, which matches every SRBench dataset on the
# PySR pipeline.

function mse_loss(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end
    diff = prediction .- dataset.y
    return L(sum(abs2, diff) / length(diff))
end

fit_greedy_correction_factor_gen1_2.name: fit_greedy_correction_factor_gen1_2
fit_greedy_correction_factor_gen1_2.code:
"""
    fit_greedy_correction_factor_gen1_2(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

A data-aware "greedy residual-factor" mutation. It asks the question *"what
multiplicative correction would turn my current prediction into the target?"*
and then tries to express that correction with one very simple, least-squares
fitted factor built out of the raw features.

Concretely: the tree is evaluated on `dataset.X` to get `ŷ`. Two correction
targets are formed pointwise, `t_mul = y/ŷ` (used as `tree * factor`) and
`t_div = ŷ/y` (used as `tree / factor`). A small library of cheap candidate
factor bodies is generated from the data columns — `x_i`, `1/x_i`, and (for a
random capped subset of feature pairs) `x_i/x_j` and `x_i*x_j`. For every
(candidate, mode) pair the operator performs an exact 1-D linear least-squares
fit `t ≈ a + b*f` and scores it by the unexplained variance fraction
`1 - r²`. The best-scoring combination (if it explains a reasonable share of
the correction) is materialised as a new root `tree * (a + b*f)` or
`tree / (a + b*f)`, with `a` or `b` dropped when they are numerically trivial
so that no complexity is wasted.

The `div` mode is the important one: whenever the true law contains a factor of
the form `(a + b*x_i/x_j)` in the *denominator* (e.g. relativistic
`1 - v/c`, Michaelis–Menten style `1 + S/K`, `1 - x/L` geometry terms), plain
mutation/constant-optimisation tends to only ever discover its Taylor
expansion in the numerator (visible in the execution trace, where
`x0*(x3 + 0.39*x4)/(x1*x2*x4)` and ever-growing `exp`/`log` patches accumulate
instead of `1/(1 - x3/x4)`). Since `ŷ/y` is *exactly* that missing denominator
factor once the rest of the formula is right, a single linear fit recovers it
in one shot and the mutation jumps straight onto the correct structure.

Heuristics/assumptions: samples are strided down to at most 256 points to keep
the operator cheap; points where `ŷ`, `y`, or the candidate are non-finite (or
too close to zero for the ratio to be meaningful) are dropped; per-sample
`dataset.weights` are ignored; requires `*` and `+` operators to be available
(`/` enables the reciprocal candidates and the divisive mode). The proposal is
returned unconditionally to the caller, so the usual accept/reject (annealing)
machinery still guards against corrections that happen to hurt the loss.
"""
function fit_greedy_correction_factor_gen1_2(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    y = dataset.y
    y === nothing && return tree
    nfeatures < 1 && return tree

    # --- locate the operators we need -------------------------------------
    binops = options.operators.binops
    mul_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (*), binops)
    add_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), binops)
    div_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (/), binops)
    (mul_idx === nothing || add_idx === nothing) && return tree

    # --- current prediction ----------------------------------------------
    y_pred, ok = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options.operators)
    ok || return tree

    # --- stride-subsample the data for speed ------------------------------
    n = dataset.n
    n < 8 && return tree
    stride = max(1, div(n, 256))
    idx = 1:stride:n
    m = length(idx)
    m < 8 && return tree

    Xs = view(dataset.X, :, idx)          # (nfeatures, m); columns are samples
    ys = Vector{Float64}(undef, m)
    ps = Vector{Float64}(undef, m)
    @inbounds for k in 1:m
        ys[k] = Float64(y[idx[k]])
        ps[k] = Float64(y_pred[idx[k]])
    end

    # --- candidate factor bodies: (kind, i, j) ----------------------------
    # kind 1 = x_i, 2 = 1/x_i, 3 = x_i/x_j, 4 = x_i*x_j
    cands = NTuple{3,Int}[]
    for i in 1:nfeatures
        push!(cands, (1, i, 0))
        div_idx !== nothing && push!(cands, (2, i, 0))
    end
    if nfeatures > 1
        # random (capped) set of pairs so cost stays O(nfeatures) not O(nfeatures^2)
        npairs = min(8, nfeatures * (nfeatures - 1))
        for _ in 1:npairs
            i = rand(rng, 1:nfeatures)
            j = rand(rng, filter(!=(i), 1:nfeatures))
            div_idx !== nothing && push!(cands, (3, i, j))
            push!(cands, (4, i, j))
        end
    end
    isempty(cands) && return tree

    # --- search for the best (candidate, mode) linear correction ----------
    fbuf = Vector{Float64}(undef, m)
    best_score = 0.9                      # must explain >=10% of the correction
    best_kind = 0
    best_i = 0
    best_j = 0
    best_mode = 0
    best_a = 0.0
    best_b = 0.0
    best_fbar = 0.0

    for (kind, i, j) in cands
        # materialise candidate values on the subsample
        @inbounds for k in 1:m
            xi = Float64(Xs[i, k])
            fbuf[k] = if kind == 1
                xi
            elseif kind == 2
                1.0 / xi
            elseif kind == 3
                xi / Float64(Xs[j, k])
            else
                xi * Float64(Xs[j, k])
            end
        end

        for mode in 1:2
            # mode 1: tree * factor  (fit y/ŷ);  mode 2: tree / factor (fit ŷ/y)
            mode == 2 && div_idx === nothing && continue

            cnt = 0
            sf = 0.0
            st = 0.0
            sff = 0.0
            sft = 0.0
            stt = 0.0
            @inbounds for k in 1:m
                f = fbuf[k]
                isfinite(f) || continue
                yk = ys[k]
                pk = ps[k]
                (isfinite(yk) && isfinite(pk)) || continue
                # pointwise correction target; skip near-zero denominators
                t = if mode == 1
                    abs(pk) > 1e-10 ? yk / pk : NaN
                else
                    abs(yk) > 1e-10 ? pk / yk : NaN
                end
                isfinite(t) || continue
                cnt += 1
                sf += f
                st += t
                sff += f * f
                sft += f * t
                stt += t * t
            end
            cnt < 8 && continue

            # closed-form 1-D least squares: t ≈ a + b*f
            w = Float64(cnt)
            fbar = sf / w
            tbar = st / w
            varf = sff / w - fbar * fbar
            vart = stt / w - tbar * tbar
            (varf > 1e-14 && vart > 1e-14) || continue
            covft = sft / w - fbar * tbar
            b = covft / varf
            resid = vart - covft * covft / varf          # residual variance
            score = max(resid, 0.0) / vart               # == 1 - r^2
            (isfinite(score) && isfinite(b)) || continue
            a = tbar - b * fbar
            isfinite(a) || continue

            if score < best_score
                best_score = score
                best_kind = kind
                best_i = i
                best_j = j
                best_mode = mode
                best_a = a
                best_b = b
                best_fbar = fbar
            end
        end
    end

    best_mode == 0 && return tree                        # nothing worthwhile found

    # --- build the factor node: (a + b*f), with trivial terms dropped -----
    scale = abs(best_b) * (abs(best_fbar) + 1.0) + abs(best_a) + 1e-12
    drop_a = abs(best_a) < 1e-4 * scale
    unit_b = abs(best_b - 1.0) < 1e-4

    local body::N
    if best_kind == 2
        # b * (1/x_i)  ==  b / x_i  (one node cheaper)
        if unit_b
            body = constructorof(N)(;
                op=div_idx,
                children=(
                    constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T)), constructorof(N)(T; feature=best_i)
                ),
            )
        else
            body = constructorof(N)(;
                op=div_idx,
                children=(
                    constructorof(N)(T; val=T(best_b)),
                    constructorof(N)(T; feature=best_i),
                ),
            )
        end
    else
        # raw candidate body first ...
        fnode = if best_kind == 1
            constructorof(N)(T; feature=best_i)
        elseif best_kind == 3
            constructorof(N)(;
                op=div_idx,
                children=(
                    constructorof(N)(T; feature=best_i),
                    constructorof(N)(T; feature=best_j),
                ),
            )
        else
            constructorof(N)(;
                op=mul_idx,
                children=(
                    constructorof(N)(T; feature=best_i),
                    constructorof(N)(T; feature=best_j),
                ),
            )
        end
        # ... then the slope, unless it is essentially 1
        body = if unit_b
            fnode
        else
            constructorof(N)(;
                op=mul_idx, children=(constructorof(N)(T; val=T(best_b)), fnode)
            )
        end
    end

    factor = if drop_a
        body
    else
        constructorof(N)(;
            op=add_idx, children=(constructorof(N)(T; val=T(best_a)), body)
        )
    end

    # --- splice in as a new root ------------------------------------------
    if best_mode == 1
        return constructorof(N)(; op=mul_idx, children=(tree, factor))
    else
        return constructorof(N)(; op=div_idx, children=(tree, factor))
    end
end

symmetric_motif_graft_init_1.name: symmetric_motif_graft_init_1
symmetric_motif_graft_init_1.code:
"""
    symmetric_motif_graft_init_1(tree, options, nfeatures, rng)

A "building-block reuse" structural mutation. Many ground-truth physical/engineering
formulas are built from a small number of *repeated motifs* that appear in several
terms, often with the variables permuted: `sqrt(x1^2 + x2^2)`, `x1*x2/x3^2 + x4*x5/x3^2`,
`sin(x1)*cos(x2) + cos(x1)*sin(x2)`, `(x1 - x2)^2 + (x3 - x4)^2`, etc. Ordinary
point mutations must rebuild such a partner term node-by-node, each intermediate step
usually being worse than the parent, so these symmetric forms are very hard to reach.
This operator constructs a partner term in a *single* move: it picks an existing
operator subtree of the tree (a "motif"), copies it, optionally relabels the features
inside the copy (rename one feature, or transpose two features globally), and grafts
the copy onto a randomly chosen leaf, combining it with that leaf through a
commutative-preferred binary operator (`+` or `*` when available).

Steps: (1) compute the size budget from `options.maxsize` so the graft cannot blow past
the complexity ceiling; (2) collect all operator subtrees that fit in the budget and
contain at least one variable leaf (constant-only motifs are useless to duplicate);
(3) pick a donor via a size-based tournament (mild bias toward compact, reusable
motifs); (4) copy it and apply one of three feature-relabelling modes — rename
(≈45%), transpose (≈25%), verbatim duplication (≈30%) — the first two generate the
"other half" of a symmetric expression, the last one generates powers/products of the
same motif; (5) splice it in at a random leaf, either as `op(leaf, motif)` (with random
argument order, so non-commutative fallback operators still explore both sides) or,
with small probability, as a direct transplant that overwrites the leaf with the motif.
Assumptions: the mutation is purely structural (no data), it always returns the same
root (the root is never replaced), and it silently returns the tree unchanged whenever
no legal donor/target exists or the budget is exhausted.
"""
function symmetric_motif_graft_init_1(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Need at least one operator node to have a "motif" to reuse.
    tree.degree == 0 && return tree

    # --- 1. Size budget -------------------------------------------------------
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? Int(options.maxsize) : 30
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    # A graft costs: donor_size (copy) + 1 (the new combining operator).
    budget = maxsize - tree_size - 1
    budget < 2 && return tree  # cannot even fit the smallest useful motif

    # --- 2. Collect legal donor motifs ---------------------------------------
    candidates = N[]
    any(tree) do t
        if t.degree > 0 && count_nodes(t) <= budget
            # Require at least one variable leaf: duplicating a constant-only
            # subtree adds complexity without adding structure.
            if any(s -> s.degree == 0 && !s.constant, t)
                push!(candidates, t)
            end
        end
        return false
    end
    isempty(candidates) && return tree

    # --- 3. Pick a donor, with a mild bias toward compact motifs -------------
    donor = rand(rng, candidates)
    if length(candidates) > 1 && rand(rng) < 0.5
        alt = rand(rng, candidates)
        # size tournament: keep the smaller of the two draws
        if count_nodes(alt) < count_nodes(donor)
            donor = alt
        end
    end
    motif = copy(donor)  # copy *before* touching the tree, so grafting is safe

    # --- 4. Relabel features inside the copy ---------------------------------
    feats = Int[]
    any(motif) do t
        if t.degree == 0 && !t.constant
            push!(feats, t.feature)
        end
        return false
    end
    unique!(feats)

    if nfeatures > 1 && !isempty(feats)
        mode = rand(rng)
        if mode < 0.45
            # RENAME: all occurrences of one feature become a different feature.
            # e.g. (x1 - x3)^2  ->  (x2 - x3)^2   (partner term of a symmetric sum)
            f = rand(rng, feats)
            g = rand(rng, filter(!=(f), 1:nfeatures))
            any(motif) do t
                if t.degree == 0 && !t.constant && t.feature == f
                    t.feature = g
                end
                return false
            end
        elseif mode < 0.70
            # TRANSPOSE: globally swap two features inside the copy.
            # e.g. sin(x1)*cos(x2) -> sin(x2)*cos(x1)  (needed for angle-sum forms)
            f = rand(rng, feats)
            g = rand(rng, filter(!=(f), 1:nfeatures))
            any(motif) do t
                if t.degree == 0 && !t.constant
                    if t.feature == f
                        t.feature = g
                    elseif t.feature == g
                        t.feature = f
                    end
                end
                return false
            end
        end
        # otherwise (≈30%): verbatim duplication (powers / repeated products)
    end

    # --- 5. Choose the combining binary operator ------------------------------
    nbin = length(options.nops) >= 2 ? options.nops[2] : 0
    op_pool = Int[]
    if nbin > 0
        # Prefer commutative accumulators: they build sums/products of motifs.
        for wanted in (+, *)
            idx = findfirst(o -> o === wanted, options.operators.binops)
            idx !== nothing && push!(op_pool, idx)
        end
        isempty(op_pool) && push!(op_pool, rand(rng, 1:nbin))
    end

    # --- 6. Pick the graft site (any leaf) and splice ------------------------
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> t.degree == 0))

    if isempty(op_pool) || rand(rng) < 0.15
        # Direct transplant: the leaf is simply replaced by the motif copy.
        # (Also the only option when no binary operators are available.)
        set_node!(target, motif)
        return tree
    end

    op_idx = rand(rng, op_pool)
    leaf_copy = copy(target)  # must copy: set_node! overwrites `target` in place
    # Randomize argument order so non-commutative fallback operators explore both sides.
    children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (leaf_copy, motif) : (motif, leaf_copy)
    new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=op_idx, children=children)
    set_node!(target, new_node)

    return tree
end

pareto_epsilon_tournament_selection_gen1.name: pareto_epsilon_tournament_selection_gen1_5
pareto_epsilon_tournament_selection_gen1.code:
"""
    pareto_epsilon_tournament_selection_gen1_5(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Tournament selection with adaptive parsimony (as in the parent operator), augmented
with two cheap, targeted improvements aimed at *ground-truth recovery* rather than
raw loss minimization:

Core steps
----------
1. Sample `tournament_selection_n` distinct members (clamped to the population size).
2. Compute each sampled member's complexity once, and its frequency-adjusted cost
   `cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * normalized_frequency[complexity])`
   exactly as the default operator does. Non-finite / NaN costs are mapped to `Inf`
   so that numerically broken members can never win a tournament.
3. **Pareto-exploration branch (new, ~10% of calls):** instead of ranking by cost,
   compute the *local* Pareto front of the sampled members in
   `(complexity, raw loss)` space and return a uniformly random front member. This
   keeps building blocks alive at *all* complexity levels (the parent operator, being
   purely cost-ranked, tends to funnel mutation effort into whatever complexity band
   currently dominates), which is what a search needs in order to walk up to the
   exact ground-truth expression rather than to a slightly-better-fitting bloated one.
4. **Rank draw:** as in the parent, the winning rank `r` is drawn from the geometric
   distribution `p (1-p)^(r-1)` (rank 1 deterministically when `p == 1`).
5. **Epsilon tie-break toward simplicity (new):** among *all* sampled members whose
   adjusted cost is within a small relative tolerance (1e-3) of the rank-`r` cost,
   return the one with the smallest complexity (ties broken by lower cost). Exactly
   equivalent-quality-but-larger expressions (a very common product of mutation, e.g.
   `x + 0*y`, `x*1`, duplicated subtrees) therefore lose to their minimal form,
   which counteracts bloat and sharpens the Pareto front around the true expression.

What changed vs. the parent
---------------------------
* NaN/Inf-safe cost handling.
* Complexity is computed once per member and reused (the parent recomputed nothing
  but also had no access to complexity when `use_frequency_in_tournament` is false).
* Added the epsilon simplicity tie-break on top of the geometric rank draw.
* Added the occasional local-Pareto-front branch for complexity diversity.
* Tournament size is clamped so small/late-stage populations cannot error out.
"""
function pareto_epsilon_tournament_selection_gen1_5(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # --- 1. Sample the tournament (clamped so we never over-request) ---
    n_requested = min(options.tournament_selection_n, length(pop.members))
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, n_requested; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)
    p = options.tournament_selection_p

    # --- 2. Complexities + frequency-adjusted costs (single pass) ---
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    use_freq = options.use_frequency_in_tournament
    scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]
        c = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = c
        cost = member.cost
        if use_freq
            frequency = if (0 < c <= options.maxsize)
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            cost = cost * exp(scaling * frequency)
        end
        # Guard against NaN (and keep Inf as-is): broken members must never win.
        adjusted_costs[i] = isnan(cost) ? L(Inf) : cost
    end

    # --- 3. Occasional Pareto-front branch: preserve complexity diversity ---
    if n > 2 && rand() < 0.1
        front = Int[]
        for i in 1:n
            # Members with non-finite loss are not eligible front candidates.
            isfinite(sample[i].loss) || continue
            dominated = false
            for j in 1:n
                j == i && continue
                isfinite(sample[j].loss) || continue
                # j dominates i if it is no worse in both axes and strictly better in one
                if (complexities[j] <= complexities[i] && sample[j].loss < sample[i].loss) ||
                    (complexities[j] < complexities[i] && sample[j].loss <= sample[i].loss)
                    dominated = true
                    break
                end
            end
            dominated || push!(front, i)
        end
        if !isempty(front)
            return copy(sample[front[rand(1:length(front))]])
        end
        # If the front is empty (all losses non-finite) fall through to cost ranking.
    end

    # --- 4. Geometric rank draw (identical semantics to the parent operator) ---
    r = if p >= 1.0
        1
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        StatsBase.sample(weights)
    end
    r = min(r, n)

    # Sort once (n is small, ~12) so we can both find the rank-r member and the
    # set of members that are effectively tied with it.
    order = sortperm(adjusted_costs)
    target_idx = order[r]
    target = adjusted_costs[target_idx]

    # --- 5. Epsilon tie-break: cheapest complexity among near-equal costs ---
    eps_rel = L(1e-3)
    threshold = isfinite(target) ? target + abs(target) * eps_rel : target
    best_idx = target_idx
    best_complexity = complexities[best_idx]
    for i in 1:n
        adjusted_costs[i] <= threshold || continue
        if complexities[i] < best_complexity ||
            (complexities[i] == best_complexity && adjusted_costs[i] < adjusted_costs[best_idx])
            best_idx = i
            best_complexity = complexities[i]
        end
    end

    return copy(sample[best_idx])
end

elite_protected_age_survival_gen1_6.name: elite_protected_age_survival_gen1_6
elite_protected_age_survival_gen1_6.code:
"""
    elite_protected_age_survival_gen1_6(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

Replace the oldest eligible member while protecting the population's single
lowest-cost member. First identify that compact, high-quality elite, then scan
for the oldest non-elite member not listed in `exclude_indices`. If the elite
is the only eligible member, replace it as a fallback.

This retains age-regularized turnover while adding only minimal elitism to
preserve promising expressions. The parent's masked birth array, typed
sentinel values, and separate `argmin_fast` call are removed; exclusion and
age selection are folded into direct scans.
"""
function elite_protected_age_survival_gen1_6(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Protect the member with the best complexity-adjusted cost.
    elite = 1
    for i in 2:pop.n
        if pop.members[i].cost < pop.members[elite].cost
            elite = i
        end
    end

    # Prefer replacing the oldest eligible non-elite member.
    replacement = 0
    for i in 1:pop.n
        if i ∉ exclude_indices && i != elite
            if replacement == 0 || pop.members[i].birth < pop.members[replacement].birth
                replacement = i
            end
        end
    end

    # Fall back to the elite only when no other member is eligible.
    if replacement == 0
        for i in 1:pop.n
            if i ∉ exclude_indices &&
               (replacement == 0 || pop.members[i].birth < pop.members[replacement].birth)
                replacement = i
            end
        end
    end

    replacement == 0 && error("No population member is eligible for replacement.")
    return replacement
end

simple_parsimony_tournament_gen1_1.name: simple_parsimony_tournament_gen1_1
simple_parsimony_tournament_gen1_1.code:
"""
    simple_parsimony_tournament_gen1_1(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Simplified tournament selection with frequency-based (adaptive) parsimony.

Core idea (kept from the parent): draw a small random tournament from the population,
rank its members by a *complexity-frequency-adjusted* cost so that over-represented
complexity sizes are penalized, and return (a copy of) a winner biased toward the
best-adjusted-cost member.

Steps:
 1. Sample `options.tournament_selection_n` distinct members from the population.
 2. For every sampled member compute `cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * freq)`,
    where `freq` is the normalized frequency of that member's complexity
    (zero if the complexity falls outside `1:maxsize`).
 3. With probability `tournament_selection_p` return the member with the lowest
    adjusted cost; otherwise return a uniformly random member of the tournament.

What was removed / merged, and why it is still sound:
 * The `use_frequency_in_tournament` branch was folded into the common path. The
   frequency penalty is the mechanism that keeps the search from collapsing onto a
   single complexity band (visible in the trace, where the front stalls on one
   structural motif), so it is always worth applying; when frequencies are flat the
   penalty is a common multiplicative factor and does not change the ranking.
 * The geometric-distribution loser sampling (`Weights` + `bottomk_fast` + the
   `tournament_winner == 1` special case) was replaced by a single Bernoulli draw:
   best-with-probability-`p`, otherwise a uniformly random tournament member. This
   removes an O(n log n) partial sort and two special-case branches while preserving
   the essential property of tournament selection with `p < 1`: strong but not
   absolute pressure toward the best individual, with a controlled amount of noise
   that maintains diversity.
"""
function simple_parsimony_tournament_gen1_1(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # 1) Random tournament (without replacement), exactly as in the parent.
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, options.tournament_selection_n; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)

    # 2) Single common scoring path: frequency-adjusted cost.
    scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        # Frequency of this complexity size; 0 if out of the tracked range.
        frequency = if 0 < size <= options.maxsize
            L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
        else
            zero(L)
        end
        # Penalize crowded complexity sizes multiplicatively (adaptive parsimony).
        adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost * exp(scaling * frequency)
    end

    # 3) Bernoulli winner rule: best with prob p, otherwise a random participant.
    p = Float64(options.tournament_selection_p)
    chosen_idx = if p >= 1.0 || rand() < p
        argmin_fast(adjusted_costs)
    else
        rand(1:n)
    end

    return copy(sample[chosen_idx])
end

pareto_crowded_age_survival_init_4.name: pareto_crowded_age_survival_init_4
pareto_crowded_age_survival_init_4.code:
"""
    pareto_crowded_age_survival_init_4(
        pop::Population{T,L,N},
        options::AbstractOptions;
        exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
    )::Int where {T,L,N}

Multi-objective survival operator for symbolic regression that balances age-regularized
evolutionary turnover, Pareto frontier preservation, and complexity-niche crowding penalty.

# Core Idea
Standard regularized evolution evicts the oldest individual regardless of whether it is a
breakthrough Pareto-optimal solution or a stagnant, heavily dominated duplicate.
This operator computes an eviction priority score for each candidate member by synthesizing
three evolutionary dynamics:
1. **Age Regularization (Exploration turnover)**: Older individuals receive higher eviction
   priority to ensure continuous turnover of genetic material.
2. **Pareto Dominance Shielding (Stepping-stone preservation)**: Solutions on or near the
   empirical Pareto front (Loss vs. Complexity) receive strong protection against premature
   eviction, preserving non-dominated stepping stones across the search space.
3. **Complexity-Niche Crowding & De-duplication**: Individuals that are dominated within
   heavily crowded complexity bins (multiple individuals at the identical complexity) are
   penalized and prioritized for eviction, freeing capacity for novel complexity niches.
4. **Immediate Sanitation**: Individuals with invalid (NaN/Inf) loss or cost are evicted
   immediately before any valid population member.

When all individuals in the population are non-dominated and uniquely distributed across
complexity bins, the dominance and crowding penalties become zero, and the operator smoothly
reduces to classic Age-Regularized Evolution.

# Returns
- `Int`: The 1-based index of the population member selected for replacement.
"""
function pareto_crowded_age_survival_init_4(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T,L,N}
    n = pop.n
    n <= 0 && return 1

    # Find first eligible index as a safe fallback for edge cases
    fallback_idx = 1
    for i in 1:n
        if !(i in exclude_indices)
            fallback_idx = i
            break
        end
    end

    # Pre-extract properties for fast vector processing
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    births = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    is_invalid = Vector{Bool}(undef, n)

    min_birth = typemax(Int)
    max_birth = typemin(Int)

    for i in 1:n
        member = pop.members[i]
        comp = compute_complexity(member, options)
        loss = Float64(member.loss)
        cost = Float64(member.cost)
        birth = member.birth

        complexities[i] = comp
        losses[i] = loss
        births[i] = birth

        # Check for non-finite / invalid numerical values
        invalid = isnan(loss) || isinf(loss) || isnan(cost) || isinf(cost)
        is_invalid[i] = invalid

        if !(i in exclude_indices)
            # Immediate eviction for non-finite solutions to sanitize the population
            invalid && return i

            if birth < min_birth
                min_birth = birth
            end
            if birth > max_birth
                max_birth = birth
            end
        end
    end

    # If all valid members are excluded or population is degenerate
    if min_birth > max_birth
        return fallback_idx
    end

    birth_span = max(1, max_birth - min_birth)

    # Compute Pareto Dominance count: how many valid members strictly dominate member i
    # Member j dominates member i if:
    #   (comp_j <= comp_i && loss_j <= loss_i) && (comp_j < comp_i || loss_j < loss_i)
    dom_counts = zeros(Int, n)
    max_dom = 0
    for i in 1:n
        (i in exclude_indices || is_invalid[i]) && continue
        comp_i = complexities[i]
        loss_i = losses[i]
        d_count = 0
        for j in 1:n
            (j == i || is_invalid[j]) && continue
            comp_j = complexities[j]
            loss_j = losses[j]
            if (comp_j <= comp_i && loss_j <= loss_i) && (comp_j < comp_i || loss_j < loss_i)
                d_count += 1
            end
        end
        dom_counts[i] = d_count
        if d_count > max_dom
            max_dom = d_count
        end
    end

    # Compute Complexity-Niche Crowding & Intra-bin Loss Rank:
    # Measures how crowded member i's complexity bin is and how sub-optimal member i is within it
    crowding_scores = zeros(Float64, n)
    for i in 1:n
        (i in exclude_indices || is_invalid[i]) && continue
        comp_i = complexities[i]
        loss_i = losses[i]

        bin_count = 0
        worse_in_bin_count = 0

        for j in 1:n
            is_invalid[j] && continue
            if complexities[j] == comp_i
                bin_count += 1
                if losses[j] < loss_i
                    worse_in_bin_count += 1
                end
            end
        end

        # Crowding penalty is non-zero only if multiple individuals share the same complexity
        if bin_count > 1
            relative_rank = worse_in_bin_count / (bin_count - 1)
            density_factor = bin_count / n
            crowding_scores[i] = relative_rank * density_factor
        end
    end

    # Compute composite eviction score:
    # Higher score -> higher priority for replacement
    best_eviction_score = -Inf
    best_idx = fallback_idx

    # Weight parameters for multi-objective eviction
    w_age = 0.40      # Base aging pressure for exploration turnover
    w_dom = 0.35      # Pareto dominance penalty (dominated solutions get evicted first)
    w_crowd = 0.25    # Complexity niche crowding penalty (prunes redundant bin duplicates)

    for i in 1:n
        (i in exclude_indices) && continue

        # Normalized age: 1.0 for oldest, 0.0 for youngest
        norm_age = (max_birth - births[i]) / birth_span

        # Normalized dominance: 0.0 for Pareto-optimal non-dominated solutions
        norm_dom = max_dom > 0 ? (dom_counts[i] / max_dom) : 0.0

        # Crowding score: 0.0 for bin champions or unique complexity bins
        norm_crowd = crowding_scores[i]

        eviction_score = w_age * norm_age + w_dom * norm_dom + w_crowd * norm_crowd

        if eviction_score > best_eviction_score
            best_eviction_score = eviction_score
            best_idx = i
        end
    end

    return best_idx
end

dynamic_range_pseudohuber_loss_gen1_0.name: dynamic_range_pseudohuber_loss_gen1_0
dynamic_range_pseudohuber_loss_gen1_0.code:
"""
    dynamic_range_pseudohuber_loss_gen1_0(tree, dataset, options)

Compute a scale-aware pseudo-Huber loss that remains quadratic near an exact fit
but only linear for large residuals. The target mean and standard deviation are
estimated with Welford's algorithm, then each residual is normalized by a blend
of the global target scale and its distance from the target mean. This modestly
downweights extreme target regimes while preserving sensitivity around typical
samples. A numerically stable pseudo-Huber formula provides robustness to noise,
outliers, and explosive early-search predictions without creating a flat,
bounded objective. The loss is zero only for an exact fit.
"""
function dynamic_range_pseudohuber_loss_gen1_0(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction) || dataset.n == 0
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n

    # Estimate target location and scale in one pass without allocating.
    mean_y = zero(L)
    m2_y = zero(L)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        yi = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !isfinite(yi)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        delta = yi - mean_y
        mean_y += delta / L(i)
        m2_y += delta * (yi - mean_y)

        if !isfinite(mean_y) || !isfinite(m2_y)
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end

    target_std = sqrt(max(zero(L), m2_y / L(n)))

    # Keep constant-target datasets well-defined without imposing a unit scale.
    scale_floor = L(8) * eps(one(L)) * max(one(L), abs(mean_y))
    global_scale = max(target_std, scale_floor)

    mean_loss = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    two_l = L(2)
    local_weight = L(0.25)

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        yi = L(dataset.y[i])
        yhat = L(prediction[i])
        if !isfinite(yhat)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # The local term prevents high-magnitude target regimes from dominating.
        denominator = global_scale + local_weight * abs(yi - mean_y)
        z = abs((yhat - yi) / denominator)
        if !isfinite(z)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Stable form of 2 * (sqrt(1 + z^2) - 1):
        # quadratic near zero and linear for large normalized residuals.
        h = hypot(one_l, z)
        rho = two_l * z * (z / (h + one_l))
        if !isfinite(rho)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Online averaging avoids a potentially overflowing raw sum.
        mean_loss += (rho - mean_loss) / L(i)
    end

    return L(mean_loss)
end

pareto_age_clone_niche_survival_gen1_7.name: pareto_age_clone_niche_survival_gen1_7
pareto_age_clone_niche_survival_gen1_7.code:
"""
    pareto_age_clone_niche_survival_gen1_7(
        pop::Population{T,L,N},
        options::AbstractOptions;
        exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
    )::Int where {T,L,N}

Survival (replacement) operator synthesizing age-regularized turnover, Pareto-front
shielding, complexity-niche crowding, and explicit clone detection.

# Core Idea
Both parent operators recognize that blindly killing the oldest member destroys
stepping-stone solutions, while purely greedy replacement collapses diversity. This
operator merges their strongest signals into one expendability score, while retaining
each parent's safety nets:

1. **Immediate Sanitation** (from parent 1): any *non-excluded* member with
   non-finite loss/cost is evicted immediately, before anything else is considered.
2. **Elitism** (from parent 2): the single best-cost member is (almost) never evicted.
3. **Pareto Dominance Pressure** (from both): members dominated by many others in
   (complexity, loss) space accumulate eviction priority; non-dominated members are
   shielded.
4. **Exact-Duplicate ("Clone") Penalty** (from parent 2): among members sharing
   identical complexity and (numerically) identical loss, only the earliest-born
   representative is left unpenalized — the rest are pure redundancy and are
   prioritized for removal, harder than mere Pareto domination.
5. **Continuous Complexity-Niche Crowding** (from parent 1): within a complexity bin,
   a member's relative loss rank times the bin's population share yields a smooth
   crowding penalty, concentrating eviction pressure on over-populated, sub-optimal
   niches without requiring exact ties.
6. **Age Regularization with Stochastic Fallback** (from both): age contributes a
   continuous eviction bonus, and with small probability the operator instead performs
   a pure oldest-first eviction among unprotected, non-elite members — guaranteeing
   that no individual can survive forever purely by sitting in a sparse niche.

The composite score is a weighted sum of normalized age, dominance, crowding, and
clone-penalty terms, with large discounts for Pareto-front members and the elite.

# Heuristics / Assumptions
* `(complexity, loss)` (not `cost`) defines dominance/clone niches, decoupling this
  from the fluctuating adaptive parsimony term.
* Complexity bins are exact integer complexities.
* Clone detection uses a relative tolerance (`1e-10`) on loss equality.
* `exclude_indices` are always respected and never returned.

# Returns
- `Int`: the 1-based index of the population member selected for replacement.
"""
function pareto_age_clone_niche_survival_gen1_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T,L,N}
    n = pop.n
    n <= 0 && return 1

    # Safe fallback: first eligible (non-excluded) index.
    fallback_idx = 1
    for i in 1:n
        if !(i in exclude_indices)
            fallback_idx = i
            break
        end
    end
    n == 1 && return fallback_idx

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Gather per-member statistics; flag invalid members for
    #    immediate sanitation.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    births = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    is_invalid = Vector{Bool}(undef, n)

    min_birth = Inf
    max_birth = -Inf

    for i in 1:n
        m = pop.members[i]
        complexities[i] = compute_complexity(m, options)
        l = Float64(m.loss)
        c = Float64(m.cost)
        births[i] = Float64(m.birth)
        is_invalid[i] = isnan(l) || isinf(l) || isnan(c) || isinf(c)
        losses[i] = is_invalid[i] ? Inf : l
        costs[i] = is_invalid[i] ? Inf : c

        if !(i in exclude_indices)
            # Immediate eviction of the first non-excluded broken member.
            is_invalid[i] && return i
            if births[i] < min_birth
                min_birth = births[i]
            end
            if births[i] > max_birth
                max_birth = births[i]
            end
        end
    end

    if min_birth > max_birth
        # All valid members were excluded; nothing sensible left to score.
        return fallback_idx
    end
    birth_range = max(max_birth - min_birth, 1.0)

    # Elite (best-cost, valid) member: protected via a huge score discount.
    best_cost_idx = fallback_idx
    best_cost_val = Inf
    for i in 1:n
        (i in exclude_indices || is_invalid[i]) && continue
        if costs[i] < best_cost_val
            best_cost_val = costs[i]
            best_cost_idx = i
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Pairwise pass over valid members: dominance counts, clone
    #    counts, and complexity-bin statistics for crowding.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    n_dom = zeros(Int, n)
    n_clone = zeros(Int, n)
    bin_count = zeros(Int, n)          # members sharing i's complexity
    worse_in_bin = zeros(Int, n)       # members in bin with strictly worse (higher) loss

    max_dom = 0
    for i in 1:n
        is_invalid[i] && continue
        ci = complexities[i]
        li = losses[i]
        bi = births[i]
        for j in 1:n
            (j == i || is_invalid[j]) && continue
            cj = complexities[j]
            lj = losses[j]

            # Strict Pareto dominance: j dominates i.
            if (cj <= ci && lj <= li) && (cj < ci || lj < li)
                n_dom[i] += 1
            end

            if cj == ci
                bin_count[i] += 1
                if lj < li
                    worse_in_bin[i] += 1  # counts members better than i for crowding rank
                end
                # Exact structural clone: identical complexity & (numerically) loss.
                same_loss = abs(lj - li) <= 1e-10 * (1.0 + abs(li))
                if same_loss && (bj_is_earlier_ac(births[j], bi, j, i))
                    n_clone[i] += 1
                end
            end
        end
        if n_dom[i] > max_dom
            max_dom = n_dom[i]
        end
        bin_count[i] += 1  # include self in bin population count
    end

    # A member sits on the Pareto front (and is not a redundant clone) if nothing
    # strictly dominates it and it is not a later duplicate of an equal twin.
    protected = [(!is_invalid[i] && n_dom[i] == 0 && n_clone[i] == 0) for i in 1:n]

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Stochastic pure-age fallback: occasionally force oldest-first
    #    eviction among unprotected, non-elite members to guarantee
    #    turnover even in sparse/well-spread populations.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    p_age = 0.15
    if rand() < p_age
        best_idx = 0
        best_birth = Inf
        for i in 1:n
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue
            i == best_cost_idx && continue
            protected[i] && continue
            if births[i] < best_birth
                best_birth = births[i]
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        best_idx != 0 && return best_idx
        # else fall through to full scoring (protections relaxed there via discounts)
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Composite expendability score.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    w_age = 0.30      # aging pressure for turnover
    w_dom = 0.30      # Pareto dominance penalty
    w_crowd = 0.20    # continuous complexity-niche crowding penalty
    w_clone = 0.20     # exact-duplicate penalty (applied per-clone, on top of dominance)

    best_score = -Inf
    best_idx = fallback_idx

    for i in 1:n
        (i in exclude_indices) && continue

        if is_invalid[i]
            # Should already have been caught, but keep as a safety net.
            return i
        end

        norm_age = (births[i] - min_birth >= 0) ? (max_birth - births[i]) / birth_range : 0.0
        norm_dom = max_dom > 0 ? (n_dom[i] / max_dom) : 0.0

        crowd = 0.0
        if bin_count[i] > 1
            relative_rank = worse_in_bin[i] / (bin_count[i] - 1)
            density_factor = bin_count[i] / n
            crowd = relative_rank * density_factor
        end

        clone_penalty = n_clone[i] > 0 ? 1.0 : 0.0  # binary: any clone-of-earlier flag

        score = w_age * norm_age + w_dom * norm_dom + w_crowd * crowd + w_clone * clone_penalty

        # Shield genuine Pareto-front, non-redundant members.
        if protected[i]
            score -= 2.0
        end
        # Elitism: effectively never replace the best-cost member.
        if i == best_cost_idx
            score -= 1.0e6
        end

        # Small tie-break jitter.
        score += 1e-6 * rand()

        if score > best_score
            best_score = score
            best_idx = i
        end
    end

    return best_idx
end

"""
    bj_is_earlier_ac(bj, bi, j, i)

Tie-break helper for clone detection: returns `true` when member `j` should be treated
as the earlier (surviving) representative of a clone cluster, using birth order first
and index as a deterministic fallback for simultaneous births.
"""
function bj_is_earlier_ac(bj::Float64, bi::Float64, j::Int, i::Int)
    return bj < bi || (bj == bi && j < i)
end

algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_1_gen1_.name: algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_1_gen1_9
algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_1_gen1_.code:
"""
    algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_1_gen1_9(tree, options, nfeatures, rng)

A *semantics-preserving* structural mutation that rewrites the expression tree using
elementary algebraic identities instead of perturbing it randomly. This is an
improved variant of `algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_0`.

Core idea (unchanged): PySR's built-in mutations are local edits, so algebraically
equivalent-but-distant forms (e.g. `x1*x2 + x1*x3` vs `x1*(x2+x3)`) are separated by
many individually-deleterious steps. This operator jumps directly between such forms
via a catalogue of rewrite rules applied at a randomly (weighted) chosen site, so that
loss-preserving complexity reduction/reshaping can happen in one move.

What changed vs. the parent:
1. **Removed the overly-eager early exit.** The parent bailed out entirely unless a
   `*` or `/` operator existed in the operator set, even though several useful rewrites
   (constant folding, `a-a`, additive identities) need only `+`/`-`. All multiplicative
   rules already self-guard via `is_times`/`is_div`/explicit `!== nothing` checks, so
   removing the blanket bail-out is safe and unlocks simplification for `+`,`-`-only
   trees (or trees with only unary operators).
2. **Generic constant folding** (new): any binary node whose two children are both
   constant leaves is folded to a single constant leaf using the *actual* operator
   function (not just `+,-,*,/`), and likewise for unary nodes applied to a constant
   leaf. This lets constant sub-expressions created by other mutations (or by this
   mutation's own rewrites) collapse immediately instead of waiting on `mutate_constant`
   or built-in simplification passes. Folds are skipped if the result is non-finite.
3. **Literal 0/1 identities** (new): `a+0`, `0+a`, `a-0` -> `a`; `a*1`, `1*a` -> `a`;
   `a*0`, `0*a` -> `0`; `a/1` -> `a`. These frequently appear after cancellation-style
   rewrites (which can produce `0`/`1` leaves) or after `mutate_constant` drifts a
   constant to exactly one of these values.
4. **Generalized self-cancellation** (new): any `a - a -> 0` and `a / a -> 1` for
   *structurally equal* subtrees `a` (not only the specific sum/product shapes handled
   by the parent's rule (1)), using the same generic non-zero/non-degenerate
   assumption already relied on by the parent's multiplicative-cancellation rules.
5. **Division distributes over its numerator** (new, symmetric to the parent's
   times-distribution rule): `(b±c)/a -> b/a ± c/a`, gated by the same "duplicated
   subtree must be small and the result must fit `maxsize`" heuristic used for `*`
   distribution, and given the same low sampling weight since it is size-increasing.
6. Constant-fold / identity / self-cancellation rewrites are given the highest sampling
   weight (5.0), since they are pure size reductions with no risk of missing an
   opportunity to further simplify in a later generation.
All other logic (structural equality check, factoring, common-denominator collection,
multiplicative cancellation, division folding/lifting, weighted site sampling) is kept
from the parent.
"""
function algebraic_refactor_mutation_init_1_gen1_9(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    tree.degree == 0 && return tree

    binops = options.operators.binops
    unaops = options.operators.unaops
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), binops)
    minus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (-), binops)
    times_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (*), binops)
    div_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (/), binops)

    # NOTE: unlike the parent, we do NOT bail out when `*`/`/` are absent: constant
    # folding, additive identities, and self-cancellation are useful even for
    # `+`/`-`-only (or purely unary) expression trees, and every multiplicative-specific
    # rule below already self-guards via `is_times`/`is_div`/explicit `!== nothing`.

    # ---- structural (syntactic) equality of two subtrees ----
    function trees_equal(a::N, b::N)
        a.degree == b.degree || return false
        if a.degree == 0
            a.constant == b.constant || return false
            return a.constant ? (a.val == b.val) : (a.feature == b.feature)
        end
        a.op == b.op || return false
        for i in 1:(a.degree)
            trees_equal(get_child(a, i), get_child(b, i)) || return false
        end
        return true
    end

    # ---- cheap operator-identity predicates ----
    is_plus(t) = t.degree == 2 && plus_idx !== nothing && t.op == plus_idx
    is_minus(t) = t.degree == 2 && minus_idx !== nothing && t.op == minus_idx
    is_sum(t) = is_plus(t) || is_minus(t)
    is_times(t) = t.degree == 2 && times_idx !== nothing && t.op == times_idx
    is_div(t) = t.degree == 2 && div_idx !== nothing && t.op == div_idx

    # Candidate rewrites: (node to overwrite, replacement subtree) plus a sampling weight.
    sites = Tuple{N,N}[]
    weights = Float64[]
    add_site!(node, repl, w) = (push!(sites, (node, repl)); push!(weights, w); nothing)

    # Build a fresh binary node / constant leaf.
    bin(op, a, b) = constructorof(N)(; op=op, children=(a, b))
    lit(v) = constructorof(N)(T; val=v)

    total = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : 30

    zeroT = zero(T)
    oneT = one(T)

    # Full traversal: `any` visits every node as long as we keep returning `false`.
    any(tree) do t
        # ---- unary constant folding: f(c) -> literal, for constant leaf c ----
        if t.degree == 1
            child = get_child(t, 1)
            if child.degree == 0 && child.constant
                folded = try
                    unaops[t.op](child.val)
                catch
                    nothing
                end
                if folded !== nothing && isfinite(folded)
                    add_site!(t, lit(T(folded)), 5.0)
                end
            end
            return false
        end

        if t.degree == 2
            c1 = get_child(t, 1)
            c2 = get_child(t, 2)

            # (0a) generic binary constant folding: op(c1, c2) -> literal
            if c1.degree == 0 && c1.constant && c2.degree == 0 && c2.constant
                folded = try
                    binops[t.op](c1.val, c2.val)
                catch
                    nothing
                end
                if folded !== nothing && isfinite(folded)
                    add_site!(t, lit(T(folded)), 5.0)
                end
            end

            # (0b) literal 0/1 identities
            if is_plus(t)
                if c1.degree == 0 && c1.constant && c1.val == zeroT
                    add_site!(t, copy(c2), 5.0)
                elseif c2.degree == 0 && c2.constant && c2.val == zeroT
                    add_site!(t, copy(c1), 5.0)
                end
            elseif is_minus(t)
                if c2.degree == 0 && c2.constant && c2.val == zeroT
                    add_site!(t, copy(c1), 5.0)
                end
            elseif is_times(t)
                if c1.degree == 0 && c1.constant && c1.val == oneT
                    add_site!(t, copy(c2), 5.0)
                elseif c1.degree == 0 && c1.constant && c1.val == zeroT
                    add_site!(t, lit(zeroT), 5.0)
                elseif c2.degree == 0 && c2.constant && c2.val == oneT
                    add_site!(t, copy(c1), 5.0)
                elseif c2.degree == 0 && c2.constant && c2.val == zeroT
                    add_site!(t, lit(zeroT), 5.0)
                end
            elseif is_div(t)
                if c2.degree == 0 && c2.constant && c2.val == oneT
                    add_site!(t, copy(c1), 5.0)
                end
            end

            # (0c) generalized self-cancellation for structurally equal subtrees
            if is_minus(t) && trees_equal(c1, c2)
                add_site!(t, lit(zeroT), 5.0)
            elseif is_div(t) && trees_equal(c1, c2)
                add_site!(t, lit(oneT), 5.0)
            end

            # (1) exact cancellation inside sums: (a+b)-b, (a+b)-a, (a-b)+b, b+(a-b)
            if is_minus(t) && is_plus(c1)
                if trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0)
                elseif trees_equal(get_child(c1, 1), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), 4.0)
                end
            elseif is_plus(t) && is_minus(c1) && trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0)
            elseif is_plus(t) && is_minus(c2) && trees_equal(get_child(c2, 2), c1)
                add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c2, 1)), 4.0)
            end

            # (2) factor a shared multiplicative term: a*b ± a*c -> a*(b±c)
            if is_sum(t) && is_times(c1) && is_times(c2)
                for i in 1:2, j in 1:2
                    if trees_equal(get_child(c1, i), get_child(c2, j))
                        common = copy(get_child(c1, i))
                        rest1 = copy(get_child(c1, 3 - i))   # the *other* factor of c1
                        rest2 = copy(get_child(c2, 3 - j))   # the *other* factor of c2
                        add_site!(t, bin(times_idx, common, bin(t.op, rest1, rest2)), 3.0)
                        break  # one factoring per node is enough
                    end
                end
            end

            # (3) common denominator: a/c ± b/c -> (a±b)/c
            if is_sum(t) &&
                is_div(c1) &&
                is_div(c2) &&
                trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), get_child(c2, 2))
                add_site!(
                    t,
                    bin(
                        div_idx,
                        bin(t.op, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), copy(get_child(c2, 1))),
                        copy(get_child(c1, 2)),
                    ),
                    3.0,
                )
            end

            # (4) multiplicative cancellation: (a*b)/a -> b  and  (a*b)/b -> a
            if is_div(t) && is_times(c1)
                if trees_equal(get_child(c1, 1), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), 4.0)
                elseif trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0)
                end
            end

            # (5) multiplicative cancellation: (a/b)*b -> a  and  b*(a/b) -> a
            if is_times(t)
                if is_div(c1) && trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0)
                elseif is_div(c2) && trees_equal(get_child(c2, 2), c1)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c2, 1)), 4.0)
                end
            end

            # (6) fold nested divisions: (a/b)/c -> a/(b*c)
            if is_div(t) && is_div(c1) && times_idx !== nothing
                add_site!(
                    t,
                    bin(
                        div_idx,
                        copy(get_child(c1, 1)),
                        bin(times_idx, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), copy(c2)),
                    ),
                    2.0,
                )
            end

            # (7) lift an inner division: a/(b/c) -> (a*c)/b
            if is_div(t) && is_div(c2) && times_idx !== nothing
                add_site!(
                    t,
                    bin(
                        div_idx,
                        bin(times_idx, copy(c1), copy(get_child(c2, 2))),
                        copy(get_child(c2, 1)),
                    ),
                    2.0,
                )
            end

            # (8) distribution over multiplication (size-increasing): a*(b±c) -> a*b ± a*c
            if is_times(t)
                for k in 1:2
                    s = get_child(t, k)          # candidate sum
                    m = get_child(t, 3 - k)      # multiplier that gets duplicated
                    if is_sum(s)
                        nm = count_nodes(m)
                        # keep the duplicated factor tiny and respect the size budget
                        if nm <= 3 && total + nm + 1 <= maxsize
                            add_site!(
                                t,
                                bin(
                                    s.op,
                                    bin(times_idx, copy(m), copy(get_child(s, 1))),
                                    bin(times_idx, copy(m), copy(get_child(s, 2))),
                                ),
                                1.0,
                            )
                        end
                    end
                end
            end

            # (9) distribution over division (size-increasing): (b±c)/a -> b/a ± c/a
            if is_div(t) && is_sum(c1)
                na = count_nodes(c2)
                if na <= 3 && total + na + 1 <= maxsize
                    add_site!(
                        t,
                        bin(
                            c1.op,
                            bin(div_idx, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), copy(c2)),
