                            bin(div_idx, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), copy(c2)),
                        ),
                        1.0,
                    )
                end
            end
        end
        return false  # never short-circuit: we want a complete traversal
    end

    isempty(sites) && return tree  # no identity applies -> leave the tree untouched

    # Weighted sampling: simplifications are much more likely than expansion.
    r = rand(rng) * sum(weights)
    idx = length(weights)
    acc = 0.0
    for (i, w) in enumerate(weights)
        acc += w
        if r <= acc
            idx = i
            break
        end
    end

    node, repl = sites[idx]
    # `repl` was built exclusively from copies, so in-place overwrite is safe
    # (this also works when `node === tree`, so the root never needs special handling).
    set_node!(node, repl)
    return tree
end

pareto_niche_crowded_aging_survival_gen1.name: pareto_niche_crowded_aging_survival_gen1_3
pareto_niche_crowded_aging_survival_gen1.code:
"""
    pareto_niche_crowded_aging_survival_gen1_3(
        pop::Population{T,L,N},
        options::AbstractOptions;
        exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
    )::Int where {T,L,N}

Multi-objective Pareto-niche crowded aging survival operator for symbolic regression.

# Core Idea
Standard regularized evolution uniformly replaces the oldest population member, which can
inadvertently eliminate rare, high-performing Pareto-optimal solutions and cause premature
loss of foundational building blocks. Conversely, purely fitness-based survival leads to
premature convergence and bloat.

This operator balances exploration, niche diversity, and age regularization by ranking
candidates using a multi-tier replacement priority:
1. Non-finite or invalid loss individuals are eliminated first.
2. Dominated, redundant individuals occupying crowded complexity niches are prioritized for removal.
3. Dominated individuals that are the best within their specific complexity bin are preserved longer.
4. Non-dominated (Pareto-optimal) individuals in crowded niches are thinned out by age.
5. Unique Pareto-optimal frontier individuals are protected from replacement until all redundant
   and dominated individuals have been cleared.
6. Within each priority tier, age regularization (replacing older individuals first) breaks ties,
   preserving continuous population turnover and preventing bloat.

# Heuristics & Assumptions
- Pareto Dominance: Solution A dominates B if `Complexity(A) <= Complexity(B)` and `Loss(A) <= Loss(B)`
  with at least one strict inequality.
- Complexity Niche Crowding: Complexity bins containing multiple members have higher replacement
  pressure to promote exploration across diverse expression sizes.
- Aging Fallback: If all unexcluded members are Pareto-optimal and unique, the operator gracefully
  reduces to classic age-regularized evolution.
"""
function pareto_niche_crowded_aging_survival_gen1_3(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T,L,N}
    n = pop.n
    # Handle small population edge cases
    n <= 0 && return 1
    n == 1 && return 1

    # Fast boolean mask for excluded indices
    is_excluded = falses(n)
    for idx in exclude_indices
        if 1 <= idx <= n
            is_excluded[idx] = true
        end
    end

    # Extract member properties: complexity, raw loss, and birth timestamps
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    births = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    min_birth = typemax(Int)
    max_birth = typemin(Int)
    max_c = 0

    for i in 1:n
        member = pop.members[i]
        c = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = c
        if c > max_c
            max_c = c
        end

        losses[i] = member.loss
        b = member.birth
        births[i] = b
        if b < min_birth
            min_birth = b
        end
        if b > max_birth
            max_birth = b
        end
    end

    # Ensure valid birth span to prevent division by zero
    birth_span = max(1, max_birth - min_birth)

    # Compute niche counts (number of members per complexity) and best loss per niche
    niche_counts = zeros(Int, max_c + 1)
    min_loss_in_niche = fill(Inf, max_c + 1)

    for i in 1:n
        c = complexities[i]
        l = losses[i]
        c_idx = (c >= 0 && c <= max_c) ? (c + 1) : 1
        niche_counts[c_idx] += 1
        
        fl = Float64(l)
        if isfinite(fl) && fl < min_loss_in_niche[c_idx]
            min_loss_in_niche[c_idx] = fl
        end
    end

    # Compute Pareto domination counts: how many members strictly dominate member i
    dom_counts = zeros(Int, n)
    for i in 1:n
        li = losses[i]
        ci = complexities[i]
        fi = isfinite(Float64(li))

        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue
            lj = losses[j]
            cj = complexities[j]
            fj = isfinite(Float64(lj))

            if !fi
                # Any finite member dominates an invalid/non-finite member
                if fj
                    dom_counts[i] += 1
                end
            elseif fj
                # Standard Pareto dominance on (complexity, loss)
                if (cj <= ci && lj <= li) && (cj < ci || lj < li)
                    dom_counts[i] += 1
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # Evaluate composite replacement score for each candidate
    best_idx = -1
    max_score = -Inf

    for i in 1:n
        if is_excluded[i]
            continue
        end

        li = losses[i]
        ci = complexities[i]
        bi = births[i]
        dom_c = dom_counts[i]
        fli = Float64(li)

        # Normalized age: 1.0 for oldest member, ~0.0 for newest
        norm_age = Float64(max_birth - bi) / Float64(birth_span)

        c_idx = (ci >= 0 && ci <= max_c) ? (ci + 1) : 1
        niche_size = niche_counts[c_idx]
        is_best_in_niche = isfinite(fli) && (fli <= min_loss_in_niche[c_idx])
        redundancy_ratio = Float64(niche_size - 1) / Float64(n)

        # Tier-based hierarchy for replacement
        tier_base = 0.0
        if !isfinite(fli)
            # Tier 0: Invalid / NaN / Inf loss expressions
            tier_base = 1000.0
        elseif dom_c > 0 && !is_best_in_niche
            # Tier 1: Dominated and suboptimal within its complexity niche
            tier_base = 300.0
        elseif dom_c > 0 && is_best_in_niche
            # Tier 2: Dominated across complexities, but best within its niche
            tier_base = 200.0
        elseif niche_size > 1
            # Tier 3: Non-dominated (Pareto front) but redundant in a crowded niche
            tier_base = 100.0
        else
            # Tier 4: Unique non-dominated Pareto front member
            tier_base = 0.0
        end

        # Domination pressure: higher domination count increases replacement priority
        dom_pressure = 10.0 * min(Float64(dom_c) / Float64(n), 1.0)

        # Niche crowding pressure: overpopulated complexity bins are thinned out
        niche_pressure = 10.0 * redundancy_ratio

        # Age pressure: older solutions within the same tier are replaced first
        age_pressure = 50.0 * norm_age

        score = tier_base + dom_pressure + niche_pressure + age_pressure

        if score > max_score
            max_score = score
            best_idx = i
        end
    end

    # Fallback to any unexcluded index if no candidate was selected
    if best_idx == -1
        for i in 1:n
            if !is_excluded[i]
                return i
            end
        end
        return 1
    end

    return best_idx
end

affine_shape_mse_loss_gen1_4.name: affine_shape_mse_loss_gen1_4
affine_shape_mse_loss_gen1_4.code:
"""
    affine_shape_mse_loss_gen1_4(tree, dataset, options)

Blend ordinary MSE with an analytically affine-calibrated shape error. The raw
MSE retains sensitivity to the expression's actual scale and offset, while a
smaller calibrated component measures how well its predictions match the target
after the best linear rescaling and intercept correction. This gives promising
structural forms a useful fitness signal before their constants are fully tuned,
without making calibration errors irrelevant.

The function evaluates the tree once, accumulates stable online moments, derives
the calibrated error from prediction-target correlation, and combines 80% raw
MSE with 20% shape error. It assumes an unweighted, unitless dataset and adds no
expression-complexity penalty.
"""
function affine_shape_mse_loss_gen1_4(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = length(dataset.y)
    if n == 0
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Welford-style online moments avoid allocating residual arrays and reduce
    # cancellation when deriving variances and covariance.
    mean_prediction = zero(L)
    mean_target = zero(L)
    m2_prediction = zero(L)
    m2_target = zero(L)
    covariance_sum = zero(L)
    squared_error_sum = zero(L)

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        predicted = L(prediction[i])
        target = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !isfinite(predicted) || !isfinite(target)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        residual = predicted - target
        squared_error_sum += abs2(residual)

        count = L(i)
        prediction_delta = predicted - mean_prediction
        target_delta = target - mean_target
        mean_prediction += prediction_delta / count
        mean_target += target_delta / count

        m2_prediction += prediction_delta * (predicted - mean_prediction)
        m2_target += target_delta * (target - mean_target)
        covariance_sum += prediction_delta * (target - mean_target)
    end

    count = L(n)
    raw_mse = squared_error_sum / count
    prediction_variance = max(m2_prediction / count, zero(L))
    target_variance = max(m2_target / count, zero(L))
    covariance = covariance_sum / count

    if !isfinite(raw_mse) || !isfinite(prediction_variance) ||
       !isfinite(target_variance) || !isfinite(covariance)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # The minimum MSE after fitting a*prediction + b is
    # var(y) * (1 - correlation(prediction, y)^2).
    calibrated_mse = target_variance
    if prediction_variance > zero(L) && target_variance > zero(L)
        correlation = (covariance / sqrt(prediction_variance)) /
                      sqrt(target_variance)
        if !isfinite(correlation)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        correlation = clamp(correlation, -one(L), one(L))
        calibrated_mse =
            target_variance * max(one(L) - abs2(correlation), zero(L))
    elseif target_variance == zero(L)
        calibrated_mse = zero(L)
    end

    # Raw accuracy remains dominant so correct constants are still uniquely
    # rewarded; the shape term only broadens the basin around useful structure.
    raw_weight = L(4) / L(5)
    loss = raw_weight * raw_mse + (one(L) - raw_weight) * calibrated_mse
    return isfinite(loss) ? L(max(loss, zero(L))) : L(Inf)
end

simple_parsimony_tournament_gen1_8.name: simple_parsimony_tournament_gen1_8
simple_parsimony_tournament_gen1_8.code:
"""
    simple_parsimony_tournament_gen1_8(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Simplified tournament selection with adaptive (frequency-based) parsimony.

Core idea (kept from the parent): sample a small tournament uniformly at random,
rank its members by a *frequency-penalized* cost, and usually pick the best one so
that selection pressure favors accurate expressions whose complexity is currently
*rare* in the search (this is what keeps the Pareto front broad instead of
collapsing onto one bloated size class).

Steps:
1. Draw `tournament_selection_n` distinct members from the population.
2. In a single loop, compute `cost * exp(scaling * normalized_frequency[complexity])`
   for every sampled member. The complexity index is clamped into `1:maxsize`
   instead of being special-cased, and the frequency term is disabled simply by
   setting `scaling = 0` when `use_frequency_in_tournament` is false.
3. With probability `tournament_selection_p` return the argmin of those adjusted
   costs; otherwise return a uniformly random member of the tournament.

Simplifications relative to the parent:
- The two nearly identical cost loops (frequency on / off) were merged into one
  loop; the on/off switch is now just a zero scaling factor, which yields
  `exp(0) == 1` and hence exactly the raw cost.
- The out-of-range complexity branch (`0 < size <= maxsize`) was folded into a
  `clamp`. Sizes outside the range are vanishingly rare (only oversized trees),
  and charging them the boundary frequency is at least as conservative as
  charging them zero penalty, so no soundness is lost.
- The geometric "k-th best wins" ladder (`Weights` construction plus
  `bottomk_fast`) was replaced by a single Bernoulli draw: best-of-tournament
  with probability `p`, else a uniform random tournament member. This preserves
  the two properties that matter — strong pressure toward the best member and a
  nonzero chance for weaker members to reproduce (diversity / escape from local
  optima) — while removing the per-call allocation of the probability vector and
  the partial sort, making each selection cheaper and thus allowing more
  mutations per unit time.
"""
function simple_parsimony_tournament_gen1_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # 1. Uniform tournament sample (without replacement), as in the parent.
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, options.tournament_selection_n; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)

    # Single scaling knob: zero disables the frequency penalty entirely,
    # which replaces the parent's duplicated "with/without frequency" loops.
    scaling = L(
        options.use_frequency_in_tournament ? options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling : 0
    )

    # 2. One pass computing frequency-penalized costs.
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]
        # Clamp instead of branching on out-of-range complexities.
        size = clamp(compute_complexity(member, options), 1, options.maxsize)
        freq = L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
        adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost * exp(scaling * freq)
    end

    # 3. Best-of-tournament with probability p, otherwise a random participant.
    #    This keeps exploitation + a diversity valve, without the geometric ladder.
    chosen_idx = if options.tournament_selection_p >= 1 ||
        rand() < options.tournament_selection_p
        argmin_fast(adjusted_costs)
    else
        rand(1:n)
    end

    return copy(sample[chosen_idx])
end

adaptive_constant_offset_gen2_5.name: adaptive_constant_offset_gen2_5
adaptive_constant_offset_gen2_5.code:
"""
    adaptive_constant_offset_gen2_5(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

Wrap a selected subtree or the root node with an addition of a data-driven constant offset:
`subtree` -> `subtree + c`.

# Improvements over `add_constant_offset`:
1. **Residual-Aware Intercept Fitting**: When wrapping the root (selected with 35% probability),
   `c` is computed directly from the mean prediction residual `mean(y - y_pred)` with optional
   stochastic jitter, allowing the expression to immediately match the global bias/intercept of the target.
2. **Subtree Centering & Scale Matching**: When wrapping an internal subtree, the sub-expression is
   evaluated on `dataset.X`. The offset `c` is strategically sampled either to center the subtree
   (`c ≈ -mean(sub_pred)`, facilitating phase shifts and radial kernels like `exp(-(x - μ)^2)`)
   or scaled proportionally to the subtree's empirical standard deviation.
3. **Avoids Redundant Constant Bloat**: Filters out existing constant leaf nodes from selection to
   prevent unsimplified additive constant chains like `(c1 + c2)`.
4. **Robust Fallbacks**: Gracefully handles evaluation failures, missing datasets, NaNs, and zero-variance
   edge cases, falling back to target-scale or standard normal perturbations.
"""
function adaptive_constant_offset_gen2_5(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Find the addition operator index in binary operators
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), options.operators.binops)
    if plus_idx === nothing
        return tree
    end

    # Determine whether dataset targets are available for data-aware calculations
    has_valid_data = (
        dataset !== nothing &&
        dataset.y !== nothing &&
        dataset.n >= 2 &&
        dataset.X !== nothing
    )

    # Bias selection towards root (35% chance) for intercept discovery,
    # otherwise pick non-constant nodes to avoid redundant (c1 + c2) bloat
    has_non_const = any(t -> !(t.degree == 0 && t.constant), tree)
    wrap_root = rand(rng) < 0.35

    node = if wrap_root
        tree
    elseif has_non_const
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> !(t.degree == 0 && t.constant)))
    else
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    end

    # Initialize constant offset value
    constant_value = zero(T)
    offset_computed = false

    if has_valid_data
        if node === tree
            # For root node, compute residual-based intercept
            y_pred, ok = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options.operators)
            if ok
                residuals = dataset.y .- y_pred
                valid_mask = isfinite.(residuals)
                n_valid = count(valid_mask)
                if n_valid >= 2
                    res_valid = view(residuals, valid_mask)
                    r_mean = T(mean(res_valid))
                    r_std = T(std(res_valid))
                    r_scale = isfinite(r_std) && r_std > T(1e-6) ? r_std : T(1)

                    # 60% chance: exact mean residual shift; 30% jittered; 10% residual-scaled random
                    p = rand(rng)
                    if p < 0.60
                        constant_value = r_mean
                    elseif p < 0.90
                        constant_value = r_mean + randn(rng, T) * T(0.1) * r_scale
                    else
                        constant_value = randn(rng, T) * r_scale
                    end
                    offset_computed = isfinite(constant_value)
                end
            end
        else
            # For subtrees, evaluate subtree response to center or scale offset
            sub_pred, ok_sub = eval_tree_array(node, dataset.X, options.operators)
            if ok_sub
                valid_sub = isfinite.(sub_pred)
                n_valid_sub = count(valid_sub)
                if n_valid_sub >= 2
                    sub_valid = view(sub_pred, valid_sub)
                    s_mean = T(mean(sub_valid))
                    s_std = T(std(sub_valid))

                    if isfinite(s_std) && s_std > T(1e-6)
                        p_sub = rand(rng)
                        if p_sub < 0.40
                            # Center the subtree distribution (e.g., for phase shifts / offsets)
                            constant_value = -s_mean + randn(rng, T) * T(0.05) * s_std
                        elseif p_sub < 0.80
                            # Offset proportional to subtree variance
                            constant_value = randn(rng, T) * s_std
                        else
                            # Scale relative to target variance
                            y_std = T(std(dataset.y))
                            constant_value = randn(rng, T) * (isfinite(y_std) && y_std > T(1e-6) ? y_std : s_std)
                        end
                        offset_computed = isfinite(constant_value)
                    end
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # Fallback if evaluation failed, data was absent, or non-finite value encountered
    if !offset_computed
        if has_valid_data
            y_std = T(std(dataset.y))
            scale = isfinite(y_std) && y_std > T(1e-6) ? y_std : one(T)
            constant_value = randn(rng, T) * scale
        else
            constant_value = randn(rng, T)
        end
        if !isfinite(constant_value)
            constant_value = randn(rng, T)
        end
    end

    # Construct the constant leaf node
    constant_node = constructorof(N)(T; val=constant_value)

    # Wrap the node with (+) and the constant, randomly choosing left or right child
    if rand(rng, Bool)
        new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(copy(node), constant_node))
    else
        new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(constant_node, copy(node)))
    end

    # In-place update of the selected subtree
    set_node!(node, new_node)

    return tree
end

lineage_guarded_pareto_breakthrough_sele.name: lineage_guarded_pareto_breakthrough_selection_gen2_4
lineage_guarded_pareto_breakthrough_sele.code:
"""
Select a parent using a lineage-guarded Pareto-breakthrough tournament.

The operator samples a standard tournament, evaluates each member by raw loss,
complexity, penalized cost, and complexity-niche frequency, then counts how many
competitors dominate it in loss-complexity space. It rewards candidates that
achieve a substantial loss improvement over every simpler sampled expression,
which targets promising "breakthroughs" on the evolving Pareto frontier.
Underrepresented complexity niches, recent individuals, and sparsely represented
lineages receive modest protection to preserve stepping stones. Selection remains
stochastic through positive weights for every candidate, while Pareto dominance
and fitness ranks keep strongly inferior members unlikely to reproduce. The
heuristic assumes lower loss and cost are better and that useful ground-truth
subexpressions often appear as unusually effective improvements per added
complexity.
"""
function lineage_guarded_pareto_breakthrough_selection_gen2_4(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    tournament_size = min(pop.n, max(2, options.tournament_selection_n))
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, tournament_size; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)

    n == 1 && return sample[1]

    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    frequencies = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)

    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]

        # Sanitize objectives so failed evaluations are always unattractive.
        loss = Float64(member.loss)
        cost = Float64(member.cost)
        losses[i] = isfinite(loss) ? loss : Inf
        costs[i] = isfinite(cost) ? cost : Inf

        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size

        frequency = if 0 < size <= options.maxsize &&
                       size <= length(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies)
            Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
        else
            0.0
        end
        frequencies[i] = isfinite(frequency) ? max(0.0, frequency) : 0.0
    end

    loss_ranks = zeros(Int, n)
    cost_ranks = zeros(Int, n)
    domination_counts = zeros(Int, n)
    niche_counts = ones(Int, n)
    lineage_counts = ones(Int, n)

    # Rank objectives, estimate local niche density, and count Pareto dominators.
    for i in 1:n
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue

            loss_ranks[i] += losses[j] < losses[i]
            cost_ranks[i] += costs[j] < costs[i]
            niche_counts[i] += complexities[j] == complexities[i]

            no_worse = losses[j] <= losses[i] &&
                       complexities[j] <= complexities[i]
            strictly_better = losses[j] < losses[i] ||
                              complexities[j] < complexities[i]
            domination_counts[i] += no_worse && strictly_better

            # Penalize crowded sibling groups and direct parent-child clusters.
            same_parent = sample[i].parent > 0 &&
                          sample[i].parent == sample[j].parent
            direct_relative = (sample[i].ref > 0 &&
                               sample[j].parent == sample[i].ref) ||
                              (sample[j].ref > 0 &&
                               sample[i].parent == sample[j].ref)
            lineage_counts[i] += same_parent || direct_relative
        end
    end

    # Measure whether each member is a genuine accuracy breakthrough over all
    # strictly simpler alternatives in this tournament.
    breakthroughs = zeros(Float64, n)
    for i in 1:n
        best_simpler_loss = Inf
        for j in 1:n
            if complexities[j] < complexities[i] && losses[j] < best_simpler_loss
                best_simpler_loss = losses[j]
            end
        end

        if isfinite(best_simpler_loss) && isfinite(losses[i]) &&
           losses[i] < best_simpler_loss
            scale = max(
                abs(best_simpler_loss) + abs(losses[i]),
                eps(Float64),
            )
            breakthroughs[i] = clamp(
                (best_simpler_loss - losses[i]) / scale,
                0.0,
                1.0,
            )
        end
    end

    min_birth = minimum(member.birth for member in sample)
    max_birth = maximum(member.birth for member in sample)
    birth_span = max_birth - min_birth

    p = clamp(Float64(options.tournament_selection_p), 0.0, 1.0)
    pressure = 0.75 + 2.25 * p
    rank_denominator = Float64(max(1, n - 1))
    dominance_scale = max(1.0, sqrt(Float64(n)))
    parsimony_scale = max(0.0, Float64(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling))

    weights = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        loss_rank = Float64(loss_ranks[i]) / rank_denominator
        cost_rank = Float64(cost_ranks[i]) / rank_denominator

        # A mixture of raw-loss and regularized-cost quality avoids committing
        # exclusively to either highly complex fits or overly simple formulas.
        quality_factor = 0.20 +
                         0.45 * exp(-pressure * loss_rank) +
                         0.35 * exp(-pressure * cost_rank)

        pareto_factor = exp(
            -pressure * Float64(domination_counts[i]) / dominance_scale,
        )
        breakthrough_factor = 1.0 + 3.0 * breakthroughs[i]

        # Protect sparse complexity niches both locally and, when requested,
        # according to the search-wide adaptive frequency statistics.
        local_niche_factor = inv(sqrt(Float64(niche_counts[i])))
        global_niche_factor = if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            inv(sqrt(1.0 + parsimony_scale * frequencies[i]))
        else
            1.0
        end

        lineage_factor = inv(sqrt(Float64(lineage_counts[i])))

        # Briefly protect fresh mutations so potentially useful stepping stones
        # can reproduce before being erased by mature lineages.
        recency = birth_span > 0 ?
            Float64(sample[i].birth - min_birth) / Float64(birth_span) : 0.5
        youth_factor = 0.8 + 0.4 * recency

        weights[i] = quality_factor *
                     pareto_factor *
                     breakthrough_factor *
                     local_niche_factor *
                     global_niche_factor *
                     lineage_factor *
                     youth_factor
    end

    total_weight = sum(weights)
    if !isfinite(total_weight) || total_weight <= 0.0
        return sample[argmin_fast(costs)]
    end

    chosen_idx = StatsBase.sample(StatsBase.Weights(weights, total_weight))
    return sample[chosen_idx]
end

parsimony_epsilon_tournament_selection_g.name: parsimony_epsilon_tournament_selection_gen2_2
parsimony_epsilon_tournament_selection_g.code:
"""
    parsimony_epsilon_tournament_selection_gen2_2(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Simplified variant of the parent operator. It keeps the parent's *single most
valuable* addition — the epsilon "prefer the simplest of the effectively tied
members" tie-break — on top of the standard adaptive-parsimony tournament, and
drops everything else that added branching complexity.

Steps
-----
1. Sample `min(tournament_selection_n, length(pop.members))` distinct members
   (the clamp keeps small/late-stage populations from erroring).
2. In one pass, compute each sampled member's complexity and its
   frequency-adjusted cost `cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * freq[complexity])`
   (exactly the default rule). NaN costs are mapped to `Inf` so numerically
   broken members can never win.
3. Draw the winning rank `r` from the usual geometric distribution
   `p (1-p)^(r-1)` (rank 1 when `p >= 1`) and find the rank-`r` adjusted cost
   with `bottomk_fast`.
4. Epsilon tie-break: among all sampled members whose adjusted cost is within a
   relative tolerance of 1e-3 of that rank-`r` cost, return the one with the
   smallest complexity (ties broken by lower cost). This removes bloated
   duplicates of equally good expressions (`x*1`, `x + 0*y`, ...) and sharpens
   the front around the exact ground-truth form.

Removed / merged relative to the parent
---------------------------------------
* The occasional (~10%) local-Pareto-front branch, with its O(n^2) domination
  loop and its separate finite-loss bookkeeping, is gone. Complexity diversity
  is still maintained by the adaptive-parsimony frequency term plus the
  simplicity tie-break, which pushes selection pressure toward smaller sizes,
  so the extra stochastic branch is not needed.
* The full `sortperm` was replaced by `bottomk_fast`, since only the rank-`r`
  cost value (not the whole ordering) is required by the tie-break.
* Inf-specific special-casing was folded into a single guarded threshold
  computation.
"""
function parsimony_epsilon_tournament_selection_gen2_2(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # --- 1. Sample the tournament (clamped so we never over-request) ---
    n_requested = min(options.tournament_selection_n, length(pop.members))
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, n_requested; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)
    p = options.tournament_selection_p

    # --- 2. Complexities + frequency-adjusted costs in a single pass ---
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    use_freq = options.use_frequency_in_tournament
    scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]
        c = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = c
        cost = member.cost
        if use_freq
            frequency = if (0 < c <= options.maxsize)
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            cost = cost * exp(scaling * frequency)
        end
        # Broken (NaN) members must never win a tournament.
        adjusted_costs[i] = isnan(cost) ? L(Inf) : cost
    end

    # --- 3. Geometric rank draw (same semantics as the default operator) ---
    r = if p >= 1.0
        1
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        min(StatsBase.sample(weights), n)
    end

    # Only the rank-r *cost value* is needed as the tie-break reference point.
    target = bottomk_fast(adjusted_costs, r)[1][end]

    # --- 4. Epsilon tie-break: simplest member among near-equal costs ---
    # (If target is non-finite, the threshold degenerates to target itself.)
    threshold = isfinite(target) ? target + abs(target) * L(1e-3) : target
    best_idx = 0
    for i in 1:n
        adjusted_costs[i] <= threshold || continue
        if best_idx == 0 ||
            complexities[i] < complexities[best_idx] ||
            (complexities[i] == complexities[best_idx] &&
             adjusted_costs[i] < adjusted_costs[best_idx])
            best_idx = i
        end
    end
    # Fallback (e.g. all costs Inf and comparisons vacuous): pick the first member.
    best_idx == 0 && (best_idx = 1)

    return copy(sample[best_idx])
end

niche_protected_age_survival_gen2_7.name: niche_protected_age_survival_gen2_7
niche_protected_age_survival_gen2_7.code:
"""
Niche-Protected Age-Regularized Survival

Core idea: Blend classic age-regularized evolution (always replace the oldest member)
with a lightweight multi-objective safeguard that protects the current Pareto-like
"champion" at each complexity level from being discarded. This prevents the search
from losing its best-known expression at a given complexity (which could be the
eventual bridge to a simpler or more accurate solution later), while still aggressively
cycling out old/redundant members to keep the population fresh and exploring.

Steps:
1. Compute the complexity of every member in the population.
2. For each distinct complexity value, identify the single member with the lowest loss
   (the "niche champion") — this member is temporarily protected from removal.
3. Build the candidate pool of replaceable members: those not excluded via
   `exclude_indices` and not a niche champion.
4. Among the candidate pool, select the oldest member (smallest birth) to replace,
   preserving the standard age-regularized evolution heuristic on the "non-elite" bulk
   of the population.
5. Fallback: if every remaining member is either excluded or a protected champion
   (e.g. tiny population, or crossover already claimed a slot), ignore the niche
   protection and simply pick the oldest non-excluded member, guaranteeing a valid
   index is always returned.

Heuristic rationale: Many SR runs prematurely lose good low-complexity or
high-accuracy solutions purely due to random age-based churn. By shielding one
representative per complexity niche, we keep a rudimentary "complexity-loss frontier"
alive across generations, improving the chance of eventually finding the true minimal
expression, while still respecting the exploratory churn of the rest of the population.
"""
function niche_protected_age_survival_gen2_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)

    # Step 1: compute complexity for every member
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, pop.n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:(pop.n)
        complexities[i] = compute_complexity(pop.members[i], options)
    end

    # Step 2: find the best-loss member (niche champion) for each complexity value
    # Dict maps complexity -> (best_loss, best_index)
    champions = Dict{Int,Tuple{L,Int}}()
    @inbounds for i in 1:(pop.n)
        c = complexities[i]
        loss_i = pop.members[i].loss
        if !haskey(champions, c) || loss_i < champions[c][1]
            champions[c] = (loss_i, i)
        end
    end
    protected_indices = Set{Int}(idx for (_, idx) in values(champions))

    # Step 3: build candidate pool (not excluded, not a protected champion)
    exclude_set = Set{Int}(exclude_indices)
    candidate_births = fill(typemax(BT), pop.n)
    any_candidate = false
    @inbounds for i in 1:(pop.n)
        if !(i in exclude_set) && !(i in protected_indices)
            candidate_births[i] = pop.members[i].birth
            any_candidate = true
        end
    end

    if any_candidate
        # Step 4: pick oldest among unprotected, non-excluded candidates
        return argmin_fast(candidate_births)
    else
        # Step 5: fallback -- ignore niche protection, just avoid excluded indices
        fallback_births = [
            (i in exclude_set) ? typemax(BT) : pop.members[i].birth for i in 1:(pop.n)
        ]
        return argmin_fast(fallback_births)
    end
end

dynamic_range_pseudohuber_loss_gen1_1_ge.name: dynamic_range_pseudohuber_loss_gen1_1_gen2_3
dynamic_range_pseudohuber_loss_gen1_1_ge.code:
"""
    dynamic_range_pseudohuber_loss_gen1_1_gen2_3(tree, dataset, options)

Simplified scale-aware pseudo-Huber loss. Like the parent, it estimates a
single global scale for the targets and uses a stable pseudo-Huber form so the
loss stays quadratic for small residuals and linear for large ones (robust to
outliers/explosive predictions) while remaining strictly zero only at an exact
fit. Simplifications relative to the parent:
  - The two-term denominator (global scale + local deviation from the target
    mean) is replaced by a single global scale (mean/std of y), removing the
    "local_weight" heuristic. The local term mainly re-weighted points in
    extreme target regions, which is a secondary effect compared to having a
    sound global scale; dropping it removes an extra hyperparameter and an
    extra pass of per-point arithmetic without changing the fundamental shape
    of the loss.
  - The Welford online mean/variance update is replaced by a direct one-pass
    sum/sum-of-squares computation, which is numerically fine for typical
    dataset sizes and avoids the branchy per-sample finiteness checks in the
    parent's online loop, cutting overhead in the hot path.
"""
function dynamic_range_pseudohuber_loss_gen1_1_gen2_3(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction) || dataset.n == 0
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n

    # Single pass to get mean and mean-of-squares of the targets.
    sum_y = zero(L)
    sum_y2 = zero(L)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        yi = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !isfinite(yi)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        sum_y += yi
        sum_y2 += yi * yi
    end
    mean_y = sum_y / L(n)
    var_y = max(zero(L), sum_y2 / L(n) - mean_y * mean_y)
    target_std = sqrt(var_y)

    # Keep constant-target datasets well-defined without imposing a unit scale.
    scale_floor = L(8) * eps(one(L)) * max(one(L), abs(mean_y))
    global_scale = max(target_std, scale_floor)

    mean_loss = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    two_l = L(2)

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        yi = L(dataset.y[i])
        yhat = L(prediction[i])
        if !isfinite(yhat)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Normalize the residual by the single global scale.
        z = abs((yhat - yi) / global_scale)
        if !isfinite(z)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Stable pseudo-Huber form: 2 * (sqrt(1 + z^2) - 1).
        h = hypot(one_l, z)
        rho = two_l * z * (z / (h + one_l))
        if !isfinite(rho)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Online averaging avoids a potentially overflowing raw sum.
        mean_loss += (rho - mean_loss) / L(i)
    end

    return L(mean_loss)
end

scale_adaptive_cauchy_loss_gen2_0.name: scale_adaptive_cauchy_loss_gen2_0
scale_adaptive_cauchy_loss_gen2_0.code:
"""
    scale_adaptive_cauchy_loss_gen2_0(tree, dataset, options)::L

A scale-adaptive Cauchy (Lorentzian) robust loss function designed to overcome the
"Taylor trap" and pole-instability bottleneck in evolutionary symbolic regression.

# Core Idea:
Standard MSE severely penalizes nascent rational and division expressions (e.g., `1 / (1 - x3/x4)`)
whenever intermediate mutations produce near-zero denominators on a few data points. The resulting
quadratically explosive errors cause tournament selection to discard structurally promising rational
hypotheses in favor of pole-free Taylor polynomials or trigonometric substitutes.

This loss employs a Cauchy/Lorentzian robust M-estimator with hybrid relative-absolute scale
normalization:
1. **Quadratic near zero (`u << 1`)**: `log(1 + u^2) ≈ u^2`, retaining standard MSE curvature and
   gradient for constant optimization and fine-grained parameter fitting.
2. **Logarithmic in the tails (`u >> 1`)**: `log(1 + u^2) ≈ 2*log(u)`, allowing promising rational
   expressions with transient pole outliers to survive tournament selection until constant/structure
   mutations eliminate the singularity.
3. **Scale-Adaptive Normalization**: Residuals are normalized by `s_i = σ_y + 0.25 * |y_i|`, seamlessly
   transitioning between absolute error (near `y ≈ 0`) and relative percentage error (at large `|y|`),
   preventing high-magnitude samples from dominating search gradients.

# Steps:
1. Evaluate the expression tree on `dataset.X`. Return `L(Inf)` on numerical failure.
2. Efficiently compute the global target dispersion (`std_y`) in a single pass over `dataset.y`.
3. Compute the per-sample adaptive scale `s_i = std_y + 0.25 * |y_i|`.
4. Calculate normalized residuals `u_i = |pred_i - y_i| / s_i`.
5. Apply the Cauchy kernel `log1p(u_i^2)` with asymptotic branch protection for extreme values.
6. Return the (optionally weighted) mean loss converted to `L`.
"""
function scale_adaptive_cauchy_loss_gen2_0(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    # 1. Evaluate candidate tree on dataset features
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    y = dataset.y
    n = dataset.n

    if n == 0
        return zero(L)
    end

    # 2. Compute target dispersion (mean and variance) in a single fast pass
    sum_y = zero(T)
    sum_y2 = zero(T)
    @inbounds @simd for i in 1:n
        yi = y[i]
        sum_y += yi
        sum_y2 += yi * yi
    end

    mean_y = sum_y / n
    var_y = max(zero(T), (sum_y2 / n) - (mean_y * mean_y))
    std_y = sqrt(var_y)

    # Global scale floor prevents division-by-zero when y is constant or centered near zero
    scale_floor = if std_y > T(1e-7)
        std_y
    elseif abs(mean_y) > T(1e-7)
        abs(mean_y) * T(0.1)
    else
        T(1.0)
    end

    # 3. Main loss accumulation loop
    total_loss = zero(T)
    total_weight = zero(T)
    has_weights = hasfield(typeof(dataset), :weights) && !isnothing(dataset.weights)

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        pred_i = prediction[i]
        y_i = y[i]

        # Early exit if prediction contains non-finite numbers
        if !isfinite(pred_i)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Local adaptive scale: blend of global dispersion and local magnitude
        s_i = scale_floor + T(0.25) * abs(y_i)

        # Scale-normalized residual
        u = abs(pred_i - y_i) / s_i

        # Cauchy M-estimator: log(1 + u^2)
        # Use asymptotic form 2*log(u) for extreme u to guarantee floating-point safety
        term = if u > T(1e150)
            T(2.0) * log(u)
        else
            log1p(u * u)
        end

        if has_weights
            w_i = T(dataset.weights[i])
            total_loss += w_i * term
            total_weight += w_i
        else
            total_loss += term
        end
    end

    # 4. Compute final normalized mean loss
    mean_loss = if has_weights
        if total_weight <= zero(T)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        total_loss / total_weight
    else
        total_loss / n
    end

    if !isfinite(mean_loss)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    return L(mean_loss)
end

adaptive_front_contribution_clone_niche_.name: adaptive_front_contribution_clone_niche_survival_gen2_1
adaptive_front_contribution_clone_niche_.code:
"""
    adaptive_front_contribution_clone_niche_survival_gen2_1(
        pop::Population{T,L,N},
        options::AbstractOptions;
        exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
    )::Int where {T,L,N}

Select a population member for replacement by combining age regularization, Pareto
quality, clone removal, and complexity-niche diversity with graded rather than absolute
front protection.

The operator proceeds as follows:

1. Immediately removes any eligible member with non-finite loss or cost.
2. Computes strict Pareto-dominance counts in `(complexity, loss)` space.
3. Detects later-born objective clones using equal complexity and tightly matching loss
   and cost, retaining the earliest representative.
4. Measures niche redundancy from both within-complexity loss rank and nearest-neighbor
   distance in normalized `(complexity, transformed-loss)` space. This catches redundant
   neighboring frontier points even when every exact complexity bin is unique.
5. Assigns non-dominated, non-clone members a graded frontier contribution based on their
   marginal loss improvement over the nearest simpler frontier point and their isolation.
   Thus, genuine breakthrough stepping stones receive more protection than long chains of
   tiny high-complexity improvements.
6. Combines age, dominance, niche redundancy, and clone status into an expendability
   score. Frontier protection decays with age, preserving new breakthroughs while still
   guaranteeing eventual turnover without a stochastic fallback.
7. Softly protects both the best-cost and best-raw-loss eligible members as complementary
   anchors, while allowing replacement in degenerate populations.

Losses are assumed to be ordered so that lower is better. A signed `log1p` transform is
used only for geometric niche and frontier-contribution calculations; exact Pareto
comparisons continue to use raw loss. All indices in `exclude_indices` are strictly
ineligible for replacement.
"""
function adaptive_front_contribution_clone_niche_survival_gen2_1(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T,L,N}
    n = pop.n
    n <= 0 && return 1

    excluded = Set(exclude_indices)
    eligible = Int[]
    for i in 1:n
        !(i in excluded) && push!(eligible, i)
    end
    isempty(eligible) && throw(ArgumentError("survival requires at least one non-excluded member"))
    length(eligible) == 1 && return eligible[1]

    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    births = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    invalid = falses(n)

    min_birth = Inf
    max_birth = -Inf

    # Gather statistics and sanitize eligible population slots immediately.
    for i in 1:n
        member = pop.members[i]
        complexities[i] = compute_complexity(member, options)
        losses[i] = Float64(member.loss)
        costs[i] = Float64(member.cost)
        births[i] = Float64(member.birth)

        invalid[i] = !isfinite(losses[i]) || !isfinite(costs[i])
        if !(i in excluded)
            invalid[i] && return i
            min_birth = min(min_birth, births[i])
            max_birth = max(max_birth, births[i])
        end
    end

    valid_count = count(!, invalid)
    birth_span = max(max_birth - min_birth, 1.0)

    # Soft elite anchors: adaptive-cost quality and pure predictive quality.
    best_cost_idx = eligible[1]
    best_loss_idx = eligible[1]
    for i in eligible
        if costs[i] < costs[best_cost_idx] ||
           (costs[i] == costs[best_cost_idx] && births[i] < births[best_cost_idx])
            best_cost_idx = i
        end
        if losses[i] < losses[best_loss_idx] ||
           (losses[i] == losses[best_loss_idx] && births[i] < births[best_loss_idx])
            best_loss_idx = i
        end
    end

    dominance = zeros(Int, n)
    bin_count = zeros(Int, n)
    better_in_bin = zeros(Int, n)
    is_later_clone = falses(n)

    # Pairwise objective comparisons also identify later near-identical twins.
    for i in 1:n
        invalid[i] && continue
        ci = complexities[i]
        li = losses[i]
        coi = costs[i]
        bi = births[i]

        for j in 1:n
            (j == i || invalid[j]) && continue
            cj = complexities[j]
            lj = losses[j]

            if (cj <= ci && lj <= li) && (cj < ci || lj < li)
                dominance[i] += 1
            end

            if cj == ci
                bin_count[i] += 1
                lj < li && (better_in_bin[i] += 1)

                # Requiring both loss and cost agreement makes accidental objective
                # collisions less likely than comparison by loss alone.
                loss_tol = 1.0e-11 * (1.0 + max(abs(li), abs(lj)))
                cost_tol = 1.0e-11 * (1.0 + max(abs(coi), abs(costs[j])))
                same_objectives =
                    abs(li - lj) <= loss_tol && abs(coi - costs[j]) <= cost_tol
                j_is_earlier = births[j] < bi || (births[j] == bi && j < i)

                if same_objectives && j_is_earlier
                    is_later_clone[i] = true
                end
            end
        end
        bin_count[i] += 1  # Include the member itself.
    end

    max_dominance = maximum(dominance)

    # Signed log transform preserves loss ordering while reducing sensitivity to scale.
    loss_coordinate = zeros(Float64, n)
    min_coordinate = Inf
    max_coordinate = -Inf
    min_complexity = typemax(Int)
    max_complexity = typemin(Int)

    for i in 1:n
        invalid[i] && continue
        l = losses[i]
        z = l >= 0.0 ? log1p(l) : -log1p(-l)
        loss_coordinate[i] = z
        min_coordinate = min(min_coordinate, z)
        max_coordinate = max(max_coordinate, z)
        min_complexity = min(min_complexity, complexities[i])
        max_complexity = max(max_complexity, complexities[i])
    end

    complexity_span = max(Float64(max_complexity - min_complexity), 1.0)
    coordinate_span = max(max_coordinate - min_coordinate, eps(Float64))

    # Nearest-neighbor objective distance supplies a continuous crowding signal
    # across adjacent complexity bins, not only within exact bins.
    nearest_distance = fill(Inf, n)
    if valid_count > 1
        for i in 1:n
            invalid[i] && continue
            for j in 1:n
                (j == i || invalid[j]) && continue
                dc = abs(complexities[i] - complexities[j]) / complexity_span
                dl = abs(loss_coordinate[i] - loss_coordinate[j]) / coordinate_span
                d = sqrt(dc * dc + dl * dl)
                nearest_distance[i] = min(nearest_distance[i], d)
            end
        end
    else
        for i in 1:n
            !invalid[i] && (nearest_distance[i] = 1.0)
        end
    end

    min_nearest = Inf
    max_nearest = -Inf
    for i in 1:n
        invalid[i] && continue
        min_nearest = min(min_nearest, nearest_distance[i])
        max_nearest = max(max_nearest, nearest_distance[i])
    end
    nearest_span = max_nearest - min_nearest

    density_penalty = zeros(Float64, n)
    for i in 1:n
        invalid[i] && continue
        if nearest_span > eps(Float64)
            # Distance near the population minimum corresponds to high redundancy.
            density_penalty[i] =
                (max_nearest - nearest_distance[i]) / nearest_span
        end
    end

    # Estimate each genuine frontier member's marginal improvement over the nearest
    # simpler frontier point. Large improvements indicate valuable stepping stones.
    frontier_gain = zeros(Float64, n)
    max_frontier_gain = 0.0

    for i in 1:n
        (invalid[i] || dominance[i] != 0 || is_later_clone[i]) && continue

        previous_complexity = typemin(Int)
        previous_coordinate = Inf

        for j in 1:n
            (invalid[j] || dominance[j] != 0 || is_later_clone[j]) && continue
            complexities[j] >= complexities[i] && continue

            if complexities[j] > previous_complexity ||
               (complexities[j] == previous_complexity &&
                loss_coordinate[j] < previous_coordinate)
                previous_complexity = complexities[j]
                previous_coordinate = loss_coordinate[j]
            end
        end

        if previous_complexity != typemin(Int)
            complexity_step = complexities[i] - previous_complexity
            gain = max(previous_coordinate - loss_coordinate[i], 0.0) /
                   max(Float64(complexity_step), 1.0)
            frontier_gain[i] = gain
            max_frontier_gain = max(max_frontier_gain, gain)
        end
    end

    # Composite expendability weights sum to one before protection discounts.
    w_age = 0.34
    w_dominance = 0.27
    w_niche = 0.18
    w_clone = 0.21
    frontier_shield = 0.55
    elite_shield = 0.65

    best_idx = eligible[1]
    best_score = -Inf

    for i in eligible
        # Oldest member receives age score 1, youngest receives 0.
        age_score = (max_birth - births[i]) / birth_span

        # Log normalization prevents one extreme individual from suppressing the
        # distinction among moderately dominated candidates.
        dominance_score =
            max_dominance > 0 ?
            log1p(Float64(dominance[i])) / log1p(Float64(max_dominance)) : 0.0

        bin_rank = bin_count[i] > 1 ?
                   better_in_bin[i] / Float64(bin_count[i] - 1) : 0.0

        # Exact-bin inferiority is emphasized, with cross-bin density as a smoother
        # secondary redundancy measure.
        niche_score = 0.65 * bin_rank + 0.35 * density_penalty[i]
        clone_score = is_later_clone[i] ? 1.0 : 0.0

        score = w_age * age_score +
                w_dominance * dominance_score +
                w_niche * niche_score +
                w_clone * clone_score

        if dominance[i] == 0 && !is_later_clone[i]
            normalized_gain =
                max_frontier_gain > 0.0 ? frontier_gain[i] / max_frontier_gain : 0.0
            isolation = 1.0 - density_penalty[i]

            # Every genuine frontier point gets a small shield, but most protection
            # is reserved for large loss jumps and isolated objective-space niches.
            contribution = 0.15 + 0.65 * normalized_gain + 0.20 * isolation

            # Protection fades as a member ages, avoiding immortal weak front points.
            protection_retention = 0.25 + 0.75 * (1.0 - age_score)
            score -= frontier_shield * contribution * protection_retention
        end

        if i == best_cost_idx || i == best_loss_idx
            score -= elite_shield
        end

        # Deterministic tie-breaking favors eviction of the older candidate.
        if score > best_score + 1.0e-12 ||
           (abs(score - best_score) <= 1.0e-12 &&
            births[i] < births[best_idx]) ||
           (abs(score - best_score) <= 1.0e-12 &&
            births[i] == births[best_idx] && i < best_idx)
            best_score = score
            best_idx = i
        end
    end

    return best_idx
end

adaptive_scale_pseudohuber_mse_loss_gen2.name: adaptive_scale_pseudohuber_mse_loss_gen2_6
adaptive_scale_pseudohuber_mse_loss_gen2.code:
"""
    adaptive_scale_pseudohuber_mse_loss_gen2_6(tree, dataset, options)

Synthesis of the two parents: keep the *exact* quadratic (MSE) behavior that
makes fine-grained ranking of near-perfect candidates possible, while inheriting
the scale-awareness and outlier tolerance of the dynamic-range pseudo-Huber.

Core idea
---------
Instead of a fixed pseudo-Huber transition point (which permanently caps the
gradient signal and flattens the objective once residuals are small), the
transition width `delta` is *adapted to the current residual distribution*.
Written in the stable form

    rho_i = 2 * z_i^2 / (sqrt(1 + (z_i/delta)^2) + 1),

the loss satisfies `rho_i -> z_i^2` (pure normalized MSE) whenever
`z_i << delta`, and `rho_i -> 2 * delta * z_i` (linear, bounded influence) only
for residuals that are gross outliers *relative to the candidate's own typical
error*. Because `delta` shrinks proportionally as the fit improves, a nearly
exact expression is scored by essentially plain MSE — so no precision is lost
during constant fine-tuning — yet a mid-search expression that fits most points
but explodes on a few is not dominated by those few points.

Steps
-----
1. One Welford pass over `y` gives the target mean and standard deviation
   (used as the global residual scale, with a floor so constant targets work).
2. Each residual is normalized by `global_scale + 0.25 * |y_i - mean_y|`
   (parent 1's dynamic-range term), so high-magnitude target regimes cannot
   monopolize the objective, but typical samples retain full sensitivity.
3. A second pass accumulates the mean absolute normalized residual
   `mean|z|` (mean absolute deviation is used rather than RMS because it is far
   less inflated by the very outliers we want to downweight), and sets
   `delta = 3 * mean|z|`, i.e. roughly a 2.4-sigma quadratic core for
   Gaussian-like residuals.
4. A third pass averages the stable pseudo-Huber terms online (avoiding
   overflow of a raw sum).

Heuristics / assumptions
------------------------
* Unweighted, unitless data (matches the SRBench PySR pipeline).
* `mean|z| == 0` means an exact fit, which returns exactly zero.
* Any non-finite target, prediction, or intermediate returns `Inf`.
* Cost is three cheap `O(n)` sweeps over already-materialized arrays, which is
  negligible next to tree evaluation itself.
"""
function adaptive_scale_pseudohuber_mse_loss_gen2_6(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction) || dataset.n == 0
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n

    # --- Pass 1: target location / scale via Welford (no allocation) ---------
    mean_y = zero(L)
    m2_y = zero(L)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        yi = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !isfinite(yi)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        delta_y = yi - mean_y
        mean_y += delta_y / L(i)
        m2_y += delta_y * (yi - mean_y)
    end
    if !isfinite(mean_y) || !isfinite(m2_y)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    target_std = sqrt(max(zero(L), m2_y / L(n)))
    # Floor keeps constant-target datasets well-defined without forcing unit scale.
    scale_floor = L(8) * eps(one(L)) * max(one(L), abs(mean_y))
    global_scale = max(target_std, scale_floor)

    one_l = one(L)
    local_weight = L(0.25)

    # --- Pass 2: mean absolute normalized residual -> adaptive transition ----
    mean_abs_z = zero(L)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        yi = L(dataset.y[i])
        yhat = L(prediction[i])
        if !isfinite(yhat)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        # Dynamic-range denominator: global scale + distance from target mean.
        denom = global_scale + local_weight * abs(yi - mean_y)
        z = abs((yhat - yi) / denom)
        if !isfinite(z)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        mean_abs_z += (z - mean_abs_z) / L(i)
    end
    if !isfinite(mean_abs_z)
        return L(Inf)
    end
    # Exact fit: nothing to score, and delta would be zero.
    if mean_abs_z <= zero(L)
        return zero(L)
    end

    # delta ~ 3 * MAD of the normalized residuals: quadratic core covers the
    # bulk of the samples, linear tail only for this candidate's own outliers.
    delta = L(3) * mean_abs_z
    inv_delta = one_l / delta

    # --- Pass 3: stable adaptive pseudo-Huber, averaged online ---------------
    mean_loss = zero(L)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        yi = L(dataset.y[i])
        yhat = L(prediction[i])
        denom = global_scale + local_weight * abs(yi - mean_y)
        z = abs((yhat - yi) / denom)
        u = z * inv_delta
        # rho = 2*delta^2*(sqrt(1+u^2)-1) rewritten as 2*z^2/(sqrt(1+u^2)+1):
        # -> z^2 (exact MSE) for u << 1, -> 2*delta*z (linear) for u >> 1.
        rho = L(2) * z * (z / (hypot(one_l, u) + one_l))
        if !isfinite(rho)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        mean_loss += (rho - mean_loss) / L(i)
    end

    return isfinite(mean_loss) ? L(mean_loss) : L(Inf)
end

streamlined_parsimony_tournament_gen2_8.name: streamlined_parsimony_tournament_gen2_8
streamlined_parsimony_tournament_gen2_8.code:
"""
    streamlined_parsimony_tournament_gen2_8(
        pop::Population{T,L,N},
        running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
        options::AbstractOptions,
    )::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}

Streamlined tournament selection with unified linear adaptive parsimony.

# Core Idea
Selects the fittest member from a random tournament sample using a smooth,
linear parsimony adjustment that penalizes over-represented expression complexities,
evaluated in a single allocation-free pass.

# Steps
1. Draw a random subset of candidates of size `options.tournament_selection_n`.
2. Compute a parsimony scaling coefficient that folds the frequency-enabled and
   disabled paths into a single expression.
3. Traverse the sample in a single pass to compute each candidate's parsimony-adjusted
   cost `cost * (1 + scaling * frequency)` and track the minimum.
4. Return the winning population member directly.

# What was removed/merged from parent
- **Unified branching**: Merged the separate `if options.use_frequency_in_tournament`
  and fallback branches into a single scaling parameter (`scaling = 0` when disabled).
- **Linearized parsimony penalty**: Replaced `exp(scaling * frequency)` with
  `(1 + scaling * frequency)` to prevent exponential score explosion and avoid
  expensive transcendental math while retaining diversity pressure.
- **Removed auxiliary allocations**: Eliminated intermediate vectors (`adjusted_costs`,
  rank indices `collect(0:(n-1))`, and geometric weight distributions).
- **Eliminated rank-sampling machinery**: Replaced `bottomk_fast` and weighted rank
  sampling with a direct, single-pass argmin loop.
- **Removed redundant copy**: Returns the winning member directly without explicit
  `copy`, letting the search dispatch manage duplication.

# Soundness
Linear parsimony preserves the relative penalty structure across complexity bins
without the risk of numerical saturation. Direct single-pass tournament selection
preserves selection pressure while significantly reducing per-generation overhead.
"""
function streamlined_parsimony_tournament_gen2_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Sample tournament candidates without replacement
    k = min(options.tournament_selection_n, length(pop.members))
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, k; replace=false)

    # Unified scaling: zero when frequency parsimony is disabled
    scaling = options.use_frequency_in_tournament ? L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling) : L(0)

    # Single-pass tournament evaluation to find the minimum adjusted cost
    best_member = sample[1]
    best_cost = typemax(L)

    for member in sample
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        freq = (0 < size <= options.maxsize) ? L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size]) : L(0)
        adj_cost = member.cost * (L(1) + scaling * freq)

        if adj_cost < best_cost
            best_cost = adj_cost
            best_member = member
        end
    end

    return best_member
end

residual_guided_linear_insertion_gen2_9.name: residual_guided_linear_insertion_gen2_9
residual_guided_linear_insertion_gen2_9.code:
"""
    residual_guided_linear_insertion_gen2_9(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

A data-aware mutation that looks at the *current* residual (`dataset.y .- prediction(tree)`)
and finds the input feature whose column in `dataset.X` is most linearly correlated with that
residual. It then fits a simple univariate least-squares line `a*x_j + b` to the residual using
that feature, and additively grafts this correction term onto the whole expression (i.e. wraps
the root with a `+` operator, `tree -> tree + (a*x_j + b)`). This is a greedy, data-driven analogue
of a single boosting/gradient step: instead of blindly inserting random operators or leaves, it
inserts the feature contribution that best explains what the current expression is still getting
wrong, along with an appropriately fit scale/offset so the correction is on the right scale
immediately (helping constant-optimization and simplification down the line).

Heuristics/assumptions:
- Requires `dataset.y` to be present (skips for multi-output datasets where it's `nothing`).
- Skips features with (numerically) zero variance to avoid degenerate correlations.
- If no feature shows a finite nonzero correlation with the residual, the tree is returned unchanged.
- Prefers using `+` and `*` binary operators if present in `options.operators.binops` to build the
  fitted linear term `a*x_j + b`; otherwise falls back to a random binary operator and/or a bare
  feature leaf (skipping the affine fit) so the mutation remains valid for arbitrary operator sets.
- The correction is grafted at the root (rather than a random interior node) since additive
  correction to the *whole* prediction is what directly targets the residual; interior insertions
  would have unpredictable, operator-dependent effects on the final output.
"""
function residual_guided_linear_insertion_gen2_9(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Need targets to compute a residual; bail out for multi-output / missing y.
    (dataset.y === nothing || nfeatures < 1) && return tree

    # Evaluate the current tree on the training features.
    y_pred, ok = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options.operators)
    (!ok || any(!isfinite, y_pred)) && return tree  # bad eval (NaN/Inf/div-by-zero) — skip

    # Residual that a new additive term could try to explain.
    residual = dataset.y .- y_pred
    (any(!isfinite, residual)) && return tree

    # Scan all features for the one most correlated (in absolute value) with the residual.
    best_j = 0
    best_abscor = zero(T)
    @inbounds for j in 1:nfeatures
        xj = view(dataset.X, j, :)
        sxj = std(xj)
        (sxj <= eps(T) || !isfinite(sxj)) && continue  # skip degenerate/constant features
        c = cor(xj, residual)
        if isfinite(c) && abs(c) > best_abscor
            best_abscor = abs(c)
            best_j = j
        end
    end

    best_j == 0 && return tree  # no informative feature found — nothing to insert

    # Fit residual ≈ a * x_best_j + b via simple closed-form least squares.
    xj = view(dataset.X, best_j, :)
    mx = mean(xj)
    my = mean(residual)
    vx = var(xj)
    a_coef = vx > eps(T) ? T(mean((xj .- mx) .* (residual .- my)) / vx) : zero(T)
    b_coef = T(my - a_coef * mx)

    # Try to find + and * operators to build the fitted affine correction a*x_j + b.
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), options.operators.binops)
    times_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (*), options.operators.binops)

    feature_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; feature=best_j)

    linear_term = if times_idx !== nothing && !iszero(a_coef)
        const_a = constructorof(N)(T; val=a_coef)
        scaled = constructorof(N)(; op=times_idx, children=(const_a, feature_leaf))
        if plus_idx !== nothing && !iszero(b_coef)
            const_b = constructorof(N)(T; val=b_coef)
            constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(scaled, const_b))
        else
            scaled
        end
    else
        # Fallback: no '*' operator available (or zero slope) — just use the raw feature.
        feature_leaf
    end

    # Graft the correction onto the whole tree via addition (or a fallback binary op).
    graft_op = plus_idx !== nothing ? plus_idx : rand(rng, 1:options.nops[2])
    newroot = constructorof(N)(; op=graft_op, children=(tree, linear_term))

    return newroot  # new root, since we wrapped the entire expression
end

balanced_rank_tournament_selection_gen3_.name: balanced_rank_tournament_selection_gen3_2
balanced_rank_tournament_selection_gen3_.code:
"""
    balanced_rank_tournament_selection_gen3_2(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Select a parent using a scale-free consensus tournament that balances adaptive
parsimony against raw predictive accuracy. The operator samples a tournament,
computes the usual frequency-adjusted costs, and independently ranks candidates
by adjusted cost and raw loss. It then combines those ranks with a 2:1 weighting
in favor of adjusted cost, preserving parsimony pressure while allowing highly
accurate building blocks to survive even when their complexity is temporarily
common. The resulting consensus order is sampled using the configured geometric
tournament pressure. The heuristic assumes finite costs and losses and treats
their ordinal ranking as more reliable than their potentially different scales.
"""
function balanced_rank_tournament_selection_gen3_2(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Permit use with temporarily undersized populations.
    sample_n = min(options.tournament_selection_n, pop.n)
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, sample_n; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)

    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{L}(undef, n)

    # Retain adaptive frequency-based parsimony from the standard tournament.
    if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
        scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
        for i in 1:n
            member = sample[i]
            size = compute_complexity(member, options)
            frequency = if 0 < size <= options.maxsize
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost * exp(scaling * frequency)
            losses[i] = member.loss
        end
    else
        for i in 1:n
            adjusted_costs[i] = sample[i].cost
            losses[i] = sample[i].loss
        end
    end

    # Average ranks avoid arbitrary preference among exactly tied candidates.
    average_ranks = function(values)
        order = sortperm(values)
        ranks = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
        first = 1
        while first <= n
            last = first
            while last < n && values[order[last + 1]] == values[order[first]]
                last += 1
            end
            rank = (first + last) / 2
            for position in first:last
                ranks[order[position]] = rank
            end
            first = last + 1
        end
        return ranks
    end

    adjusted_ranks = average_ranks(adjusted_costs)
    loss_ranks = average_ranks(losses)

    # Adaptive cost remains primary, while raw loss protects useful accurate forms.
    consensus_scores = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        consensus_scores[i] = 2.0 * adjusted_ranks[i] + loss_ranks[i]
    end

    selection_order = collect(1:n)
    sort!(
        selection_order;
        by=i -> (consensus_scores[i], adjusted_ranks[i], loss_ranks[i]),
    )

    # Apply the configured geometric tournament pressure to the consensus order.
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_rank = if p == 1.0
        1
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        StatsBase.sample(weights)
    end

    return copy(sample[selection_order[chosen_rank]])
end

affine_tail_continuation_loss_gen3_9.name: affine_tail_continuation_loss_gen3_9
affine_tail_continuation_loss_gen3_9.code:
"""
    affine_tail_continuation_loss_gen3_9(tree, dataset, options)

Variance-normalized error with two complementary correction terms, computed in a single
cheap pass over the data:

1. **Raw fit term** — `log1p(SSE / SS_y)`, the usual normalized-MSE signal.
2. **Tail-concentration term** — `log1p(sqrt(mean(u^4)))` where `u_i = d_i / sd(y)` are the
   normalized residuals. Because `sqrt(mean(u^4)) >= mean(u^2)`, this term only exceeds the
   raw term when the residuals are *concentrated* in a subregion of the data. Smooth
   truncated-series surrogates (e.g. `x0 + x0*x1^2/(2*x2^2)` standing in for
   `x0/sqrt(1-x1^2/x2^2)`) fit most of the domain almost perfectly and dump all of their
   error near the singular/extreme region; the L4 term makes those plateaus visibly worse
   than structurally correct forms, discouraging the epicycle-stacking seen in the parent's
   Pareto fronts. Its weight is kept modest (1/3 in log space) so i.i.d. observation noise
   — whose residuals are spread out, giving `mean(u^4) ~ 3*mean(u^2)^2` — is not
   over-penalized on noisy real-world data.
3. **Affine-calibration scaffold** — the least-squares residual of `a*prediction + b`,
   obtained analytically from a Welford pass (`SS_y - cov(p,y)^2/var(p)`). This rewards
   expressions with the right functional shape before their constants are tuned, and its
   weight `0.75 * nmse / (1 + nmse)` fades continuously to zero as the raw fit improves, so
   only genuinely correct predictions attain zero loss.

Changes vs. the parent (`affine_continuation_loss_init_8`):
* Added the L4 tail-concentration term (main new signal), normalized to be directly
  comparable to the raw NMSE and folded in with a small, fixed log-space weight.
* Replaced the parent's Welford pass over the residuals with direct accumulation of
  `sum d^2` and `sum d^4`; these are sums of non-negative terms, so there is no
  cancellation to protect against, and it removes three updates per sample.
* Added an overflow-safe fallback: if the fourth-power sum is not finite, the tail term
  degrades gracefully to the raw term instead of returning `Inf`.
* Kept the relative variance floors, constant-target/constant-prediction guards, and the
  continuation schedule of the parent unchanged. No complexity penalty is included.
"""
function affine_tail_continuation_loss_gen3_9(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)

    # Welford state for the affine calibration (needs centered moments of p and y).
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l

    # Residual power sums: both are sums of non-negative terms, so plain
    # accumulation is exact enough (no catastrophic cancellation possible).
    sse = zero_l
    s4 = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        d = p - y

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y) && isfinite(d))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        k = L(i)

        delta_p = p - mean_p
        mean_p += delta_p / k

        delta_y = y - mean_y
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        # Covariance update uses the freshly updated target mean (standard form).
        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)

        d2 = d * d
        sse += d2
        s4 += d2 * d2
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py) && isfinite(sse))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Centered sums can drift microscopically negative from roundoff.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)
    sse = max(sse, zero_l)

    if sse == zero_l
        return zero_l
    end

    n_l = L(n)

    # Relative floors suppress unstable calibration on numerically constant data.
    y_reference = max(one_l, abs(mean_y))
    p_reference = max(one_l, abs(mean_p))
    scale_floor = n_l * eps(L) * y_reference * y_reference
    prediction_floor = n_l * eps(L) * p_reference * p_reference
    if !(isfinite(scale_floor) && isfinite(prediction_floor))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    scale_sse = max(m2_y, scale_floor)
    target_is_variable = m2_y > scale_floor

    # --- affine-calibrated structural error -------------------------------------
    affine_sse = sse
    if target_is_variable
        if m2_p > prediction_floor
            # Explained SSE of the least-squares fit a*p+b is cov(p,y)^2 / var(p).
            normalized_covariance = cov_py / sqrt(m2_p)
            explained_sse = normalized_covariance * normalized_covariance
            if !isfinite(explained_sse)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            affine_sse = clamp(m2_y - explained_sse, zero_l, m2_y)
        else
            # A constant prediction can only capture the target intercept.
            affine_sse = m2_y
        end
    end

    raw_nmse = sse / scale_sse
    affine_nmse = affine_sse / scale_sse
    if !(isfinite(raw_nmse) && isfinite(affine_nmse))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # --- tail-concentration term -------------------------------------------------
    # With u_i = d_i / sd(y): mean(u^2) == raw_nmse and
    # sqrt(mean(u^4)) == sqrt(n * s4) / scale_sse (>= raw_nmse, equal iff |d| constant).
    tail_nmse = raw_nmse
    if isfinite(s4) && s4 > zero_l
        candidate = sqrt(n_l * s4) / scale_sse
        # Fall back to the raw term on overflow; clamp guards roundoff below raw.
        tail_nmse = isfinite(candidate) ? max(candidate, raw_nmse) : raw_nmse
    end

    raw_term = log1p(max(raw_nmse, zero_l))
    tail_term = log1p(max(tail_nmse, zero_l))
    affine_term = log1p(max(affine_nmse, zero_l))

    # Modest, fixed weight on residual concentration: enough to break ties between
    # globally-smooth-but-locally-wrong surrogates and correct structure, small
    # enough that spread-out observation noise is not over-penalized.
    tail_weight = L(1) / L(3)
    fit_term = (one_l - tail_weight) * raw_term + tail_weight * tail_term

    # Structural (affine) guidance is strong far from the target and vanishes near a fit,
    # so only exact predictions can reach zero loss.
    scaffold_strength = L(3) / L(4)
    blend = scaffold_strength * raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse)
    loss_value = (one_l - blend) * fit_term + blend * affine_term

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

shape_guided_log_nmse_loss_gen3_3.name: shape_guided_log_nmse_loss_gen3_3
shape_guided_log_nmse_loss_gen3_3.code:
"""
    shape_guided_log_nmse_loss_gen3_3(tree, dataset, options)

Evaluate an expression with a scale-normalized MSE augmented by a lightweight
shape-matching signal. The direct error is normalized by target energy and
log-compressed so numerically poor candidates do not overwhelm useful structural
differences. A secondary `1 - r²` term measures agreement after the best implicit
affine rescaling, helping promising nonlinear structure survive before its
constants and offset are fully optimized.

Compared with the parent MSE, this loss is scale-independent, less dominated by
large aggregate errors, allocation-free, and provides affine-invariant shape
guidance. Online moments compute all statistics in one pass. Constant targets
disable the shape term, exact predictions return zero, and no expression
complexity penalty is included.
"""
function shape_guided_log_nmse_loss_gen3_3(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = length(dataset.y)
