    function trees_equal(a, b)
        a.degree == b.degree || return false
        if a.degree == 0
            a.constant == b.constant || return false
            return a.constant ? (a.val == b.val) : (a.feature == b.feature)
        end
        a.op == b.op || return false
        for i in 1:(a.degree)
            trees_equal(get_child(a, i), get_child(b, i)) || return false
        end
        return true
    end

    # Node constructors.
    bin(op, a, b) = constructorof(N)(; op=op, children=(a, b))
    lit(v) = constructorof(N)(T; val=v)

    # Operator-identity predicates.
    is_plus(t) = t.degree == 2 && plus_idx !== nothing && t.op == plus_idx
    is_minus(t) = t.degree == 2 && minus_idx !== nothing && t.op == minus_idx
    is_sum(t) = is_plus(t) || is_minus(t)
    is_times(t) = t.degree == 2 && times_idx !== nothing && t.op == times_idx
    is_div(t) = t.degree == 2 && div_idx !== nothing && t.op == div_idx

    # Feature-space helpers (from parent 1).
    function _collect_features!(node, feats::Vector{Int})
        if node.degree == 0
            !node.constant && push!(feats, node.feature)
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _collect_features!(get_child(node, i), feats)
            end
        end
        return feats
    end
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int, num_features::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, num_features)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift, num_features)
            end
        end
        return node
    end
    function _remap_feature!(node, from_f::Int, to_f::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant && node.feature == from_f
                node.feature = to_f
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _remap_feature!(get_child(node, i), from_f, to_f)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Rewrite-site catalogue (parent 2, extended with `a + a -> 2*a`).
    # Each site is (node_to_overwrite, replacement, sampling_weight, is_pure_reduction)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    function gather_sites(root)
        sites = Tuple{N,N,Float64,Bool}[]
        add_site!(node, repl, w, red) = (push!(sites, (node, repl, w, red)); nothing)
        total = count_nodes(root)

        any(root) do t
            # ---- unary constant folding: f(c) -> literal ----
            if t.degree == 1
                child = get_child(t, 1)
                if child.degree == 0 && child.constant
                    folded = try
                        unaops[t.op](child.val)
                    catch
                        nothing
                    end
                    if folded !== nothing && isfinite(folded)
                        add_site!(t, lit(T(folded)), 5.0, true)
                    end
                end
                return false
            end

            if t.degree == 2
                c1 = get_child(t, 1)
                c2 = get_child(t, 2)
                c1_is_const = c1.degree == 0 && c1.constant
                c2_is_const = c2.degree == 0 && c2.constant

                # (0a) generic binary constant folding
                if c1_is_const && c2_is_const
                    folded = try
                        binops[t.op](c1.val, c2.val)
                    catch
                        nothing
                    end
                    if folded !== nothing && isfinite(folded)
                        add_site!(t, lit(T(folded)), 5.0, true)
                    end
                end

                # (0b) literal 0/1 identities
                if is_plus(t)
                    if c1_is_const && c1.val == zeroT
                        add_site!(t, copy(c2), 5.0, true)
                    elseif c2_is_const && c2.val == zeroT
                        add_site!(t, copy(c1), 5.0, true)
                    end
                elseif is_minus(t)
                    if c2_is_const && c2.val == zeroT
                        add_site!(t, copy(c1), 5.0, true)
                    end
                elseif is_times(t)
                    if c1_is_const && c1.val == oneT
                        add_site!(t, copy(c2), 5.0, true)
                    elseif c1_is_const && c1.val == zeroT
                        add_site!(t, lit(zeroT), 5.0, true)
                    elseif c2_is_const && c2.val == oneT
                        add_site!(t, copy(c1), 5.0, true)
                    elseif c2_is_const && c2.val == zeroT
                        add_site!(t, lit(zeroT), 5.0, true)
                    end
                elseif is_div(t)
                    if c2_is_const && c2.val == oneT
                        add_site!(t, copy(c1), 5.0, true)
                    end
                end

                # (0c) generalized self-cancellation on structurally equal subtrees
                if is_minus(t) && trees_equal(c1, c2)
                    add_site!(t, lit(zeroT), 5.0, true)
                elseif is_div(t) && trees_equal(c1, c2)
                    add_site!(t, lit(oneT), 5.0, true)
                end

                # (0d) NEW (motif-duplication companion): a + a -> 2*a
                if is_plus(t) &&
                    times_idx !== nothing &&
                    !(c1_is_const && c2_is_const) &&
                    trees_equal(c1, c2)
                    add_site!(t, bin(times_idx, lit(twoT), copy(c1)), 4.0, true)
                end

                # (1) exact cancellation inside sums
                if is_minus(t) && is_plus(c1)
                    if trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                        add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0, true)
                    elseif trees_equal(get_child(c1, 1), c2)
                        add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), 4.0, true)
                    end
                elseif is_plus(t) && is_minus(c1) && trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0, true)
                elseif is_plus(t) && is_minus(c2) && trees_equal(get_child(c2, 2), c1)
                    add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c2, 1)), 4.0, true)
                end

                # (2) factor a shared multiplicative term: a*b ± a*c -> a*(b±c)
                # (exploratory reshaping -> not used by the greedy cleanup pass)
                if is_sum(t) && is_times(c1) && is_times(c2)
                    for i in 1:2, j in 1:2
                        if trees_equal(get_child(c1, i), get_child(c2, j))
                            common = copy(get_child(c1, i))
                            rest1 = copy(get_child(c1, 3 - i))
                            rest2 = copy(get_child(c2, 3 - j))
                            add_site!(
                                t,
                                bin(times_idx, common, bin(t.op, rest1, rest2)),
                                3.0,
                                false,
                            )
                            break
                        end
                    end
                end

                # (3) common denominator: a/c ± b/c -> (a±b)/c
                if is_sum(t) &&
                    is_div(c1) &&
                    is_div(c2) &&
                    trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), get_child(c2, 2))
                    add_site!(
                        t,
                        bin(
                            div_idx,
                            bin(t.op, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), copy(get_child(c2, 1))),
                            copy(get_child(c1, 2)),
                        ),
                        3.0,
                        false,
                    )
                end

                # (4) multiplicative cancellation: (a*b)/a -> b, (a*b)/b -> a
                if is_div(t) && is_times(c1)
                    if trees_equal(get_child(c1, 1), c2)
                        add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), 4.0, true)
                    elseif trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                        add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0, true)
                    end
                end

                # (5) multiplicative cancellation: (a/b)*b -> a, b*(a/b) -> a
                if is_times(t)
                    if is_div(c1) && trees_equal(get_child(c1, 2), c2)
                        add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), 4.0, true)
                    elseif is_div(c2) && trees_equal(get_child(c2, 2), c1)
                        add_site!(t, copy(get_child(c2, 1)), 4.0, true)
                    end
                end

                # (6) fold nested divisions: (a/b)/c -> a/(b*c)
                if is_div(t) && is_div(c1) && times_idx !== nothing
                    add_site!(
                        t,
                        bin(
                            div_idx,
                            copy(get_child(c1, 1)),
                            bin(times_idx, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), copy(c2)),
                        ),
                        2.0,
                        false,
                    )
                end

                # (7) lift an inner division: a/(b/c) -> (a*c)/b
                if is_div(t) && is_div(c2) && times_idx !== nothing
                    add_site!(
                        t,
                        bin(
                            div_idx,
                            bin(times_idx, copy(c1), copy(get_child(c2, 2))),
                            copy(get_child(c2, 1)),
                        ),
                        2.0,
                        false,
                    )
                end

                # (8) distribution over multiplication (size-increasing)
                if is_times(t)
                    for k in 1:2
                        s = get_child(t, k)
                        m = get_child(t, 3 - k)
                        if is_sum(s)
                            nm = count_nodes(m)
                            if nm <= 3 && total + nm + 1 <= maxsize
                                add_site!(
                                    t,
                                    bin(
                                        s.op,
                                        bin(times_idx, copy(m), copy(get_child(s, 1))),
                                        bin(times_idx, copy(m), copy(get_child(s, 2))),
                                    ),
                                    1.0,
                                    false,
                                )
                            end
                        end
                    end
                end

                # (9) distribution over division (size-increasing)
                if is_div(t) && is_sum(c1)
                    na = count_nodes(c2)
                    if na <= 3 && total + na + 1 <= maxsize
                        add_site!(
                            t,
                            bin(
                                c1.op,
                                bin(div_idx, copy(get_child(c1, 1)), copy(c2)),
                                bin(div_idx, copy(get_child(c1, 2)), copy(c2)),
                            ),
                            1.0,
                            false,
                        )
                    end
                end
            end
            return false  # full traversal, never short-circuit
        end
        return sites
    end

    # Greedy, bounded cleanup: apply only pure size reductions.
    function canonicalize!(root)
        for _ in 1:3
            s = gather_sites(root)
            reducing = [x for x in s if x[4]]
            isempty(reducing) && break
            node, repl, _, _ = reducing[rand(rng, 1:length(reducing))]
            set_node!(node, repl)
        end
        return root
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Mode selection: pure algebraic rewrite vs. symmetry move + cleanup
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    sites = tree.degree == 0 ? Tuple{N,N,Float64,Bool}[] : gather_sites(tree)
    if !isempty(sites)
        # Simplifications available -> more likely to take the algebraic route.
        has_reducing = any(x -> x[4], sites)
        p_algebraic = has_reducing ? 0.55 : 0.3
        if rand(rng) < p_algebraic
            weights = [x[3] for x in sites]
            r = rand(rng) * sum(weights)
            idx = length(weights)
            acc = 0.0
            for (i, w) in enumerate(weights)
                acc += w
                if r <= acc
                    idx = i
                    break
                end
            end
            node, repl, _, _ = sites[idx]
            set_node!(node, repl)  # `repl` built only from copies -> safe in-place
            return tree
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Symmetry move: motif duplication with feature-space transformation
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    if options.nops[2] == 0
        # No binary operators: fall back to a unary wrap (parent 1 behaviour).
        if options.nops[1] > 0
            node = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
            new_node = constructorof(N)(;
                op=rand(rng, 1:options.nops[1]), children=(copy(node),)
            )
            set_node!(node, new_node)
        end
        return canonicalize!(tree)
    end

    # Step 1: pick a donor motif and clone it.
    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    donor_clone = copy(donor)

    # Step 2: apply a feature-space symmetry transformation to the clone.
    feats = _collect_features!(donor_clone, Int[])
    if !isempty(feats) && nfeatures > 1
        roll = rand(rng)
        if roll < 0.45
            # Cyclic permutation: preserves relational structure across variables.
            _shift_features!(donor_clone, rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1)), nfeatures)
        elseif roll < 0.70
            # Targeted single-feature substitution (asymmetric couplings).
            f_old = rand(rng, feats)
            valid_targets = [f for f in 1:nfeatures if f != f_old]
            if !isempty(valid_targets)
                _remap_feature!(donor_clone, f_old, rand(rng, valid_targets))
            end
        else
            # Identity: enables powers (u*u) and rational self-coupling.
        end
    end

    # Step 3: integrate the transformed motif back into the tree.
    total_nodes = count_nodes(tree)
    if total_nodes > 3 && rand(rng) < 0.35
        # Homologous grafting: overwrite a random node with the evolved motif.
        target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
        set_node!(target, donor_clone)
    else
        # Binary coupling of a target node with the motif.
        target = rand(rng, Bool) ? donor : rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
        target_copy = copy(target)

        # Structure-aware operator choice: identical operands must not be coupled
        # by `-` or `/` (they would cancel to 0/1); prefer the symmetric `+`/`*`
        # couplings that dominate physically symmetric laws.
        identical = trees_equal(target_copy, donor_clone)
        preferred = Int[]
        plus_idx !== nothing && push!(preferred, plus_idx)
        times_idx !== nothing && push!(preferred, times_idx)

        bin_op = if !isempty(preferred) && (identical || rand(rng) < 0.6)
            rand(rng, preferred)
        else
            cands = [
                k for k in 1:options.nops[2] if !(
                    identical && (
                        (minus_idx !== nothing && k == minus_idx) ||
                        (div_idx !== nothing && k == div_idx)
                    )
                )
            ]
            isempty(cands) ? rand(rng, 1:options.nops[2]) : rand(rng, cands)
        end

        # Randomize operand order for non-commutative operators.
        children_tuple = if rand(rng, Bool)
            (target_copy, donor_clone)
        else
            (donor_clone, target_copy)
        end
        set_node!(target, constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children_tuple))
    end

    # Step 4: canonicalize the freshly duplicated material (collapse degeneracies
    # such as `a-a`, `a/a`, `a+a`, constant sub-expressions) so the offspring is
    # judged on its symmetric hypothesis rather than on redundant bloat.
    return canonicalize!(tree)
end

streamlined_age_survival_gen8_9.code:
"""
    streamlined_age_survival_gen8_9(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

Replace the oldest eligible population member, preserving the parent's age-regularized
selection pressure. The population is scanned once: excluded slots are skipped, lower
birth values are preferred, and equal-age ties select the member with worse cost rather
than depending on array order. This removes the temporary birth vector, typed sentinel,
and separate `argmin_fast` pass while retaining the core age-based behavior.
"""
function streamlined_age_survival_gen8_9(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    candidate = 0

    for i in 1:pop.n
        i in exclude_indices && continue

        # Age is primary; cost only resolves members born at the same time.
        if candidate == 0 ||
           pop.members[i].birth < pop.members[candidate].birth ||
           (pop.members[i].birth == pop.members[candidate].birth &&
            pop.members[i].cost > pop.members[candidate].cost)
            candidate = i
        end
    end

    candidate == 0 && throw(ArgumentError("No population member is eligible for replacement"))
    return candidate
end

pareto_frontier_slope_selection_gen8_6.name: pareto_frontier_slope_selection_gen8_6
pareto_frontier_slope_selection_gen8_6.code:
"""
    pareto_frontier_slope_selection_gen8_6(
        pop::Population{T,L,N},
        running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
        options::AbstractOptions,
    )::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}

Select a parent using Pareto-front layering, logarithmic trade-off gradient
(loss improvement per unit complexity), and dual-level niche protection.

# Core Idea & Heuristics
1. **Pareto Front Layering**: Evaluates loss-complexity trade-offs by partitioning
   the sampled tournament into non-dominated Pareto fronts (Front 0 = non-dominated,
   Front 1 = second-tier, etc.). Front level provides a much stronger structural
   signal than flat domination counts.
2. **Log-Scale Pareto Slope Breakthrough**: Quantifies breakthrough significance as
   the rate of logarithmic loss reduction relative to the best simpler sampled candidate
   per unit of added complexity: `slope = (log(L_simpler) - log(L_i)) / (C_i - C_simpler)`.
   Passed through `tanh`, this rewards true Occam breakthroughs (massive accuracy gains
   for small complexity increments) invariantly across varying loss magnitudes.
3. **Dual-Level Niche Protection**:
   - *Tournament-local de-crowding*: Penalizes multiple members sharing the exact same
     complexity size in the tournament (`1 / sqrt(count)`), preserving structural diversity.
   - *Global adaptive parsimony*: Softly dampens over-explored complexity bins search-wide
     using `1 / (1 + scaling * frequency)`.
4. **Balanced Quality Anchor**: Blends Pareto front level with regularized cost rank
   and raw loss rank to anchor search to user objective preferences while promoting
   efficient exploration.

# Changes vs. Parent
- Replaced raw Pareto domination counts with exact iterative Pareto front peeling
  (NSGA-II front ranks 0, 1, ...).
- Replaced the parent's linear loss-difference ratio with a scale-invariant logarithmic
  gradient (`Δ log(loss) / Δ complexity`), preventing saturation and appropriately rewarding
  order-of-magnitude accuracy improvements.
- Added tournament-local complexity de-crowding to prevent identical-complexity clusters
  from dominating the selection pool.
- Replaced exponential global frequency scaling with rational damping for improved
  numerical stability across wide parsimony scaling settings.
"""
function pareto_frontier_slope_selection_gen8_6(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    tournament_size = min(pop.n, max(2, options.tournament_selection_n))
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, tournament_size; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)

    n == 1 && return sample[1]

    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    frequencies = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)

    # 1. Extract and sanitize objectives and search statistics
    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]

        loss = Float64(member.loss)
        cost = Float64(member.cost)
        losses[i] = isfinite(loss) ? loss : Inf
        costs[i] = isfinite(cost) ? cost : Inf

        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size

        frequency = if 0 < size <= options.maxsize &&
                       size <= length(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies)
            Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
        else
            0.0
        end
        frequencies[i] = isfinite(frequency) ? max(0.0, frequency) : 0.0
    end

    # 2. Objective ranks and local complexity crowding counts
    loss_ranks = zeros(Int, n)
    cost_ranks = zeros(Int, n)
    complexity_counts = zeros(Int, n)

    for i in 1:n
        for j in 1:n
            if i != j
                loss_ranks[i] += losses[j] < losses[i]
                cost_ranks[i] += costs[j] < costs[i]
            end
            complexity_counts[i] += (complexities[j] == complexities[i])
        end
    end

    # 3. Iterative Pareto front peeling (NSGA-II front ranks: 0 = non-dominated, 1 = second front, ...)
    front_ranks = fill(-1, n)
    assigned = 0
    current_rank = 0
    in_front = falses(n)

    while assigned < n
        fill!(in_front, false)
        for i in 1:n
            front_ranks[i] >= 0 && continue
            dominated = false
            for j in 1:n
                (i == j || front_ranks[j] >= 0) && continue
                no_worse = losses[j] <= losses[i] && complexities[j] <= complexities[i]
                strictly_better = losses[j] < losses[i] || complexities[j] < complexities[i]
                if no_worse && strictly_better
                    dominated = true
                    break
                end
            end
            if !dominated
                in_front[i] = true
            end
        end

        for i in 1:n
            if in_front[i]
                front_ranks[i] = current_rank
                assigned += 1
            end
        end
        current_rank += 1

        # Fallback guard against non-progress
        if current_rank > n
            for i in 1:n
                front_ranks[i] < 0 && (front_ranks[i] = current_rank)
            end
            break
        end
    end

    # 4. Logarithmic Pareto slope: evaluate loss reduction rate per unit complexity
    breakthroughs = zeros(Float64, n)
    for i in 1:n
        losses[i] == Inf && continue

        best_simpler_loss = Inf
        best_simpler_complexity = 0
        for j in 1:n
            if complexities[j] < complexities[i] && losses[j] < best_simpler_loss
                best_simpler_loss = losses[j]
                best_simpler_complexity = complexities[j]
            end
        end

        if isfinite(best_simpler_loss) && losses[i] < best_simpler_loss
            # Logarithmic reduction across positive loss scales
            delta_log = if losses[i] > 0.0 && best_simpler_loss > 0.0
                log(best_simpler_loss) - log(losses[i])
            elseif losses[i] <= 0.0 && best_simpler_loss > 0.0
                log(best_simpler_loss) + 5.0
            else
                (best_simpler_loss - losses[i]) / max(1e-12, abs(best_simpler_loss))
            end

            delta_complexity = max(1, complexities[i] - best_simpler_complexity)
            slope = max(0.0, delta_log) / Float64(delta_complexity)
            breakthroughs[i] = tanh(slope)
        end
    end

    # 5. Composite selection probability weight calculation
    p = clamp(Float64(options.tournament_selection_p), 0.0, 1.0)
    pressure = 0.80 + 2.20 * p
    rank_denom = Float64(max(1, n - 1))
    parsimony_scale = max(0.0, Float64(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling))

    weights = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        norm_cost_rank = Float64(cost_ranks[i]) / rank_denom
        norm_loss_rank = Float64(loss_ranks[i]) / rank_denom

        # Blended regularized-cost and raw-loss quality factors
        quality_factor = 0.20 +
                         0.50 * exp(-pressure * norm_cost_rank) +
                         0.30 * exp(-pressure * norm_loss_rank)

        # Exponential preference for lower (better) Pareto fronts
        pareto_factor = exp(-pressure * Float64(front_ranks[i]))

        # Breakthrough bonus for high marginal efficiency
        breakthrough_factor = 1.0 + 2.5 * breakthroughs[i]

        # Local complexity niche de-crowding
        local_niche_factor = inv(sqrt(Float64(complexity_counts[i])))

        # Population-wide adaptive parsimony damping
        global_niche_factor = if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            inv(1.0 + parsimony_scale * frequencies[i])
        else
            1.0
        end

        weights[i] = quality_factor *
                     pareto_factor *
                     breakthrough_factor *
                     local_niche_factor *
                     global_niche_factor
    end

    total_weight = sum(weights)
    if !isfinite(total_weight) || total_weight <= 0.0
        return sample[argmin_fast(costs)]
    end

    chosen_idx = StatsBase.sample(StatsBase.Weights(weights, total_weight))
    return sample[chosen_idx]
end

data_guided_residual_pursuit_gen8_5.name: data_guided_residual_pursuit_gen8_5
data_guided_residual_pursuit_gen8_5.code:
"""
    data_guided_residual_pursuit_gen8_5(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

A data-aware mutation operator inspired by gradient boosting and orthogonal matching pursuit.
It analyzes the regression residuals of the current expression, identifies the input feature
most correlated with the unexplained residual variance, computes an optimal closed-form
linear scaling coefficient via ordinary least squares (OLS), and grafts this residual-compensating
term into the expression.

### Steps:
1. **Residual Evaluation**: Evaluates `tree` on `dataset.X` to obtain predictions and residuals `r = y - y_pred`.
   If evaluation fails, produces non-finite values, or target is missing, the mutation safely returns `tree`.
2. **Feature Correlation Screening**: Computes sample-weighted Pearson correlation and covariance
   between each input feature and the residual vector.
3. **Stochastic Selection**: Samples a promising feature with probability proportional to its squared
   correlation (explained residual variance), maintaining population diversity while prioritizing high-signal features.
4. **OLS Coefficient Estimation**: Computes the optimal linear slope `α = Cov(x_j, r) / Var(x_j)` for the chosen feature.
5. **Structural Grafting**:
   - If binary addition (`+`) is available, wraps the root (or splices into a leaf) with an additive term `α * x_j`.
   - If addition is unavailable, replaces an existing leaf with the chosen feature.

### Assumptions and Heuristics:
- Linear residual correlation serves as a fast, robust first-order proxy for discovering missing additive components.
- Closed-form OLS initialization bypasses slow random constant exploration, providing immediate fitness improvement.
- Probabilistic selection over squared correlations avoids greedy fixation on a single feature.
"""
function data_guided_residual_pursuit_gen8_5(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Safety check: dataset must contain single-output targets and sufficient samples
    if dataset.y === nothing || dataset.n < 2 || nfeatures < 1
        return tree
    end

    # Evaluate the current expression tree on the dataset
    y_pred, ok = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options.operators)
    if !ok || any(!isfinite, y_pred)
        return tree
    end

    n = dataset.n
    y = dataset.y
    weights = dataset.weights
    has_weights = weights !== nothing

    # Compute (weighted) mean of residuals
    sum_w = zero(T)
    mean_r = zero(T)
    for i in 1:n
        w_i = has_weights ? T(weights[i]) : one(T)
        sum_w += w_i
        r_i = y[i] - y_pred[i]
        mean_r += w_i * r_i
    end

    if sum_w <= zero(T) || !isfinite(mean_r)
        return tree
    end
    mean_r /= sum_w

    # Compute (weighted) variance of residuals
    var_r = zero(T)
    for i in 1:n
        w_i = has_weights ? T(weights[i]) : one(T)
        r_i = y[i] - y_pred[i]
        var_r += w_i * (r_i - mean_r)^2
    end
    var_r /= sum_w

    # If residual variance is effectively zero, the model already fits perfectly
    if var_r <= eps(T) * T(100) || !isfinite(var_r)
        return tree
    end

    # Calculate correlation and OLS slope for each input feature against the residual
    scores = zeros(T, nfeatures)
    slopes = zeros(T, nfeatures)

    for j in 1:nfeatures
        # Feature mean
        mean_xj = zero(T)
        for i in 1:n
            w_i = has_weights ? T(weights[i]) : one(T)
            mean_xj += w_i * dataset.X[j, i]
        end
        mean_xj /= sum_w

        # Feature variance and covariance with residual
        cov_xr = zero(T)
        var_xj = zero(T)
        for i in 1:n
            w_i = has_weights ? T(weights[i]) : one(T)
            dx = dataset.X[j, i] - mean_xj
            dr = (y[i] - y_pred[i]) - mean_r
            cov_xr += w_i * dx * dr
            var_xj += w_i * dx * dx
        end
        cov_xr /= sum_w
        var_xj /= sum_w

        # If feature has non-zero variance, record its correlation and OLS slope
        if var_xj > eps(T) * T(100) && isfinite(var_xj) && isfinite(cov_xr)
            corr = cov_xr / sqrt(var_xj * var_r)
            if isfinite(corr)
                scores[j] = corr^2  # R^2 weighting for feature sampling
                slopes[j] = cov_xr / var_xj
            end
        end
    end

    total_score = sum(scores)
    if total_score <= zero(T) || !isfinite(total_score)
        return tree
    end

    # Stochastic selection of feature proportional to explained variance
    threshold = rand(rng, T) * total_score
    cumulative = zero(T)
    chosen_feature = 1
    for j in 1:nfeatures
        cumulative += scores[j]
        if cumulative >= threshold
            chosen_feature = j
            break
        end
    end

    chosen_slope = slopes[chosen_feature]
    if !isfinite(chosen_slope) || abs(chosen_slope) <= eps(T)
        return tree
    end

    # Identify available binary operators
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), options.operators.binops)
    mul_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (*), options.operators.binops)

    # Construct the residual correction term: (α * x_j) or simply (x_j)
    feat_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; feature=chosen_feature)
    correction_term = if mul_idx !== nothing
        const_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=chosen_slope)
        constructorof(N)(; op=mul_idx, children=(const_leaf, feat_leaf))
    else
        feat_leaf
    end

    # Graft the correction term into the expression
    if plus_idx !== nothing
        # With 70% probability (or if tree is small), perform additive boosting at the root
        if count_nodes(tree) <= 3 || rand(rng) < 0.7
            return constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(tree, correction_term))
        else
            # Otherwise, splice additively onto a random leaf to refine a local sub-expression
            target_leaf = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> t.degree == 0))
            new_sub = constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(copy(target_leaf), correction_term))
            set_node!(target_leaf, new_sub)
            return tree
        end
    else
        # Fallback if addition is not available: replace a leaf with the correlated feature
        target_leaf = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> t.degree == 0))
        set_node!(target_leaf, feat_leaf)
        return tree
    end
end

adaptive_shape_continuation_nmse_loss_ge.name: adaptive_shape_continuation_nmse_loss_gen8_3
adaptive_shape_continuation_nmse_loss_ge.code:
"""
    adaptive_shape_continuation_nmse_loss_gen8_3(tree, dataset, options)

Combine the *affine continuation* idea of parent 1 with the *bounded shape signal*
of parent 2 into a single-pass, allocation-free loss.

Core idea:
  * One numerically stable Welford pass accumulates the raw sum of squared
    residuals together with the first/second moments of the prediction and the
    target and their covariance, plus the raw target energy as a fallback scale.
  * Fidelity term: the raw SSE is normalized by the target variance (falling back
    to target energy, then to `n`, for numerically constant targets) and
    compressed with `log1p`, so catastrophic candidates cannot drown out
    structurally useful ones while relative accuracy stays scale-free.
  * Shape term: `1 - r²`, i.e. the *bounded* normalized residual left after the
    best implicit affine map `a * prediction + b`. This rewards candidates whose
    functional shape is already correct even though their constants/offset have
    not been tuned yet. Being bounded in `[0, 1]`, it can never dominate the
    ranking the way an unbounded calibrated error can.
  * Continuation schedule: the weight on the shape term is not fixed but grows
    with the raw error, `w = w_max * raw_nmse / (1 + raw_nmse)`, so structural
    guidance is strong far from a fit and fades smoothly to zero as the raw
    error vanishes. Only genuinely correct predictions reach zero loss, avoiding
    the degenerate optimum of a purely affine-invariant objective.

Heuristics/assumptions: `w_max = 0.5` keeps direct fidelity at least half the
loss everywhere; constant targets disable the shape term (correlation is
undefined); a constant prediction against a variable target gets the maximal
shape penalty of 1. No expression-complexity penalty is included.
"""
function adaptive_shape_continuation_nmse_loss_gen8_3(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)

    # Welford accumulators: stable variances/covariance without raw power sums.
    mean_y = zero_l
    mean_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    covariance = zero_l
    squared_error = zero_l
    target_energy = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        p = L(prediction[i])
        if !(isfinite(y) && isfinite(p))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        residual = p - y
        squared_error = muladd(residual, residual, squared_error)
        target_energy = muladd(y, y, target_energy)

        count = L(i)
        delta_y = y - mean_y
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        mean_y += delta_y / count
        mean_p += delta_p / count

        # Updates use the freshly advanced means (standard Welford form).
        m2_y = muladd(delta_y, y - mean_y, m2_y)
        m2_p = muladd(delta_p, p - mean_p, m2_p)
        covariance = muladd(delta_p, y - mean_y, covariance)
    end

    # Preserve the exact zero optimum even if auxiliary sums are extreme.
    if squared_error == zero_l
        return zero_l
    end

    if !(isfinite(squared_error) && isfinite(target_energy) &&
         isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(covariance) &&
         isfinite(mean_y) && isfinite(mean_p))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Roundoff can make centered sums microscopically negative.
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)

    # Relative floors keep us from "calibrating" numerically constant data.
    n_l = L(n)
    y_reference = max(one_l, abs(mean_y))
    p_reference = max(one_l, abs(mean_p))
    target_floor = n_l * eps(L) * y_reference * y_reference
    prediction_floor = n_l * eps(L) * p_reference * p_reference
    if !(isfinite(target_floor) && isfinite(prediction_floor))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    target_is_variable = m2_y > target_floor

    # Scale-free normalizer: prefer target variance, fall back to energy, then n.
    normalizer = if target_is_variable
        m2_y
    elseif target_energy > zero_l
        target_energy
    else
        n_l
    end

    raw_nmse = squared_error / normalizer
    if !isfinite(raw_nmse) || raw_nmse < zero_l
        return L(Inf)
    end
    fidelity_term = log1p(raw_nmse)

    # Bounded shape term: normalized residual after the best affine map a*p + b.
    shape_term = zero_l
    if target_is_variable
        if m2_p > prediction_floor
            correlation = covariance / sqrt(m2_p) / sqrt(m2_y)
            if !isfinite(correlation)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            bounded_correlation = min(abs(correlation), one_l)
            shape_term = one_l - bounded_correlation * bounded_correlation
        else
            # A constant prediction can match only the target mean: worst shape.
            shape_term = one_l
        end
    end

    # Continuation: structural guidance is strong far away, vanishes near a fit.
    max_shape_weight = L(0.5)
    shape_weight = max_shape_weight * raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse)

    loss_value = (one_l - shape_weight) * fidelity_term + shape_weight * shape_term
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

relative_aware_shape_log_nmse_loss_simpl.name: relative_aware_shape_log_nmse_loss_simplified_gen8_0
relative_aware_shape_log_nmse_loss_simpl.code:
"""
    relative_aware_shape_log_nmse_loss_simplified_gen8_0(tree, dataset, options)

A streamlined version of the three-term blend (energy-normalized log-MSE +
soft relative error + affine-invariant shape term) that keeps the same three
loss ingredients but removes the two-pass Welford bookkeeping in favor of a
single pass with plain running sums.

Rationale for the simplification:
* The parent computes target moments in a dedicated first pass using Welford's
  algorithm for numerical stability, then a second pass accumulates
  prediction-dependent sums (also partly Welford for `p`). For typical
  regression targets (finite, moderate dynamic range) plain sums
  `Σy, Σy², Σp, Σp², Σyp` are numerically adequate and let everything —
  target energy, target variance, prediction variance, covariance, squared
  error, and the relative term — be computed in *one* sweep, halving the
  number of loop iterations over the dataset.
* The overflow-clamping branch on the relative term's numerator/denominator
  is folded into a single small epsilon added to the denominator; this keeps
  the term bounded without extra branching logic.
* All three loss components (log-compressed normalized MSE, soft symmetric
  relative error, affine-invariant `1 - r²` shape term) are retained with the
  same weights, since removing any of them was found to hurt performance on
  multiplicative/power-law benchmarks (the relative and shape terms are what
  let the search discover factorized skeletons before constant-tuning).
* Exact-zero SSE and non-finite short circuits are preserved for correctness.
"""
function relative_aware_shape_log_nmse_loss_simplified_gen8_0(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    y_vec = dataset.y
    n = length(y_vec)
    if n == 0 || length(prediction) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Single pass: accumulate all raw sums needed for every term at once.
    # (Plain running sums instead of the parent's two-pass Welford scheme.)
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    sum_y = zero(L)
    sum_y2 = zero(L)
    sum_p = zero(L)
    sum_p2 = zero(L)
    sum_yp = zero(L)
    squared_error = zero(L)
    relative_sum = zero(L)

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        y = L(y_vec[i])
        p = L(prediction[i])
        if !isfinite(y) || !isfinite(p)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        sum_y += y
        sum_y2 = muladd(y, y, sum_y2)
        sum_p += p
        sum_p2 = muladd(p, p, sum_p2)
        sum_yp = muladd(y, p, sum_yp)

        residual = p - y
        sq_residual = residual * residual
        squared_error = muladd(residual, residual, squared_error)

        # Soft symmetric relative error, epsilon-stabilized instead of the
        # parent's separate overflow-clamp branch.
        denom = muladd(y, y, muladd(p, p, L(1e-12)))
        relative_sum += sq_residual / denom
    end

    # Preserve an exact zero optimum regardless of other sums.
    if squared_error == zero(L)
        return zero(L)
    end

    if !isfinite(squared_error) || !isfinite(sum_y2) || !isfinite(sum_p2) ||
       !isfinite(sum_yp) || !isfinite(relative_sum)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n_L = L(n)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Term 1: energy-normalized, log-compressed MSE.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    energy_y = sum_y2
    normalizer = energy_y > zero(L) ? energy_y : n_L
    normalized_mse = squared_error / normalizer
    if !isfinite(normalized_mse)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Term 2: mean soft relative error (bounded by construction, ~[0, 2]).
    relative_loss = relative_sum / n_L

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Term 3: affine-invariant shape mismatch, 1 - r², derived algebraically
    # from the raw sums (no need for a dedicated target-only prepass).
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    mean_y = sum_y / n_L
    mean_p = sum_p / n_L
    m2_y = sum_y2 - n_L * mean_y * mean_y
    m2_p = sum_p2 - n_L * mean_p * mean_p
    cov_sum = sum_yp - n_L * mean_y * mean_p

    shape_loss = zero(L)
    if m2_y > zero(L)
        shape_loss = one(L)   # constant predictions explain no target variance
        if m2_p > zero(L)
            correlation = cov_sum / sqrt(m2_p) / sqrt(m2_y)
            if !isfinite(correlation)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            bounded_correlation = min(abs(correlation), one(L))
            shape_loss = one(L) - bounded_correlation * bounded_correlation
        end
    end

    # Direct fidelity stays dominant; the relative term equalizes magnitudes and
    # the shape term supplies pre-constant-tuning guidance.
    loss_value = L(0.55) * log1p(normalized_mse) +
                 L(0.30) * relative_loss +
                 L(0.15) * shape_loss
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
end

epsilon_pareto_clone_purge_survival_gen8.name: epsilon_pareto_clone_purge_survival_gen8_2
epsilon_pareto_clone_purge_survival_gen8.code:
"""
    epsilon_pareto_clone_purge_survival_gen8_2(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

Survival ("who dies") operator designed to fight the two dominant failure modes seen in
long PySR runs: (1) **structural takeover / cloning**, where one lucky motif fills the
population so no alternative skeleton can ever be assembled, and (2) **Pareto bloat**,
where huge expressions that add micro-corrections with negligible loss gain (e.g.
`... - ((x0 - cos(...)) * -0.00015)`) sit on the exact Pareto front and are therefore
immortal under naive front-protection, consuming slots that structural exploration needs.

Core idea: instead of always killing the oldest member, kill the member that is the most
*expendable* under an **ε-Pareto** criterion combined with **clone purging** and a mild
age/size pressure.

Steps:
 1. Collect complexity, (positive, finite-guarded) loss and birth for every member.
 2. ε-dominance: member `i` is considered dominated by `j` if `c[j] <= c[i]` and
    `loss[j] <= loss[i] * (1 + ε)^(c[i] - c[j])`. That is, extra complexity must "pay for
    itself" with a *constant fractional loss reduction per unit of complexity*
    (a constant slope in log-loss vs. complexity space). With ε ≈ 5%, a genuinely better
    structure (2 nodes bigger, 2× lower loss) survives, while a 27-node micro-correction
    chain that only gains 3× is flagged as expendable bloat.
 3. Clone purging: members with identical complexity and (relatively) identical loss are
    near-certain duplicates of the same skeleton; all but the earliest-born one are
    flagged, which directly slows genotypic takeover and preserves the diversity that
    lets crossover/mutation reach a different basin.
 4. Score all admissible indices with a soft priority: clones > ε-dominated bloat >
    ε-dominated > old > large; the global best-loss member and the very newest member are
    strongly protected (offspring need a grace period to be optimized/expanded).
 5. Return the argmax of that score, never returning an index in `exclude_indices`.

Assumptions/heuristics: `member.loss` is comparable across members (same dataset), losses
are non-negative (non-finite losses are treated as maximally bad and purged first), and
ε = 0.05 per complexity unit is a reasonable "worth it" threshold; the exponent is capped
to avoid overflow. When the population is genuinely diverse and non-bloated, no member is
flagged and the score degenerates to age-regularized replacement (the default behaviour).
"""
function epsilon_pareto_clone_purge_survival_gen8_2(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n

    # ---- admissible replacement slots ---------------------------------------------
    allowed = trues(n)
    for i in exclude_indices
        if 1 <= i <= n
            allowed[i] = false
        end
    end
    if !any(allowed)
        # Degenerate case (should not happen): fall back to the first index not excluded.
        for i in 1:n
            if !(i in exclude_indices)
                return i
            end
        end
        return 1
    end

    # ---- gather per-member statistics ---------------------------------------------
    cplx = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    lss = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    births = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        m = pop.members[i]
        cplx[i] = compute_complexity(m, options)
        lv = Float64(m.loss)
        # Guard: non-finite losses are maximally bad; exact zeros get a tiny positive
        # value so that the multiplicative ε-dominance test stays well defined.
        lss[i] = if !isfinite(lv)
            1e300
        elseif lv <= 0.0
            1e-300
        else
            lv
        end
        births[i] = Float64(m.birth)
    end

    maxsize = max(1, options.maxsize)
    min_birth, max_birth = extrema(births)
    birth_span = max(max_birth - min_birth, 1.0)
    best_i = argmin_fast(lss)                      # global best-loss member: protect it
    median_c = sum(cplx) / n                       # cheap "typical size" reference

    # ---- ε-Pareto dominance --------------------------------------------------------
    # ε per unit complexity: extra nodes must buy a constant fractional loss reduction.
    eps_per_c = 0.05
    dominated = falses(n)
    for i in 1:n
        li = lss[i]
        ci = cplx[i]
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue
            cj = cplx[j]
            cj > ci && continue                    # j must not be larger than i
            if cj == ci
                # Same size: strictly lower loss dominates; exact ties broken by age so
                # that only one representative of a duplicate pair stays protected.
                if lss[j] < li || (lss[j] == li && births[j] < births[i])
                    dominated[i] = true
                    break
                end
            else
                # Cap the exponent to avoid overflow on very large size gaps.
                d = min(ci - cj, 100)
                if lss[j] <= li * (1.0 + eps_per_c)^d
                    dominated[i] = true
                    break
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # ---- clone detection (same complexity + relatively identical loss) -------------
    clone = falses(n)
    for i in 2:n
        for j in 1:(i - 1)
            if cplx[i] == cplx[j]
                scale = max(lss[i], lss[j], 1e-300)
                if abs(lss[i] - lss[j]) <= 1e-8 * scale
                    # Keep the earliest-born copy; flag the younger duplicate.
                    if births[i] >= births[j]
                        clone[i] = true
                    else
                        clone[j] = true
                    end
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # ---- expendability score -------------------------------------------------------
    best_score = -Inf
    best_idx = 0
    for i in 1:n
        allowed[i] || continue
        s = 0.0
        # Redundant duplicates are the top purge target: they cost diversity, not accuracy.
        clone[i] && (s += 3.0)
        # ε-dominated members are not paying for their size.
        if dominated[i]
            s += 2.0
            # Extra pressure on ε-dominated members that are also *large* (Pareto bloat).
            if cplx[i] > median_c
                s += 1.5 * (cplx[i] / maxsize)
            end
        end
        # Retain age-regularized flavour: older members are preferred for replacement.
        s += 0.8 * (max_birth - births[i]) / birth_span
        # Very mild size pressure to keep the population from drifting upward.
        s += 0.3 * (cplx[i] / maxsize)
        # Hard protections: never discard the current best-loss member, and give the
        # newest offspring a grace period so it can be mutated/optimized at least once.
        i == best_i && (s -= 100.0)
        births[i] == max_birth && (s -= 5.0)
        # Deterministic, index-based tie-break (keeps behaviour reproducible).
        s += 1e-9 * i
        if s > best_score
            best_score = s
            best_idx = i
        end
    end

    # `best_idx` is guaranteed set because at least one index is allowed.
    return best_idx
end

deterministic_adaptive_tournament_select.name: deterministic_adaptive_tournament_selection_gen8_7
deterministic_adaptive_tournament_select.code:
"""
    deterministic_adaptive_tournament_selection_gen8_7(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Select a parent by sampling one tournament and deterministically choosing its lowest-cost
member. Candidate costs retain the parent's optional frequency-based adaptive parsimony:
members at common complexity levels receive a multiplicative penalty.

The duplicated adjusted-cost branches are merged into one loop, and the geometric
rank lottery controlled by `tournament_selection_p` is removed. Random tournament
sampling still supplies exploration, while always choosing the tournament winner
reduces selection noise and preserves the main diversity mechanism.
"""
function deterministic_adaptive_tournament_selection_gen8_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    sample = StatsBase.sample(
        pop.members,
        options.tournament_selection_n;
        replace=false,
    )

    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, length(sample))
    use_frequency = options.use_frequency_in_tournament
    scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    # Score every candidate through one common path.
    for (i, member) in pairs(sample)
        penalty = one(L)
        if use_frequency
            size = compute_complexity(member, options)
            if 1 <= size <= options.maxsize
                frequency = L(
                    running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size],
                )
                penalty = exp(scaling * frequency)
            end
        end
        adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost * penalty
    end

    # Tournament sampling supplies randomness; the best adjusted candidate wins.
    return copy(sample[argmin_fast(adjusted_costs)])
end

fit_offset_wrap_mutation_gen8_8.name: fit_offset_wrap_mutation_gen8_8
fit_offset_wrap_mutation_gen8_8.code:
"""
    fit_offset_wrap_mutation_gen8_8(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

**Data-aware "offset / driver / pole" wrap.**  This operator synthesizes the two
parents into a single idea: *wrapping a subtree with an additive correction whose
constant is chosen by the data instead of by chance*.

Parent 1 (`add_constant_offset`) wraps a random subtree as `s -> s + c` with a
random `c`; that is cheap and structurally useful (it creates additive terms that
`add_node`/`insert_node` cannot), but the random `c` almost always makes the
expression worse, so the move is wasted most of the time.  Parent 2
(`fit_rational_pole_mutation`) shows how to make such a structural jump *pay off
immediately*: propose the new structure with coefficients obtained in closed form
by (weighted) least squares, verify the actual MSE, and only accept if the gain
justifies the extra nodes.

This mutation applies that recipe to the whole "additive wrap" family, in
increasing order of structural boldness (all linear-in-parameters at the root, so
all solvable in closed form):

1. `p -> p + b`            — `b` = weighted mean residual (the *fitted* version of
   parent 1's random offset; only 2 extra nodes).
2. `p -> p + b*q`          — a fitted additive *term*, where `q` (the "driver") is
   drawn from a handful of the tree's own subtrees, a bare feature, or a random
   product of two features (candidate generation borrowed from parent 2).  `b` is
   the 1-D least-squares projection of the residual onto `q`.
3. `p -> a*p / (1 + b*q)`  — parent 2's rational/pole wrap: `(a,b)` from the 2x2
   weighted normal equations of `y*(1 + b*q) ≈ a*p`, with the pole-safety test
   (the fitted denominator must keep one sign and stay away from 0 on the data).

If none of the root-level fits earns its keep, the operator falls back to a
*local* version of parent 1: pick a random interior subtree `s`, wrap it as
`s + c`, and choose `c` by a short line search (coarse grid scaled by `std(s)`
plus the centering value `-mean(s)`, then one refinement step), scoring the
**full** tree's MSE.  The tree is nonlinear in an interior offset, so a numeric
search replaces the closed form here; the search is run on a strided subsample
when `n` is large and the winner is re-verified on all data.

Acceptance heuristics (shared by every branch): a candidate must reduce the
weighted MSE by at least `1%` per extra node (capped at 50%), must respect
`options.maxsize`, and among accepted candidates the one minimizing
`mse * (1 + 0.02*added_nodes)` is chosen, which biases toward parsimony.  If the
data are unusable (multi-output, `n < 8`, evaluation failure) the operator
degrades gracefully to parent 1's purely random offset, with the random constant
scaled to the residual magnitude.
"""
function fit_offset_wrap_mutation_gen8_8(
    tree::N, dataset, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    ops = options.operators
    binops = ops.binops
    i_add = findfirst(op -> op === (+), binops)
    i_add === nothing && return tree            # cannot express any additive wrap
    i_mul = findfirst(op -> op === (*), binops)
    i_div = findfirst(op -> op === (/), binops)

    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    cur_nodes = count_nodes(tree)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- fallback
    # Parent-1 behaviour: wrap a random node with a random constant offset.
    function random_offset!(scale::Float64)
        cur_nodes + 2 > maxsize && return tree
        node = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
        c = constructorof(N)(T; val=T(randn(rng) * (isfinite(scale) && scale > 0 ? scale : 1.0)))
        wrapped = if rand(rng, Bool)
            constructorof(N)(; op=i_add, children=(copy(node), c))
        else
            constructorof(N)(; op=i_add, children=(c, copy(node)))
        end
        set_node!(node, wrapped)
        return tree
    end

    y = dataset.y
    X = dataset.X
    n = dataset.n
    (y === nothing || n < 8) && return random_offset!(1.0)   # can't fit anything

    w = dataset.weights
    wsum = 0.0
    @inbounds for k in 1:n
        wsum += w === nothing ? 1.0 : Float64(w[k])
    end
    (isfinite(wsum) && wsum > 0) || return tree

    # -------------------------------------------------- current predictions p
    p_raw, ok = eval_tree_array(tree, X, ops)
    (ok && all(isfinite, p_raw)) || return random_offset!(1.0)
    p = Float64.(p_raw)

    base_acc = 0.0
    @inbounds for k in 1:n
        r = Float64(y[k]) - p[k]
        base_acc += (w === nothing ? 1.0 : Float64(w[k])) * r * r
    end
    base_mse = base_acc / wsum
    (isfinite(base_mse) && base_mse > 0) || return tree   # already exact: leave alone
    resid_scale = sqrt(base_mse)

    # Weighted MSE of an arbitrary prediction vector on the full data.
    function wmse_full(pred::Vector{Float64})
        acc = 0.0
        @inbounds for k in 1:n
            v = pred[k]
            isfinite(v) || return Inf
            r = Float64(y[k]) - v
            acc += (w === nothing ? 1.0 : Float64(w[k])) * r * r
        end
        return acc / wsum
    end

    # --------------------------------------------- root-level candidate search
    best_kind = :none            # :const | :lin | :ratio
    best_adj = Inf
    best_q = nothing
    best_a = 1.0
    best_b = 0.0

    # Accept-if-worth-it bookkeeping shared by all root-level candidates.
    function consider!(kind::Symbol, q, a::Float64, b::Float64, pred::Vector{Float64}, added::Int)
        cur_nodes + added > maxsize && return nothing
        mse = wmse_full(pred)
        isfinite(mse) || return nothing
        # demand ~1% relative gain per added node (never more than 50%)
        thresh = base_mse * max(0.5, 1.0 - 0.01 * added)
        mse > thresh && return nothing
        adj = mse * (1.0 + 0.02 * added)     # parsimony-biased ranking
        if adj < best_adj
            best_adj = adj
            best_kind = kind
            best_q = q
            best_a = a
            best_b = b
        end
        return nothing
    end

    # (1) fitted pure offset: b = weighted mean residual  (parent 1, but optimal)
    b0 = 0.0
    @inbounds for k in 1:n
        b0 += (w === nothing ? 1.0 : Float64(w[k])) * (Float64(y[k]) - p[k])
    end
    b0 /= wsum
    if isfinite(b0) && abs(b0) > 1e-10 * max(1.0, resid_scale)
        consider!(:const, nothing, 1.0, b0, p .+ b0, 2)
    end

    # ---- driver candidates q (parent-2 style candidate generation) ----------
    q_cands = N[]
    if i_mul !== nothing
        subs = N[]
        any(tree) do t
            # operator nodes and variable leaves only: constants make useless drivers
            if t.degree > 0 || !t.constant
                push!(subs, t)
            end
            return false                     # visit every node
        end
        for _ in 1:min(length(subs), 4)
            push!(q_cands, subs[rand(rng, 1:length(subs))])
        end
        push!(q_cands, constructorof(N)(T; feature=rand(rng, 1:nfeatures)))
        if nfeatures >= 2
            push!(
                q_cands,
                constructorof(N)(;
                    op=i_mul,
                    children=(
                        constructorof(N)(T; feature=rand(rng, 1:nfeatures)),
                        constructorof(N)(T; feature=rand(rng, 1:nfeatures)),
                    ),
                ),
            )
        end
    end

    for q in q_cands
        qv_raw, qok = eval_tree_array(q, X, ops)
        qok || continue
        all(isfinite, qv_raw) || continue
        qv = Float64.(qv_raw)
        sq = Float64(std(qv))
        (!isfinite(sq) || sq <= 1e-12) && continue     # constant driver ⇒ no structure
        qn = count_nodes(q)

        # (2) fitted additive term:  p + b*q   (1-D weighted LS projection)
        num = 0.0
        den = 0.0
        @inbounds for k in 1:n
            wk = w === nothing ? 1.0 : Float64(w[k])
            num += wk * (Float64(y[k]) - p[k]) * qv[k]
            den += wk * qv[k] * qv[k]
        end
        if isfinite(num) && isfinite(den) && den > 1e-12
            b = num / den
            if isfinite(b) && abs(b) * sq > 1e-8 * max(1.0, resid_scale)
                pred = similar(p)
                @inbounds for k in 1:n
                    pred[k] = p[k] + b * qv[k]
                end
                # nodes: add + mul + b-leaf + q   (mul/b dropped later if b≈1)
                consider!(:lin, q, 1.0, b, pred, 3 + qn)
            end
        end

        # (3) rational / pole wrap:  a*p / (1 + b*q)  (2x2 weighted normal eqns)
        if i_div !== nothing && i_mul !== nothing
            S11 = 0.0; S12 = 0.0; S22 = 0.0; r1 = 0.0; r2 = 0.0
            @inbounds for k in 1:n
                wk = w === nothing ? 1.0 : Float64(w[k])
                yk = Float64(y[k])
                uk = yk * qv[k]                     # column multiplying b
                S11 += wk * uk * uk
                S12 += wk * uk * p[k]
                S22 += wk * p[k] * p[k]
                r1 += wk * uk * yk
                r2 += wk * p[k] * yk
            end
            D = S11 * S22 - S12 * S12
            if isfinite(D) && abs(D) > 1e-12 * max(1.0, S11 * S22)
                b = (S12 * r2 - r1 * S22) / D
                a = (S11 * r2 - r1 * S12) / D
                if isfinite(a) && isfinite(b) && abs(a) > 1e-12 && abs(b) * sq > 1e-6
                    # pole safety: 1 + b*q must keep one sign and stay away from 0
                    dmin = Inf; dmax = -Inf
                    @inbounds for k in 1:n
                        dk = 1.0 + b * qv[k]
                        dmin = min(dmin, dk)
                        dmax = max(dmax, dk)
                    end
                    if !(dmin <= 0.1 && dmax >= -0.1)
                        pred = similar(p)
                        @inbounds for k in 1:n
                            pred[k] = a * p[k] / (1.0 + b * qv[k])
                        end
                        # nodes: div + add + one-leaf + mul + b-leaf + q (+ a*mul)
                        extra_a = abs(a - 1.0) < 1e-3 ? 0 : 2
                        consider!(:ratio, q, a, b, pred, 5 + qn + extra_a)
                    end
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------- build the winning wrap
    if best_kind === :const
        c = constructorof(N)(T; val=T(best_b))
        return constructorof(N)(; op=i_add, children=(tree, c))       # new root!
    elseif best_kind === :lin
        qc = copy(best_q)                                  # q may live inside tree
        term = if abs(best_b - 1.0) < 1e-3
            qc                                             # skip a useless *1
        else
            constructorof(N)(; op=i_mul, children=(constructorof(N)(T; val=T(best_b)), qc))
        end
        return constructorof(N)(; op=i_add, children=(tree, term))    # new root!
    elseif best_kind === :ratio
        qc = copy(best_q)
        bq = constructorof(N)(; op=i_mul, children=(constructorof(N)(T; val=T(best_b)), qc))
        denom = constructorof(N)(; op=i_add, children=(constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T)), bq))
        numer = if abs(best_a - 1.0) < 1e-3
            tree
        else
            constructorof(N)(; op=i_mul, children=(constructorof(N)(T; val=T(best_a)), tree))
        end
        return constructorof(N)(; op=i_div, children=(numer, denom))  # new root!
    end

    # ------------------------- local branch: fitted offset on interior subtree
    # (parent 1's move, but with the constant chosen by a short line search)
    cur_nodes + 2 > maxsize && return tree
    has_target = any(t -> (t.degree > 0 || !t.constant), tree)
    has_target || return random_offset!(resid_scale)

    node = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> (t.degree > 0 || !t.constant)))

    sv_raw, sok = eval_tree_array(node, X, ops)
    (sok && all(isfinite, sv_raw)) || return random_offset!(resid_scale)
    sv = Float64.(sv_raw)
    sc = Float64(std(sv))
    if !isfinite(sc) || sc <= 1e-8
        sc = max(1e-3, Float64(mean(abs.(sv))))
    end
    isfinite(sc) || return random_offset!(resid_scale)
    smean = Float64(mean(sv))

    # Splice in `node + c` with a mutable constant leaf we can retune in place.
    restore = copy(node)                     # for rollback
    orig = copy(node)                        # becomes the child of the wrap
    cleaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=zero(T))
    set_node!(node, constructorof(N)(; op=i_add, children=(orig, cleaf)))
    cref = get_child(node, 2)                # the tunable constant

    # Score on a strided subsample when n is large; verify the winner on all data.
    step = max(1, cld(n, 128))
    cols = 1:step:n
    Xs = step == 1 ? X : view(X, :, cols)
    function score(c::Float64)
        cref.val = T(c)
        pv, pok = eval_tree_array(tree, Xs, ops)
        pok || return Inf
        acc = 0.0; sw = 0.0
        @inbounds for (j, k) in enumerate(cols)
            v = Float64(pv[j])
            isfinite(v) || return Inf
            wk = w === nothing ? 1.0 : Float64(w[k])
            r = Float64(y[k]) - v
            acc += wk * r * r
            sw += wk
        end
        return sw > 0 ? acc / sw : Inf
    end

    # coarse grid: multiples of the subtree's own spread, plus a centering shift
    grid = Float64[-2sc, -sc, -0.5sc, -0.25sc, 0.25sc, 0.5sc, sc, 2sc, -smean]
    best_c = 0.0
    best_s = score(0.0)                      # baseline (offset 0 ≈ current tree)
    for c in grid
        isfinite(c) || continue
        s = score(c)
        if s < best_s
            best_s = s
            best_c = c
        end
    end
    # one refinement step around the winner
    if best_c != 0.0
        for c in (best_c - 0.35 * sc, best_c + 0.35 * sc)
            s = score(c)
            if s < best_s
                best_s = s
                best_c = c
            end
        end
    end

    if best_c == 0.0 || !isfinite(best_s)
        set_node!(node, restore)             # nothing found: undo the wrap
        return random_offset!(resid_scale)
    end

    # Final verification on the *full* data set with the same 2-node threshold.
    cref.val = T(best_c)
    pf, pok = eval_tree_array(tree, X, ops)
    if !pok
        set_node!(node, restore)
        return random_offset!(resid_scale)
    end
    mse_full = wmse_full(Float64.(pf))
    if !isfinite(mse_full) || mse_full > 0.98 * base_mse
        set_node!(node, restore)
        return random_offset!(resid_scale)
    end

    return tree
end

age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen9_3.name: age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen9_3
age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen9_3.code:
"""
age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen9_3

Since both parent operators are identical pure age-regularized survival
strategies (replace the oldest member), the synthesis here goes beyond
concatenation: it preserves the core age-regularization principle (older
members are preferred for replacement, ensuring diversity and turnover)
but adds a cost-aware tiebreak/selection refinement to avoid prematurely
discarding old-but-excellent members and to bias replacement toward
old members that are also relatively poor performers.

Steps:
1. Compute birth times for all non-excluded members (excluded members get
   an effectively infinite birth so they're never chosen).
2. Identify the "oldest quartile" (or at least the single oldest if pop is
   small) of non-excluded members by birth time — this respects the
   original age-regularization heuristic that old members should cycle out.
3. Among that oldest-quartile candidate set, break ties/select using cost
   (higher cost = worse fit) so that if multiple old members exist, we
   preferentially replace the worst-performing one rather than blindly
   picking the single oldest, protecting old-but-high-quality solutions
   from unnecessary replacement.
4. Fall back to pure oldest-birth logic if the candidate set is degenerate
   (e.g., only one eligible member remains).
"""
function age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen9_3(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)
    n = pop.n

    # Step 1: gather births, excluding forbidden indices via sentinel value
    births = [(i in exclude_indices) ? typemax(BT) : pop.members[i].birth for i in 1:n]

    # Collect indices that are actually eligible (not excluded)
    eligible = [i for i in 1:n if !(i in exclude_indices)]

    if isempty(eligible)
        # Degenerate case: nothing eligible, just return argmin over births
        # (will point at an excluded slot only if all are excluded, which
        # should not normally happen given caller contract).
        return argmin_fast(births)
    end

    if length(eligible) == 1
        # Only one candidate: no tiebreak needed, must replace it
        return eligible[1]
    end

    # Step 2: determine the "oldest quartile" cutoff among eligible members
    sorted_births = sort(births[eligible])
    quartile_size = max(1, ceil(Int, length(eligible) / 4))
    cutoff_birth = sorted_births[quartile_size]

    # Candidate pool: eligible members whose birth is <= cutoff (i.e., among
    # the oldest ~25% of the population)
    candidates = [i for i in eligible if births[i] <= cutoff_birth]

    if length(candidates) == 1
        # Unambiguous oldest member, mirrors pure age-regularized behavior
        return candidates[1]
    end

    # Step 3: among old candidates, pick the one with worst (highest) cost,
    # so that we preferentially cull weak old solutions rather than
    # arbitrarily replacing a possibly-excellent old member.
    costs = [pop.members[i].cost for i in candidates]
    worst_idx_in_candidates = argmax(costs)

    return candidates[worst_idx_in_candidates]
end

symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_6.name: symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_6
symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_6.code:
"""
    symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_6(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

A streamlined structural mutation operator that duplicates subexpression motifs and couples
them into the expression tree with optional cyclic feature-space shifts.

# Core Idea
Physical laws and mathematical models frequently feature repeated functional forms across different
variables or dimensions (e.g., kinetic energy `0.5*m*(vx^2 + vy^2)` or distances `(x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2`).
This operator extracts an evolved subtree motif, optionally cyclically shifts its feature indices to
replicate functional structures across variables, and couples it with a target node via a binary operator.

# Steps
1. Return early if no binary operators are configured.
2. Sample a donor subtree and deep-copy it into an independent motif.
3. If `nfeatures > 1`, select a cyclic shift `shift ∈ 0:(nfeatures - 1)` and shift all variable leaves
   in the motif. A shift of 0 keeps variables identical for powers/rational self-couplings.
4. Select a target node in the tree and wrap it with the motif under a random binary operator.

# Simplifications from Parent
- Unified three distinct feature transformation paths (cyclic permutation, targeted substitution,
  and identity mapping) into a single cyclic shift offset (`shift ∈ 0:(nfeatures - 1)`). This eliminates
  the need for `_collect_features!`, `_remap_feature!`, and multi-way branch logic.
- Removed homologous grafting heuristics and unary fallback logic in favor of direct, uniform
  binary operator coupling, streamlining code paths while maintaining modular symmetry discovery.
"""
function symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_6(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Guard: binary coupling requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # Helper: cyclically permute feature indices in the motif leaves
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int, num_features::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, num_features)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift, num_features)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Step 1: Sample a donor subtree motif and duplicate it
    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    motif = copy(donor)

    # Step 2: Apply cyclic feature transformation (shift == 0 preserves features for self-coupling)
    if nfeatures > 1
        shift = rand(rng, 0:(nfeatures - 1))
        if shift > 0
            _shift_features!(motif, shift, nfeatures)
        end
    end

    # Step 3: Couple target node with the transformed motif under a random binary operator
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    target_copy = copy(target)
    bin_op = rand(rng, 1:options.nops[2])

    # Randomize operand ordering to support non-commutative operators
    children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
    new_node = constructorof(N)(;
        op=bin_op,
        children=children,
    )
    set_node!(target, new_node)

    return tree
end

residual_guided_basis_augmentation_gen9_.name: residual_guided_basis_augmentation_gen9_8
residual_guided_basis_augmentation_gen9_.code:
"""
    residual_guided_basis_augmentation_gen9_8(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

A data-aware "boosting" mutation: it looks at what the current expression gets *wrong*
and appends the single basis function that best explains the leftover error, with its
coefficient fitted by least squares on the training data.

Steps:
1. Evaluate the tree on (a strided subsample of) `dataset.X`. If evaluation fails or
   produces non-finite values, switch to a **repair** branch: locate the *smallest*
   subtree that itself evaluates to NaN/Inf on the data and replace it with a benign
   constant leaf (`avg_y` or `1`). This removes the numerically-broken part of the tree
   while keeping the rest of the (potentially useful) structure.
2. Otherwise compute the residual `r = y - ŷ`. If the residual is already negligible
   compared to `std(y)`, there is nothing to gain and the tree is returned unchanged.
3. Build a small library of candidate basis functions and score each by `|cor(basis, r)|`:
   (a) every raw feature `x_f`; (b) each unary operator applied to the few
   most residual-correlated features (`g(x_f)`); (c) products `x_f * x_g` among those
   same top features (including squares). Restricting (b)/(c) to the top features keeps
   the cost O(nfeatures · n) even with hundreds of features.
4. Pick a candidate *stochastically* from the top-3 scorers (probability ∝ score) so the
   operator stays exploratory rather than greedy/deterministic, then fit
   `r ≈ c·basis + b` by (centered) least squares. `c` is snapped to a nearby integer when
   it is close, which helps recover exact ground-truth coefficients.
5. Return `tree + c·basis` (plus the intercept `b` if it is non-negligible and the size
   budget allows). Requires `+` in the operator set; `*` is used for the coefficient when
   available, otherwise the basis is added unscaled.

Assumptions/heuristics: correlation with the residual is a cheap proxy for "which term is
missing"; a least-squares coefficient on a subsample generalizes; the extra complexity is
justified only if the parent search accepts it (the normal selection pressure decides).
Sample weights are ignored for simplicity.
"""
function residual_guided_basis_augmentation_gen9_8(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # ---- basic guards -------------------------------------------------------
    dataset.y === nothing && return tree
    n = dataset.n
    n < 5 && return tree
    nfeatures < 1 && return tree

    # Subsample columns (samples) for speed; keep a strided view of the data.
    max_pts = 512
    if n <= max_pts
        Xs = dataset.X
        ys = dataset.y
    else
        idx = round.(Int, range(1, n; length=max_pts))
        Xs = dataset.X[:, idx]
        ys = dataset.y[idx]
    end
    ns = length(ys)

    # ---- 1. evaluate current tree ------------------------------------------
    pred, ok = eval_tree_array(tree, Xs, options.operators)

    if !ok || any(!isfinite, pred)
        # ---- REPAIR BRANCH: excise the smallest NaN/Inf-producing subtree ----
        worst = Ref{Any}(nothing)
        worst_size = Ref(typemax(Int))
        any(tree) do t
            if t.degree > 0
                sub, sok = eval_tree_array(t, Xs, options.operators)
                if !sok || any(!isfinite, sub)
                    sz = count_nodes(t)
                    if sz < worst_size[]
                        worst_size[] = sz
                        worst[] = t
                    end
                end
            end
            return false  # never short-circuit: visit every node
        end
        bad = worst[]
        bad === nothing && return tree
        # Replace the offending subtree with a harmless constant (mean of y, or 1).
        safe_val = dataset.avg_y === nothing ? one(T) : T(dataset.avg_y)
        repl = constructorof(N)(T; val=safe_val)
        if bad === tree
            return repl  # the whole tree was broken -> new root
        else
            set_node!(bad, repl)
            return tree
        end
    end

    # ---- 2. residual --------------------------------------------------------
    y64 = Float64.(ys)
    r64 = y64 .- Float64.(pred)
    sy = std(y64)
    sr = std(r64)
    (isfinite(sr) && sr > 1e-10 * max(1.0, abs(mean(y64)))) || return tree
    # Already essentially perfect on this subsample: nothing to add.
    (sy > 0 && sr < 1e-6 * sy) && return tree

    # Operator indices we need.
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), options.operators.binops)
    plus_idx === nothing && return tree            # cannot append a term without `+`
    mul_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (*), options.operators.binops)
    n_una = options.nops[1]

    # Size budget (do not blow past maxsize).
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : 30
    base_size = count_nodes(tree)
    base_size + 4 > maxsize && return tree

    # ---- 3. candidate library, scored by |cor(basis, residual)| -------------
    # kinds: 1 = raw feature, 2 = unary(feature), 3 = feature * feature
    kinds = Int[]
    f1s = Int[]
    f2s = Int[]
    uops = Int[]
    vals = Vector{Vector{Float64}}()
    scores = Float64[]
