    function push_candidate!(kind, f1, f2, uop, v)
        # Reject non-finite or constant candidate columns; else score by |cor|.
        all(isfinite, v) || return nothing
        sv = std(v)
        (isfinite(sv) && sv > 1e-12) || return nothing
        c = cor(v, r64)
        isfinite(c) || return nothing
        push!(kinds, kind); push!(f1s, f1); push!(f2s, f2); push!(uops, uop)
        push!(vals, v); push!(scores, abs(c))
        return nothing
    end

    # (a) raw features
    for f in 1:nfeatures
        push_candidate!(1, f, 0, 0, Float64.(@view Xs[f, :]))
    end
    isempty(scores) && return tree

    # Top few features (by |cor| with residual) get nonlinear expansion.
    raw_order = sortperm(scores; rev=true)
    ntop = min(4, length(raw_order))
    topf = [f1s[i] for i in raw_order[1:ntop]]

    # (b) unary transforms of the top features
    for f in topf, k in 1:n_una
        g = options.operators.unaops[k]
        v = try
            Float64.(g.(@view Xs[f, :]))
        catch
            continue
        end
        push_candidate!(2, f, 0, k, v)
    end

    # (c) pairwise products (and squares) among the top features
    if mul_idx !== nothing
        for i in 1:ntop, j in i:ntop
            fa, fb = topf[i], topf[j]
            v = Float64.(@view Xs[fa, :]) .* Float64.(@view Xs[fb, :])
            push_candidate!(3, fa, fb, 0, v)
        end
    end

    # ---- 4. stochastic pick among the top-3 candidates ---------------------
    order = sortperm(scores; rev=true)
    K = min(3, length(order))
    top = order[1:K]
    wsum = sum(scores[i] for i in top)
    pick = top[1]
    if wsum > 0
        u = rand(rng) * wsum
        acc = 0.0
        for i in top
            acc += scores[i]
            if u <= acc
                pick = i
                break
            end
        end
    end
    v = vals[pick]

    # Least-squares fit of r ≈ c * v + b (centered, numerically safe).
    mv = mean(v)
    mr = mean(r64)
    vc = v .- mv
    denom = sum(abs2, vc)
    denom > 1e-14 || return tree
    c = sum(vc .* (r64 .- mr)) / denom
    b = mr - c * mv
    (isfinite(c) && isfinite(b)) || return tree
    abs(c) > 1e-12 || return tree
    # Snap near-integer coefficients (helps hit exact ground-truth constants).
    if abs(c - round(c)) < 0.02 * max(1.0, abs(c))
        c = round(c)
    end

    # ---- 5. assemble  tree + c*basis (+ b) ---------------------------------
    kind = kinds[pick]
    basis = if kind == 1
        constructorof(N)(T; feature=f1s[pick])
    elseif kind == 2
        constructorof(N)(;
            op=uops[pick], children=(constructorof(N)(T; feature=f1s[pick]),)
        )
    else
        constructorof(N)(;
            op=mul_idx,
            children=(
                constructorof(N)(T; feature=f1s[pick]),
                constructorof(N)(T; feature=f2s[pick]),
            ),
        )
    end

    term = if mul_idx !== nothing && !(isapprox(c, 1.0; atol=1e-8))
        # scale the basis by the fitted coefficient
        constructorof(N)(;
            op=mul_idx, children=(constructorof(N)(T; val=T(c)), basis)
        )
    else
        basis  # no `*` operator available (or coefficient ≈ 1): add unscaled
    end

    newroot = constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(tree, term))

    # Optionally add the intercept if it matters and we still have size budget.
    added = count_nodes(term) + 1
    if abs(b) > 0.05 * sr && base_size + added + 2 <= maxsize
        newroot = constructorof(N)(;
            op=plus_idx, children=(newroot, constructorof(N)(T; val=T(b)))
        )
    end

    return newroot  # new root!
end

adaptive_pareto_efficiency_rank_tourname.name: adaptive_pareto_efficiency_rank_tournament_selection_gen9_7
adaptive_pareto_efficiency_rank_tourname.code:
"""
Select a parent with an adaptive-parsimony tournament reranked by Pareto
efficiency and lineage-aware diversity.

The operator first applies the standard frequency-adjusted cost heuristic, then
evaluates each sampled member by adjusted-cost rank, raw-loss rank, and its
number of loss-complexity Pareto dominators. Candidates receive an additional
bonus when they deliver a substantial loss improvement over every simpler
sampled expression; this bonus is discounted across large complexity jumps so
tiny improvements from bloated formulas are not mistaken for useful frontier
breakthroughs. Crowded complexity niches and closely related lineages receive
small penalties, while recent individuals receive brief protection. Finally,
the resulting priorities are sampled with the standard geometric tournament
rank distribution, preserving the familiar meaning of `tournament_selection_p`.
The heuristic assumes lower loss and cost are preferable, costs are normally
nonnegative, and efficient frontier improvements are promising stepping stones
toward compact ground-truth expressions.
"""
function adaptive_pareto_efficiency_rank_tournament_selection_gen9_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    tournament_size = min(pop.n, max(1, options.tournament_selection_n))
    sample = StatsBase.sample(
        pop.members,
        tournament_size;
        replace=false,
    )
    n = length(sample)

    n == 1 && return sample[1]

    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    frequencies = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)

    raw_parsimony_scale = Float64(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    parsimony_scale = isfinite(raw_parsimony_scale) ?
        max(0.0, raw_parsimony_scale) : 0.0

    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]

        raw_loss = Float64(member.loss)
        raw_cost = Float64(member.cost)
        losses[i] = isfinite(raw_loss) ? raw_loss : Inf
        costs[i] = isfinite(raw_cost) ? raw_cost : Inf

        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size

        frequency = if 0 < size <= options.maxsize &&
                       size <= length(
                           running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies,
                       )
            Float64(
                running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size],
            )
        else
            0.0
        end
        frequencies[i] = isfinite(frequency) ? max(0.0, frequency) : 0.0

        # Reproduce adaptive parsimony while preventing numerical overflow from
        # making an otherwise valid tournament computation fail.
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament && isfinite(costs[i])
            exponent = clamp(
                parsimony_scale * frequencies[i],
                0.0,
                700.0,
            )
            adjusted = costs[i] * exp(exponent)
            adjusted_costs[i] = isfinite(adjusted) ? adjusted : Inf
        else
            adjusted_costs[i] = costs[i]
        end
    end

    loss_ranks = zeros(Int, n)
    adjusted_cost_ranks = zeros(Int, n)
    domination_counts = zeros(Int, n)
    niche_counts = ones(Int, n)
    lineage_counts = ones(Int, n)

    for i in 1:n
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue

            loss_ranks[i] += losses[j] < losses[i]
            adjusted_cost_ranks[i] += adjusted_costs[j] < adjusted_costs[i]
            niche_counts[i] += complexities[j] == complexities[i]

            # Pareto dominance uses raw predictive quality and expression size,
            # independently of the regularized cost used by the base tournament.
            no_worse = losses[j] <= losses[i] &&
                       complexities[j] <= complexities[i]
            strictly_better = losses[j] < losses[i] ||
                              complexities[j] < complexities[i]
            domination_counts[i] += no_worse && strictly_better

            same_parent = sample[i].parent > 0 &&
                          sample[i].parent == sample[j].parent
            direct_relative = (
                sample[i].ref > 0 &&
                sample[j].parent == sample[i].ref
            ) || (
                sample[j].ref > 0 &&
                sample[i].parent == sample[j].ref
            )

            if same_parent || direct_relative
                lineage_counts[i] += 1
            end
        end
    end

    # Reward accuracy breakthroughs, but discount gains requiring a large jump
    # in complexity. The raw-gain component still permits multi-node structural
    # innovations when their improvement is genuinely substantial.
    breakthrough_efficiencies = zeros(Float64, n)
    for i in 1:n
        best_simpler_loss = Inf
        best_simpler_complexity = 0

        for j in 1:n
            if complexities[j] < complexities[i]
                if losses[j] < best_simpler_loss
                    best_simpler_loss = losses[j]
                    best_simpler_complexity = complexities[j]
                elseif losses[j] == best_simpler_loss &&
                       complexities[j] > best_simpler_complexity
                    best_simpler_complexity = complexities[j]
                end
            end
        end

        if isfinite(best_simpler_loss) &&
           isfinite(losses[i]) &&
           losses[i] < best_simpler_loss
            scale = max(
                abs(best_simpler_loss) + abs(losses[i]),
                eps(Float64),
            )
            relative_gain = clamp(
                (best_simpler_loss - losses[i]) / scale,
                0.0,
                1.0,
            )
            complexity_jump = max(
                1,
                complexities[i] - best_simpler_complexity,
            )

            breakthrough_efficiencies[i] = relative_gain * (
                0.5 + 0.5 / sqrt(Float64(complexity_jump))
            )
        end
    end

    min_birth = minimum(member.birth for member in sample)
    max_birth = maximum(member.birth for member in sample)
    birth_span = max_birth - min_birth
    rank_denominator = Float64(max(1, n - 1))

    priorities = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        adjusted_cost_rank =
            Float64(adjusted_cost_ranks[i]) / rank_denominator
        loss_rank = Float64(loss_ranks[i]) / rank_denominator
        domination = Float64(domination_counts[i]) / rank_denominator
        niche_crowding =
            Float64(niche_counts[i] - 1) / rank_denominator
        lineage_crowding =
            Float64(lineage_counts[i] - 1) / rank_denominator

        recency = birth_span > 0 ?
            Float64(sample[i].birth - min_birth) / Float64(birth_span) :
            0.5

        # Lower priority is better. Adaptive cost remains the main signal;
        # Pareto quality and efficient breakthroughs refine its ordering.
        priority = 0.55 * adjusted_cost_rank +
                   0.20 * loss_rank +
                   0.25 * domination -
                   0.35 * breakthrough_efficiencies[i] +
                   0.06 * niche_crowding +
                   0.05 * lineage_crowding -
                   0.03 * recency

        # Failed objective evaluations should never benefit from tied ranks.
        !isfinite(losses[i]) && (priority += 2.0)
        !isfinite(adjusted_costs[i]) && (priority += 2.0)

        priorities[i] = priority
    end

    ordered_indices = sortperm(priorities)

    raw_p = Float64(options.tournament_selection_p)
    p = isfinite(raw_p) ? clamp(raw_p, 0.0, 1.0) : 1.0

    chosen_rank = if p >= 1.0
        1
    elseif p <= 0.0
        StatsBase.sample(1:n)
    else
        # The common factor `p` cancels during normalization, leaving a stable
        # truncated geometric distribution over the synthesized ranking.
        q = 1.0 - p
        rank_weights = q .^ collect(0:(n - 1))
        StatsBase.sample(
            StatsBase.Weights(rank_weights, sum(rank_weights)),
        )
    end

    return sample[ordered_indices[chosen_rank]]
end

relative_scale_invariant_loss_gen9_0.name: relative_scale_invariant_loss_gen9_0
relative_scale_invariant_loss_gen9_0.code:
"""
Scale-invariant relative squared error loss.

Many symbolic-regression benchmarks (e.g. Feynman equations) produce targets whose
magnitude spans several orders of magnitude across the training set (products/quotients
of physical constants, squares, exponentials, etc.). Ordinary MSE is dominated by the
few largest-magnitude samples, so the search effectively ignores the shape of the
expression over low-magnitude regions and gets stuck fitting only the "big" values —
exactly the pathology visible in Pareto fronts that plateau with structurally wrong
low-complexity candidates before eventually discovering divisive/multiplicative structure.

This loss instead measures *relative* squared error: each residual is divided by an
estimate of the local target scale (|y|), so errors of similar relative size are
weighted similarly regardless of the absolute magnitude of y at that point. To avoid
blow-up when y is near zero (common with signed physical quantities that cross zero),
a small adaptive floor derived from the mean absolute value of y across the dataset is
added to the denominator. This keeps the computation just as cheap as MSE (a single
pass, elementwise ops) while making the fitness landscape much more informative for
targets with wide dynamic range.

Heuristics/assumptions:
  - Uses mean(|y|) as a robust, cheap-to-compute proxy for the "typical" scale of the
    dataset, then uses a small fraction of it (plus a tiny absolute constant) as a floor
    to regularize the denominator near y ≈ 0.
  - Falls back to `L(Inf)` on any evaluation failure, consistent with other losses.
"""
function relative_scale_invariant_loss_gen9_0(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    y = dataset.y
    n = dataset.n

    # Estimate the typical magnitude of the target to build an adaptive floor.
    # This prevents the relative error from exploding when y crosses/approaches zero.
    mean_abs_y = sum(abs, y) / n
    floor_scale = L(1e-3) * max(mean_abs_y, L(1e-6)) + L(1e-12)
    eps2 = floor_scale * floor_scale

    # Accumulate relative squared error: (pred - y)^2 / (y^2 + eps^2)
    total = zero(L)
    @inbounds for i in eachindex(y, prediction)
        diff = prediction[i] - y[i]
        denom = y[i] * y[i] + eps2
        total += (diff * diff) / denom
    end

    return L(total / n)
end

residual_basis_graft_mutation_gen9_1.name: residual_basis_graft_mutation_gen9_1
residual_basis_graft_mutation_gen9_1.code:
"""
    residual_basis_graft_mutation_gen9_1(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

Fit a compact, data-driven correction to the current expression's residuals. The
mutation searches a randomized subset of features and tests three representable
basis functions: `x_j`, `x_j^2`, and `tree(x) * x_j`. For each basis it performs
weighted least squares with an intercept, then selects the correction with the
largest complexity-adjusted reduction in residual sum of squares.

The selected term is grafted onto the expression using only `+` and `*`.
Interaction corrections are factored as `tree * (1 + a*x_j) + b` to avoid
duplicating the original tree. Invalid observations, nonpositive weights, nearly
constant bases, nonfinite coefficients, and numerically negligible improvements
are ignored.
"""
function residual_basis_graft_mutation_gen9_1(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    y = dataset.y
    y === nothing && return tree

    # This mutation needs representable affine corrections.
    add_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), options.operators.binops)
    mul_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (*), options.operators.binops)
    (add_idx === nothing || mul_idx === nothing) && return tree

    y_pred, ok = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options.operators)
    ok || return tree

    usable_features = min(nfeatures, dataset.nfeatures, size(dataset.X, 1))
    usable_features == 0 && return tree

    nobs = min(dataset.n, length(y), length(y_pred), size(dataset.X, 2))
    if dataset.weights !== nothing
        nobs = min(nobs, length(dataset.weights))
    end
    nobs < 2 && return tree

    # Cache observations on which the current expression and target are valid.
    valid_indices = Int[]
    residuals = Float64[]
    predictions = Float64[]
    observation_weights = Float64[]

    total_weight = 0.0
    weighted_residual_sum = 0.0
    baseline_sse = 0.0

    for i in 1:nobs
        yi = Float64(y[i])
        pi = Float64(y_pred[i])
        wi = dataset.weights === nothing ? 1.0 : Float64(dataset.weights[i])

        if isfinite(yi) && isfinite(pi) && isfinite(wi) && wi > 0.0
            ri = yi - pi
            isfinite(ri) || continue

            push!(valid_indices, i)
            push!(residuals, ri)
            push!(predictions, pi)
            push!(observation_weights, wi)

            total_weight += wi
            weighted_residual_sum += wi * ri
            baseline_sse += wi * ri * ri
        end
    end

    length(valid_indices) < 2 && return tree
    if !(isfinite(total_weight) && total_weight > 0.0 &&
         isfinite(baseline_sse) && baseline_sse > 0.0)
        return tree
    end

    mean_residual = weighted_residual_sum / total_weight

    # A pure intercept correction is the fallback candidate.
    intercept_gain = weighted_residual_sum^2 / total_weight
    best_kind = 0
    best_feature = 0
    best_slope = 0.0
    best_intercept = mean_residual
    best_gain = intercept_gain
    best_score = intercept_gain / 1.04

    # Reservoir sampling bounds mutation cost on very wide datasets while
    # allowing every feature to participate over repeated mutations.
    max_examined_features = 32
    if usable_features <= max_examined_features
        feature_indices = collect(1:usable_features)
    else
        feature_indices = collect(1:max_examined_features)
        for j in (max_examined_features + 1):usable_features
            replacement_index = rand(rng, 1:j)
            if replacement_index <= max_examined_features
                feature_indices[replacement_index] = j
            end
        end
    end

    for feature_index in feature_indices
        # kind 1: x_j; kind 2: x_j^2; kind 3: prediction * x_j.
        for kind in 1:3
            weighted_z_sum = 0.0
            weighted_z2_sum = 0.0
            candidate_valid = true

            for q in eachindex(valid_indices)
                i = valid_indices[q]
                x = Float64(dataset.X[feature_index, i])
                if !isfinite(x)
                    candidate_valid = false
                    break
                end

                z = if kind == 1
                    x
                elseif kind == 2
                    x * x
                else
                    predictions[q] * x
                end

                if !isfinite(z)
                    candidate_valid = false
                    break
                end

                w = observation_weights[q]
                weighted_z_sum += w * z
                weighted_z2_sum += w * z * z
            end

            candidate_valid || continue
            if !(isfinite(weighted_z_sum) && isfinite(weighted_z2_sum))
                continue
            end

            mean_z = weighted_z_sum / total_weight
            centered_z2 = 0.0
            centered_zr = 0.0

            for q in eachindex(valid_indices)
                i = valid_indices[q]
                x = Float64(dataset.X[feature_index, i])
                z = if kind == 1
                    x
                elseif kind == 2
                    x * x
                else
                    predictions[q] * x
                end

                dz = z - mean_z
                dr = residuals[q] - mean_residual
                w = observation_weights[q]
                centered_z2 += w * dz * dz
                centered_zr += w * dz * dr
            end

            # Reject numerically constant bases rather than creating huge constants.
            variance_floor = 64.0 * eps(Float64) *
                             max(weighted_z2_sum, floatmin(Float64))
            if !(isfinite(centered_z2) && isfinite(centered_zr) &&
                 centered_z2 > variance_floor)
                continue
            end

            slope = centered_zr / centered_z2
            intercept = mean_residual - slope * mean_z
            slope_gain = centered_zr^2 / centered_z2
            gain = intercept_gain + slope_gain

            if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept) && isfinite(gain))
                continue
            end

            # Slightly prefer structurally cheaper residual explanations.
            added_cost = kind == 1 ? 3.0 : 4.0
            score = gain / (1.0 + 0.04 * added_cost)

            if score > best_score
                best_kind = kind
                best_feature = feature_index
                best_slope = slope
                best_intercept = intercept
                best_gain = gain
                best_score = score
            end
        end
    end

    # Do not graft corrections explained only by floating-point noise.
    improvement_floor = 1.0e-10 * max(baseline_sse, floatmin(Float64))
    best_gain > improvement_floor || return tree

    slope_t = T(best_slope)
    intercept_t = T(best_intercept)
    if !(isfinite(slope_t) && isfinite(intercept_t))
        return tree
    end

    make_constant(value) = constructorof(N)(T; val=value)
    make_feature(index) = constructorof(N)(T; feature=index)
    make_binary(op, left, right) =
        constructorof(N)(; op=op, children=(left, right))

    # If the selected slope underflows in T, retain only the fitted mean shift.
    if best_kind == 0 || slope_t == zero(T)
        intercept_t == zero(T) && return tree
        return make_binary(add_idx, tree, make_constant(intercept_t))
    end

    feature_node = make_feature(best_feature)

    corrected_tree = if best_kind == 1
        # tree + a*x_j
        scaled_feature = make_binary(
            mul_idx,
            make_constant(slope_t),
            feature_node,
        )
        make_binary(add_idx, tree, scaled_feature)
    elseif best_kind == 2
        # tree + a*x_j^2
        squared_feature = make_binary(
            mul_idx,
            feature_node,
            make_feature(best_feature),
        )
        scaled_square = make_binary(
            mul_idx,
            make_constant(slope_t),
            squared_feature,
        )
        make_binary(add_idx, tree, scaled_square)
    else
        # tree + a*tree*x_j, factored to avoid duplicating the original tree.
        scaled_feature = make_binary(
            mul_idx,
            make_constant(slope_t),
            feature_node,
        )
        multiplicative_factor = make_binary(
            add_idx,
            make_constant(one(T)),
            scaled_feature,
        )
        make_binary(mul_idx, tree, multiplicative_factor)
    end

    # Preserve the jointly fitted intercept unless it rounds exactly to zero.
    if intercept_t != zero(T)
        corrected_tree = make_binary(
            add_idx,
            corrected_tree,
            make_constant(intercept_t),
        )
    end

    return corrected_tree
end

age_and_quality_regularized_survival_gen.name: age_and_quality_regularized_survival_gen9_2
age_and_quality_regularized_survival_gen.code:
"""
Age-regularized survival with a quality-aware tie-break.

Both parents implement identical pure age-regularized survival: always
replace the globally oldest population member. This is robust for
diversity/exploration, but it can occasionally evict an old-but-excellent
solution just because a slightly younger member happens to be worse,
letting weak members linger in the population and slowing convergence
(visible in the trace as long plateaus on the Pareto front before jumps
to lower-loss expressions).

This operator synthesizes the two identical parents into a refined
strategy: we still enforce age-regularization (so the population keeps
turning over and doesn't stagnate on stale genotypes), but instead of
blindly picking the single oldest member, we first gather a pool of the
oldest members (e.g. the oldest ~25% of eligible members) and then, within
that pool, replace the one with the *worst* cost. This preserves the
turnover/diversity benefits of age-regularization while sparing old but
high-quality solutions from being discarded prematurely, giving weaker
old members priority for replacement.

`exclude_indices` is respected by never including those indices in the
eligible pool.
"""
function age_and_quality_regularized_survival_gen9_2(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    # Build the set of indices eligible for replacement (i.e. not excluded).
    valid_indices = [i for i in 1:n if !(i in exclude_indices)]

    # Fallback: if somehow everything is excluded (shouldn't normally happen),
    # just defer to the plain age-regularized rule as a safe default.
    if isempty(valid_indices)
        BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)
        births = [(i in exclude_indices) ? typemax(BT) : pop.members[i].birth
                   for i in 1:n]
        return argmin_fast(births)
    end

    # Sort eligible indices by birth (ascending: oldest first).
    sorted_by_age = sort(valid_indices; by=i -> pop.members[i].birth)

    # Take the oldest quartile (at least 1 member) as the replacement pool.
    # This keeps the age-regularization pressure (turnover among old members)
    # while allowing quality to decide who exactly gets replaced.
    pool_size = max(1, ceil(Int, length(sorted_by_age) * 0.25))
    oldest_pool = sorted_by_age[1:pool_size]

    # Within the oldest pool, replace the member with the highest (worst) cost,
    # sparing old-but-good solutions and prioritizing weak old members.
    costs = [pop.members[i].cost for i in oldest_pool]
    worst_local_idx = argmax(costs)

    return oldest_pool[worst_local_idx]
end

tail_aware_bounded_shape_continuation_lo.name: tail_aware_bounded_shape_continuation_loss_gen9_4
tail_aware_bounded_shape_continuation_lo.code:
"""
    tail_aware_bounded_shape_continuation_loss_gen9_4(tree, dataset, options)

Synthesis of the two parents into a single cheap pass that carries **three
complementary signals**, each addressing a different failure mode of plain NMSE:

1. **Scale-free fidelity** (both parents) — `log1p(SSE / S)` where `S` is the
   centered target energy `m2_y`, with graceful fallbacks to the raw target
   energy and then to `n` for numerically constant targets. `log1p` compression
   keeps catastrophic candidates from drowning out structurally useful ones.

2. **Tail-concentration correction** (parent 1) — with normalized residuals
   `u_i = d_i / sd(y)` we have `mean(u^2) == raw_nmse` and
   `sqrt(mean(u^4)) == sqrt(n * s4) / S >= raw_nmse`, with equality iff `|d|` is
   constant. Blending a modest fraction (1/3 in log space) of the L4 term into
   the fidelity signal penalizes candidates whose error is *concentrated* in a
   subregion — exactly the signature of truncated-series / epicycle surrogates
   that fit most of the domain and dump all their error near a singular or
   extreme region. The weight is deliberately small so i.i.d. observation noise
   (whose kurtosis gives `sqrt(mean(u^4)) ~ sqrt(3) * mean(u^2)`) is not
   over-penalized on noisy real-world data.

3. **Bounded shape scaffold** (parent 2) — `1 - r²`, the fraction of target
   variance left unexplained by the best implicit affine map `a*prediction + b`.
   This rewards candidates whose *functional shape* is right before their
   constants have been tuned. Being bounded in `[0, 1]`, it can never dominate
   the ranking the way parent 1's unbounded affine-NMSE scaffold can when the
   raw error is huge; it behaves purely as structural guidance / tie-breaking.

The shape term is folded in with parent 2's **continuation schedule**,
`w = w_max * raw_nmse / (1 + raw_nmse)` with `w_max = 0.5`: guidance is strong
far from a fit and fades continuously to zero as the raw error vanishes, so only
genuinely correct predictions (not merely affinely-correlated ones) reach zero
loss, while direct fidelity always retains at least half the weight.

Implementation notes / heuristics:
  * One Welford pass gives stable centered moments of `p` and `y` plus their
    covariance; the residual power sums `sum d^2`, `sum d^4` are sums of
    non-negative terms, so plain accumulation suffices (no cancellation).
  * If the fourth-power sum overflows or is non-finite, the tail term degrades
    gracefully to the raw term instead of returning `Inf`.
  * Relative `eps`-based floors disable calibration on numerically constant
    targets/predictions; a constant prediction against a variable target gets
    the maximal shape penalty of 1.
  * No expression-complexity penalty is included (handled by PySR's parsimony).
"""
function tail_aware_bounded_shape_continuation_loss_gen9_4(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)

    # --- single pass: Welford moments + residual power sums ----------------------
    mean_y = zero_l
    mean_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    covariance = zero_l
    target_energy = zero_l   # fallback normalizer for (near-)constant targets
    sse = zero_l             # sum d^2
    s4 = zero_l              # sum d^4  (tail-concentration signal)

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        p = L(prediction[i])
        if !(isfinite(y) && isfinite(p))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        d = p - y
        d2 = d * d
        # Non-negative accumulations: no catastrophic cancellation possible.
        sse += d2
        s4 = muladd(d2, d2, s4)
        target_energy = muladd(y, y, target_energy)

        count = L(i)
        delta_y = y - mean_y
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        mean_y += delta_y / count
        mean_p += delta_p / count

        # Standard Welford form: updates use the freshly advanced means.
        m2_y = muladd(delta_y, y - mean_y, m2_y)
        m2_p = muladd(delta_p, p - mean_p, m2_p)
        covariance = muladd(delta_p, y - mean_y, covariance)
    end

    # Preserve the exact zero optimum regardless of auxiliary sums.
    if sse == zero_l
        return zero_l
    end

    if !(isfinite(sse) && isfinite(target_energy) &&
         isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(covariance) &&
         isfinite(mean_y) && isfinite(mean_p))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Roundoff can push centered sums microscopically negative.
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    sse = max(sse, zero_l)

    # --- relative floors: never "calibrate" numerically constant data -----------
    n_l = L(n)
    y_reference = max(one_l, abs(mean_y))
    p_reference = max(one_l, abs(mean_p))
    target_floor = n_l * eps(L) * y_reference * y_reference
    prediction_floor = n_l * eps(L) * p_reference * p_reference
    if !(isfinite(target_floor) && isfinite(prediction_floor))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    target_is_variable = m2_y > target_floor

    # Scale-free normalizer: target variance, then target energy, then n.
    normalizer = if target_is_variable
        m2_y
    elseif target_energy > zero_l
        target_energy
    else
        n_l
    end

    raw_nmse = sse / normalizer
    if !isfinite(raw_nmse) || raw_nmse < zero_l
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # --- tail-concentration term ------------------------------------------------
    # sqrt(mean(u^4)) = sqrt(n * s4) / normalizer >= mean(u^2) = raw_nmse.
    tail_nmse = raw_nmse
    if isfinite(s4) && s4 > zero_l
        candidate = sqrt(n_l * s4) / normalizer
        # Fall back to the raw term on overflow; max() guards roundoff below raw.
        tail_nmse = isfinite(candidate) ? max(candidate, raw_nmse) : raw_nmse
    end

    raw_term = log1p(raw_nmse)
    tail_term = log1p(tail_nmse)

    # Modest fixed weight: breaks ties between globally-smooth-but-locally-wrong
    # surrogates and correct structure without over-punishing spread-out noise.
    tail_weight = L(1) / L(3)
    fidelity_term = muladd(tail_weight, tail_term - raw_term, raw_term)

    # --- bounded shape scaffold: 1 - r^2 ---------------------------------------
    shape_term = zero_l
    if target_is_variable
        if m2_p > prediction_floor
            correlation = covariance / sqrt(m2_p) / sqrt(m2_y)
            if !isfinite(correlation)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            bounded_correlation = min(abs(correlation), one_l)
            shape_term = one_l - bounded_correlation * bounded_correlation
        else
            # Constant prediction can match only the target mean: worst shape.
            shape_term = one_l
        end
    end

    # --- continuation: strong structural guidance far away, none at a fit -------
    max_shape_weight = L(0.5)
    shape_weight = max_shape_weight * raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse)

    loss_value = (one_l - shape_weight) * fidelity_term + shape_weight * shape_term
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

pareto_guarded_age_survival_gen9_5.name: pareto_guarded_age_survival_gen9_5
pareto_guarded_age_survival_gen9_5.code:
"""
    pareto_guarded_age_survival_gen9_5(pop::Population{T,L,N}, options::AbstractOptions; exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[])::Int

Pareto-Guarded Age-Regularized Survival Operator.

# Core Idea & Motivation
Standard age-regularized evolution replaces the oldest member regardless of quality.
In symbolic regression, this causes two critical failure modes:
1. Crucial Pareto-optimal building blocks (e.g. `x0`, `x1/x2`) get evicted when they reach
   maximum age, forcing the search to re-derive them or settle for bloated Taylor approximations.
2. Dominated or redundant bloated expressions linger for a full lifespan, crowding
   selection tournaments and spawning increasingly complex local-optimum bloat.

# Mechanism & Steps
1. Precompute complexities, losses, and birth orders for all population members to avoid
   repeated tree traversals.
2. Detect invalid members (NaN or Inf loss) and assign them immediate eviction priority.
3. Compute 2D empirical Pareto dominance `(complexity, loss)` across the active sub-population:
   - Member `j` dominates `i` if `comp[j] <= comp[i]` and `loss[j] < loss[i]` (or vice versa).
   - Identical duplicates (`comp[j] == comp[i]` and `loss[j] == loss[i]`) are resolved such that
     younger copies dominate older ones, pruning redundant clones and freeing population capacity.
4. Replacement Priority:
   a. Oldest member with invalid (NaN/Inf) loss (immediate eviction of non-evaluable trees).
   b. Oldest dominated member (preserves uniform exploration lifespan for exploratory branches
      while shielding the empirical Pareto frontier from premature extinction).
   c. Oldest member overall (graceful fallback to standard age-regularization when all members
      are non-dominated).
5. Excluded indices (`exclude_indices`) are strictly respected to prevent replacing the same slot twice.

# Changes vs. Parent (`age_regularized_survival`)
- Introduces Pareto-front protection: non-dominated expressions are shielded from age eviction
  as long as dominated candidates exist.
- Implements duplicate pruning so redundant clones are marked as dominated and recycled.
- Prioritizes invalid (NaN/Inf) individuals for instant replacement.
- Preserves the uniform lifespan exploration property for dominated individuals without hyperparameter tuning.
"""
function pareto_guarded_age_survival_gen9_5(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    if n <= 1
        return 1
    end

    # Precompute member metrics to avoid repeated tree traversals during pairwise comparisons
    complexities = [compute_complexity(pop.members[i], options) for i in 1:n]
    losses = [pop.members[i].loss for i in 1:n]
    births = [pop.members[i].birth for i in 1:n]
    BT = eltype(births)

    # Track dominance and validity status
    is_dominated = falses(n)
    is_invalid = falses(n)

    for i in 1:n
        loss_i = losses[i]
        comp_i = complexities[i]
        birth_i = births[i]
        bad_i = isnan(loss_i) || isinf(loss_i)
        is_invalid[i] = bad_i

        for j in 1:n
            j == i && continue
            loss_j = losses[j]
            comp_j = complexities[j]
            birth_j = births[j]
            bad_j = isnan(loss_j) || isinf(loss_j)

            if bad_i
                # Invalid members are dominated by any valid member or younger invalid member
                if !bad_j || (birth_j > birth_i || (birth_j == birth_i && j > i))
                    is_dominated[i] = true
                    break
                end
            elseif !bad_j
                # Strict Pareto dominance: j is at least as good in both criteria and strictly better in one
                if (comp_j <= comp_i && loss_j < loss_i) ||
                   (comp_j < comp_i && loss_j <= loss_i) ||
                   # Duplicate resolution: younger duplicate dominates older duplicate to prune redundancy
                   (comp_j == comp_i && loss_j == loss_i && (birth_j > birth_i || (birth_j == birth_i && j > i)))
                    is_dominated[i] = true
                    break
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # Find replacement candidates across three priority tiers
    oldest_invalid_idx = -1
    oldest_invalid_birth = typemax(BT)

    oldest_dominated_idx = -1
    oldest_dominated_birth = typemax(BT)

    oldest_any_idx = -1
    oldest_any_birth = typemax(BT)

    for i in 1:n
        # Always respect excluded indices (e.g. from crossover dual replacement)
        if i in exclude_indices
            continue
        end

        birth_i = births[i]

        # Tier 3 fallback: overall oldest available member
        if birth_i < oldest_any_birth
            oldest_any_birth = birth_i
            oldest_any_idx = i
        end

        # Tier 1: oldest invalid member (highest priority for immediate cleanup)
        if is_invalid[i] && (birth_i < oldest_invalid_birth)
            oldest_invalid_birth = birth_i
            oldest_invalid_idx = i
        end

        # Tier 2: oldest dominated member with valid loss
        if is_dominated[i] && !is_invalid[i] && (birth_i < oldest_dominated_birth)
            oldest_dominated_birth = birth_i
            oldest_dominated_idx = i
        end
    end

    # Return the highest priority candidate available
    if oldest_invalid_idx != -1
        return oldest_invalid_idx
    elseif oldest_dominated_idx != -1
        return oldest_dominated_idx
    elseif oldest_any_idx != -1
        return oldest_any_idx
    else
        # Safety fallback in the rare event all members were excluded
        return 1
    end
end

lineage_guarded_frontier_bridge_selectio.name: lineage_guarded_frontier_bridge_selection_gen9_9
lineage_guarded_frontier_bridge_selectio.code:
"""
Select a parent with a lineage-guarded frontier-bridge tournament.

The tournament combines loss/cost ranking, loss-complexity Pareto dominance,
adaptive complexity niching, and lineage protection with a two-sided frontier
heuristic. Each sampled expression is rewarded for a complexity-normalized loss
breakthrough over the best simpler candidate. The simpler candidate that enabled
that breakthrough also receives "bridge" credit, preserving compact structural
launchpads that might otherwise be discarded while the search pursues a tail of
increasingly complex approximations. Bounded youth, niche, and lineage factors
maintain stepping-stone diversity without overwhelming objective quality.

The heuristic assumes lower loss and cost are better, useful symbolic structure
often lies on or near the sampled loss-complexity frontier, and large improvements
made with small complexity increments are more informative than marginal gains
from substantial growth. Selection remains stochastic, while invalid objectives
and Pareto-dominated candidates retain only small positive probability.
"""
function lineage_guarded_frontier_bridge_selection_gen9_9(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    tournament_size = min(pop.n, max(2, options.tournament_selection_n))
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, tournament_size; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)

    n == 1 && return sample[1]

    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    frequencies = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    valid_losses = Vector{Bool}(undef, n)
    valid_costs = Vector{Bool}(undef, n)
    valid_complexities = Vector{Bool}(undef, n)

    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]

        raw_loss = Float64(member.loss)
        raw_cost = Float64(member.cost)
        valid_losses[i] = isfinite(raw_loss)
        valid_costs[i] = isfinite(raw_cost)
        losses[i] = valid_losses[i] ? raw_loss : Inf
        costs[i] = valid_costs[i] ? raw_cost : Inf

        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size
        valid_complexities[i] = 0 < size <= options.maxsize

        frequency = if valid_complexities[i] &&
                       size <= length(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies)
            Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
        else
            0.0
        end
        frequencies[i] = isfinite(frequency) ? max(0.0, frequency) : 0.0
    end

    loss_ranks = zeros(Int, n)
    cost_ranks = zeros(Int, n)
    domination_counts = zeros(Int, n)
    niche_counts = ones(Int, n)
    lineage_counts = ones(Int, n)

    # Estimate objective quality, Pareto status, and local crowding.
    for i in 1:n
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue

            if losses[j] < losses[i]
                loss_ranks[i] += 1
            end
            if costs[j] < costs[i]
                cost_ranks[i] += 1
            end
            if complexities[j] == complexities[i]
                niche_counts[i] += 1
            end

            no_worse = losses[j] <= losses[i] &&
                       complexities[j] <= complexities[i]
            strictly_better = losses[j] < losses[i] ||
                              complexities[j] < complexities[i]
            if no_worse && strictly_better
                domination_counts[i] += 1
            end

            # Count siblings and direct parent-child pairs as one local lineage.
            same_parent = sample[i].parent > 0 &&
                          sample[i].parent == sample[j].parent
            direct_relative = (sample[i].ref > 0 &&
                               sample[j].parent == sample[i].ref) ||
                              (sample[j].ref > 0 &&
                               sample[i].parent == sample[j].ref)
            if same_parent || direct_relative
                lineage_counts[i] += 1
            end
        end
    end

    breakthrough_scores = zeros(Float64, n)
    bridge_scores = zeros(Float64, n)

    # Give frontier progress credit to a breakthrough and bridge credit to its
    # best simpler launchpad. Complexity-gap normalization discourages bloat.
    for i in 1:n
        valid_losses[i] || continue

        best_simpler_idx = 0
        best_simpler_loss = Inf
        for j in 1:n
            if valid_losses[j] &&
               complexities[j] < complexities[i] &&
               losses[j] < best_simpler_loss
                best_simpler_loss = losses[j]
                best_simpler_idx = j
            end
        end

        if best_simpler_idx > 0 && losses[i] < best_simpler_loss
            scale = max(
                abs(best_simpler_loss) + abs(losses[i]),
                eps(Float64),
            )
            relative_gain = clamp(
                (best_simpler_loss - losses[i]) / scale,
                0.0,
                1.0,
            )
            complexity_gap = max(
                1,
                complexities[i] - complexities[best_simpler_idx],
            )
            efficient_gain = relative_gain / sqrt(Float64(complexity_gap))

            breakthrough_scores[i] = efficient_gain
            bridge_scores[best_simpler_idx] = max(
                bridge_scores[best_simpler_idx],
                efficient_gain,
            )
        end
    end

    min_birth = minimum(member.birth for member in sample)
    max_birth = maximum(member.birth for member in sample)
    birth_span = max_birth - min_birth

    raw_p = Float64(options.tournament_selection_p)
    p = isfinite(raw_p) ? clamp(raw_p, 0.0, 1.0) : 1.0
    pressure = 0.60 + 2.40 * p
    rank_denominator = Float64(max(1, n - 1))
    dominance_scale = max(1.0, sqrt(Float64(n)))

    raw_parsimony_scale = Float64(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    parsimony_scale = isfinite(raw_parsimony_scale) ?
        max(0.0, raw_parsimony_scale) : 0.0

    weights = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        loss_rank = Float64(loss_ranks[i]) / rank_denominator
        cost_rank = Float64(cost_ranks[i]) / rank_denominator

        # Raw loss retains accuracy pressure while penalized cost limits growth.
        quality_factor = 0.15 +
                         0.50 * exp(-pressure * loss_rank) +
                         0.35 * exp(-pressure * cost_rank)

        pareto_factor = exp(
            -pressure * Float64(domination_counts[i]) / dominance_scale,
        )
        if domination_counts[i] == 0
            pareto_factor *= 1.10
        end

        # Reward both frontier advances and compact expressions from which a
        # strong advance was reached.
        frontier_role_factor = 1.0 +
                               2.75 * breakthrough_scores[i] +
                               1.75 * bridge_scores[i]

        local_niche_factor = inv(sqrt(Float64(niche_counts[i])))
        global_niche_factor = if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            inv(sqrt(1.0 + parsimony_scale * frequencies[i]))
        else
            1.0
        end
        lineage_factor = inv(sqrt(Float64(lineage_counts[i])))

        # Bound diversity protection so novelty cannot erase fitness pressure.
        diversity_factor = 0.35 + 0.65 *
            local_niche_factor *
            global_niche_factor *
            lineage_factor

        recency = if birth_span > 0
            Float64(sample[i].birth - min_birth) / Float64(birth_span)
        else
            0.5
        end
        youth_factor = 0.85 + 0.30 * recency

        # Invalid members retain a positive weight but are very unlikely to win.
        validity_factor = if valid_losses[i] &&
                             valid_costs[i] &&
                             valid_complexities[i]
            1.0
        elseif valid_losses[i] && valid_complexities[i]
            0.05
        else
            1.0e-8
        end

        weights[i] = validity_factor *
                     quality_factor *
                     pareto_factor *
                     frontier_role_factor *
                     diversity_factor *
                     youth_factor
    end

    total_weight = sum(weights)
    if !isfinite(total_weight) || total_weight <= 0.0
        return sample[argmin_fast(costs)]
    end

    chosen_idx = StatsBase.sample(StatsBase.Weights(weights, total_weight))
    return sample[chosen_idx]
end

affine_shape_nrmse_loss_simplified_gen10.name: affine_shape_nrmse_loss_simplified_gen10_7
affine_shape_nrmse_loss_simplified_gen10.code:
"""
    affine_shape_nrmse_loss_simplified_gen10_7(tree, dataset, options)

Simplified affine-shape loss: score an expression by the *shape* of its output
(the normalized RMSE that remains after the best least-squares affine
recalibration `a * prediction + b`), plus a small bounded raw-error term that
breaks ties toward the correctly calibrated representative.

Steps:
 1. One pass of Welford moments to get `mean_p, mean_y, m2_p, m2_y, cov_py`
    (and `max_abs_y`, used only as a fallback scale).
 2. Fit the affine coefficients in closed form; if the prediction is constant
    the fit degenerates to the target mean (`slope = 0`).
 3. One pass over the fitted residuals (evaluated directly, which avoids the
    catastrophic cancellation of `var(y) - cov^2/var(p)` near an exact match),
    accumulating both the affine NMSE and the raw NMSE with the same
    `sqrt(m2_y)` normalization.
 4. Return `sqrt(clamp(affine_nmse, 0, 1)) + (1/256) * raw/(1+raw)`.

Simplifications versus the parent:
 * The separate constant-target branch (and its whole extra accumulation loop)
   is folded into the common path: when `m2_y` is ~0 the normalizer falls back
   to a data scale, the affine fit reduces to the constant `mean_y`, so the
   shape term vanishes and the loss becomes a monotone function of raw error —
   exactly the behavior the special case implemented.
 * Kahan compensation and the `raw_overflowed` state machine are removed; a
   single `isfinite` test on the raw accumulator saturates it to 1, and the
   affine term is clamped to `[0, 1]` (the affine optimum can never be worse
   than fitting the mean), so both terms stay bounded and well defined.
 * Per-element finiteness checks in the moment pass are replaced by checks on
   the aggregates, since any NaN/Inf sample propagates into the moments.
These changes keep the two-pass, cancellation-free core idea while reducing the
kernel to two lean loops with MSE-comparable cost.
"""
function affine_shape_nrmse_loss_simplified_gen10_7(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # ---- Pass 1: stable Welford moments (no per-element checks; NaN/Inf
    # propagate into the accumulators and are caught right after the loop).
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y
        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k
        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)   # uses updated target mean
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Roundoff can make Welford sums microscopically negative.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    # ---- Normalizer: sqrt of the total target variation, with a data-scale
    # fallback for (near-)constant targets so the common path stays valid.
    target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)
    if !(target_norm > sqrt(eps(L)) * max_abs_y * sqrt(n_l))
        target_norm = sqrt(n_l) * max(one_l, max_abs_y)
    end

    # ---- Affine fit; a constant prediction degenerates to the target mean.
    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if m2_p > zero_l
        slope = cov_py / m2_p
        intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
        if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
            slope = zero_l
            intercept = mean_y
        end
    end

    # ---- Pass 2: evaluate the fitted residuals directly (cancellation-free)
    # together with the raw residuals, both under the same normalization.
    affine_sum = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_normalized = (p - y) / target_norm
        raw_sum += raw_normalized * raw_normalized

        affine_normalized = (muladd(slope, p, intercept) - y) / target_norm
        affine_sum += affine_normalized * affine_normalized
    end

    if !isfinite(affine_sum)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # The affine optimum can never be worse than fitting the target mean,
    # so the shape NMSE lives in [0, 1]; RMSE form magnifies near-exact fits.
    shape_term = sqrt(clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l))

    # Bounded calibration tie-breaker: saturating, monotone in raw error, and
    # small enough that it cannot outweigh shape differences.
    bounded_raw = if isfinite(raw_sum) && raw_sum >= zero_l
        raw_sum / (one_l + raw_sum)
    else
        one_l
    end

    loss_value = shape_term + bounded_raw / L(256)
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

tournament_age_survival_gen10_1.name: tournament_age_survival_gen10_1
tournament_age_survival_gen10_1.code:
"""
Simplified age-regularized survival via a small random "death tournament".

Core idea kept from the parent: still remove an *old* member to implement
age-regularized evolution (the same principle as `age_regularized_survival` /
`default_survival`). What is removed/simplified:

- Instead of building a full `births` vector over the entire population
  (an O(n) allocation + scan every call) and always picking the *globally*
  oldest member, we draw a small random tournament of `ts` members and
  replace the oldest one *within that tournament*.
- This merges the "exclusion check" and "oldest search" into a single loop
  with early exit, avoiding the extra array allocation and the `typemax`
  sentinel trick except as a rare fallback.
- The small stochastic tournament also has a beneficial side effect: it
  avoids deterministically always evicting the single oldest individual
  every generation, which can cause premature convergence/stagnation
  (as seen in search traces where the Pareto front gets stuck for long
  stretches). Occasionally sparing the oldest member preserves diversity
  while still biasing replacement toward older members overall.

Soundness: with tournament size `ts` capped at population size, and a
fallback full scan when no valid (non-excluded) candidate is found in the
random draws, the function always returns a valid index not in
`exclude_indices`.
"""
function tournament_age_survival_gen10_1(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)
    n = pop.n

    # Small fixed tournament size, capped by population size.
    ts = min(3, n)

    best_idx = 0
    best_birth = typemax(BT)

    # Randomly sample candidates (with replacement, for simplicity) and
    # track the oldest non-excluded member seen so far.
    tried = 0
    attempts = 0
    max_attempts = ts * 10  # avoid infinite loop if many indices are excluded
    while tried < ts && attempts < max_attempts
        i = rand(1:n)
        attempts += 1
        if i in exclude_indices
            continue
        end
        tried += 1
        if pop.members[i].birth < best_birth
            best_birth = pop.members[i].birth
            best_idx = i
        end
    end

    # Fallback: if random sampling failed to find any valid candidate
    # (e.g., most indices excluded), do a full deterministic scan.
    if best_idx == 0
        births = [(i in exclude_indices) ? typemax(BT) : pop.members[i].birth
                  for i in 1:n]
        return argmin_fast(births)
    end

    return best_idx
end

simplified_tournament_selection_gen10_0.name: simplified_tournament_selection_gen10_0
simplified_tournament_selection_gen10_0.code:
"""
Simplified tournament selection with folded parsimony branch and rank-based
sampling.

Core idea: same as the parent (sample `tournament_selection_n` members,
optionally penalize by complexity-frequency, then pick a winner via a
truncated-geometric-like tournament), but the two separate code paths for
"use_frequency" vs "not" and for "p==1" vs "p<1" are merged into single,
shared code paths:

  1. A single loop always builds `adjusted_costs`, using a multiplier of
     `exp(scaling * freq)` where `scaling` is set to 0 when frequency-based
     parsimony is disabled (so the exponential term becomes 1 and the cost
     is unchanged) — this removes the need for two separate loops.
  2. Instead of computing a full `Weights` distribution over all n ranks
     and then handling the `winner == 1` case specially (falling back to
     `argmin_fast`) or otherwise calling `bottomk_fast`, we sort the
     adjusted costs once (`sortperm`) to get a rank ordering, then draw a
     single random number and map it analytically to a geometric-like rank
     via the closed-form inverse CDF `1 + floor(log(1-r)/log(1-p))`,
     clamped to `n`. This is mathematically equivalent in spirit to the
     parent's `p * (1-p)^k` tournament-weight scheme (it samples earlier
     ranks with higher probability, decaying by factor `(1-p)` per rank)
     but avoids allocating a `Weights` vector and avoids the special-cased
     branch for `p == 1` (which is just the limiting case where the
     geometric draw always returns rank 1).

This keeps the essential tournament-with-parsimony behavior while removing
redundant branches and vector allocations.
"""
function simplified_tournament_selection_gen10_0(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, options.tournament_selection_n; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)
    p = options.tournament_selection_p

    # Single unified loop: when frequency-based parsimony is off, `scaling` is
    # zero so the exponential multiplier collapses to 1, leaving cost unchanged.
    scaling = options.use_frequency_in_tournament ? L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling) : L(0)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]
        cost = member.cost
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            size = compute_complexity(member, options)
            freq = (0 < size <= options.maxsize) ? L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size]) : L(0)
            cost = cost * exp(scaling * freq)
        end
        adjusted_costs[i] = cost
    end

    # Rank members once by adjusted cost (rank 1 = best).
    order = sortperm(adjusted_costs)

    # Draw a rank via the closed-form inverse CDF of a truncated geometric
    # distribution with success probability p: this reproduces the parent's
    # p * (1-p)^k tournament-weight decay without building a Weights vector
    # or special-casing p == 1 (which just always returns rank 1 here).
    chosen_rank = 1
    if p < 1.0
        r = rand()
        chosen_rank = min(n, 1 + floor(Int, log(1 - r) / log(1 - p)))
    end

    chosen_idx = order[chosen_rank]
    return copy(sample[chosen_idx])
end

symmetric_motif_offset_coupling_gen10_2.name: symmetric_motif_offset_coupling_gen10_2
symmetric_motif_offset_coupling_gen10_2.code:
"""
    symmetric_motif_offset_coupling_gen10_2(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

Structural mutation that synthesizes *motif duplication with cyclic feature shifts*
(parent 2) and *additive constant offsets* (parent 1) into one coherent operator.

# Core idea
Many ground-truth laws are built from a repeated functional motif that appears across
several variables, each instance offset or shifted by an additive constant, e.g.
`(x1 - c)^2 + (x2 - c)^2`, `sin(x1) + sin(x2) + c`, `m*(vx^2 + vy^2)`. Reaching such
forms by single-node edits is very unlikely: the search must (a) *replicate* an already
evolved motif onto other features, and (b) have a free additive constant available so
that least-squares/constant-optimization can position the replicated block correctly.

This operator does both in one move:

1. Bail out if no binary operator is available (coupling requires one).
2. Sample a donor subtree and deep-copy it into an independent *motif*.
3. If `nfeatures > 1`, cyclically shift all variable indices in the motif by a random
   offset `shift ∈ 0:(nfeatures-1)`; `shift == 0` keeps the motif identical, which is
   what is needed for powers / self-couplings (`u*u`, `u/u`-style rational forms).
4. With probability 1/2 (and only if `+` exists), wrap the motif as `motif + c`, where
   `c` is a fresh normal constant scaled by `std(y)` from the dataset. Scaling by the
   target's spread makes the offset *dimensionally plausible* instead of always O(1),
   which is the main weakness of a plain `randn` constant.
5. Sample a target node and replace it with a binary coupling of the target and the
   (shifted, offset) motif. The coupling operator is biased toward `+` (probability 1/2)
   because additive superposition of motifs is by far the most common structure in
   physical laws; otherwise a uniformly random binary operator is used. Operand order
   is randomized so non-commutative operators (`-`, `/`, `^`) are reachable both ways.

# Assumptions / heuristics
- Cyclic shifting assumes neighboring feature indices are exchangeable; over many
  proposals it covers all feature relabelings of the motif.
- The fresh constant is a *hook* for constant optimization, so only its magnitude
  scale matters, not its precise initial value.
- `dataset.y === nothing` (multi-output) simply falls back to unit scale.
"""
function symmetric_motif_offset_coupling_gen10_2(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Step 1: binary coupling requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # Locate `+` once; used both for the offset and for the biased coupling choice
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), options.operators.binops)

    # Helper: cyclically permute feature indices inside the duplicated motif
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int, num_features::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, num_features)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift, num_features)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Data-aware magnitude for the offset constant: spread of the target signal
    scale = one(T)
    if dataset.y !== nothing && dataset.n > 1
        sy = std(dataset.y)
        if isfinite(sy) && sy > 0
            scale = T(sy)
        end
    end

    # Step 2: sample a donor subtree and duplicate it into an independent motif
    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    motif = copy(donor)

    # Step 3: optional cyclic feature relabeling of the motif (shift 0 == self-coupling)
    if nfeatures > 1
        shift = rand(rng, 0:(nfeatures - 1))
        if shift > 0
            _shift_features!(motif, shift, nfeatures)
        end
    end

    # Step 4: half the time, give the motif its own additive constant hook: motif + c
    if plus_idx !== nothing && rand(rng) < 0.5
        constant_node = constructorof(N)(T; val=scale * randn(rng, T))
        motif = constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(motif, constant_node))
    end

    # Step 5: couple a target node with the transformed motif under a binary operator,
    # biased toward additive superposition when `+` is available
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    target_copy = copy(target)
    bin_op = if plus_idx !== nothing && rand(rng) < 0.5
        plus_idx
    else
        rand(rng, 1:(options.nops[2]))
    end

    # Randomize operand order so non-commutative operators are fully reachable
    children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
    new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children)
    set_node!(target, new_node)

    return tree
end

crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen.name: crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen10_4
crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen.code:
"""
    crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen10_4(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Tournament selection that actively fights the two failure modes most visible in
long PySR runs: **lineage monopoly** (one champion skeleton and its near-identical
clones fill the population, so search degenerates into constant-tuning of a single
structure) and **complexity-niche starvation** (whole complexity bands go extinct,
removing the mid-size building blocks needed to assemble the true expression).

Core idea: score a slightly enlarged tournament pool with the usual
frequency-adjusted cost, then *inflate* the score of members that are redundant
copies of a better pool member (same complexity + essentially the same loss, or a
shared parent reference), *slightly discount* the freshest members to keep lineage
turnover going, and occasionally (with probability `p_rare_niche`) deliberately
select the pool member sitting in the rarest complexity niche instead of the
fittest one.

Steps:
 1. Sample a pool of `~1.5 * tournament_selection_n` distinct members (a bit larger
    than the default tournament, so that redundancy/niche information exists).
 2. Compute complexity and the default adaptive-parsimony-adjusted cost
    (`cost * exp(scaling * normalized_frequency[complexity])`).
 3. Redundancy (crowding) suppression: sort the pool by adjusted cost; for each
    member count how many *better* pool members are effectively the same solution
    (identical complexity and loss within a relative tolerance -> weight 1.0) or a
    sibling from the same parent (-> weight `sibling_weight`). Inflate the score
    geometrically with that accumulated redundancy weight. The best representative
    of each cluster is untouched, its twins are progressively demoted.
 4. Youth discount: members born most recently get up to `youth_discount`
    relative cost reduction, which prevents an ancient champion from being
    re-selected forever and re-tuned in place.
 5. With probability `p_rare_niche`, return the pool member whose complexity has
    the lowest `normalized_frequencies` value (ties broken by score) — an explicit
    exploration move that repopulates starved complexity bands. Otherwise run the
    standard geometric tournament ladder (`tournament_selection_p`) over the
    penalized scores.

Assumptions / heuristics:
 - Equal complexity plus (relatively) equal loss is a cheap, allocation-free proxy
   for "structurally the same expression"; false positives merely nudge selection
   toward a slightly different equally-good member, which is harmless.
 - Costs are usually positive; the `inflate` helper handles non-positive costs by
   dividing instead of multiplying so that "worse" always means "worse".
 - All penalties are multiplicative and mild, so behaviour degrades gracefully to
   the default tournament when the pool contains no redundancy.
"""
function crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen10_4(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # ---------------- tunables (kept mild so we degrade to default behaviour) ----
    pool_scale = 1.5          # pool size relative to tournament_selection_n
    clone_penalty = 1.35      # score inflation per unit of redundancy weight
    sibling_weight = 0.4      # a shared parent counts as a partial twin
    loss_rtol = 1e-6          # relative tolerance for "same loss"
    youth_discount = 0.05     # max relative cost discount for the newest members
    p_rare_niche = 0.10       # probability of the explicit rare-complexity pick

    # Multiplicative penalty/bonus that is sign-safe (f > 1 always means worse).
    inflate = function (x::L, f::Float64)
        fl = L(f)
        return x > zero(L) ? x * fl : x / fl
    end

    # ---------------- 1. sample the pool -----------------------------------------
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # ---------------- 2. base (frequency-adjusted) scores ------------------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 3. redundancy (clone / sibling) suppression -----------------
    # Process from best to worst so the best representative of a cluster is free of
    # penalty and each of its twins gets progressively demoted.
    order = sortperm(scores)
    redundancy = zeros(Float64, n)
    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        wi = 0.0
        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            # near-identical solution: same complexity and (relatively) same loss
            same_loss = abs(li - lj) <= L(loss_rtol) * max(abs(li), abs(lj), eps(L))
            if complexities[i] == complexities[j] && same_loss
                wi += 1.0
            elseif pool[i].parent != 0 && pool[i].parent == pool[j].parent
                # siblings from the same parent: partial redundancy
                wi += sibling_weight
            end
        end
        redundancy[i] = wi
    end

    # ---------------- 4. youth discount ------------------------------------------
    birth_min = pool[1].birth
    birth_max = pool[1].birth
    for i in 2:n
        b = pool[i].birth
        b < birth_min && (birth_min = b)
        b > birth_max && (birth_max = b)
    end
    birth_span = max(birth_max - birth_min, 1)

    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        # redundancy inflation (>= 1) and recency discount (<= 1) combined
        recency = (pool[i].birth - birth_min) / birth_span  # 0 (oldest) .. 1 (newest)
        factor = (clone_penalty^redundancy[i]) * (1.0 - youth_discount * recency)
        penalized[i] = inflate(scores[i], factor)
    end

    # ---------------- 5a. occasional rare-complexity (niche) pick -----------------
    if rand() < p_rare_niche
        best_idx = 1
        best_freq = Inf
        best_score = penalized[1]
        for i in 1:n
            c = complexities[i]
            f = if (0 < c <= options.maxsize)
                Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
            else
                0.0  # out-of-range sizes count as maximally rare
            end
            # prefer the rarest complexity; break ties with the penalized score
            if f < best_freq || (f == best_freq && penalized[i] < best_score)
                best_freq = f
                best_score = penalized[i]
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        return pool[best_idx]
    end

    # ---------------- 5b. standard geometric tournament ladder --------------------
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        if tournament_winner == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, tournament_winner)[2][end]
        end
    end
    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

rank_normalized_lineage_pareto_breakthro.name: rank_normalized_lineage_pareto_breakthrough_selection_gen10_6
rank_normalized_lineage_pareto_breakthro.code:
"""
Select a parent using a rank-normalized, lineage-guarded Pareto-breakthrough
tournament.

This operator merges the tournament machinery from both parents (which were
identical) and strengthens the parts most likely to affect SRBench-style
discovery: (1) the breakthrough signal is made scale-invariant by combining a
relative-loss-improvement term with a per-added-complexity efficiency term, so
that a big loss gain achieved with only a little extra complexity is rewarded
even when absolute loss magnitudes are tiny or huge; (2) niche protection is
computed as a geometric blend of local tournament niche density and the
global adaptive-parsimony frequency statistic, rather than only locally
diluting or only chaining through options; (3) Pareto dominance counts are
softened by a continuous "crowding margin" (how close, not just whether,
competitors beat a candidate) so near-dominated points are not punished as
harshly as clearly-dominated ones; (4) lineage and youth protection are kept
to preserve stepping-stones and encourage exploration of fresh mutations.
The heuristic still assumes lower loss/cost is better, that useful
ground-truth subexpressions manifest as unusually efficient loss reductions
per unit of added complexity, and that maintaining a spread of complexity
niches and lineages helps avoid premature convergence.
"""
function rank_normalized_lineage_pareto_breakthrough_selection_gen10_6(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    tournament_size = min(pop.n, max(2, options.tournament_selection_n))
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, tournament_size; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)

    n == 1 && return sample[1]

    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    frequencies = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)

    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]

        # Sanitize objectives so failed evaluations are always unattractive.
        loss = Float64(member.loss)
        cost = Float64(member.cost)
        losses[i] = isfinite(loss) ? loss : Inf
        costs[i] = isfinite(cost) ? cost : Inf

        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size

        frequency = if 0 < size <= options.maxsize &&
                       size <= length(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies)
            Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
        else
            0.0
        end
        frequencies[i] = isfinite(frequency) ? max(0.0, frequency) : 0.0
    end

    loss_ranks = zeros(Int, n)
    cost_ranks = zeros(Int, n)
    domination_counts = zeros(Int, n)
    crowding_margin = zeros(Float64, n)
    niche_counts = ones(Int, n)
    lineage_counts = ones(Int, n)

    # Rank objectives, estimate local niche density, count Pareto dominators,
    # and accumulate a soft "how badly dominated" margin.
    for i in 1:n
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue

            loss_ranks[i] += losses[j] < losses[i]
            cost_ranks[i] += costs[j] < costs[i]
            niche_counts[i] += complexities[j] == complexities[i]

            no_worse = losses[j] <= losses[i] &&
                       complexities[j] <= complexities[i]
            strictly_better = losses[j] < losses[i] ||
                              complexities[j] < complexities[i]
            is_dominator = no_worse && strictly_better
            domination_counts[i] += is_dominator

            if is_dominator
                # Relative margin by which j beats i in loss, used to soften
                # the penalty for near-dominated (vs. clearly-dominated) points.
                denom = max(abs(losses[i]) + abs(losses[j]), eps(Float64))
                crowding_margin[i] += clamp((losses[i] - losses[j]) / denom, 0.0, 1.0)
            end

            # Penalize crowded sibling groups and direct parent-child clusters.
            same_parent = sample[i].parent > 0 &&
                          sample[i].parent == sample[j].parent
            direct_relative = (sample[i].ref > 0 &&
                               sample[j].parent == sample[i].ref) ||
                              (sample[j].ref > 0 &&
                               sample[i].parent == sample[j].ref)
            lineage_counts[i] += same_parent || direct_relative
        end
    end

    # Measure whether each member is a genuine, complexity-efficient
    # accuracy breakthrough over strictly simpler alternatives in this
    # tournament: blend relative loss improvement with per-complexity gain.
    breakthroughs = zeros(Float64, n)
    for i in 1:n
        best_simpler_loss = Inf
        best_simpler_complexity = 0
        for j in 1:n
            if complexities[j] < complexities[i] && losses[j] < best_simpler_loss
                best_simpler_loss = losses[j]
                best_simpler_complexity = complexities[j]
            end
        end

        if isfinite(best_simpler_loss) && isfinite(losses[i]) &&
           losses[i] < best_simpler_loss
            scale = max(abs(best_simpler_loss) + abs(losses[i]), eps(Float64))
            relative_gain = clamp(
                (best_simpler_loss - losses[i]) / scale, 0.0, 1.0
            )

            added_complexity = max(1, complexities[i] - best_simpler_complexity)
            # Efficiency: how much relative gain per unit of added complexity,
            # normalized so a single added node yields the full relative_gain.
            efficiency = relative_gain / sqrt(Float64(added_complexity))

            breakthroughs[i] = clamp(0.5 * relative_gain + 0.5 * efficiency, 0.0, 1.0)
        end
    end

    min_birth = minimum(member.birth for member in sample)
    max_birth = maximum(member.birth for member in sample)
    birth_span = max_birth - min_birth

    p = clamp(Float64(options.tournament_selection_p), 0.0, 1.0)
    pressure = 0.75 + 2.25 * p
    rank_denominator = Float64(max(1, n - 1))
    dominance_scale = max(1.0, sqrt(Float64(n)))
    parsimony_scale = max(0.0, Float64(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling))

    weights = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        loss_rank = Float64(loss_ranks[i]) / rank_denominator
        cost_rank = Float64(cost_ranks[i]) / rank_denominator

        # A mixture of raw-loss and regularized-cost quality avoids committing
        # exclusively to either highly complex fits or overly simple formulas.
        quality_factor = 0.20 +
                         0.45 * exp(-pressure * loss_rank) +
                         0.35 * exp(-pressure * cost_rank)

        # Soft Pareto penalty: combine dominator count with the average margin
        # by which dominators beat this candidate, so marginal dominance hurts
