   adjusted cost), which injects parents from thinly-populated size classes.

Assumptions / heuristics
========================
* Lower `loss` and lower complexity are both desirable; non-finite losses are
  treated as `Inf` so they are always dominated.
* Crowding is measured in (complexity, log-loss) space because losses span many
  orders of magnitude.
* Weights (0.30 crowding, 0.30 rarity, 0.10 youth) are deliberately smaller than
  the exploitation term so selection pressure toward low cost is preserved.
* Cost is O(n^2) in the tournament size (n ~ 18), i.e. negligible.
"""
function pareto_crowding_novelty_tournament_gen13_3(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Degenerate population guard
    if pop.n <= 1
        return pop.members[1]
    end

    # --- 1. Draw an enlarged tournament (without replacement) ----------------
    base_n = max(2, options.tournament_selection_n)
    n_sample = min(pop.n, base_n + base_n ÷ 2)
    idxs = StatsBase.sample(1:(pop.n), n_sample; replace=false)

    # --- 2. Gather per-member quantities -------------------------------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n_sample)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_sample)
    adj_costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_sample)
    freqs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_sample)
    births = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_sample)

    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = Float64(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n_sample
        member = pop.members[idxs[i]]
        c = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = c
        # Non-finite losses/costs are pushed to Inf so they are always dominated
        lval = Float64(member.loss)
        losses[i] = isfinite(lval) ? lval : Inf
        cval = Float64(member.cost)
        cval = isfinite(cval) ? cval : Inf
        # Frequency of this complexity size (used both for parsimony and rarity)
        f = if 0 < c <= options.maxsize
            Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
        else
            0.0
        end
        freqs[i] = f
        # Same frequency-based parsimony adjustment as the default selector
        adj_costs[i] = if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            cval * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * f)
        else
            cval
        end
        births[i] = Float64(member.birth)
    end

    # --- 3. Occasional pure-exploration step: rarest complexity niche --------
    if rand() < 0.06
        best_i = 1
        for i in 2:n_sample
            # strictly rarer niche wins; equal rarity broken by adjusted cost
            if (freqs[i] < freqs[best_i]) ||
                (freqs[i] == freqs[best_i] && adj_costs[i] < adj_costs[best_i])
                best_i = i
            end
        end
        return pop.members[idxs[best_i]]
    end

    # --- 4. Local Pareto front in (complexity, loss) --------------------------
    dominated = falses(n_sample)
    for i in 1:n_sample
        for j in 1:n_sample
            i == j && continue
            dominated[i] && break
            if (complexities[j] <= complexities[i] && losses[j] <= losses[i]) && (
                complexities[j] < complexities[i] || losses[j] < losses[i]
            )
                dominated[i] = true
            end
        end
    end
    front = [i for i in 1:n_sample if !dominated[i]]
    dominated_idx = [i for i in 1:n_sample if dominated[i]]

    F = length(front)

    # --- 5. Crowding distance along the front (complexity vs log-loss) -------
    crowd = zeros(Float64, F)
    if F > 2
        perm = sortperm([complexities[i] for i in front])
        sorted_front = front[perm]
        cc = [Float64(complexities[i]) for i in sorted_front]
        # log-loss makes spacing scale-free across many orders of magnitude
        ll = [log(max(losses[i], eps(Float64))) for i in sorted_front]
        crange = max(cc[end] - cc[1], 1.0)
        lrange = max(abs(ll[1] - ll[end]), 1e-12)
        d = zeros(Float64, F)
        d[1] = 1.0          # boundary solutions are maximally "uncrowded"
        d[F] = 1.0
        for t in 2:(F - 1)
            d[t] =
                0.5 * (
                    (cc[t + 1] - cc[t - 1]) / crange +
                    abs(ll[t - 1] - ll[t + 1]) / lrange
                )
        end
        for t in 1:F
            crowd[perm[t]] = min(max(d[t], 0.0), 1.0)
        end
    end

    # --- 6. Refined ordering of the front ------------------------------------
    # (a) adjusted-cost rank within the front, normalized to [0, 1]
    cost_perm = sortperm([adj_costs[i] for i in front])
    cost_rank = zeros(Float64, F)
    for (r, pos) in enumerate(cost_perm)
        cost_rank[pos] = (r - 1) / max(F - 1, 1)
    end
    # (b) rarity and (c) youth, both min-max normalized within the front
    front_freqs = [freqs[i] for i in front]
    fmin, fmax = minimum(front_freqs), maximum(front_freqs)
    front_births = [births[i] for i in front]
    bmin, bmax = minimum(front_births), maximum(front_births)

    scores = Vector{Float64}(undef, F)
    for t in 1:F
        rarity = (fmax > fmin) ? (fmax - front_freqs[t]) / (fmax - fmin) : 0.0
        youth = (bmax > bmin) ? (front_births[t] - bmin) / (bmax - bmin) : 0.0
        # Lower score is better: exploit cost, reward isolation / rarity / novelty
        scores[t] = cost_rank[t] - 0.30 * crowd[t] - 0.30 * rarity - 0.10 * youth
    end

    # Front members (best score first), then dominated members by adjusted cost
    order = front[sortperm(scores)]
    if !isempty(dominated_idx)
        append!(order, dominated_idx[sortperm([adj_costs[i] for i in dominated_idx])])
    end

    # --- 7. Geometric rank sampling (identical semantics to the default) -----
    p = Float64(options.tournament_selection_p)
    winner_rank = if p >= 1.0
        1
    else
        k = collect(0:(length(order) - 1))
        prob_each = p .* ((1 - p) .^ k)
        StatsBase.sample(StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each)))
    end

    return pop.members[idxs[order[winner_rank]]]
end

affine_log_shape_uniformity_loss_gen13_g.name: affine_log_shape_uniformity_loss_gen13_gen13_0
affine_log_shape_uniformity_loss_gen13_g.code:
"""
    affine_log_shape_uniformity_loss_gen13_gen13_0(tree, dataset, options)

Shape-first loss that grades an expression by (i) how well the *best affine calibration*
`a * prediction + b` reproduces the target, (ii) how *uniform* the fit is in **log
(relative) space**, (iii) whether the prediction is at least a *power/scaling* of the
target, and (iv) a magnitude-calibration ramp that keeps a usable gradient at any error
scale.

Core idea (inherited from the parent)
-------------------------------------
The primary signal is the normalized residual of the least-squares affine calibration of
the prediction onto the target, evaluated *directly* from the fitted residuals in a second
pass (no `var(y) - cov^2/var(p)` cancellation), reported as an RMSE-like quantity so that
near-exact and exact structures stay distinguishable.  This makes the criterion invariant
to a globally wrong outer scale/offset, which is what lets structurally-correct but
badly-tuned candidates survive long enough for constant optimization to fix them.

Observed failure mode being fixed
---------------------------------
Runs such as `exp(-x0^2/2)/sqrt(2*pi)` show the frontier being colonized by rational /
`sin`-over-`exp` surrogates (`square(sin(x0)+0.99)/exp(1.579*(x0+0.688))`) that reach tiny
magnitude-weighted NMSE and then absorb all search effort with cosmetic complexity
refinements.  Such surrogates are wrong *precisely in the tail*, i.e. in **relative**, not
absolute error, and the truth belongs to a family (`exp(c*x0^2)`) whose members only look
good once `c` is nearly right, so no low-complexity landmark ever appears.

Changes vs. the parent
----------------------
1. **Relative uniformity is now measured in log space.**  Instead of the ad-hoc
   `(fitted - y) / (|y| + rms/8)` damping (which dilutes the small-`|y|` tail by ~3x on
   decaying targets), we accumulate `r_i = log|p_i| - log|y_i|` and use `std(r)` (squashed
   into `[0,1)`).  This is exactly scale-invariant, weighs every decade equally, and is the
   sharpest available discriminator for the multiplicative/exponential structures that
   dominate SR benchmarks.  Whether the log path is used depends **only on the target**
   (single sign, bounded away from zero), so every candidate on a given dataset is graded
   with the same formula; on zero-crossing / mixed-sign targets we fall back to the
   parent's damped-relative terms.
2. **New "power-shape" term.**  The log-space affine NMSE of `log|y|` on `log|p|` is zero
   iff `p = k*|y|^a` for some `k, a`, i.e. it recognizes predictions that are right *up to
   a power transform*.  This creates a cheap landmark for whole families such as
   `exp(c*x0^2)`, `x0^a*x1^b`, ... irrespective of the inner constant, guiding the search
   into the correct basin.  It is computed stably from Welford moments of `(log|y|, r)`
   (the parametrization makes the residual identically zero at the perfect-power point) and
   only carries weight 1/8, so power impostors cannot dominate the frontier.
3. **Calibration term is log-scaled instead of saturating.**  The parent's
   `raw/(1+raw)` at weight 1/256 is numerically flat for badly scaled predictions, which
   removes the descent direction the constant optimizer needs when a constant lives inside
   a nonlinearity.  We use `min(log1p(raw_nmse), 20)/20` (weight 1/4): constant slope in
   log-error, so gradient survives at *any* magnitude, yet the penalty grows only
   logarithmically and is capped, so mis-scaled correct structures still beat well-scaled
   wrong ones.
4. **Peak term is now the bounded half-spread of the log-ratio** (max minus min of `r`),
   which is cheaper and scale-free, and directly punishes locally-bad surrogates.

All terms are bounded in `[0, 1]`, all vanish simultaneously only for an exact fit, and no
complexity penalty is applied.  Cost is one tree evaluation plus two linear passes with
Kahan/Welford compensation and two `log` calls per sample on the log path.
"""
function affine_log_shape_uniformity_loss_gen13_gen13_0(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Pass 1: numerically stable Welford moments for the affine fit, plus the
    # target magnitude statistics needed to decide whether a log-space
    # (relative) analysis is meaningful for this dataset.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l
    min_abs_y = L(Inf)
    n_neg_y = 0

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        ap = abs(p)
        ay = abs(y)
        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, ap)
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, ay)
        min_abs_y = min(min_abs_y, ay)
        n_neg_y += ifelse(y < zero_l, 1, 0)

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        # Covariance update uses the freshly updated target mean.
        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Welford sums of squares can go microscopically negative after roundoff.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    relative_tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))
    target_rms = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    prediction_rms = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)
    target_is_variable = target_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_y
    prediction_is_variable = prediction_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_p

    if !target_is_variable
        # Affine shape is undefined for a constant target: fall back to a
        # scale-normalized raw MSE (normalize before squaring to avoid overflow).
        target_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_y)
        raw_sum = zero_l
        raw_compensation = zero_l

        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            p = L(prediction[i])
            y = L(dataset.y[i])
            residual = p - y
            if !isfinite(residual)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            normalized_residual = residual / target_scale
            term = normalized_residual * normalized_residual
            if !isfinite(term)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            corrected = term - raw_compensation
            updated = raw_sum + corrected
            if !isfinite(updated)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            raw_compensation = (updated - raw_sum) - corrected
            raw_sum = updated
        end

        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum / n_l, zero_l)
        loss_value = log1p(raw_nmse)
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
    end

    target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)  # = sqrt(n) * target_rms
    if !(isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Least-squares affine calibration; a constant prediction collapses to mean(y).
    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if prediction_is_variable
        slope = cov_py / m2_p
        intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
        if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Log-path viability depends ONLY on the target, so all candidates on a
    # given dataset are graded with the same functional form: the target must be
    # of one sign and bounded away from zero relative to its own magnitude.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    log_path = ((n_neg_y == 0) || (n_neg_y == n)) &&
               isfinite(min_abs_y) &&
               min_abs_y > L(1e-6) * max_abs_y

    # Predictions may still touch zero; floor them well below any legitimate
    # target magnitude so that log|p| stays finite while a vanishing prediction
    # is (correctly) recorded as a large relative deviation.
    p_floor = L(1e-8) * max_abs_y

    # Damping floor for the fallback relative denominator (parent's scheme).
    rel_floor = target_rms / L(8)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Pass 2: fitted residuals (absolute), raw residuals, and either log-space
    # (relative) statistics or the parent's damped-relative statistics.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    affine_sum = zero_l
    affine_compensation = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l
    raw_compensation = zero_l
    raw_overflowed = false

    # Fallback (linear-space damped relative) accumulators.
    rel_sum = zero_l
    rel_compensation = zero_l
    max_rel_sq = zero_l
    rel_overflowed = false

    # Log-space accumulators: joint Welford over (log|y|, r = log|p| - log|y|).
    mean_ly = zero_l
    mean_r = zero_l
    m2_ly = zero_l
    m2_r = zero_l
    c_lyr = zero_l
    max_r = L(-Inf)
    min_r = L(Inf)

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_residual = p - y
        if !isfinite(raw_residual)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # --- raw calibration term (normalized by ||y - mean(y)||) ---
        if !raw_overflowed
            raw_normalized = raw_residual / target_norm
            raw_term = raw_normalized * raw_normalized
            if isfinite(raw_term)
                corrected = raw_term - raw_compensation
                updated = raw_sum + corrected
                if isfinite(updated)
                    raw_compensation = (updated - raw_sum) - corrected
                    raw_sum = updated
                else
                    raw_overflowed = true
                end
            else
                raw_overflowed = true
            end
        end

        # --- affine-calibrated residual (primary shape signal) ---
        fitted = prediction_is_variable ? muladd(slope, p, intercept) : mean_y
        affine_residual = fitted - y
        affine_normalized = affine_residual / target_norm
        affine_term = affine_normalized * affine_normalized

        if !(isfinite(fitted) && isfinite(affine_residual) &&
             isfinite(affine_normalized) && isfinite(affine_term))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        corrected = affine_term - affine_compensation
        updated = affine_sum + corrected
        if !isfinite(updated)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        affine_compensation = (updated - affine_sum) - corrected
        affine_sum = updated

        # --- fallback: scale-damped relative residual of the calibrated fit ---
        # (always accumulated; it is only used if the log path is unavailable)
        if !rel_overflowed
            rel_denominator = abs(y) + rel_floor
            rel_residual = affine_residual / rel_denominator
            rel_term = rel_residual * rel_residual
            if isfinite(rel_term)
                max_rel_sq = max(max_rel_sq, rel_term)
                corrected_rel = rel_term - rel_compensation
                updated_rel = rel_sum + corrected_rel
                if isfinite(updated_rel)
                    rel_compensation = (updated_rel - rel_sum) - corrected_rel
                    rel_sum = updated_rel
                else
                    rel_overflowed = true
                end
            else
                rel_overflowed = true
            end
        end

        # --- log-space (relative / power) statistics on the raw prediction ---
        if log_path
            ly = log(abs(y))                       # finite: |y| > 0 and finite
            lp = log(max(abs(p), p_floor))          # finite: floor > 0
            # Bound the log-ratio so a single pathological point cannot swamp
            # the statistics (it is already a maximal relative deviation).
            r = clamp(lp - ly, L(-40), L(40))

            max_r = max(max_r, r)
            min_r = min(min_r, r)

            k = L(i)
            d_ly = ly - mean_ly
            d_r = r - mean_r
            mean_ly += d_ly / k
            mean_r += d_r / k
            c_lyr += d_ly * (r - mean_r)
            m2_ly += d_ly * (ly - mean_ly)
            m2_r += d_r * (r - mean_r)
        end
    end

    # The affine optimum can never be worse than predicting mean(y), i.e. NMSE <= 1.
    affine_nmse = clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l)
    shape_term = sqrt(affine_nmse)  # RMSE-like: keeps resolution near exactness

    log_usable = log_path && isfinite(m2_r) && isfinite(m2_ly) &&
                 isfinite(c_lyr) && isfinite(max_r) && isfinite(min_r)

    rel_term_value = zero_l
    peak_term_value = zero_l
    # Neutral default for the power term: mirrors the primary shape signal, so
    # datasets without a usable log path are neither rewarded nor punished.
    power_term_value = shape_term

    if log_usable
        # Dispersion of the log-ratio == scale-invariant relative RMSE.
        var_r = max(m2_r / n_l, zero_l)
        dispersion = sqrt(var_r)
        rel_term_value = dispersion / (one_l + dispersion)

        # Peak (worst-case) relative deviation, bounded.
        half_spread = max((max_r - min_r) / L(2), zero_l)
        peak_term_value = half_spread / (one_l + half_spread)

        # Power-shape: NMSE of the affine fit log|y| ~ a*log|p| + b, expressed
        # through (log|y|, r) moments so that it is *exactly* zero whenever
        # p = k*|y|^a (r affine in log|y|), with no cancellation.
        m2_ly_c = max(m2_ly, zero_l)
        m2_lp = m2_ly_c + L(2) * c_lyr + m2_r
        log_rms_y = sqrt(m2_ly_c / n_l)
        if m2_lp > zero_l && m2_ly_c > zero_l && log_rms_y > L(1e-4)
            cov_lp_ly = m2_ly_c + c_lyr
            ss_res = m2_ly_c - (cov_lp_ly * cov_lp_ly) / m2_lp
            power_nmse = clamp(ss_res / m2_ly_c, zero_l, one_l)
            power_term_value = sqrt(power_nmse)
        end
    else
        # Parent's linear-space damped-relative uniformity (zero-crossing or
        # mixed-sign targets).
        if rel_overflowed
            rel_term_value = one_l
            peak_term_value = one_l
        else
            rel_mse = max(rel_sum / n_l, zero_l)
            rel_term_value = sqrt(rel_mse / (one_l + rel_mse))
            peak_rel = sqrt(max(max_rel_sq, zero_l))
            peak_term_value = peak_rel / (one_l + peak_rel)
        end
    end

    # Magnitude calibration: linear in log-error (constant gradient in log space,
    # so the constant optimizer always has a descent direction), capped so that a
    # wildly mis-scaled but structurally correct candidate is never crushed.
    calibration_value = if raw_overflowed
        one_l
    else
        t = log1p(max(raw_sum, zero_l))
        isfinite(t) ? min(t, L(20)) / L(20) : one_l
    end

    # Weights: shape dominates; log-relative uniformity is the strong secondary
    # signal; power-shape is a mild landmark bonus; peak deviation regularizes;
    # calibration keeps the magnitude honest without dictating the search.
    relative_weight = one_l / L(4)
    peak_weight = one_l / L(16)
    power_weight = one_l / L(8)
    calibration_weight = one_l / L(4)

    loss_value =
        shape_term +
        relative_weight * rel_term_value +
        peak_weight * peak_term_value +
        power_weight * power_term_value +
        calibration_weight * calibration_value

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

pareto_age_density_tournament_gen13_2.name: pareto_age_density_tournament_gen13_2
pareto_age_density_tournament_gen13_2.code:
"""
    pareto_age_density_tournament_gen13_2(
        pop::Population{T,L,N},
        running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
        options::AbstractOptions,
    )::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}

Multi-objective tournament selection operator integrating local Pareto non-domination,
adaptive complexity-frequency niching, and lineage youth regularization.

# Core Idea & Motivation
Standard tournament selection on scalar parsimony costs frequently falls into deep local
minima where bloated expressions with marginal numerical improvements crowd out simpler,
structurally correct building blocks. This operator combats premature convergence and bloat
through three complementary mechanisms:

1. **Tournament Pareto Dominance Filtering**: Evaluates candidates simultaneously on Loss
   and Complexity. Non-dominated candidates (Pareto dominance count = 0) are strictly prioritized
   over dominated ones, preserving simpler structural stepping stones at lower complexities.
2. **Adaptive Complexity Density Niching**: Incorporates normalized complexity frequencies
   to penalize over-crowded complexity bins and incentivize exploration of sparse structural sizes.
3. **Youth Novelty Regularization**: Uses candidate birth order to apply a modest discount
   to recent mutations and crossovers, preventing stagnant ancient lineages from monopolizing
   the selection pool and giving new algebraic topologies time to optimize constants.

# Steps
1. Sample `tournament_selection_n` candidates without replacement from the population.
2. Extract sanitized loss, complexity, and birth order for each candidate.
3. Compute pairwise Pareto dominance counts within the sample: candidate `j` dominates `i`
   iff `(loss_j <= loss_i && comp_j <= comp_i) && (loss_j < loss_i || comp_j < comp_i)`.
4. Calculate adjusted parsimony-youth cost combining base cost, adaptive parsimony scaling,
   and relative youth bonus.
5. Rank candidates lexicographically by `(dominance_count, adjusted_cost)`.
6. Select the top candidate (if `p == 1.0`) or sample according to the geometric rank
   probability distribution (if `p < 1.0`).
"""
function pareto_age_density_tournament_gen13_2(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Guard against tournament size exceeding population count
    sample_size = min(options.tournament_selection_n, pop.n)
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, sample_size; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)

    # Fast path for trivial tournament
    n == 1 && return sample[1]

    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    use_frequency = options.use_frequency_in_tournament

    # Pre-allocate feature vectors for the tournament sample
    losses = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    births = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)

    min_birth = typemax(Int)
    max_birth = typemin(Int)

    # Extract sanitized metrics for all tournament candidates
    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]
        raw_loss = member.loss
        losses[i] = if isnan(raw_loss) || isinf(raw_loss)
            typemax(L) / L(4)
        else
            raw_loss
        end

        raw_cost = member.cost
        costs[i] = if isnan(raw_cost) || isinf(raw_cost)
            typemax(L) / L(4)
        else
            raw_cost
        end

        c = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = c

        b = member.birth
        births[i] = b
        min_birth = min(min_birth, b)
        max_birth = max(max_birth, b)
    end

    # Compute pairwise Pareto dominance count within the tournament sample.
    # An individual j dominates i iff it is as good in both loss & complexity and strictly better in at least one.
    dom_counts = zeros(Int, n)
    for i in 1:n
        l_i = losses[i]
        c_i = complexities[i]
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue
            l_j = losses[j]
            c_j = complexities[j]
            if (l_j <= l_i && c_j <= c_i) && (l_j < l_i || c_j < c_i)
                dom_counts[i] += 1
            end
        end
    end

    # Calculate adjusted costs integrating frequency parsimony scaling and youth bonus
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    birth_range = max(max_birth - min_birth, 1)
    youth_scale = L(0.15) # Gentle 15% discount for the freshest innovations

    for i in 1:n
        # Parsimony factor based on complexity bin density
        parsimony_factor = if use_frequency
            c = complexities[i]
            freq = if (0 < c <= length(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies))
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * freq)
        else
            L(1)
        end

        # Youth factor: younger candidates (higher birth) receive a slight discount
        relative_youth = L(births[i] - min_birth) / L(birth_range)
        youth_factor = L(1) - (youth_scale * relative_youth)

        base_cost = costs[i]
        adjusted_costs[i] = if base_cost >= L(0)
            base_cost * parsimony_factor * youth_factor
        else
            (base_cost * youth_factor) / parsimony_factor
        end
    end

    # Tournament selection with Pareto-lexicographic priority
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        # Deterministic winner: lowest dominance count first, lowest adjusted cost as tiebreaker
        best_idx = 1
        for i in 2:n
            if dom_counts[i] < dom_counts[best_idx]
                best_idx = i
            elseif dom_counts[i] == dom_counts[best_idx] && adjusted_costs[i] < adjusted_costs[best_idx]
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        best_idx
    else
        # Stochastic tournament: sort candidates lexicographically by (dom_count, adjusted_cost)
        perm = sortperm(1:n; by=i -> (dom_counts[i], adjusted_costs[i]))
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        perm[tournament_winner]
    end

    return sample[chosen_idx]
end

symmetric_motif_duplication_gen10_1_gen1.name: symmetric_motif_duplication_gen10_1_gen13_4
symmetric_motif_duplication_gen10_1_gen1.code:
"""
    symmetric_motif_duplication_gen10_1_gen13_4(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

A structural mutation operator that duplicates an evolved subexpression *motif*, optionally
re-indexes its feature leaves (identity / targeted substitution / cyclic shift), and couples the
copy back into the tree with a symmetry-friendly binary operator, occasionally wrapping the
coupled pair in a unary envelope.

# Core Idea
Physical laws are full of repeated functional forms coupled together: `0.5*m*(vx^2 + vy^2)`,
`(x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2`, `sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)`, `exp(-E/kT)`. Such structures are extremely hard to
reach by single-node edits, but trivial to reach if an already-discovered motif can be *cloned*,
*re-indexed*, and *re-coupled*. This operator performs exactly that macro-move.

# Steps
1. Bail out if no binary operators exist.
2. Compute a **size budget** from `options.maxsize` so the produced tree can actually survive the
   complexity filter; refuse to act (no-op) if there is no room.
3. Sample a donor subtree that (a) fits the budget and (b) actually contains a feature leaf
   (constant-only motifs carry no structure); fall back to any budget-fitting node.
4. Apply one of three feature transforms to the deep copy:
   * identity (prob ~0.35) → self-coupling, yields powers / rational self-terms like `(x/y)^2`;
   * targeted substitution (prob ~0.35) → swap *one* feature that occurs in the motif for another,
     yielding partial symmetries (`f(x1,x2) ⊕ f(x1,x3)`);
   * cyclic shift (prob ~0.30) → shift all features, yielding full dimensional replication.
5. Pick a coupling target: with prob 0.3 the **root** (whole-expression coupling, the move needed
   to build `A ⊕ B` top-level laws), otherwise a uniformly random node.
6. Pick the coupling operator with a bias toward `+`, `*`, `-` (the operators that actually express
   physical symmetry), while *avoiding* degenerate couplings (`x + x`, `x - x`, `x / x`) when the
   motif is structurally identical to the target and no feature transform was applied.
7. With prob 0.25 (and if the budget allows) wrap the coupled pair in a random unary operator,
   enabling composite forms like `sqrt(a^2 + b^2)`, `exp(a*b)`, `1/sqrt(1 - (v/c)^2)` — precisely the
   kind of envelope the search trace failed to reach (it plateaued on rational surrogates of
   `x0/sqrt(1 - x1^2/x2^2)`).

# Changes vs. Parent
- **Size-aware**: the parent could nearly double the tree, so most proposals were discarded by the
  complexity limit. Donors are now filtered by a `maxsize` budget, and the operator becomes a
  cheap no-op instead of emitting an unusable tree.
- **Informative donors**: motifs must contain at least one variable leaf (constant clones were pure
  waste in the parent).
- **Degeneracy guard**: structural equality test prevents `x + x` / `x - x` / `x / x` couplings,
  routing identical motif/target pairs to multiplicative coupling (i.e. squaring), which is useful.
- **Operator bias**: symmetry couplings are drawn preferentially from `+`, `*`, `-` instead of
  uniformly over all binary operators.
- **Reintroduced (cheaply) the targeted feature substitution path** the parent dropped, since pure
  cyclic shifts cannot express partial symmetries; all three modes share one weighted branch.
- **Unary envelope** restored in a budgeted, probabilistic form to allow `g(A ⊕ B)` composites.
- **Root-biased target selection** to make top-level additive/multiplicative coupling reachable.
"""
function symmetric_motif_duplication_gen10_1_gen13_4(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Guard: binary coupling requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # ---------------- helpers ----------------

    # Cyclically permute every feature index in the motif
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int, nf::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nf)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift, nf)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Replace one specific feature index by another (targeted substitution)
    function _remap_feature!(node, from::Int, to::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant && node.feature == from
                node.feature = to
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _remap_feature!(get_child(node, i), from, to)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Collect the distinct feature indices used by a subtree
    function _collect_features!(acc::Vector{Int}, node)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant && !(node.feature in acc)
                push!(acc, node.feature)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _collect_features!(acc, get_child(node, i))
            end
        end
        return acc
    end

    # Structural (syntactic) equality, used only for degeneracy detection
    function _structurally_equal(a, b)
        a.degree == b.degree || return false
        if a.degree == 0
            a.constant == b.constant || return false
            return a.constant ? (a.val == b.val) : (a.feature == b.feature)
        end
        a.op == b.op || return false
        for i in 1:(a.degree)
            _structurally_equal(get_child(a, i), get_child(b, i)) || return false
        end
        return true
    end

    _has_feature(node) = any(t -> t.degree == 0 && !t.constant, node)

    # ---------------- Step 2: size budget ----------------
    # New size = tree_size + size(motif) + 1 (coupling op) [+ 1 if unary envelope]
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : 30
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    budget = maxsize - tree_size - 1           # max allowed motif size
    budget < 1 && return tree                  # no room: cheap no-op

    # ---------------- Step 3: donor selection ----------------
    _donor_ok(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget && _has_feature(t)
    local donor
    if any(_donor_ok, tree)
        donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_donor_ok))
    else
        _fits(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget
        any(_fits, tree) || return tree
        donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_fits))
    end
    motif = copy(donor)

    # ---------------- Step 4: feature transform ----------------
    transformed = false
    if nfeatures > 1
        r = rand(rng)
        if r < 0.35
            # identity: self-coupling (squares, rational self-terms)
        elseif r < 0.70
            # targeted substitution: partial symmetry f(x1,x2) ⊕ f(x1,x3)
            feats = _collect_features!(Int[], motif)
            if !isempty(feats)
                from = feats[rand(rng, 1:length(feats))]
                to = rand(rng, filter(!=(from), 1:nfeatures))
                _remap_feature!(motif, from, to)
                transformed = true
            end
        else
            # full cyclic shift: dimensional replication
            shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
            _shift_features!(motif, shift, nfeatures)
            transformed = true
        end
    end

    # ---------------- Step 5: target selection ----------------
    # Bias toward the root so that whole-expression couplings (A ⊕ B) are reachable
    target = rand(rng) < 0.3 ? tree : rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))

    # ---------------- Step 6: coupling operator ----------------
    binops = options.operators.binops
    nbin = options.nops[2]
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (+), binops)
    times_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (*), binops)
    minus_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (-), binops)
    div_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (/), binops)

    # If motif and target are literally the same expression, `+`/`-`/`/` collapse trivially
    degenerate = !transformed && _structurally_equal(motif, target)

    local bin_op::Int
    if degenerate
        if times_idx !== nothing
            bin_op = times_idx                 # x*x = square: informative
        else
            cands = [i for i in 1:nbin if i != plus_idx && i != minus_idx && i != div_idx]
            bin_op = isempty(cands) ? rand(rng, 1:nbin) : cands[rand(rng, 1:length(cands))]
        end
    else
        preferred = Int[]
        for idx in (plus_idx, times_idx, minus_idx)
            idx === nothing || push!(preferred, idx)
        end
        bin_op = if !isempty(preferred) && rand(rng) < 0.7
            preferred[rand(rng, 1:length(preferred))]
        else
            rand(rng, 1:nbin)
        end
    end

    # ---------------- Step 7: build and splice ----------------
    target_copy = copy(target)
    # Randomize operand order to support non-commutative operators
    children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
    new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children)

    # Optional unary envelope g(A ⊕ B): sqrt(a^2+b^2), exp(a*b), 1/sqrt(1-(v/c)^2), ...
    if options.nops[1] > 0 && (count_nodes(motif) + 1) <= budget && rand(rng) < 0.25
        new_node = constructorof(N)(;
            op=rand(rng, 1:options.nops[1]),
            children=(new_node,),
        )
    end

    set_node!(target, new_node)

    return tree
end

age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen13_.name: age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen13_5
age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen13_.code:
"""
Synthesizes the age-regularized replacement strategy with a cost-awareness safeguard.

Core idea: pure age-based survival (as in both parents) cycles out the oldest member
regardless of fitness, which can accidentally evict a fresh good solution while
protecting a stale mediocre one, contributing to search stagnation (e.g. getting
trapped in local complexity/loss plateaus as seen in long-running Pareto fronts).
This operator keeps age as the dominant signal (preserving the original
age-regularized evolution behavior and its diversity benefits) but:
  1. Never selects the single best-cost member in the population for replacement,
     acting as an elitism safeguard so a lucky good discovery is not lost to age alone.
  2. Among the remaining (non-elite, non-excluded) members, computes a combined
     replacement-priority score that mixes normalized age (older -> higher priority)
     with normalized cost (worse cost -> higher priority), so that when several
     members are similarly old, the search preferentially discards the worse
     performer, freeing slots for exploration while protecting promising young or
     elite members.
  3. Falls back to pure age-based selection if all members are excluded/elite-tied,
     to remain robust in edge cases (e.g. tiny populations).
"""
function age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen13_5(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)

    # Identify the global best (lowest cost) member to protect it from eviction,
    # unless doing so would leave us with no valid candidates.
    costs = [pop.members[i].cost for i in 1:n]
    best_idx = argmin_fast(costs)

    # Build the exclusion mask: explicitly excluded indices plus the elite best.
    protected = Set(exclude_indices)
    push!(protected, best_idx)

    # Gather births and costs for non-protected members.
    births = [(i in protected) ? typemax(BT) : pop.members[i].birth for i in 1:n]
    valid_mask = [!(i in protected) for i in 1:n]

    if !any(valid_mask)
        # Fallback: nothing left but excluded/elite members, so just use pure
        # age-regularized selection over the truly excluded set (ignore elite
        # protection) to guarantee a valid return.
        fallback_births = [(i in exclude_indices) ? typemax(BT) : pop.members[i].birth
                            for i in 1:n]
        return argmin_fast(fallback_births)
    end

    # Normalize age: older members (smaller birth) get higher removal priority.
    valid_births = [births[i] for i in 1:n if valid_mask[i]]
    min_b, max_b = extrema(valid_births)
    age_span = max(max_b - min_b, one(BT))

    # Normalize cost: worse (higher) cost gets higher removal priority.
    valid_costs = [costs[i] for i in 1:n if valid_mask[i]]
    min_c, max_c = extrema(valid_costs)
    cost_span = max(max_c - min_c, eps(L))

    # Weight age more heavily than cost to preserve the age-regularized character
    # of the original strategy, while still nudging the search away from stale,
    # underperforming members.
    age_weight = 0.7
    cost_weight = 0.3

    best_score = -Inf
    replace_idx = -1
    for i in 1:n
        if !valid_mask[i]
            continue
        end
        # Higher score = higher priority for replacement.
        age_priority = Float64(max_b - births[i]) / Float64(age_span)
        cost_priority = Float64(costs[i] - min_c) / Float64(cost_span)
        score = age_weight * age_priority + cost_weight * cost_priority
        if score > best_score
            best_score = score
            replace_idx = i
        end
    end

    return replace_idx
end

soft_relative_affine_shape_loss_gen13_6.name: soft_relative_affine_shape_loss_gen13_6
soft_relative_affine_shape_loss_gen13_6.code:
"""
    soft_relative_affine_shape_loss_gen13_6(tree, dataset, options)

Measure both numerical accuracy and structural agreement with the target. Targets and
predictions are normalized by a stably computed target RMS, then softly weighted by
`1 / (0.05 + ŷ²)` so samples near zero remain well-conditioned while no output-magnitude
regime dominates the search. The loss blends the direct weighted squared error with the
residual from the best weighted affine calibration `ŷ ≈ a * prediction̂ + b`. This
affine-profiled component rewards candidates that discover the correct functional shape
before constants and offsets are fully optimized, while the direct component ensures
that only correctly calibrated predictions achieve zero loss. The fixed 65/35 blend and
5% relative-error floor are heuristics intended for mixed-scale symbolic-regression data.
"""
function soft_relative_affine_shape_loss_gen13_6(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)

    # Compute the target RMS with a scaled sum-of-squares algorithm to avoid overflow.
    target_scale = zero_l
    scaled_ssq = zero_l
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        yi = L(dataset.y[i])
        pi = L(prediction[i])
        if !isfinite(yi) || !isfinite(pi)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        ayi = abs(yi)
        if ayi != zero_l
            if target_scale < ayi
                ratio = target_scale / ayi
                scaled_ssq = one_l + scaled_ssq * ratio * ratio
                target_scale = ayi
            else
                ratio = ayi / target_scale
                scaled_ssq += ratio * ratio
            end
        end
    end

    if target_scale != zero_l
        rms_scale = target_scale * sqrt(scaled_ssq / L(n))
        target_scale = rms_scale > zero_l ? rms_scale : target_scale
    else
        # A unit scale keeps an identically zero target well-defined.
        target_scale = one_l
    end

    relative_floor = L(0.05)
    weight_sum = zero_l
    direct_sum = zero_l

    # Weighted online moments provide a stable affine-profiled residual in one pass.
    mean_prediction = zero_l
    mean_target = zero_l
    prediction_ss = zero_l
    target_ss = zero_l
    prediction_target_ss = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        pn = L(prediction[i]) / target_scale
        yn = L(dataset.y[i]) / target_scale
        if !isfinite(pn) || !isfinite(yn)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        weight = inv(relative_floor + yn * yn)
        residual = pn - yn
        direct_sum += (weight * residual) * residual

        new_weight_sum = weight_sum + weight
        delta_prediction = pn - mean_prediction
        delta_target = yn - mean_target
        fraction = weight / new_weight_sum

        new_mean_prediction = mean_prediction + fraction * delta_prediction
        new_mean_target = mean_target + fraction * delta_target

        prediction_ss += weight * delta_prediction * (pn - new_mean_prediction)
        target_ss += weight * delta_target * (yn - new_mean_target)
        prediction_target_ss +=
            weight * delta_prediction * (yn - new_mean_target)

        weight_sum = new_weight_sum
        mean_prediction = new_mean_prediction
        mean_target = new_mean_target
    end

    if !isfinite(weight_sum) || weight_sum <= zero_l ||
       !isfinite(direct_sum) || !isfinite(prediction_ss) ||
       !isfinite(target_ss) || !isfinite(prediction_target_ss)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    direct_loss = direct_sum / weight_sum

    # The best affine residual equals target variance times one minus correlation².
    prediction_ss = max(prediction_ss, zero_l)
    target_ss = max(target_ss, zero_l)
    shape_sum = target_ss
    if prediction_ss > zero_l && target_ss > zero_l
        correlation = abs(prediction_target_ss) /
                      sqrt(prediction_ss) / sqrt(target_ss)
        correlation = min(one_l, max(zero_l, correlation))
        shape_sum = target_ss * max(zero_l, one_l - correlation * correlation)
    end
    shape_loss = shape_sum / weight_sum

    loss = (L(13) * direct_loss + L(7) * shape_loss) / L(20)
    return isfinite(loss) ? max(zero_l, L(loss)) : L(Inf)
end

motif_symmetry_duplication_gen5_gen13_7.name: motif_symmetry_duplication_gen5_gen13_7
motif_symmetry_duplication_gen5_gen13_7.code:
"""
    motif_symmetry_duplication_gen5_gen13_7(tree::N, dataset, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

A structural, size-aware and *data-aware* mutation operator that extracts a modular
subexpression ("motif"), permutes its feature indices, and recombines it with the host
expression either by binary coupling or by homologous grafting.

# Motivation & Core Idea
Ground-truth scientific formulas are dominated by repeated structural motifs under
feature permutations: Euclidean distances `(x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2`, coupled oscillators
`sin(x1) + sin(x2)`, multilinear products `x1*x2*x3`, rational envelopes `u/(1+u^2)`,
and polynomial powers `u*u`. Reaching such structures by independent point mutations
requires many simultaneous lucky steps. This operator instead *replicates an already
evolved subtree* and re-indexes its variables, giving a single-step route to symmetric
and self-coupled forms.

# Steps & Heuristics
1. **Donor selection (structure-biased, size-capped).** Sample the motif preferentially
   from *operator* nodes (leaves carry no structure to replicate) whose size fits the
   remaining complexity budget `maxsize - size(tree)`.
2. **Candidate feature transformations.** Build a small set of transformed clones:
   cyclic feature shift (preserves relational sub-structure), targeted single-feature
   substitution *biased toward features not yet used anywhere in the tree* (drives
   coverage of all relevant variables), and identity (enables powers / self-coupling).
3. **Data-driven pick.** Evaluate the host tree once on a random subsample of the data,
   form the residual, then score each candidate motif by `|cor(motif, residual)|` and
   keep the best (with 20% random exploration to avoid greedy collapse). The sign of the
   correlation also selects `+` vs `-` and the operand order.
4. **Integration.**
   - *Binary coupling*: wrap the donor, the tree root, or a random node together with the
     motif under a binary operator, biased toward `+`/`*` (the way motifs actually combine
     in physical laws). Occasionally the motif is first wrapped in a unary envelope
     (`x2 -> sin(x2)`) to build things like `sin(x1)+sin(x2)` from a bare leaf.
   - *Homologous grafting*: replace a node **other than the donor itself** (avoids no-op
     mutations) with the evolved motif, choosing a target large enough that the size budget
     is respected.

# What changed vs. the parent
- Accepts and *uses* `dataset`: residual-correlation ranking of the candidate feature
  permutations instead of a blind random roll (parent chose the mapping by coin flip).
- Feature substitution now prefers *unused* features, which is what actually completes a
  symmetry over all variables.
- Complexity-budget awareness (`options.maxsize`): donor size caps, graft-target size
  filtering, and a graft-preferring mode when the tree is nearly at max size — this
  drastically reduces mutations rejected for being oversized.
- Donor sampling biased to operator nodes (real motifs) rather than uniform over all nodes.
- Guarantees graft targets differ from the donor, removing the parent's silent no-op case.
- Operator choice biased to `+`/`*`, with `-` selected (and operand order fixed) when the
  motif is anti-correlated with the residual.
- Optional unary envelope on the duplicated motif.
- All previous fallbacks (no binary operators, no features, single feature) are preserved.
"""
function motif_symmetry_duplication_gen5_gen13_7(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # ---------------- local helpers ----------------
    # Collect all active feature indices inside a subtree
    function _collect_features!(node, feats::Vector{Int})
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                push!(feats, node.feature)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _collect_features!(get_child(node, i), feats)
            end
        end
        return feats
    end

    # Cyclically shift every feature leaf of a subtree
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int, num_features::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, num_features)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift, num_features)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Replace one specific feature index by another throughout a subtree
    function _remap_feature!(node, from_f::Int, to_f::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant && node.feature == from_f
                node.feature = to_f
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _remap_feature!(get_child(node, i), from_f, to_f)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # ---------------- 0. fallback: no binary operators configured ----------------
    if options.nops[2] == 0
        if options.nops[1] > 0
            node = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
            new_node = constructorof(N)(;
                op=rand(rng, 1:options.nops[1]), children=(copy(node),)
            )
            set_node!(node, new_node)
        end
        return tree
    end

    total_nodes = count_nodes(tree)
    # Remaining complexity budget (fall back to a sane default if maxsize is absent)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : 30
    room = maxsize - total_nodes

    # ---------------- 1. choose integration mode & donor size cap ----------------
    can_graft = total_nodes > 3
    # When the tree is nearly at max size, grafting (which can shrink) is much safer
    p_graft = can_graft ? (room <= 2 ? 0.85 : 0.30) : 0.0
    do_graft = rand(rng) < p_graft
    if room < 2 && !do_graft
        # No room to grow by coupling: graft if possible, otherwise leave the tree alone
        can_graft || return tree
        do_graft = true
    end

    # Donor must fit the budget when we are going to *add* it (coupling adds size(motif)+1)
    donor_cap = do_graft ? total_nodes : max(1, room - 1)
    _size_ok(t) = count_nodes(t) <= donor_cap

    # ---------------- 2. donor selection (structure-biased) ----------------
    n_op_cand = count(t -> t.degree > 0 && _size_ok(t), tree)
    donor = if n_op_cand > 0 && rand(rng) < 0.75
        # Prefer genuine motifs (operator subtrees) over bare leaves
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> t.degree > 0 && _size_ok(t)))
    else
        n_any = count(_size_ok, tree)
        n_any == 0 && return tree
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_size_ok))
    end

    # ---------------- 3. build candidate feature-space transformations ----------------
    donor_feats = unique(_collect_features!(donor, Int[]))
    tree_feats = unique(_collect_features!(tree, Int[]))
    unused_feats = [f for f in 1:nfeatures if !(f in tree_feats)]

    candidates = N[]
    if isempty(donor_feats) || nfeatures <= 1
        # Constant-only motif or single-feature problem: only the identity map exists
        push!(candidates, copy(donor))
    else
        # (a) cyclic permutation of all variables (keeps relational structure intact)
        c_shift = copy(donor)
        _shift_features!(c_shift, rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1)), nfeatures)
        push!(candidates, c_shift)

        # (b) targeted substitution, preferring a feature the tree does not use yet
        f_old = rand(rng, donor_feats)
        pool = isempty(unused_feats) ? [f for f in 1:nfeatures if f != f_old] : unused_feats
        if !isempty(pool)
            c_sub = copy(donor)
            _remap_feature!(c_sub, f_old, rand(rng, pool))
            push!(candidates, c_sub)
            # (b2) a second, different substitution target when several remain
            if length(pool) > 1
                c_sub2 = copy(donor)
                _remap_feature!(c_sub2, rand(rng, donor_feats), rand(rng, pool))
                push!(candidates, c_sub2)
            end
        end

        # (c) identity: fosters powers (u*u) and rational self-coupling u/(1+u)
        push!(candidates, copy(donor))
    end

    # ---------------- 4. data-driven selection among candidates ----------------
    motif = candidates[1]
    chosen_cor = 0.0
    if length(candidates) > 1
        best_k, best_score, best_cor = 0, -1.0, 0.0
        y = dataset.y
        if y !== nothing && dataset.n > 3
            # Cheap evaluation on a bounded random subsample of columns (samples)
            nsub = min(dataset.n, 128)
            idx = nsub == dataset.n ? collect(1:dataset.n) : rand(rng, 1:dataset.n, nsub)
            Xs = dataset.X[:, idx]
            ys = y[idx]
            base, ok = eval_tree_array(tree, Xs, options.operators)
            if ok && all(isfinite, base)
                resid = ys .- base
                sr = std(resid)
                if isfinite(sr) && sr > 0
                    for (k, cand) in enumerate(candidates)
                        vals, ok2 = eval_tree_array(cand, Xs, options.operators)
                        (ok2 && all(isfinite, vals)) || continue
                        sv = std(vals)
                        (isfinite(sv) && sv > 0) || continue
                        cval = cor(vals, resid)
                        isfinite(cval) || continue
                        score = abs(Float64(cval))
                        if score > best_score
                            best_score, best_k, best_cor = score, k, Float64(cval)
                        end
                    end
                end
            end
        end
        if best_k == 0 || rand(rng) < 0.2
            # No usable data signal, or deliberate exploration step
            motif = candidates[rand(rng, 1:length(candidates))]
        else
            motif = candidates[best_k]
            chosen_cor = best_cor
        end
    end

    motif_size = count_nodes(motif)

    # ---------------- 5. integration ----------------
    if do_graft
        # Homologous grafting: replace some *other* node with the evolved motif.
        # Prefer targets large enough that the size budget is not blown.
        min_target = motif_size - room
        n_fit = count(t -> t !== donor && count_nodes(t) >= min_target, tree)
        target = if n_fit > 0
            rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> t !== donor && count_nodes(t) >= min_target))
        else
            n_other = count(t -> t !== donor, tree)
            n_other > 0 ? rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> t !== donor)) : donor
        end
        set_node!(target, motif)
    else
        # Occasionally wrap the motif in a unary envelope: turns `x1 + x2` seeds into
        # `x1 + sin(x2)`-type structures in a single step.
        if options.nops[1] > 0 && room >= motif_size + 2 && rand(rng) < 0.15
            motif = constructorof(N)(;
                op=rand(rng, 1:options.nops[1]), children=(motif,)
            )
        end

        # Coupling site: the donor itself (local symmetry), the root (global additive
        # symmetry, e.g. f(x1) + f(x2)), or any random node.
        roll = rand(rng)
        target = roll < 0.40 ? donor : (roll < 0.70 ? tree : rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree)))
        target_copy = copy(target)

        # Operator choice: strongly bias to `+` / `*`, the way motifs combine in real laws
        bin_op = rand(rng, 1:options.nops[2])
        plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (+), options.operators.binops)
        times_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (*), options.operators.binops)
        minus_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (-), options.operators.binops)
        flip_order = rand(rng, Bool)

        if abs(chosen_cor) > 0.3 && (plus_idx !== nothing || minus_idx !== nothing)
            # Data says the motif tracks (or anti-tracks) the residual: add or subtract it
            if chosen_cor > 0
                bin_op = plus_idx === nothing ? minus_idx : plus_idx
                flip_order = false
            else
                bin_op = minus_idx === nothing ? plus_idx : minus_idx
                flip_order = false  # (target - motif): order matters for subtraction
            end
        elseif rand(rng) < 0.7
            prefs = Int[]
            plus_idx === nothing || push!(prefs, plus_idx)
            times_idx === nothing || push!(prefs, times_idx)
            isempty(prefs) || (bin_op = rand(rng, prefs))
        end

        children_tuple = flip_order ? (motif, target_copy) : (target_copy, motif)
        new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children_tuple)
        set_node!(target, new_node)
    end

    return tree
end

motif_symmetry_envelope_mutation_gen13_8.name: motif_symmetry_envelope_mutation_gen13_8
motif_symmetry_envelope_mutation_gen13_8.code:
"""
    motif_symmetry_envelope_mutation_gen13_8(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

A structural mutation operator that duplicates an evolved subexpression *motif*, optionally maps it
into a different part of feature space (symmetry replication), and then re-inserts it either by
direct coupling, homologous grafting, or by wrapping it inside a **constant-anchored envelope**
(e.g. `sqrt(1 - u)`, `1/(1 + u)`, `exp(-u)`).

# Core idea (synthesis of both parents)
Parent 1 contributed a rich set of feature-space symmetry maps (cyclic permutation, targeted
single-feature substitution, identity for self-coupling) plus two insertion modes (binary coupling
and homologous grafting) and a unary fallback. Parent 2 contributed a lean, uniform code path with
cheap cyclic shifts. This operator keeps Parent 1's expressive symmetry maps and insertion choices
in a compact, Parent-2-style single pass, and adds one new synthesized capability motivated by
observed search failures:

Traces on tasks such as `x0 / sqrt(1 - x1^2/x2^2)` show that search quickly discovers the correct
*inner* motif (`x1/x2`, `square(x1/x2)`) but then wastes enormous effort on additive/multiplicative
patch-ups (`x0 + x0*x1*sqrt(x1)/(x2-x1)`, `x0*exp(square(x1/x2))`) because reaching the true form
requires *several simultaneous* structural steps: pair the motif with a unit constant, apply a
binary operator, and wrap the result in a unary op. The **envelope** insertion mode performs exactly
that composite step atomically, biasing the constant toward `±1` since saturating/relativistic/
rational envelopes in physics are almost always anchored at unity.

# Steps
1. Guard: if no binary operators exist, degrade gracefully to a unary wrap (Parent 1's fallback).
2. Sample a donor subtree, biased (75%) toward composite (operator) nodes so motifs are meaningful
   functional units rather than bare leaves; deep-copy it into an independent motif.
3. Apply one feature-space transformation to the motif (only if it contains variables and
   `nfeatures > 1`):
   - cyclic shift of all feature indices (replicates relational structure across dimensions),
   - targeted substitution of one present feature (asymmetric couplings),
   - identity (enables powers `u*u` and rational self-coupling).
4. Re-insert the motif using one of three modes:
   - **Envelope (≈30%)**: build `binop(const, motif)` with a unit-biased constant, optionally wrap
     in a unary op, then graft it over a target node or couple it to the target.
   - **Homologous graft (≈20%, trees with >3 nodes)**: replace a random node with the motif.
   - **Binary coupling (rest)**: wrap a target node and the motif under a random binary operator,
     with randomized operand order for non-commutative ops.

# Assumptions
Operations are in-place on `tree`; the root is never removed, so the same node object is returned.
"""
function motif_symmetry_envelope_mutation_gen13_8(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # ---- local helpers -------------------------------------------------------
    # Collect all active (non-constant) feature indices inside a subtree
    function _collect_features!(node, feats::Vector{Int})
        if node.degree == 0
            !node.constant && push!(feats, node.feature)
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _collect_features!(get_child(node, i), feats)
            end
        end
        return feats
    end

    # Cyclically shift every feature leaf in a subtree
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int, num_features::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, num_features)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift, num_features)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Replace one specific feature index by another throughout a subtree
    function _remap_feature!(node, from_f::Int, to_f::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant && node.feature == from_f
                node.feature = to_f
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _remap_feature!(get_child(node, i), from_f, to_f)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    nuna = options.nops[1]
    nbin = options.nops[2]

    # ---- Step 1: fallback when binary coupling is impossible -----------------
    if nbin == 0
        if nuna > 0
            node = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
            set_node!(
                node,
                constructorof(N)(; op=rand(rng, 1:nuna), children=(copy(node),)),
            )
        end
        return tree
    end

    # ---- Step 2: sample the donor motif, biased toward composite subtrees ----
    has_op = any(t -> t.degree > 0, tree)
    donor = if has_op && rand(rng) < 0.75
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> t.degree > 0))
    else
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    end
    motif = copy(donor)

    # ---- Step 3: feature-space symmetry transformation -----------------------
    if nfeatures > 1
        feats = _collect_features!(motif, Int[])
        if !isempty(feats)
            roll = rand(rng)
            if roll < 0.45
                # Cyclic permutation: replicate the same relational form on other variables
                _shift_features!(motif, rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1)), nfeatures)
            elseif roll < 0.70
                # Targeted substitution: swap a single variable occurring in the motif
                f_old = rand(rng, feats)
                targets = [f for f in 1:nfeatures if f != f_old]
                if !isempty(targets)
                    _remap_feature!(motif, f_old, rand(rng, targets))
                end
            end
            # else: identity map -> powers (u*u) / rational self-coupling
        end
    end

    # ---- Step 4: re-insertion --------------------------------------------------
    total_nodes = count_nodes(tree)
    mode = rand(rng)

    if mode < 0.30
        # Envelope mode: build const∘motif, optionally under a unary op, in one atomic step.
        # Unit-biased constants because physical envelopes are anchored at 1 (1-u, 1+u, u/(1+u)).
        cval = if rand(rng) < 0.65
            rand(rng, Bool) ? one(T) : -one(T)
        else
            T(randn(rng))
        end
        const_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=cval)
        inner_children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (const_leaf, motif) : (motif, const_leaf)
        enveloped = constructorof(N)(; op=rand(rng, 1:nbin), children=inner_children)

        # Optional unary jacket: yields sqrt(1-u), exp(-u), log(1+u), ...
        if nuna > 0 && rand(rng) < 0.6
            enveloped = constructorof(N)(; op=rand(rng, 1:nuna), children=(enveloped,))
        end

        target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
        if rand(rng) < 0.5
            # Graft the envelope over an existing (often redundant) subtree
            set_node!(target, enveloped)
        else
            # Or couple it multiplicatively/divisively with the target term
            tcopy = copy(target)
            kids = rand(rng, Bool) ? (tcopy, enveloped) : (enveloped, tcopy)
            set_node!(target, constructorof(N)(; op=rand(rng, 1:nbin), children=kids))
        end
    elseif total_nodes > 3 && mode < 0.50
        # Homologous grafting: transplant the transformed motif over another node
        target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
        set_node!(target, motif)
    else
        # Binary coupling: pair the motif with the donor itself or another node
        target = rand(rng, Bool) ? donor : rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
        tcopy = copy(target)
        kids = rand(rng, Bool) ? (tcopy, motif) : (motif, tcopy)
        set_node!(target, constructorof(N)(; op=rand(rng, 1:nbin), children=kids))
    end

    return tree
end

symmetry_aware_motif_coupling_gen14_8.name: symmetry_aware_motif_coupling_gen14_8
symmetry_aware_motif_coupling_gen14_8.code:
"""
    symmetry_aware_motif_coupling_gen14_8(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

A structural mutation operator that reuses an already-evolved subexpression *motif* by cloning it,
re-indexing its variables, and coupling the clone back into the tree with a (usually additive or
multiplicative) binary operator.

# Core Idea
Ground-truth laws are overwhelmingly built from *repeated functional forms* evaluated on different
variables or dimensions: `0.5*m*(vx^2 + vy^2)`, `(x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2`, `a*b + c*d`, `sin(x)/x`.
Discovering each copy independently through point mutations is exponentially unlikely, so this
operator recycles structure evolution has already found: duplicate a subtree, remap its features,
and attach it to a target site.

# Synthesis of the two parents
* From parent 1 (`symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_6`): a single, compact feature-remapping traversal
  and a lean control flow — no homologous-grafting heuristics, no unary fallbacks, one coupling path.
* From parent 2 (`..._gen10_1_gen11_9`): a `maxsize`-derived size budget so the offspring is actually
  admissible, tiered donor sampling that prefers compound variable-bearing motifs (avoiding
  degeneration into `insert_random_op`), targeted feature substitution alongside the cyclic shift,
  self-coupling degeneracy avoidance, and a bias toward the canonical accumulators `+` / `*`.
* New in this version:
  - **Root-biased target selection.** Symmetric motifs in real laws almost always accumulate near the
    *top* of an expression (`f(x) + f(y)`, not deep inside a nonlinearity). With probability `0.35`
    the target is the root, otherwise a uniformly sampled node; this makes the common `A + A'` /
    `A * A'` outer structures reachable in one step.
  - **Adaptive remap-mode weights.** The remap mode is chosen conditioned on the motif itself: if the
    motif carries no variables (constant-only) only the identity map is meaningful; if it carries a
    single feature, targeted substitution and cyclic shift coincide, so the cheaper shift is favored;
    with multiple features targeted substitution is up-weighted, since only it can express pairwise
    exchanges like `x1 → x2` inside `(x1 - x2)`.
  - **Substitution can introduce an unused feature**, which lets the mutation import variables that
    do not yet appear anywhere in the tree (useful early in a run).

# Steps
1. Bail out if there is no binary operator or no size headroom (`maxsize - size(tree) - 1 < 1`).
2. Sample a donor subtree that fits the budget, with tiered preference:
   compound & variable-bearing → variable-bearing → anything that fits.
3. Deep-copy it into an independent motif.
4. Pick the target: the root with probability 0.35, else a uniformly random node.
5. Remap the motif's feature indices via cyclic shift, targeted substitution, or identity
   (forcing a nonzero shift when donor === target and identity was drawn, to avoid trivial `u ⊕ u`).
6. Wrap the target with `motif ⊕ copy(target)` under a binary operator biased toward `+`/`*`,
   with randomized operand order for non-commutative operators.

# Assumptions
* Feature indices are `1:nfeatures`, so `mod1` shifts are always valid.
* Duplication grows the tree by exactly `size(motif) + 1` nodes, which is what the budget enforces.
"""
function symmetry_aware_motif_coupling_gen14_8(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Guard: coupling a duplicated motif requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ size budget
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    # Result size == tree_size + size(motif) + 1 (target subtree is duplicated in place)
    budget = maxsize - tree_size - 1
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ helpers
    # Apply an arbitrary index map to every variable leaf of a subtree
    function _map_features!(node, fmap)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = fmap(node.feature)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _map_features!(get_child(node, i), fmap)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Distinct feature indices appearing in a subtree
    function _collect_features(node)
        acc = Int[]
        function _walk(n)
            if n.degree == 0
                if !n.constant && !(n.feature in acc)
                    push!(acc, n.feature)
                end
            else
                for i in 1:(n.degree)
                    _walk(get_child(n, i))
                end
            end
            return nothing
        end
        _walk(node)
        return acc
    end

    _fits(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget
    _has_var(t) = any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, t)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ Step 1: donor
    # Tier 1: compound, variable-bearing motifs — the genuine symmetry carriers
    _tier1(t) = t.degree > 0 && _fits(t) && _has_var(t)
    _tier2(t) = _fits(t) && _has_var(t)

    donor = if count(_tier1, tree) > 0 && rand(rng) < 0.8
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_tier1))
    elseif count(_tier2, tree) > 0
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_tier2))
    elseif count(_fits, tree) > 0
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_fits))
    else
        return tree  # nothing fits within the complexity budget
    end

    motif = copy(donor)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ Step 2: target
    # Root-biased: symmetric accumulations (`f(x) + f(y)`) live near the top of real laws.
    target = if rand(rng) < 0.35
        tree
    else
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    end
    self_coupling = target === donor

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ Step 3: remap features
    if nfeatures > 1
        feats = _collect_features(motif)
        nf = length(feats)

        if nf == 0
            # Constant-only motif: no remapping is meaningful (identity map).
            nothing
        else
            # Adaptive mode weights: multi-feature motifs benefit most from targeted swaps
            # (e.g. `x1 - x2` → `y1 - y2` needs per-feature substitution, not a global shift).
            p_shift = nf == 1 ? 0.60 : 0.35
            p_subst = nf == 1 ? 0.15 : 0.45
            r = rand(rng)

            if r < p_shift
                # (a) cyclic shift: replicate the whole functional form on the next variable block
                shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
                _map_features!(motif, f -> mod1(f + shift, nfeatures))
            elseif r < p_shift + p_subst
                # (b) targeted substitution: replace exactly one feature of the motif everywhere,
                # possibly importing a feature not yet present anywhere in the tree.
                src = feats[rand(rng, 1:nf)]
                dst = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
                dst >= src && (dst += 1)  # uniform over destinations != src
                _map_features!(motif, f -> (f == src ? dst : f))
            else
                # (c) identity: enables powers (`u*u`) and rational self-couplings (`u/u'`).
                # If donor and target coincide, half the time force a shift so we do not
                # produce the trivially simplifiable `u ⊕ u`.
                if self_coupling && rand(rng, Bool)
                    shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
                    _map_features!(motif, f -> mod1(f + shift, nfeatures))
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ Step 4: couple
    # Bias toward `+` and `*`, the canonical symmetric accumulators of physical laws.
    binops = options.operators.binops
    pref = Int[]
    for i in 1:(options.nops[2])
        op = binops[i]
        (op === (+) || op === (*)) && push!(pref, i)
    end
    bin_op = if !isempty(pref) && rand(rng) < 0.7
        pref[rand(rng, 1:length(pref))]
    else
        rand(rng, 1:(options.nops[2]))
    end

    target_copy = copy(target)
    # Randomize operand ordering so non-commutative operators explore both arrangements
    children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
    new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children)
    set_node!(target, new_node)

    return tree
end

affine_shape_rmse_loss_simple_gen14_0.name: affine_shape_rmse_loss_simple_gen14_0
affine_shape_rmse_loss_simple_gen14_0.code:
"""
    affine_shape_rmse_loss_simple_gen14_0(tree, dataset, options)

Simplified affine-shape loss. The idea is unchanged from the parent: score an
expression mainly by the *shape* of its output — the normalized RMSE that remains
after the best affine recalibration `a * prediction + b` — and add a tiny bounded
raw-error term so that, among affine-equivalent structures, the one whose constants
are actually correct is preferred (and only it can reach zero loss).

Steps:
1. One pass of plain running sums (`Σp, Σy, Σp², Σpy, Σy²`, `max|y|`) with a
   finiteness guard on the samples.
2. Closed-form least-squares slope/intercept from those sums (slope is zeroed when
   the prediction is constant, in which case the affine fit degenerates to `mean(y)`).
3. One pass evaluating the fitted residual and the raw residual directly, both
   normalized by a single positive scale `‖y - mean(y)‖` (floored by
   `sqrt(n) * max(1, max|y|)` when the target has no variance). Evaluating the fitted
   residual instead of `1 - r²` avoids catastrophic cancellation near an exact match.
4. Loss = `sqrt(clamp(affine_nmse, 0, 1)) + (1/256) * raw/(1 + raw)`.

Removed / merged relative to the parent (and why this is still sound):
* Welford moment updates and Kahan compensated summation were replaced by plain
  sums with a single finiteness check at the end; the moments are only used for the
  calibration coefficients, and the accuracy-critical residual terms are still
  computed directly in the second pass.
* The separate constant-target branch (with its own normalized-MSE loop and
  `log1p`) was folded into the common path via the scale floor: with a constant
  target the shape term is identically zero, so the monotone bounded raw term
  already ranks candidates correctly.
* The scale-relative variability tests and the raw-overflow bookkeeping flag were
  dropped in favor of simple positivity/finiteness checks, which cover the same
  degenerate cases with far less branching.
"""
function affine_shape_rmse_loss_simple_gen14_0(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # --- Pass 1: plain running sums for the affine least-squares coefficients. ---
    sum_p = zero_l
    sum_y = zero_l
    sum_pp = zero_l
    sum_py = zero_l
    sum_yy = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end
        sum_p += p
        sum_y += y
        sum_pp += p * p
        sum_py += p * y
        sum_yy += y * y
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))
    end

    if !(isfinite(sum_p) && isfinite(sum_y) && isfinite(sum_pp) &&
         isfinite(sum_py) && isfinite(sum_yy))
