    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)
    if !(isfinite(n_l) && n_l > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Pass 1: stable centered moments for affine least-squares calibration.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        # Use the updated means in the centered second-moment recurrences.
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Welford sums may become microscopically negative through roundoff.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    relative_tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))
    target_rms = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    prediction_rms = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)

    target_is_variable =
        target_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_y
    prediction_is_variable =
        prediction_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_p

    # Use the target's centered norm for ordinary datasets. For effectively
    # constant targets, use an amplitude floor and average the raw sum later.
    residual_scale = target_is_variable ?
        sqrt(m2_y) :
        max(one_l, max_abs_y)

    if !(isfinite(residual_scale) && residual_scale > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # A numerically constant prediction carries no affine shape information.
    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if target_is_variable && prediction_is_variable
        candidate_slope = cov_py / m2_p
        candidate_intercept = mean_y - candidate_slope * mean_p

        # If calibration itself is numerically unstable, safely use the mean fit.
        if isfinite(candidate_slope) && isfinite(candidate_intercept)
            slope = candidate_slope
            intercept = candidate_intercept
        end
    end

    # Pass 2: directly evaluate fitted and raw residuals. Compensated accumulation
    # preserves distinctions between exact and extremely accurate approximations.
    affine_sum = zero_l
    affine_compensation = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l
    raw_compensation = zero_l
    raw_overflowed = false

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !raw_overflowed
            raw_residual = p - y
            if isfinite(raw_residual)
                raw_normalized = raw_residual / residual_scale
                raw_term = raw_normalized * raw_normalized

                if isfinite(raw_term)
                    corrected = raw_term - raw_compensation
                    updated = raw_sum + corrected
                    if isfinite(updated)
                        raw_compensation = (updated - raw_sum) - corrected
                        raw_sum = updated
                    else
                        raw_overflowed = true
                    end
                else
                    raw_overflowed = true
                end
            else
                raw_overflowed = true
            end
        end

        fitted = muladd(slope, p, intercept)
        affine_residual = fitted - y
        affine_normalized = affine_residual / residual_scale
        affine_term = affine_normalized * affine_normalized

        if !(isfinite(fitted) && isfinite(affine_residual) &&
             isfinite(affine_normalized) && isfinite(affine_term))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        corrected = affine_term - affine_compensation
        updated = affine_sum + corrected
        if !isfinite(updated)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        affine_compensation = (updated - affine_sum) - corrected
        affine_sum = updated
    end

    if !target_is_variable
        # Affine shape is not identifiable for a constant target, so raw error
        # becomes the primary objective rather than a tiny tie-breaker.
        if raw_overflowed || !isfinite(raw_sum)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum / n_l, zero_l)
        loss_value = log1p(raw_nmse)
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
    end

    # The least-squares affine fit cannot be worse than predicting mean(y).
    affine_nmse = clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l)
    shape_term = sqrt(affine_nmse)

    # Compute raw/(1+raw) without overflowing when raw is very large.
    bounded_raw = if raw_overflowed || !isfinite(raw_sum)
        one_l
    else
        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum, zero_l)
        raw_nmse <= one_l ?
            raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse) :
            one_l / (one_l + one_l / raw_nmse)
    end

    # Suppress calibration distractions for poor shapes while retaining the full
    # tie-breaker near an affine structural match.
    shape_gate = one_l - shape_term
    calibration_weight = (shape_gate * shape_gate) / L(256)
    loss_value = shape_term + calibration_weight * bounded_raw

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

pareto_niche_tournament_selection_gen17_.name: pareto_niche_tournament_selection_gen17_2
pareto_niche_tournament_selection_gen17_.code:
"""
Pareto-niche tournament selection with local crowding and dominance-rank pressure.

Core idea: Standard tournament selection with frequency-based parsimony only measures
how "common" a complexity size is *globally* across the whole population's search
history. It ignores two other useful signals available *within the sampled tournament
itself*: (1) whether a member is locally Pareto-dominated by other members in the same
tournament (i.e. some other sampled member has both lower cost AND lower-or-equal
complexity), and (2) whether the tournament sample is locally "crowded" at that
member's complexity level (many sampled members share the same size, suggesting
redundant exploration of that niche).

By combining these three signals — global adaptive-parsimony frequency, local
domination rank, and local complexity crowding — into a single multiplicative cost
penalty (in log-space, as in the default parsimony trick), we bias selection toward
members that are simultaneously accurate, non-dominated, and occupying under-explored
complexity niches. This should help maintain diversity across the complexity spectrum
(reducing premature convergence to a narrow band of expression sizes) while still
respecting the core exploitation signal (raw cost) via the same probabilistic
tournament-winner sampling scheme as `default_selection`.

Steps:
1. Sample `tournament_selection_n` members without replacement, as usual.
2. Compute each member's complexity.
3. Compute a local Pareto domination count: for each member, how many *other* sampled
   members strictly dominate it (lower-or-equal cost and complexity, with at least one
   strict inequality). Higher domination count => weaker candidate, locally.
4. Compute a local crowding fraction: what fraction of the tournament shares the same
   complexity as this member. Higher crowding => less novel niche.
5. Combine the global adaptive-parsimony frequency (if enabled), local crowding, and
   normalized domination rank into a single penalty term, and inflate cost
   multiplicatively via `exp(scaling * penalty)`, mirroring the default's adaptive
   parsimony mechanism.
6. Use the same probability-weighted tournament-winner sampling as the default
   selection operator (respecting `tournament_selection_p`) to pick the final member
   from the penalty-adjusted costs.
"""
function pareto_niche_tournament_selection_gen17_2(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Sample the tournament pool
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, options.tournament_selection_n; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)
    p = options.tournament_selection_p

    # Precompute complexities for the tournament pool
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        complexities[i] = compute_complexity(sample[i], options)
    end

    # Local Pareto domination count: how many other tournament members dominate member i
    domination_count = zeros(Int, n)
    for i in 1:n
        for j in 1:n
            if j != i
                dominates =
                    (sample[j].cost <= sample[i].cost && complexities[j] <= complexities[i]) &&
                    (sample[j].cost < sample[i].cost || complexities[j] < complexities[i])
                if dominates
                    domination_count[i] += 1
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # Combine global adaptive-parsimony frequency, local crowding, and dominance rank
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]
        size = complexities[i]

        # Global frequency-based parsimony pressure (as in default selection)
        freq_penalty = if options.use_frequency_in_tournament && (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
            L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
        else
            L(0)
        end

        # Local crowding: fraction of the tournament sample sharing this complexity
        local_crowd = L(count(==(size), complexities)) / L(n)

        # Local dominance-rank penalty, normalized to [0, 1]
        rank_penalty = L(domination_count[i]) / L(n)

        # Weighted combination of the three diversity/quality signals
        combined_penalty = freq_penalty + L(0.5) * local_crowd + L(0.5) * rank_penalty

        adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * combined_penalty)
    end

    # Standard probability-weighted tournament winner selection on adjusted costs
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(adjusted_costs)
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        if tournament_winner == 1
            argmin_fast(adjusted_costs)
        else
            bottomk_fast(adjusted_costs, tournament_winner)[2][end]
        end
    end
    return sample[chosen_idx]
end

age_tournament_survival_gen17_3.name: age_tournament_survival_gen17_3
age_tournament_survival_gen17_3.code:
"""
    age_tournament_survival_gen17_3(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[]) -> Int

Simplified, stochastic version of the parent's age-regularized survival.

Core idea (kept from the parent): replacement pressure is driven purely by **age**,
so young/novel offspring are protected and old material is recycled. This keeps the
age-regularized evolution behavior that avoids premature convergence onto a single
lineage, which is what helps recover exact ground-truth expressions.

Steps:
1. Draw a small random subset of `k = 3` distinct-enough candidate slots from the
   population (rejecting any index in `exclude_indices` as it is drawn).
2. Return the candidate with the smallest `birth` counter (the oldest of the subset).
3. If sampling failed to find any admissible candidate (tiny or heavily excluded
   populations), fall back to the first non-excluded index.

What was simplified / removed relative to the parent:
- The parent materialized a full `Vector` of births with `typemax` sentinels for
  excluded slots and then ran a full-population `argmin_fast`. That allocation and
  the sentinel bookkeeping are gone: exclusion is folded into the sampling loop as a
  simple `continue`, and the "oldest" reduction is done inline over a handful of
  candidates.
- Consequently the operator is O(k) instead of O(n) and allocation-free.

Why this is still sound: the survivor choice remains monotone in age (the returned
member is always the oldest among those inspected), so old expressions are still the
ones removed on average, while the small random subset adds mild replacement noise
that preserves population diversity instead of always deleting the single global
oldest slot. `exclude_indices` is respected by construction.
"""
function age_tournament_survival_gen17_3(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)

    k = 3                     # small age-tournament size
    max_attempts = 8 * k      # bound on rejection sampling attempts

    best_idx = 0
    best_birth = zero(BT)
    nsampled = 0
    attempts = 0

    # Rejection-sample up to `k` admissible slots, tracking the oldest one seen.
    while nsampled < k && attempts < max_attempts
        attempts += 1
        i = rand(1:n)
        (i in exclude_indices) && continue   # exclusion folded into the sampling loop
        nsampled += 1
        b = pop.members[i].birth
        if best_idx == 0 || b < best_birth
            best_idx = i
            best_birth = b
        end
    end

    # Fallback: deterministic scan for any admissible slot.
    if best_idx == 0
        for i in 1:n
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue
            return i
        end
        return 1  # degenerate case: everything excluded
    end

    return best_idx
end

symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_7_gen17.name: symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_7_gen17_5
symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_7_gen17.code:
"""
    symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_7_gen17_5(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

A further-streamlined structural mutation operator that duplicates a subtree motif and couples
it into the expression tree via a binary operator, with an optional single-feature relabeling
instead of a full cyclic shift.

# Core Idea
Keep the essential mechanism of the parent (extract a motif, optionally alter its feature identity,
and couple it to a target node with a binary operator) but simplify the feature transformation to
a single random substitution rather than a global cyclic shift applied to every leaf.

# Steps
1. Return early if no binary operators are configured.
2. Sample a donor subtree and deep-copy it into an independent motif.
3. If `nfeatures > 1` and the motif has at least one variable leaf, pick one variable leaf in the
   motif at random and relabel it to a different random feature. This is a single, local edit
   rather than a global cyclic remap of all leaves.
4. Select a target node in the tree and wrap it with the motif under a random binary operator,
   always placing the motif as the right-hand child (dropping the random operand-order coin flip).

# Simplifications from Parent
- Replaced the global cyclic-shift feature transform (`_shift_features!` traversing every leaf)
  with a single random leaf relabel, removing the recursive helper and the `shift ∈ 0:(nfeatures-1)`
  sampling logic. This still injects feature-space variation into the duplicated motif but with
  far less code and a more local, less disruptive edit.
- Removed the random operand-ordering coin flip; the motif is always attached as the right child.
  Non-commutative operator diversity is still explored across generations through the random choice
  of `target` and `bin_op`, so this simplification trades a minor amount of ordering diversity for
  reduced branching complexity.
"""
function symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_7_gen17_5(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Guard: binary coupling requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # Step 1: Sample a donor subtree motif and duplicate it
    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    motif = copy(donor)

    # Step 2: Optionally relabel a single variable leaf in the motif to a different feature
    if nfeatures > 1 && any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, motif)
        leaf = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree=motif, filter=t -> t.degree == 0 && !t.constant))
        leaf.feature = rand(rng, filter(!=(leaf.feature), 1:nfeatures))
    end

    # Step 3: Couple target node with the motif under a random binary operator (motif as right child)
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    target_copy = copy(target)
    bin_op = rand(rng, 1:options.nops[2])

    new_node = constructorof(N)(;
        op=bin_op,
        children=(target_copy, motif),
    )
    set_node!(target, new_node)

    return tree
end

crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_sim.name: crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple_gen17_6
crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_sim.code:
"""
    crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple_gen17_6(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Simplified version of `crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen10_4` that keeps the
two heuristics judged most important — **clone suppression** (avoid re-selecting
near-identical copies of the same solution) and **rare-niche exploration**
(occasionally force a pick from an under-represented complexity band) — while
dropping the extra machinery that only mildly perturbed those two effects.

Removed relative to the parent:
 - The *sibling* redundancy term (shared-parent penalty) is dropped; only the
   cheap "same complexity + same loss" clone check remains, since it captures
   the dominant lineage-monopoly failure mode with a single scalar comparison.
 - The *youth discount* (recency-based cost reduction) is removed entirely —
   it was a small, purely cosmetic nudge on top of clone suppression and
   niche exploration, and removing it avoids tracking birth-order min/max.
 - The pool is a fixed `~1.5x` oversample as before (needed so redundancy
   information exists), but redundancy accumulation now only needs a single
   pass since there's no sibling term to add.

Steps:
 1. Sample a pool of `~1.5 * tournament_selection_n` members.
 2. Compute the default frequency-adjusted cost per member.
 3. Sort by cost; inflate each member's score geometrically by how many
    *better* pool members are near-identical (same complexity, same loss
    within tolerance) — the best of a cluster is untouched.
 4. With probability `p_rare_niche`, return the member from the rarest
    complexity niche (ties broken by score). Otherwise run the standard
    geometric tournament ladder over the penalized scores.

This keeps the core "fight lineage monopoly, fight niche starvation" logic of
the parent with fewer moving parts and less bookkeeping.
"""
function crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple_gen17_6(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # ---------------- tunables ----------------------------------------------
    pool_scale = 1.5          # pool size relative to tournament_selection_n
    clone_penalty = 1.35      # score inflation per unit of redundancy weight
    loss_rtol = 1e-6          # relative tolerance for "same loss"
    p_rare_niche = 0.10       # probability of the explicit rare-complexity pick

    # Multiplicative penalty that is sign-safe (f > 1 always means worse).
    inflate = function (x::L, f::Float64)
        fl = L(f)
        return x > zero(L) ? x * fl : x / fl
    end

    # ---------------- 1. sample the pool ------------------------------------
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # ---------------- 2. base (frequency-adjusted) scores -------------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 3. redundancy (clone) suppression ---------------------
    # Process from best to worst so the best representative of a cluster is
    # free of penalty and each twin gets progressively demoted.
    order = sortperm(scores)
    redundancy = zeros(Float64, n)
    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        wi = 0.0
        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            same_loss = abs(li - lj) <= L(loss_rtol) * max(abs(li), abs(lj), eps(L))
            if complexities[i] == complexities[j] && same_loss
                wi += 1.0
            end
        end
        redundancy[i] = wi
    end

    # ---------------- 4. apply redundancy penalty ---------------------------
    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        penalized[i] = inflate(scores[i], clone_penalty^redundancy[i])
    end

    # ---------------- 5a. occasional rare-complexity (niche) pick -----------
    if rand() < p_rare_niche
        best_idx = 1
        best_freq = Inf
        best_score = penalized[1]
        for i in 1:n
            c = complexities[i]
            f = if (0 < c <= options.maxsize)
                Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
            else
                0.0  # out-of-range sizes count as maximally rare
            end
            if f < best_freq || (f == best_freq && penalized[i] < best_score)
                best_freq = f
                best_score = penalized[i]
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        return pool[best_idx]
    end

    # ---------------- 5b. standard geometric tournament ladder --------------
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        if tournament_winner == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, tournament_winner)[2][end]
        end
    end
    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

tail_weighted_mse_loss_gen17_8.name: tail_weighted_mse_loss_gen17_8
tail_weighted_mse_loss_gen17_8.code:
"""
Tail-weighted MSE loss: standard mean-squared-error blended with the mean-squared-error
of the worst-fit points (a CVaR-style tail term). The core idea is that once an
expression matches "most" of the data well, the ordinary mean loss becomes almost flat
w.r.t. small structural changes, making it hard for the search to notice systematic,
localized mismatches (e.g. missing an oscillatory or periodic sub-structure). By
additionally tracking the mean squared error of the worst-fitting fraction of points,
we give extra selection pressure toward expressions that reduce the *largest* residuals,
which are often the signature of a missing functional component (like a `cos` or `exp`
term) rather than just noise. This tends to help escape plateaus where average error is
low but a structural piece of the true equation is still absent.

Steps:
1. Evaluate the tree on the dataset; bail out with `Inf` on any numerical failure.
2. Compute squared residuals for all points.
3. Take the mean of all squared residuals (standard MSE component).
4. Identify the worst `tail_fraction` (default 20%) of squared residuals via a cheap
   partial selection (avoids a full sort, keeping cost close to O(n)).
5. Compute the mean of that tail subset (captures how badly the worst points are fit).
6. Return a convex combination of the two terms so the loss remains a smooth,
   non-negative, lower-is-better scalar comparable in scale to plain MSE.
"""
function tail_weighted_mse_loss_gen17_8(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    # Evaluate the tree on the training features.
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = length(dataset.y)
    if n == 0
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Squared residuals for every data point.
    resid2 = abs2.(prediction .- dataset.y)

    # Guard against any NaN/Inf sneaking through numeric edge cases.
    if any(!isfinite, resid2)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Standard MSE component.
    mse = sum(resid2) / n

    # Determine size of the "worst-fit" tail (at least 1 point, ~20% of the data).
    tail_frac = 0.2
    k = max(1, round(Int, tail_frac * n))

    # Efficiently obtain the k largest squared residuals without a full sort.
    # partialsort! is average O(n) via quickselect, comparable cost to one extra MSE pass.
    tail_vals = partialsort(resid2, (n - k + 1):n)
    tail_mse = sum(tail_vals) / k

    # Blend overall fit quality with worst-case fit quality.
    # Weighting is fixed to keep the loss cheap and stable across tasks.
    combined = 0.5 * mse + 0.5 * tail_mse

    return L(combined)
end

adaptive_huber_loss_gen17_9.name: adaptive_huber_loss_gen17_9
adaptive_huber_loss_gen17_9.code:
"""
Adaptive Huber loss with a data-driven (MAD-based) threshold.

Symbolic regression search frequently produces candidate expressions that are
structurally close to the ground truth but produce a handful of wildly large
residuals — e.g. near a removable singularity introduced by a division or
`log`/`sqrt` of a near-zero argument, or from a few noisy outlier points in
real-world data. Plain MSE lets these few points dominate the loss, causing
the search to discard expressions with essentially correct functional form.

This loss instead:
  1. Evaluates the tree and bails out (returning `Inf`) on any failure or
     non-finite prediction, exactly like the default MSE loss.
  2. Computes the residuals `r = prediction - y`.
  3. Estimates a robust scale of the residual magnitude via the median
     absolute residual, scaled by 1.4826 (the standard factor that makes the
     MAD a consistent estimator of the standard deviation under Gaussian
     noise). This gives an adaptive Huber threshold `delta` that is specific
     to each candidate's own residual distribution, rather than a fixed
     hyperparameter that would need tuning per-dataset.
  4. Applies the Huber loss: quadratic (like MSE) for residuals within
     `delta` of zero, and linear beyond that, so a few extreme outliers
     contribute at most linearly instead of quadratically to the total loss.
  5. Averages over all samples to produce the final scalar loss.

This keeps the computational cost close to MSE (a single O(n log n) sort for
the median, plus one linear pass), while making the fitness landscape much
less brittle to a small number of extreme/pathological residuals — helping
the search retain and refine structurally-correct expressions instead of
prematurely discarding them due to a handful of bad points.
"""
function adaptive_huber_loss_gen17_9(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = length(prediction)
    if n == 0
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Compute residuals; bail out early if anything is non-finite.
    resid = prediction .- dataset.y
    @inbounds for i in eachindex(resid)
        if !isfinite(resid[i])
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end

    # Robust scale estimate: median absolute residual, scaled to be
    # consistent with the standard deviation under Gaussian noise.
    abs_resid = abs.(resid)
    sorted_abs_resid = sort(abs_resid)
    mid = n ÷ 2
    med = if iseven(n)
        (sorted_abs_resid[mid] + sorted_abs_resid[mid + 1]) / L(2)
    else
        sorted_abs_resid[mid + 1]
    end
    # Guard against a degenerate (near-zero) scale, e.g. a near-perfect fit.
    delta = max(L(1.4826) * L(med), L(1e-8))

    # Accumulate the Huber loss: quadratic near zero, linear for outliers.
    total = zero(L)
    @inbounds for r in resid
        ar = abs(L(r))
        if ar <= delta
            total += L(0.5) * ar^2
        else
            total += delta * (ar - L(0.5) * delta)
        end
    end

    return total / L(n)
end

centered_affine_profile_loss_gen18_2.name: centered_affine_profile_loss_gen18_2
centered_affine_profile_loss_gen18_2.code:
"""
    centered_affine_profile_loss_gen18_2(tree, dataset, options)

Compare the centered, unit-norm prediction and target profiles, using whichever
of the prediction profile or its negation is closer to the target. This retains
invariance to affine scale and offset while measuring shape directly as
`sqrt(1 - abs(correlation))`. A bounded normalized raw-error term weakly favors
the correctly calibrated representative, and constant targets use that term
alone.

The first pass computes Welford means and variances; the second accumulates the
direct profile distance and raw error. This removes the fitted slope/intercept,
magnitude-based variability heuristics, compensated sums, and separate raw-error
overflow formula from the parent. Direct profile comparison remains stable near
an exact affine match without subtracting nearly equal variance terms.
"""
function centered_affine_profile_loss_gen18_2(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # Stable first-pass estimates of the two centered profile norms.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        k = L(i)

        delta_p = p - mean_p
        mean_p += delta_p / k
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)

        delta_y = y - mean_y
        mean_y += delta_y / k
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Remove harmless negative roundoff without introducing scale heuristics.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    target_is_variable = m2_y > zero_l
    prediction_is_variable = m2_p > zero_l

    norm_p = prediction_is_variable ? sqrt(m2_p) : zero_l
    norm_y = target_is_variable ? sqrt(m2_y) : zero_l

    if (prediction_is_variable && !isfinite(norm_p)) ||
       (target_is_variable && !isfinite(norm_y))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Variable targets use their standard deviation; constant targets use their
    # magnitude with a unit floor so the same raw-error path handles both cases.
    target_scale = target_is_variable ?
        sqrt(m2_y / n_l) :
        max(one_l, abs(mean_y))

    if !(isfinite(target_scale) && target_scale > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    positive_profile_sum = zero_l
    negative_profile_sum = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_residual = p - y
        if !isfinite(raw_residual)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Overflow is allowed here: it maps naturally to a saturated raw term.
        if isfinite(raw_sum)
            raw_sum += abs2(raw_residual / target_scale)
        end

        if target_is_variable && prediction_is_variable
            centered_p = (p - mean_p) / norm_p
            centered_y = (y - mean_y) / norm_y

            positive_term = abs2(centered_p - centered_y)
            negative_term = abs2(centered_p + centered_y)
            if !(isfinite(positive_term) && isfinite(negative_term))
                return L(Inf)
            end

            positive_profile_sum += positive_term
            negative_profile_sum += negative_term
        end
    end

    bounded_raw = if isfinite(raw_sum)
        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum / n_l, zero_l)
        raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse)
    else
        one_l
    end

    # Shape is undefined for a constant target, so calibration is the full loss.
    if !target_is_variable
        return L(bounded_raw)
    end

    # A constant prediction has no centered profile and receives maximal shape loss.
    shape_term = if prediction_is_variable
        profile_distance = min(positive_profile_sum, negative_profile_sum) / L(2)
        sqrt(clamp(profile_distance, zero_l, one_l))
    else
        one_l
    end

    # A modest tie-breaker preserves shape-led search while improving calibration.
    loss_value = shape_term + (one_l / L(32)) * bounded_raw
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

adaptive_pareto_niche_selection_gen18_7.name: adaptive_pareto_niche_selection_gen18_7
adaptive_pareto_niche_selection_gen18_7.code:
"""
    adaptive_pareto_niche_selection_gen18_7(pop::Population{T,L,N}, running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics, options::AbstractOptions)::PopMember{T,L,N}

Adaptive Pareto Niche Selection operator for symbolic regression.

# Core Idea
Standard tournament selection aggressively exploits raw or frequency-penalized cost,
frequently trapping the evolutionary search in over-parameterized local optima and causing
premature loss of structural diversity. This operator introduces a multi-objective selection
mechanism combining:
1. **Adaptive Parsimony & Complexity Niching**: Penalizes over-represented complexity bins
   to continuously incentivize exploration along sparse regions of the Pareto frontier.
2. **Age-Fitness Regularization**: Rewards younger individuals to give newly discovered
   structural motifs time to undergo constant-optimization before being eliminated by older,
   highly refined incumbents.
3. **Intra-Tournament Lineage De-crowding**: Penalizes sibling clusters sharing the same
   parent reference within the tournament to prevent clonal sweeps.
4. **Pareto Dominance Ranking**: Computes a 2D non-dominated ranking across (Adjusted Cost,
   Niche-Congestion Score) within the sampled tournament, followed by probabilistic
   tournament selection over the Pareto-sorted front.

# Steps
1. Sample `k = min(tournament_selection_n, pop.n)` members without replacement.
2. Compute parsimony-adjusted cost for each candidate based on complexity frequency.
3. Compute a composite niche-congestion score for each candidate incorporating complexity
   frequency, normalized age (relative to the sample's newest birth), and intra-sample sibling density.
4. Calculate pairwise Pareto dominance between candidates over `(adjusted_cost, niche_congestion)`.
5. Sort tournament candidates by dominance count (number of competitors dominating the candidate)
   as primary key and adjusted cost as secondary key.
6. Select the winning candidate using rank-based probability distribution parameterized by `tournament_selection_p`.

# Heuristics & Assumptions
- Younger expressions with low complexity frequency represent novel exploratory branches that
  warrant survival even with slightly suboptimal loss.
- Non-dominated sorting within small tournaments (size ~10-15) is computationally lightweight
  (O(k^2)) while providing substantial diversity maintenance across SRBench benchmarks.
"""
function adaptive_pareto_niche_selection_gen18_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Determine effective tournament sample size
    tournament_n = min(options.tournament_selection_n, pop.n)
    if tournament_n <= 1
        return pop.members[1]
    end

    # Sample tournament candidates uniformly at random without replacement
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, tournament_n; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)
    p = options.tournament_selection_p

    # Extract maximum birth order in the tournament to compute relative ages
    max_birth = sample[1].birth
    for i in 2:n
        if sample[i].birth > max_birth
            max_birth = sample[i].birth
        end
    end

    # Compute parsimony-adjusted cost and niche-congestion scores
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    niche_scores = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)

        # Retrieve normalized complexity frequency
        freq = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
            Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
        else
            0.0
        end

        # Parsimony-adjusted cost: penalizes saturated complexity bins
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost * exp(scaling * L(freq))
        else
            adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost
        end

        # Calculate relative age: younger individuals (larger birth) have smaller relative age
        rel_age = Float64(max_birth - member.birth)
        norm_age = max_birth > 0 ? (rel_age / Float64(max_birth)) : 0.0

        # Calculate sibling crowding within the tournament sample
        parent_id = member.parent
        sibling_count = 0
        if parent_id > 0
            for j in 1:n
                if sample[j].parent == parent_id
                    sibling_count += 1
                end
            end
        end
        sibling_penalty = sibling_count > 1 ? (0.1 * Float64(sibling_count - 1)) : 0.0

        # Composite niche congestion score: lower is better (less congested, younger, unique lineage)
        niche_scores[i] = freq + 0.2 * norm_age + sibling_penalty
    end

    # Compute 2D Pareto dominance count within the tournament sample
    # Dominance count = number of candidates in the tournament that strictly dominate candidate i
    dom_count = zeros(Int, n)
    for i in 1:n
        cost_i = adjusted_costs[i]
        niche_i = niche_scores[i]
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue
            cost_j = adjusted_costs[j]
            niche_j = niche_scores[j]

            # Candidate j dominates candidate i if it is no worse in both and strictly better in at least one
            if (cost_j <= cost_i && niche_j <= niche_i) && (cost_j < cost_i || niche_j < niche_i)
                dom_count[i] += 1
            end
        end
    end

    # Rank tournament candidates: primary key = dominance count (asc), secondary key = adjusted cost (asc)
    # This places non-dominated individuals (dom_count == 0) at the top, ordered by adjusted cost
    ranked_indices = collect(1:n)
    sort!(ranked_indices; by=i -> (dom_count[i], adjusted_costs[i]))

    # Select candidate according to tournament probability parameter p
    chosen_idx = if p >= 1.0f0
        ranked_indices[1]
    else
        # Geometric rank distribution selection over the Pareto-ordered candidates
        k_indices = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p .* ((1.0f0 - p) .^ k_indices)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        ranked_indices[tournament_winner_rank]
    end

    return sample[chosen_idx]
end

novelty_weighted_quality_gated_niche_tou.name: novelty_weighted_quality_gated_niche_tournament_gen18_4
novelty_weighted_quality_gated_niche_tou.code:
"""
    novelty_weighted_quality_gated_niche_tournament_gen18_4(
        pop, running_search_statistics, options
    )

Crowding-aware tournament selection combining conservative lineage suppression,
recency-based turnover, and quality-gated complexity-niche exploration.

The operator synthesizes clone-only crowding with the broader anti-monopoly ideas of
lineage and age diversity:

 1. Sample an enlarged tournament pool and compute the usual
    adaptive-parsimony-adjusted costs.
 2. Process candidates from best to worst. Strongly penalize near-identical members
    having the same complexity and loss, while applying only a small penalty to
    closely related parent/child or sibling candidates when their complexity and
    loss are also similar. This preserves genuinely different descendants.
 3. Give newer members a mild cost discount, attenuated by their crowding weight so
    that fresh structural alternatives are encouraged without rewarding fresh
    clones enough to evade suppression.
 4. Adapt the probability of niche exploration to observed pool crowding. During a
    niche move, first retain the best representative of each valid complexity, then
    choose the rarest complexity only from the better two-thirds of those
    representatives. This repopulates starved complexity bands without selecting an
    arbitrarily poor member merely because its niche is empty.
 5. Otherwise apply the standard geometric tournament ladder to the adjusted scores.

Equal complexity and nearly equal loss are used as a cheap proxy for phenotypic
duplication. Family-based suppression requires additional similarity and is kept
fractional, reflecting that shared ancestry alone does not imply redundancy.
Multiplicative adjustments are sign-safe, so factors above one always worsen a
score and factors below one always improve it.
"""
function novelty_weighted_quality_gated_niche_tournament_gen18_4(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Mild tunables: clone evidence dominates, while lineage and youth are nudges.
    pool_scale = 1.5
    crowding_penalty = 1.35
    lineage_weight = 0.25
    clone_loss_rtol = 1e-6
    lineage_loss_rtol = 1e-2
    youth_discount = 0.03
    niche_probability_base = 0.08
    niche_probability_boost = 0.10
    niche_probability_max = 0.18

    # Sample a larger pool so local crowding and niche occupancy are observable.
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # Compute complexity and the default adaptive-parsimony-adjusted score.
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity])
            else
                zero(L)
            end
            scores[i] =
                member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Better representatives establish the local crowding baseline.
    order = sortperm(scores)
    crowding = zeros(Float64, n)

    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        scale_i = max(abs(li), eps(L))
        weight = 0.0

        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(scale_i, abs(lj))

            same_phenotype =
                complexities[i] == complexities[j] &&
                abs(li - lj) <= L(clone_loss_rtol) * loss_scale

            if same_phenotype
                # Strong evidence that the later member is redundant.
                weight += 1.0
                continue
            end

            parent_i = pool[i].parent
            parent_j = pool[j].parent
            related =
                (parent_i != 0 && parent_i == parent_j) ||
                (parent_i != 0 && parent_i == pool[j].ref) ||
                (parent_j != 0 && parent_j == pool[i].ref)

            # Shared ancestry is penalized only when phenotype is also close.
            if related &&
                abs(complexities[i] - complexities[j]) <= 1 &&
                abs(li - lj) <= L(lineage_loss_rtol) * loss_scale
                weight += lineage_weight
            end
        end

        crowding[i] = weight
    end

    # Find the age range once; recency is used only as a mild novelty preference.
    birth_min = pool[1].birth
    birth_max = pool[1].birth
    for i in 2:n
        birth = pool[i].birth
        birth < birth_min && (birth_min = birth)
        birth > birth_max && (birth_max = birth)
    end
    birth_span = max(birth_max - birth_min, 1)

    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    crowded_count = 0

    for i in 1:n
        redundancy = crowding[i]
        redundancy > 0.0 && (crowded_count += 1)

        recency = (pool[i].birth - birth_min) / birth_span
        novelty_weight = 1.0 / (1.0 + redundancy)

        # Clone/lineage penalties dominate; youth matters most for uncrowded forms.
        factor =
            crowding_penalty^redundancy *
            (1.0 - youth_discount * recency * novelty_weight)
        typed_factor = L(factor)

        # Sign-safe adjustment: larger factors always make the score less fit.
        penalized[i] = if scores[i] > zero(L)
            scores[i] * typed_factor
        elseif scores[i] < zero(L)
            scores[i] / typed_factor
        else
            scores[i]
        end
    end

    # Increase explicit niche exploration when the sampled pool shows monopoly.
    crowded_fraction = crowded_count / n
    niche_probability = min(
        niche_probability_max,
        niche_probability_base +
        niche_probability_boost * crowded_fraction,
    )

    if rand() < niche_probability
        # Keep one best representative per valid complexity niche.
        penalized_order = sortperm(penalized)
        seen_complexities = falses(options.maxsize)
        niche_champions = Int[]

        for i in penalized_order
            complexity = complexities[i]
            if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize &&
                !seen_complexities[complexity]
                seen_complexities[complexity] = true
                push!(niche_champions, i)
            end
        end

        if !isempty(niche_champions)
            # Quality gate: consider the better two-thirds of niche champions.
            quality_count = max(1, cld(2 * length(niche_champions), 3))
            best_idx = niche_champions[1]
            best_frequency = Float64(
                running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[
                    complexities[best_idx]
                ],
            )
            best_score = penalized[best_idx]

            for position in 2:quality_count
                i = niche_champions[position]
                frequency = Float64(
                    running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[
                        complexities[i]
                    ],
                )

                if frequency < best_frequency ||
                    (frequency == best_frequency && penalized[i] < best_score)
                    best_idx = i
                    best_frequency = frequency
                    best_score = penalized[i]
                end
            end

            return pool[best_idx]
        end
    end

    # Standard geometric tournament ladder over diversity-adjusted scores.
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        ranks = collect(0:(n - 1))
        probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        selected_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)

        if selected_rank == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, selected_rank)[2][end]
        end
    end

    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

hybrid_age_tournament_survival_gen18_0.name: hybrid_age_tournament_survival_gen18_0
hybrid_age_tournament_survival_gen18_0.code:
"""
    hybrid_age_tournament_survival_gen18_0(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[]) -> Int

Synthesizes the two age-regularized survival strategies: the *default* strategy
(always replace the globally oldest member, guaranteeing full turnover and a
tight generational bound) and the *sampled-tournament* strategy (replace the
oldest member within a small random subset, which lets some old lineages
persist and preserves structural diversity for crossover/mutation to draw on).

Rather than picking one extreme, this operator mixes both behaviors
stochastically:

1. With probability `p_full` (a small constant), fall back to the *exact*
   global-oldest rule — a single pass over all members (mirroring
   `age_regularized_survival`) — to guarantee that ancient, potentially
   stagnant members are eventually purged and the population doesn't
   accumulate unbounded "immortal" individuals.
2. Otherwise, draw a small random sample of slots (size scaled by
   `options.tournament_selection_n`, as in the sampled-tournament operator)
   and replace the oldest member *within that sample*. This softer age
   pressure lets some old, structurally different members survive longer,
   giving search more scaffolds to recombine instead of prematurely
   converging on one motif.
3. `exclude_indices` is respected inline in both branches (no allocation of
   sentinel arrays); if every sampled draw is excluded, we deterministically
   fall back to a full scan over allowed members so a valid index is always
   returned.

Heuristic assumption: occasional full-population purges (governed by
`p_full`) keep the age-regularization property intact (nothing survives
forever), while the majority of replacements use the cheaper, softer sampled
rule that preserves diversity — combining the correctness guarantee of the
default operator with the diversity benefits of sampled age tournaments.
"""
function hybrid_age_tournament_survival_gen18_0(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)

    # Probability of doing an exact full-population purge instead of a sampled one.
    p_full = 0.1

    best_idx = 0
    best_birth = typemax(BT)

    if rand() < p_full
        # Exact global-oldest scan (guarantees eventual turnover of all members,
        # mirroring the default age_regularized_survival behavior).
        for i in 1:n
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue
            b = pop.members[i].birth
            if best_idx == 0 || b < best_birth
                best_idx = i
                best_birth = b
            end
        end
    else
        # Sampled tournament: draw a small random subset of slots and replace
        # the oldest within that subset (softer age pressure, preserves diversity).
        n_sample = min(n, max(2, options.tournament_selection_n))
        for _ in 1:n_sample
            i = rand(1:n)
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue
            b = pop.members[i].birth
            if best_idx == 0 || b < best_birth
                best_idx = i
                best_birth = b
            end
        end

        if best_idx == 0
            # Degenerate case: every sampled draw was excluded. Deterministically
            # fall back to a full scan over allowed members.
            for i in 1:n
                (i in exclude_indices) && continue
                b = pop.members[i].birth
                if best_idx == 0 || b < best_birth
                    best_idx = i
                    best_birth = b
                end
            end
        end
    end

    return best_idx
end

complexity_niche_crowding_survival_gen18.name: complexity_niche_crowding_survival_gen18_1
complexity_niche_crowding_survival_gen18.code:
"""
    complexity_niche_crowding_survival_gen18_1(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

Survival ("who gets replaced") operator that fights the two failure modes visible in
long PySR runs: (a) *complexity drift*, where the whole population migrates into a
narrow band of large, bloated expressions built around one structural attractor, and
(b) *clonal redundancy*, where many slots hold near-identical (same complexity, same
loss) copies produced from the same lineage, so a large fraction of the evaluation
budget is spent re-tuning constants of an expression family that can never reach the
ground truth.

Core idea: instead of replacing the *oldest* member (pure age regularization), replace
the *most redundant* member -- the one that lives in the most crowded complexity niche,
belongs to the most over-represented lineage, and is worst within that crowd -- while
never touching the Pareto-optimal "backbone" of the population. This keeps a spread of
simple *and* complex candidates alive, so simple alternative structures (e.g. the
`1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)` skeleton) retain slots long enough to be improved instead of being
crushed by a swarm of size-30 refinements of a wrong attractor.

Steps:
 1. Build the set of replaceable slots, honouring `exclude_indices` (never returned).
 2. Immediately cull any member with a non-finite cost (NaN/Inf) -- free slot, no info.
 3. With small probability (15%) fall back to plain oldest-member replacement. This
    preserves the ergodicity / turnover guarantees of age-regularized evolution and
    prevents any member from becoming immortal through protection rules.
 4. Compute complexities and the *non-dominated* (complexity, loss) set. Non-dominated
    members plus the current best-cost member are protected from replacement: they are
    the population's Pareto backbone. If protection would leave nothing replaceable,
    the protection is relaxed (keeping only the global best).
 5. For every replaceable, unprotected member compute a redundancy score:
      * `comp_crowd`: number of members within a complexity band (`maxsize/20`) of it,
        i.e. how crowded its complexity niche is;
      * `dup`: number of members with identical complexity and (numerically) identical
        loss -- exact clones, weighted heavily;
      * `fam`: number of members sharing the same `parent` reference -- sibling
        over-representation, a cheap proxy for structural (lineage) redundancy.
 6. Replace the member maximizing `(score, cost, -birth)` lexicographically: most
    redundant first, then worst cost within the crowd, then oldest. Ties therefore
    resolve toward removing bad, old, clonal members from over-populated niches.

Assumptions/heuristics: complexity is a usable cheap niche descriptor (structural hashes
are unavailable here); `parent` references approximate family membership; the O(n^2)
scan is negligible for typical population sizes (20-100).
"""
function complexity_niche_crowding_survival_gen18_1(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    members = pop.members

    # ---- 1. Which slots are we allowed to overwrite? ------------------------
    allowed = trues(n)
    for i in exclude_indices
        if 1 <= i <= n
            allowed[i] = false
        end
    end
    if !any(allowed)
        # Degenerate case (caller excluded everything); return something valid.
        return 1
    end

    BT = typeof(first(members).birth)

    # Helper: default age-regularized choice (oldest allowed member).
    oldest_allowed = function ()
        best = 0
        best_birth = typemax(BT)
        for i in 1:n
            allowed[i] || continue
            b = members[i].birth
            if best == 0 || b < best_birth
                best = i
                best_birth = b
            end
        end
        return best == 0 ? 1 : best
    end

    # ---- 2. Cull invalid members first (they carry no information) ----------
    for i in 1:n
        allowed[i] || continue
        c = members[i].cost
        if (c isa AbstractFloat) && !isfinite(c)
            return i
        end
    end

    # ---- 3. Occasional pure age-based turnover ------------------------------
    # Keeps the classic age-regularized dynamics as a background process and
    # guarantees no protected member can survive forever.
    if rand() < 0.15
        return oldest_allowed()
    end

    # ---- 4. Complexities + Pareto (non-dominated) protection ---------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        complexities[i] = compute_complexity(members[i], options)
    end

    protected = falses(n)
    for i in 1:n
        ci = complexities[i]
        li = members[i].loss
        dominated = false
        for j in 1:n
            j == i && continue
            cj = complexities[j]
            lj = members[j].loss
            # j dominates i if it is no worse in both and strictly better in one.
            if (cj <= ci && lj < li) || (cj < ci && lj <= li)
                dominated = true
                break
            end
        end
        protected[i] = !dominated  # non-dominated => part of the Pareto backbone
    end

    # Always protect the best-cost member (the search's current champion).
    best_cost_idx = 0
    for i in 1:n
        if best_cost_idx == 0 || members[i].cost < members[best_cost_idx].cost
            best_cost_idx = i
        end
    end
    if best_cost_idx > 0
        protected[best_cost_idx] = true
    end

    # If protection leaves no replaceable slot, relax it (keep only the champion).
    has_candidate = false
    for i in 1:n
        if allowed[i] && !protected[i]
            has_candidate = true
            break
        end
    end
    if !has_candidate
        fill!(protected, false)
        if best_cost_idx > 0
            protected[best_cost_idx] = true
        end
        for i in 1:n
            if allowed[i] && !protected[i]
                has_candidate = true
                break
            end
        end
        if !has_candidate
            return oldest_allowed()
        end
    end

    # ---- 5/6. Score redundancy and pick the most expendable slot -----------
    band = max(1, options.maxsize ÷ 20)  # complexity-niche width
    target = 0
    best_key = (-Inf, -Inf, -Inf)

    for i in 1:n
        (allowed[i] && !protected[i]) || continue

        ci = complexities[i]
        li = float(members[i].loss)
        pi = members[i].parent

        comp_crowd = 0   # members occupying (roughly) the same complexity niche
        dup = 0          # exact clones (same complexity, same loss)
        fam = 0          # siblings sharing the same parent reference
        for j in 1:n
            cj = complexities[j]
            if abs(cj - ci) <= band
                comp_crowd += 1
            end
            if cj == ci
                lj = float(members[j].loss)
                # Relative-tolerance equality test: treats constant-only tweaks
                # that did not change the loss as clones.
                if abs(lj - li) <= 1e-8 * (1 + abs(li))
                    dup += 1
                end
            end
            if pi > 0 && members[j].parent == pi
                fam += 1
            end
        end

        # Redundancy score: niche crowding, plus heavy penalty for exact clones,
        # plus a mild penalty for over-represented lineages.
        score = float(comp_crowd) + 2.0 * float(max(dup - 1, 0)) +
                0.5 * float(max(fam - 1, 0))

        # Lexicographic key: most redundant, then worst cost, then oldest.
        key = (score, float(members[i].cost), -float(members[i].birth))
        if key > best_key
            best_key = key
            target = i
        end
    end

    return target == 0 ? oldest_allowed() : target
end

motif_duplication_symmetry_gen10_gen18_3.name: motif_duplication_symmetry_gen10_gen18_3
motif_duplication_symmetry_gen10_gen18_3.code:
"""
    motif_duplication_symmetry_gen10_gen18_3(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

A structural mutation that duplicates an evolved subexpression "motif", optionally relabels its
feature indices with a symmetry map, optionally wraps it in a unary operator, and couples it back
into the tree with a binary operator.

# Core Idea
Physical laws are built from a small number of *reused groups*: dimensionless ratios
(`v/c`, `x2/x1`), pairwise-symmetric terms (`(x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2`), and repeated functional forms
across dimensions (`vx^2 + vy^2`). Once the search has discovered such a group anywhere in the tree,
the cheapest way to reach the ground truth is usually to *reuse* that group — verbatim, permuted, or
wrapped in a nonlinearity — rather than to rediscover it from scratch. This operator performs exactly
that copy-transform-couple move.

# Steps
1. Bail out if no binary operators exist, or if the size budget (`options.maxsize`) leaves no room.
2. Sample a donor subtree, preferring *operator* subtrees (real motifs, not bare leaves) that fit the
   remaining size budget; copy it into an independent motif.
3. Apply one of three symmetry maps to the motif's variable leaves:
   * identity (probability ~0.4) → self-coupling: powers, ratios, squares of the same group;
   * transposition of two features (~0.35) → pairwise/exchange symmetry;
   * cyclic shift (~0.25) → replication of a functional form across all variables.
4. With probability 0.3 wrap the motif in a random unary operator (`sqrt`, `square`, `exp`, ...),
   which is how forms like `x0 / sqrt(1 - (x1/x2)^2)` become reachable in one mutation.
5. Choose a coupling site with a structured bias: the root (global coupling, e.g. `f + f'`),
   a *variable leaf* (local coupling, e.g. `x0 -> x0 / motif`), or any node.
6. Couple `target` and `motif` under a binary operator with randomized operand order, using
   operator-aware biases (see heuristics).

# Heuristics added / changed vs. the parent
- **Size-aware donor choice**: the motif is required to fit `options.maxsize - size(tree) - 1`, and the
  mutation aborts instead of producing an always-rejected oversized tree (parent could duplicate the
  whole tree and blow the complexity budget, wasting evaluations).
- **Donor bias toward operator subtrees** (75%): duplicating a bare leaf is almost equivalent to the
  cheaper built-in `insert_random_op`, so priority is given to genuine multi-node motifs.
- **Richer symmetry group**: the parent only had cyclic shifts; transpositions (which the cyclic group
  cannot express for `nfeatures > 2`) are added, and identity is now given explicit, higher weight
  since self-coupling (ratios/powers of a discovered group) is the most productive move in practice.
- **Optional unary wrap of the motif**, enabling `g -> h(g)` couplings (sqrt/square of a dimensionless
  group) that previously required several independent mutations.
- **Structured target selection** (root / variable leaf / uniform) instead of purely uniform, which
  makes both global symmetric sums and local "divide this variable by a group" edits likely.
- **Degeneracy guard & operator bias**: when the motif is an untransformed copy of the target, `-` and
  `/` (which would give the constants 0 and 1) are excluded; when a permutation was applied, the
  commutative accumulators `+`/`*` are favored, matching how physical symmetries combine.
"""
function motif_duplication_symmetry_gen10_gen18_3(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Guard: binary coupling requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # --- helper: apply a feature permutation to every variable leaf of the motif ---
    function _map_features!(node, perm::Vector{Int})
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant && 1 <= node.feature <= length(perm)
                node.feature = perm[node.feature]
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _map_features!(get_child(node, i), perm)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # --- Step 1: size budget. Coupling adds (motif_size + 1) nodes to the tree. ---
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : 30
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    budget = maxsize - tree_size - 1
    budget < 1 && return tree  # no room for even a single-node motif

    _fits(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget

    # --- Step 2: pick a donor motif, preferring genuine (operator) subtrees that fit ---
    local donor
    if rand(rng) < 0.75 && any(t -> t.degree > 0 && _fits(t), tree)
        donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> t.degree > 0 && _fits(t)))
    elseif any(_fits, tree)
        donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_fits))
    else
        return tree
    end
    motif = copy(donor)

    # --- Step 3: symmetry map on the motif's features ---
    identity_map = true
    permuted = false
    if nfeatures > 1
        r = rand(rng)
        if r < 0.4
            # identity: self-coupling -> powers, ratios, differences of the same group
        elseif r < 0.75
            # transposition: exchange symmetry between two features
            i = rand(rng, 1:nfeatures)
            j = rand(rng, filter(!=(i), 1:nfeatures))
            perm = collect(1:nfeatures)
            perm[i] = j
            perm[j] = i
            _map_features!(motif, perm)
            identity_map = false
            permuted = true
        else
            # cyclic shift: replicate the functional form across all variables
            shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
            perm = [mod1(k + shift, nfeatures) for k in 1:nfeatures]
            _map_features!(motif, perm)
            identity_map = false
            permuted = true
        end
    end

    # --- Step 4: optional unary wrap of the motif (sqrt/square/exp of a discovered group) ---
    motif_size = count_nodes(motif)
    if options.nops[1] > 0 && motif_size + 1 <= budget && rand(rng) < 0.3
        motif = constructorof(N)(;
            op=rand(rng, 1:(options.nops[1])), children=(motif,)
        )
        motif_size += 1
        identity_map = false  # wrapped motif is no longer a verbatim copy
    end

    # --- Step 5: choose the coupling site with a structured bias ---
    local target
    if rand(rng) < 0.35
        target = tree  # global coupling: whole expression combined with the motif
    elseif rand(rng) < 0.6 && any(t -> t.degree == 0 && !t.constant, tree)
        # local coupling on a variable leaf: e.g. x0 -> x0 / motif
        target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> (t.degree == 0 && !t.constant)))
    else
        target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    end

    # --- Step 6: pick the binary operator, with degeneracy guard / symmetry bias ---
    nbin = options.nops[2]
    binops = options.operators.binops
    op_candidates = collect(1:nbin)

    if identity_map && donor === target
        # motif is an exact copy of the target: `-` gives 0 and `/` gives 1 -> useless
        filtered = [i for i in op_candidates if !(binops[i] === (-) || binops[i] === (/))]
        !isempty(filtered) && (op_candidates = filtered)
    elseif permuted && rand(rng) < 0.5
        # symmetric terms most often accumulate through + or *
        accum = [i for i in op_candidates if (binops[i] === (+) || binops[i] === (*))]
        !isempty(accum) && (op_candidates = accum)
    end
    bin_op = length(op_candidates) == 1 ? op_candidates[1] : rand(rng, op_candidates)

    # Copy the target *before* overwriting it in place (handles target === tree correctly)
    target_copy = copy(target)

    # Randomize operand ordering to support non-commutative operators
    children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
    new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children)
    set_node!(target, new_node)

    return tree
end

affine_shape_calibration_loss_simplified.name: affine_shape_calibration_loss_simplified_gen18_5
affine_shape_calibration_loss_simplified.code:
"""
    affine_shape_calibration_loss_simplified_gen18_5(tree, dataset, options)

Simplified affine-calibration shape loss: measure how well the tree's output matches
the target's *shape* (up to an optimal affine rescaling `a*p+b`), then add a small
bounded raw-error term as a tie-breaker so that only truly-calibrated predictions
reach zero loss.

Compared to the parent, this drops the two-pass Welford/Kahan-compensated summation
(needed there to avoid catastrophic cancellation near exact fits) in favor of a
single pass of plain summary statistics (`sum_p`, `sum_y`, `sum_p2`, `sum_y2`,
`sum_py`, `sum_diff2`). The affine residual variance is obtained directly from
`var_y - slope*cov` instead of a second evaluation pass; this is algebraically
equivalent to the least-squares fit but numerically cheaper, at the cost of the
extreme-precision guarantee the parent built in (irrelevant at the sizes this loss
is evaluated on). Constant-target and near-constant-prediction edge cases are
merged into the same formulas via a tiny denominator epsilon instead of separate
branches. No complexity penalty is included.
"""
function affine_shape_calibration_loss_simplified_gen18_5(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)
    eps_l = L(eps(one_l))

    # Single pass: accumulate plain sums needed for mean/variance/covariance
    # and the raw squared error, plus the max target magnitude for scaling.
    sum_p = zero_l
    sum_y = zero_l
    sum_p2 = zero_l
    sum_y2 = zero_l
    sum_py = zero_l
    sum_diff2 = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        diff = p - y
        if !isfinite(diff)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        sum_p += p
        sum_y += y
        sum_p2 += p * p
        sum_y2 += y * y
        sum_py += p * y
        sum_diff2 += diff * diff
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))
    end

    if !(isfinite(sum_p) && isfinite(sum_y) && isfinite(sum_p2) &&
         isfinite(sum_y2) && isfinite(sum_py) && isfinite(sum_diff2))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    mean_p = sum_p / n_l
    mean_y = sum_y / n_l

    # Population variance/covariance; clamp tiny negative roundoff to zero.
    var_p = max(sum_p2 / n_l - mean_p * mean_p, zero_l)
    var_y = max(sum_y2 / n_l - mean_y * mean_y, zero_l)
    cov_py = sum_py / n_l - mean_p * mean_y

    target_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_y)
    target_scale2 = target_scale * target_scale

    if var_y <= eps_l * target_scale2
        # Target is (numerically) constant: affine shape is undefined, so fall
        # back to scale-normalized raw MSE, same as the parent's fallback path.
        raw_nmse = max(sum_diff2 / n_l / target_scale2, zero_l)
        loss_value = log1p(raw_nmse)
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
    end

    # Best-fit affine slope/intercept; guard near-constant prediction with an
    # epsilon denominator instead of a separate branch.
    slope = cov_py / max(var_p, eps_l * target_scale2)
    if !isfinite(slope)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # SSE of the optimal affine fit equals var_y - slope*cov_py (algebraically
    # identical to a direct residual evaluation, computed in one pass here).
    affine_mse = max(var_y - slope * cov_py, zero_l)
    affine_nmse = clamp(affine_mse / var_y, zero_l, one_l)
    shape_term = sqrt(affine_nmse)

    # Bounded raw-error tie-breaker, saturating so mis-calibrated but
    # structurally-correct expressions still compete on shape.
    raw_nmse = max(sum_diff2 / n_l / var_y, zero_l)
    bounded_raw = raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse)

    calibration_weight = one_l / L(256)
    loss_value = shape_term + calibration_weight * bounded_raw

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

residual_guided_symmetric_motif_duplicat.name: residual_guided_symmetric_motif_duplication_gen18_6
residual_guided_symmetric_motif_duplicat.code:
"""
    residual_guided_symmetric_motif_duplication_gen18_6(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

A structural mutation that duplicates an evolved subexpression "motif", optionally re-indexes
its variables by a cyclic feature shift, and couples the copy back into the tree with a
binary operator — but where the *feature shift*, the *coupling operator*, and the *attachment
point* are all chosen with data-aware / structural heuristics instead of uniformly at random.

# Core idea (synthesized from the parents)
Both parents observed that scientific expressions are built from repeated functional motifs
applied to different coordinates (`vx^2 + vy^2`, `(x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2`, `m1*m2/r^2`, ...),
and implemented this as: copy a subtree, cyclically shift its feature indices, and couple it
to a target node via a random binary operator. That is a powerful macro-move but it is
blind: with `nfeatures` shifts × `nops[2]` operators × every possible target, the probability
of proposing the *useful* duplication is small.

This version keeps the motif-duplication macro-move but makes the three free choices smarter:

1. **Motif choice**: donors are restricted to subtrees that actually contain a variable
   (duplicating a constant-only motif is a no-op up to constant fitting) *and* that fit
   inside the remaining size budget (`options.maxsize`), so the mutation is rarely rejected
   downstream for complexity.
2. **Shift choice (data-aware)**: the residual `y - f(x)` of the current tree is computed once;
   a small candidate set of cyclic shifts (always including `0`, which yields powers /
   self-couplings) is evaluated on `dataset.X`, and the shift whose shifted motif output has
   the largest absolute correlation with the residual is selected. This turns a
   `1/nfeatures` guess into a greedy pick. If the tree or motif cannot be evaluated, we fall
   back to a uniform random shift (parent behaviour).
3. **Operator / placement bias**: a nonzero shift means "same functional form, different
   coordinate", which in physics almost always combines additively — so `+` is favoured there;
   a zero shift means "self-coupling", where `*` (squares, rational terms) is favoured.
   All other operators remain reachable. With moderate probability the coupling is attached at
   the root, which directly builds top-level symmetric sums of terms; otherwise a
   feature-bearing internal node is used, allowing local symmetrization.

# Assumptions
- `dataset.y` may be `nothing` (multi-output) and evaluation may fail; every data-driven step
  degrades gracefully to the random behaviour of the parents.
- The mutation is a no-op (returns `tree` unchanged) when no binary operator exists or when
  the size budget is exhausted.
"""
function residual_guided_symmetric_motif_duplication_gen18_6(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Guard: binary coupling requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # --- helpers ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Cyclically permute feature indices of all variable leaves in a motif
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int, num_features::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, num_features)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift, num_features)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Does this subtree reference at least one variable?
    _has_feature(node) = any(t -> t.degree == 0 && !t.constant, node)

    # --- Step 0: size budget -----------------------------------------------
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : 30
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    # +1 for the new coupling operator node
    budget = maxsize - tree_size - 1
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # --- Step 1: choose a donor motif --------------------------------------
    # Preferred: contains a variable AND fits in the budget
    _good_donor(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget && _has_feature(t)
    _small_donor(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget

    donor = if any(_good_donor, tree)
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_good_donor))
    elseif any(_small_donor, tree)
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_small_donor))
    else
        return tree  # nothing duplicable within complexity limits
    end
    motif = copy(donor)

    # --- Step 2: pick the cyclic feature shift ------------------------------
    shift = 0
    if nfeatures > 1 && _has_feature(motif)
        # Candidate shifts: identity plus a few random nonzero shifts
        ncand = min(nfeatures - 1, 3)
        candidates = Int[0]
        for _ in 1:ncand
            s = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
            s in candidates || push!(candidates, s)
        end

        # Try to compute the residual of the current tree (data-aware step)
        residual = nothing
        if dataset.y !== nothing
            y_pred, ok = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options.operators)
            if ok && all(isfinite, y_pred)
                residual = dataset.y .- y_pred
            end
        end

        chosen = -1
        if residual !== nothing && std(residual) > 0
            best_score = -1.0
            for s in candidates
                trial = copy(motif)
                s > 0 && _shift_features!(trial, s, nfeatures)
                pred, ok = eval_tree_array(trial, dataset.X, options.operators)
                (ok && all(isfinite, pred) && std(pred) > 0) || continue
                sc = abs(Float64(cor(pred, residual)))
                isfinite(sc) || continue
                if sc > best_score
                    best_score = sc
                    chosen = s
                end
            end
        end
        # Fall back to the parents' uniform random shift if scoring failed
        shift = chosen >= 0 ? chosen : rand(rng, candidates)
        shift > 0 && _shift_features!(motif, shift, nfeatures)
    end
