    # --- Step 3: pick the coupling operator, biased by the shift semantics --
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), options.operators.binops)
    times_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (*), options.operators.binops)
    bin_op = rand(rng, 1:(options.nops[2]))
    if shift > 0
        # Same form on a different coordinate -> most often an additive symmetry
        if plus_idx !== nothing && rand(rng) < 0.6
            bin_op = plus_idx
        end
    else
        # Self-coupling -> powers / products are the common ground-truth pattern
        r = rand(rng)
        if times_idx !== nothing && r < 0.45
            bin_op = times_idx
        elseif plus_idx !== nothing && r < 0.65
            bin_op = plus_idx
        end
    end

    # --- Step 4: choose where to attach the coupling ------------------------
    # Root attachment builds top-level sums of symmetric terms; otherwise
    # symmetrize locally at a variable-bearing node.
    target = if rand(rng) < 0.35
        tree
    elseif any(_has_feature, tree)
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_has_feature))
    else
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    end
    target_copy = copy(target)

    # Randomize operand ordering to support non-commutative operators
    children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
    new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children)

    # In-place content replacement keeps the root valid even when target === tree
    set_node!(target, new_node)

    return tree
end

elbow_lineage_pareto_selection_gen18_8.name: elbow_lineage_pareto_selection_gen18_8
elbow_lineage_pareto_selection_gen18_8.code:
"""
Select a parent from an elbow-aware, lineage-diverse loss–complexity Pareto frontier.

The operator samples a tournament, removes candidates dominated in both raw loss and
expression complexity, and ranks the survivors by frequency-adjusted cost. It then
assigns stochastic selection weights using four signals: cost rank for exploitation,
Pareto crowding for objective-space coverage, local frontier curvature for emphasizing
promising loss-versus-complexity elbows, and complexity-frequency rarity for niche
preservation. Siblings from overrepresented parent lineages are mildly downweighted.
The heuristic assumes that ground-truth expressions often appear near an abrupt elbow
of the loss–complexity frontier, while sparse complexity niches and distinct lineages
provide useful structural stepping stones.
"""
function elbow_lineage_pareto_selection_gen18_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Draw a local tournament while remaining safe for unusually small populations.
    tournament_n = min(pop.n, max(1, options.tournament_selection_n))
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, tournament_n; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)
    n == 1 && return sample[1]

    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    frequencies = zeros(Float64, n)
    valid_frequency = falses(n)

    frequency_table = running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies
    parsimony_scale = Float64(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]
        size = Int(compute_complexity(member, options))
        complexities[i] = size

        # Non-finite objectives are retained only as last-resort candidates.
        loss = Float64(member.loss)
        losses[i] = isfinite(loss) ? loss : Inf

        if 1 <= size <= options.maxsize && size <= length(frequency_table)
            frequency = Float64(frequency_table[size])
            if isfinite(frequency) && frequency >= 0.0
                frequencies[i] = frequency
                valid_frequency[i] = true
            end
        end

        cost = Float64(member.cost)
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament && valid_frequency[i]
            exponent = clamp(parsimony_scale * frequencies[i], -50.0, 50.0)
            cost *= exp(exponent)
        end
        adjusted_costs[i] = isfinite(cost) ? cost : Inf
    end

    # Retain candidates that are not dominated in raw loss and complexity.
    frontier = Int[]
    for i in 1:n
        dominated = false
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue
            no_worse = complexities[j] <= complexities[i] && losses[j] <= losses[i]
            strictly_better =
                complexities[j] < complexities[i] || losses[j] < losses[i]
            if no_worse && strictly_better
                dominated = true
                break
            end
        end
        !dominated && push!(frontier, i)
    end

    # This is defensive; a finite nonempty tournament normally has a Pareto survivor.
    if isempty(frontier)
        return sample[argmin_fast(adjusted_costs)]
    end

    m = length(frontier)
    quality_order = sort(
        frontier;
        by=i -> (adjusted_costs[i], losses[i], complexities[i]),
    )
    quality_rank = fill(m, n)
    for (rank, i) in enumerate(quality_order)
        quality_rank[i] = rank
    end

    # NSGA-style crowding keeps both simple and highly accurate frontier extremes,
    # as well as isolated intermediate stepping stones.
    crowding = zeros(Float64, n)
    complexity_order = sort(frontier; by=i -> complexities[i])
    loss_order = sort(frontier; by=i -> losses[i])

    if m == 1
        crowding[frontier[1]] = 2.0
    else
        complexity_span =
            Float64(complexities[complexity_order[end]] - complexities[complexity_order[1]])
        if complexity_span > 0.0
            crowding[complexity_order[1]] += 1.0
            crowding[complexity_order[end]] += 1.0
            for k in 2:(m - 1)
                neighbor_span = Float64(
                    complexities[complexity_order[k + 1]] -
                    complexities[complexity_order[k - 1]],
                )
                crowding[complexity_order[k]] += neighbor_span / complexity_span
            end
        end

        loss_span = losses[loss_order[end]] - losses[loss_order[1]]
        if isfinite(loss_span) && loss_span > 0.0
            crowding[loss_order[1]] += 1.0
            crowding[loss_order[end]] += 1.0
            for k in 2:(m - 1)
                neighbor_span =
                    losses[loss_order[k + 1]] - losses[loss_order[k - 1]]
                crowding[loss_order[k]] += neighbor_span / loss_span
            end
        end
    end

    # A normalized triangle area estimates local curvature of the Pareto front.
    # Large bends often mark a useful minimum-description-length "elbow."
    knee_score = zeros(Float64, n)
    if m >= 3
        cmin = Float64(complexities[complexity_order[1]])
        cspan = Float64(
            complexities[complexity_order[end]] -
            complexities[complexity_order[1]],
        )
        finite_frontier_losses = all(isfinite(losses[i]) for i in frontier)
        lmin = minimum(losses[i] for i in frontier)
        lmax = maximum(losses[i] for i in frontier)
        lspan = lmax - lmin

        if cspan > 0.0 && finite_frontier_losses && isfinite(lspan) && lspan > 0.0
            for k in 2:(m - 1)
                previous = complexity_order[k - 1]
                current = complexity_order[k]
                following = complexity_order[k + 1]

                x1 = (Float64(complexities[previous]) - cmin) / cspan
                x2 = (Float64(complexities[current]) - cmin) / cspan
                x3 = (Float64(complexities[following]) - cmin) / cspan
                y1 = (losses[previous] - lmin) / lspan
                y2 = (losses[current] - lmin) / lspan
                y3 = (losses[following] - lmin) / lspan

                twice_area = abs((x2 - x1) * (y3 - y1) - (y2 - y1) * (x3 - x1))
                knee_score[current] = min(1.0, 4.0 * twice_area)
            end
        end
    end

    # Normalize rarity relative to the most common frontier complexity.
    frequency_max = 0.0
    for i in frontier
        valid_frequency[i] && (frequency_max = max(frequency_max, frequencies[i]))
    end
    frequency_floor = 1.0 / Float64(max(1, options.population_size))

    weights = Vector{Float64}(undef, m)
    tournament_p = clamp(Float64(options.tournament_selection_p), 0.0, 1.0)
    rank_decay = 0.35 + 0.75 * tournament_p

    for (position, i) in enumerate(frontier)
        # Geometric rank pressure preserves exploitation without making it absolute.
        quality_weight = exp(-rank_decay * Float64(quality_rank[i] - 1))

        shape_bonus =
            1.0 +
            0.55 * min(crowding[i], 2.0) +
            1.50 * knee_score[i]

        rarity_bonus = 1.0
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament && valid_frequency[i]
            rarity_bonus = sqrt(
                (frequency_max + frequency_floor) /
                (frequencies[i] + frequency_floor),
            )
            rarity_bonus = clamp(rarity_bonus, 1.0, 3.0)
        end

        # Count siblings on the eligible frontier; roots use their own reference ID.
        lineage_id = sample[i].parent != 0 ? sample[i].parent : sample[i].ref
        lineage_count = 0
        for j in frontier
            other_lineage =
                sample[j].parent != 0 ? sample[j].parent : sample[j].ref
            lineage_count += other_lineage == lineage_id
        end
        lineage_penalty = sqrt(Float64(max(1, lineage_count)))

        weights[position] =
            quality_weight * shape_bonus * rarity_bonus / lineage_penalty
    end

    total_weight = sum(weights)
    if !(isfinite(total_weight) && total_weight > 0.0)
        return sample[quality_order[1]]
    end

    chosen_position =
        StatsBase.sample(StatsBase.Weights(weights, total_weight))
    return sample[frontier[chosen_position]]
end

streamlined_affine_shape_rmse_loss_gen18.name: streamlined_affine_shape_rmse_loss_gen18_9
streamlined_affine_shape_rmse_loss_gen18.code:
"""
    streamlined_affine_shape_rmse_loss_gen18_9(tree, dataset, options)

Streamlined affine-shape objective. It primarily measures the RMSE remaining
after the best affine recalibration of the prediction, while a small raw-error
term distinguishes affine-equivalent expressions and rewards correct constants.

Steps:
1. Evaluate the tree and accumulate only the four sums needed for the affine
   slope and intercept.
2. In a second pass, directly accumulate the fitted, raw, and centered-target
   squared errors.
3. Form the shape term from the ratio of fitted and target residual norms.
4. Add `1/256` times a bounded normalized raw RMSE. A mean-based scale is used
   only when the target residual norm is zero.

Compared with the parent, this removes `Σy²`, `max|y|`, the shared per-sample
normalization, and separate raw-overflow bookkeeping. It also uses bounded raw
RMSE instead of bounded raw NMSE, placing both components on an RMSE scale and
giving a stronger but still tiny preference for exact calibration. Directly
accumulating residual norms preserves the numerically important affine-shape
idea without additional moment or scale heuristics.
"""
function streamlined_affine_shape_rmse_loss_gen18_9(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # First pass: moments required by the least-squares affine calibration.
    sum_p = zero_l
    sum_y = zero_l
    sum_pp = zero_l
    sum_py = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        sum_p += p
        sum_y += y
        sum_pp += p * p
        sum_py += p * y
    end

    if !(isfinite(sum_p) && isfinite(sum_y) &&
         isfinite(sum_pp) && isfinite(sum_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    mean_p = sum_p / n_l
    mean_y = sum_y / n_l
    centered_pp = sum_pp - sum_p * mean_p
    centered_py = sum_py - sum_p * mean_y

    if !(isfinite(centered_pp) && isfinite(centered_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Constant predictions contain no shape information.
    variance_p = max(centered_pp, zero_l)
    slope = variance_p > zero_l ? centered_py / variance_p : zero_l
    if !isfinite(slope)
        slope = zero_l
    end

    intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
    if !isfinite(intercept)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Second pass: direct residual norms avoid cancellation near exact matches.
    affine_sse = zero_l
    raw_sse = zero_l
    target_sse = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        target_residual = y - mean_y
        target_sse += target_residual * target_residual

        raw_residual = p - y
        raw_sse += raw_residual * raw_residual

        fitted_residual = muladd(slope, p, intercept) - y
        affine_sse += fitted_residual * fitted_residual
    end

    if !(isfinite(target_sse) && isfinite(raw_sse) && isfinite(affine_sse))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # The optimal affine fit is bounded by the mean-prediction baseline.
    shape_term = if target_sse > zero_l
        min(sqrt(affine_sse) / sqrt(target_sse), one_l)
    else
        zero_l
    end

    # Use target variation normally and a relative level scale for constants.
    raw_reference = if target_sse > zero_l
        target_sse
    else
        target_level = max(one_l, abs(mean_y))
        n_l * target_level * target_level
    end

    if !(isfinite(raw_reference) && raw_reference > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Bounded normalized raw RMSE in [0, 1], used only as a small tie-breaker.
    raw_norm = sqrt(raw_sse)
    reference_norm = sqrt(raw_reference)
    bounded_raw = raw_norm / (raw_norm + reference_norm)

    loss_value = shape_term + bounded_raw / L(256)
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen19_.name: age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen19_0
age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen19_.code:
"""
Synthesizes the age-regularized replacement strategy (favor removing the
oldest genome) with a quality-aware tie-break so that, among genomes of
similar age, the search preferentially discards the *worse* performer
rather than blindly picking whichever happens to be oldest.

Motivation: pure age-regularized survival (both parents) guarantees healthy
turnover and protects young, still-unevaluated offspring, but it is blind to
fitness — a mediocre-but-old member can be kept alive far too long relative
to peers, or a decent old member can be evicted purely due to birth order
even while a worse, slightly younger member persists. This is visible in
the trace above: complexity keeps climbing with vanishing loss gains,
suggesting bloated members are not being pruned efficiently.

Approach:
1. Rank all eligible (non-excluded) members by age (older -> higher rank)
   and by cost (worse cost -> higher rank).
2. Combine the two ranks into a single score using a tunable weight that
   keeps age as the dominant signal (preserving the original
   age-regularized character and its diversity/turnover guarantees) while
   letting cost break ties and nudge borderline decisions towards removing
   under-performing members.
3. Return the index with the highest combined score, i.e., the oldest and
   (secondarily) worst member, excluding any indices in `exclude_indices`.
"""
function age_and_cost_regularized_survival_gen19_0(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    eligible = [i for i in 1:n if !(i in exclude_indices)]
    @assert !isempty(eligible) "No eligible members to replace"

    # Extract raw birth and cost values for eligible members
    births = [pop.members[i].birth for i in eligible]
    costs = [pop.members[i].cost for i in eligible]

    # Rank by age: oldest (smallest birth) gets highest age-rank
    age_order = sortperm(births)  # ascending birth -> first is oldest
    age_rank = similar(age_order, Float64)
    for (r, idx) in enumerate(age_order)
        age_rank[idx] = (length(eligible) - r + 1) / length(eligible)  # oldest -> 1.0
    end

    # Rank by cost: worst (largest cost) gets highest cost-rank
    cost_order = sortperm(costs)  # ascending cost -> last is worst
    cost_rank = similar(cost_order, Float64)
    for (r, idx) in enumerate(cost_order)
        cost_rank[idx] = r / length(eligible)  # worst -> 1.0
    end

    # Combine ranks: age dominates (weight 0.75) but cost breaks ties and
    # nudges the decision toward removing poor performers among similarly-aged peers.
    age_weight = 0.75
    combined_score = age_weight .* age_rank .+ (1 - age_weight) .* cost_rank

    # Pick eligible member with highest combined score (oldest & worst-biased)
    best_local = argmax(combined_score)
    return eligible[best_local]
end

elite_protected_oldest_survival_gen19_5.name: elite_protected_oldest_survival_gen19_5
elite_protected_oldest_survival_gen19_5.code:
"""
Simplified survival operator: elite-protected oldest replacement.

Core idea kept from the parent: still purely age-regularized -- the
population member to be replaced is chosen as the one with the smallest
`birth` value (i.e. the oldest), exactly like `age_regularized_survival`.

What is removed/merged relative to a more elaborate multi-factor scheme
(age + loss + complexity combined into a weighted score) is that we do
**not** compute any weighted combination of factors. Instead we fold in a
single, cheap extra rule directly into the same birth-based argmin pass:
the current best (lowest-cost) member is treated as "unkillable" for this
call, exactly as if it were in `exclude_indices`. This prevents the pure
age heuristic from occasionally discarding a long-surviving elite solution
just because it happens to be the oldest, which the trace shows can lead
to stagnation (good early solutions being purged before better variants
are found). All other complexity (tournaments, adaptive parsimony scaling,
frequency weighting, etc.) that a fuller heuristic might add is
deliberately omitted to keep the operator O(n) and easy to reason about.
"""
function elite_protected_oldest_survival_gen19_5(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)

    # Identify the single best (lowest-cost) member in the population;
    # this member is protected from replacement so elite solutions
    # persist even if they are old.
    costs = [pop.members[i].cost for i in 1:(pop.n)]
    best_idx = argmin_fast(costs)

    # Build birth vector, masking out excluded indices and the protected
    # elite with typemax so they are never chosen as the oldest.
    births = [
        (i in exclude_indices || i == best_idx) ? typemax(BT) : pop.members[i].birth
        for i in 1:(pop.n)
    ]

    # Replace the oldest remaining (non-protected, non-excluded) member.
    return argmin_fast(births)
end

signed_centered_profile_calibrated_loss_.name: signed_centered_profile_calibrated_loss_gen19_1
signed_centered_profile_calibrated_loss_.code:
"""
    signed_centered_profile_calibrated_loss_gen19_1(tree, dataset, options)

Compare centered, unit-norm prediction and target profiles while preserving their
orientation, so negatively correlated expressions are no longer treated as
equivalent to the target. Two Welford accumulators first estimate stable means
and centered norms; a second pass measures the direct profile distance and the
normalized raw squared error.

Unlike the parent, this variant removes the prediction-negation branch, uses a
bounded normalized RMSE rather than bounded NMSE so calibration remains visible
near an exact fit, and raises the calibration weight to one quarter. Shape still
leads the search, while incorrectly scaled or shifted affine representatives
receive a meaningful penalty. Constant targets use calibration alone, and
constant predictions receive the zero-correlation profile penalty.
"""
function signed_centered_profile_calibrated_loss_gen19_1(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # Stable first-pass estimates of both centered profile norms.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        k = L(i)

        delta_p = p - mean_p
        mean_p += delta_p / k
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)

        delta_y = y - mean_y
        mean_y += delta_y / k
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Welford variances can only become slightly negative through roundoff.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    prediction_is_variable = m2_p > zero_l
    target_is_variable = m2_y > zero_l

    norm_p = prediction_is_variable ? sqrt(m2_p) : zero_l
    norm_y = target_is_variable ? sqrt(m2_y) : zero_l

    if (prediction_is_variable && !isfinite(norm_p)) ||
       (target_is_variable && !isfinite(norm_y))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Population target deviation makes the mean-target predictor have unit
    # normalized MSE. Constant targets instead use a magnitude-aware unit floor.
    target_scale = target_is_variable ?
        sqrt(m2_y / n_l) :
        max(one_l, abs(mean_y))

    if !(isfinite(target_scale) && target_scale > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    profile_sum = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        residual = p - y
        if !isfinite(residual)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Overflow saturates the bounded calibration term rather than invalidating
        # an otherwise valid expression evaluation.
        if isfinite(raw_sum)
            scaled_residual = residual / target_scale
            raw_sum += abs2(scaled_residual)
        end

        if target_is_variable && prediction_is_variable
            centered_p = (p - mean_p) / norm_p
            centered_y = (y - mean_y) / norm_y
            profile_term = abs2(centered_p - centered_y)

            if !isfinite(profile_term)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            profile_sum += profile_term
        end
    end

    bounded_nrmse = if isfinite(raw_sum)
        normalized_mse = max(raw_sum / n_l, zero_l)
        normalized_rmse = sqrt(normalized_mse)
        normalized_rmse / (one_l + normalized_rmse)
    else
        one_l
    end

    # Centered shape is undefined for a constant target.
    if !target_is_variable
        return L(bounded_nrmse)
    end

    shape_term = if prediction_is_variable
        if !isfinite(profile_sum)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # For unit profiles this equals sqrt(1 - correlation). Retaining the
        # upper range through sqrt(2) explicitly penalizes reversed orientation.
        profile_distance = profile_sum / L(2)
        sqrt(clamp(profile_distance, zero_l, L(2)))
    else
        # A constant prediction corresponds to zero usable correlation.
        one_l
    end

    loss_value = shape_term + (one_l / L(4)) * bounded_nrmse
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

algebraic_fidelity_loss_gen19_2.name: algebraic_fidelity_loss_gen19_2
algebraic_fidelity_loss_gen19_2.code:
"""
    algebraic_fidelity_loss_gen19_2(tree, dataset, options)

A multi-scale, shape-aware loss function designed to overcome the classic failure modes of MSE
in symbolic regression, such as premature convergence into bloated Taylor/rational polynomial
approximations and severe penalization of uncalibrated radical/transcendental backbones.

### Core Idea:
Standard MSE is heavily dominated by points with large absolute values and quadratic penalties
on domain-edge deviations. When searching for complex expressions (e.g., relativistic factors
`x0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)`), MSE frequently traps the evolutionary search in deep polynomial
patches that overfit the interior while discarding partially calibrated true functional forms.

This loss guides the search toward the true mathematical expression via four complementary,
scale-invariant terms:
1. **Normalized Pseudo-Huber Error (`loss_huber`)**: Computes smooth Charbonnier/pseudo-Huber
   loss on variance-normalized residuals. Becomes quadratic for fine-tuning near zero error
   and linear for large deviations, preventing domain-edge spikes from killing candidate skeletons.
2. **Scale-Invariant Relative Error (`loss_rel`)**: Balances errors across the dynamic range
   of the target by normalizing point errors by local target magnitude and variance.
3. **Pearson Functional Shape Loss (`corr_loss`)**: Measures `1 - Pearson correlation`,
   providing an affine-invariant shape reward that identifies expressions with the correct
   algebraic curvature even before constants are tuned by local optimization.
4. **Asymptotic Tail Penalty (`loss_tail`)**: Computes the normalized fourth-root fourth-power
   (L4) discrepancy to quickly penalize polynomial approximations that diverge near asymptotes
   or domain boundaries.

### Heuristics and Assumptions:
- Target variance `var_y` provides a natural normalization scale for dimensional invariance.
- When prediction variance is near zero (flat prediction), correlation loss defaults to 1.0.
- All terms are non-negative, dimensionless, and evaluate to 0.0 only upon exact match.
- Evaluates in two fast, non-allocating SIMD passes over dataset arrays for maximum throughput.
"""
function algebraic_fidelity_loss_gen19_2(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    # Evaluate tree on feature matrix
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n == 0
        return L(0)
    end

    y = dataset.y
    pred = prediction
    eps_T = T(1e-10)

    # Pass 1: Accumulate sums for mean and early invalid value detection
    sum_y = zero(T)
    sum_pred = zero(T)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = pred[i]
        yi = y[i]
        # Reject expressions producing NaN or Inf
        if isnan(p) || isinf(p)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        sum_y += yi
        sum_pred += p
    end

    mean_y = sum_y / n
    mean_pred = sum_pred / n

    # Compute second-order moments for scale and correlation
    var_y_acc = zero(T)
    var_pred_acc = zero(T)
    cov_acc = zero(T)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        dy = y[i] - mean_y
        dp = pred[i] - mean_pred
        var_y_acc += dy * dy
        var_pred_acc += dp * dp
        cov_acc += dy * dp
    end

    var_y = var_y_acc / n
    var_pred = var_pred_acc / n
    cov_yp = cov_acc / n

    std_y = sqrt(var_y + eps_T)
    std_pred = sqrt(var_pred + eps_T)

    # Pearson functional shape correlation loss (1 - r)
    corr_loss = if std_pred > T(1e-6)
        r = cov_yp / (std_y * std_pred + eps_T)
        r_clamped = clamp(r, T(-1), T(1))
        max(zero(T), one(T) - r_clamped)
    else
        one(T)
    end

    # Pass 2: Accumulate multi-scale robust loss terms
    sum_huber = zero(T)
    sum_rel = zero(T)
    sum_l4 = zero(T)
    scale_sq = var_y + eps_T

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        yi = y[i]
        pi = pred[i]
        diff = pi - yi
        diff_sq = diff * diff

        # Variance-normalized squared residual
        u = diff_sq / scale_sq

        # Pseudo-Huber (Charbonnier) discrepancy
        sum_huber += sqrt(one(T) + u) - one(T)

        # Dynamic-range relative error
        denom_rel = abs(yi) + std_y + eps_T
        sum_rel += abs(diff) / denom_rel

        # Fourth-power residual accumulation for tail/asymptotic divergence
        sum_l4 += u * u
    end

    loss_huber = sum_huber / n
    loss_rel = sum_rel / n
    loss_tail = sqrt(sqrt(sum_l4 / n))

    # Balanced composite loss combining magnitude precision, dynamic-range balance,
    # functional shape alignment, and asymptotic boundary fidelity
    total_loss = loss_huber + T(0.5) * loss_rel + T(0.5) * corr_loss + T(0.25) * loss_tail

    return L(total_loss)
end

crowded_clone_purge_survival_gen19_3.name: crowded_clone_purge_survival_gen19_3
crowded_clone_purge_survival_gen19_3.code:
"""
    crowded_clone_purge_survival_gen19_3(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

Diversity-preserving replacement operator ("clone purge + crowding + age").

Motivation
----------
Age-regularized replacement (the default) removes the oldest member regardless of
what it contributes to the search. In long runs this lets the population collapse
onto a single structural motif: dozens of members become near-identical clones or
slightly-bloated re-parameterizations of one scaffold (e.g. in the observed trace,
almost every high-complexity member was a variant of
`x0/exp(x0+square(x0-sqrt(x0)))/(x0+square(x0-sqrt(x0)))`, and several Pareto
entries had *identical* losses at different complexities). Once that happens,
mutation only shuffles constants and the true expression is never reached.

Core idea
---------
Instead of asking "who is oldest?", ask "who is *least informative*?". A member is
uninformative if (a) another member is functionally the same (same complexity and,
to floating-point tolerance, the same loss -> a clone), or (b) it is bloated: a
smaller member already achieves essentially the same loss, or (c) it sits in an
already over-crowded region of complexity space. Members that are unique, on the
current cost-complexity Pareto front, or young are protected. Everything is folded
into a single scalar "replacement priority" and we return the argmax.

Steps
-----
1. Collect complexity, raw loss, cost and birth for every member.
2. Flag non-finite members (NaN/Inf cost or loss) -> replace them first.
3. Clone detection: within each exact-complexity group, members whose losses agree
   to a relative tolerance are duplicates; keep the one with best cost (tie-break
   older birth, then lower index) and flag the rest as redundant.
4. Bloat detection: flag member i if some j is strictly smaller and has a loss no
   worse than (1 + tol) times i's loss, i.e. i pays complexity for nothing.
5. Crowding: count members within +/-1 complexity of i (soft niche occupancy),
   normalized by population size, so over-represented sizes are pruned first.
6. Elitism: members not dominated in (complexity, cost) get a strong protection
   bonus, and the single global best-cost member is protected the most; clones of
   an elite are *not* protected (the kept copy already carries the information).
7. Age: older members get a mild replacement bonus, retaining the pressure of
   age-regularized evolution as the tie-breaker / background drift.
8. Return `argmax(priority)` while never returning an index in `exclude_indices`.

Assumptions / heuristics
------------------------
* Equal complexity + equal loss (to ~1e-6 relative) is a reliable, tree-free proxy
  for structural/functional duplication; this avoids traversing expressions.
* Weights are chosen so ordering is: non-finite > clone > bloat > crowd/age, and a
  Pareto-optimal non-clone is essentially never replaced unless it is the only
  legal choice.
* The function is total: if every index is excluded it still returns a valid index.
"""
function crowded_clone_purge_survival_gen19_3(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    members = pop.members

    # Trivial cases: nothing to choose from.
    if n <= 1
        return 1
    end

    # ---- 1. descriptors -------------------------------------------------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    births = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        m = members[i]
        complexities[i] = compute_complexity(m, options)
        losses[i] = Float64(m.loss)
        costs[i] = Float64(m.cost)
        births[i] = Float64(m.birth)
    end

    # ---- 2. non-finite members are always the first to go --------------------
    bad = falses(n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        bad[i] = !isfinite(costs[i]) || !isfinite(losses[i])
    end

    # ---- 3. clone (duplicate) detection --------------------------------------
    # Same complexity + (relatively) identical loss => functionally the same
    # individual. Keep the best-cost / oldest representative, purge the others.
    rel_tol_clone = 1e-6
    redundant = falses(n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        bad[i] && continue
        for j in 1:n
            (j == i) && continue
            bad[j] && continue
            (complexities[j] == complexities[i]) || continue
            scale = max(abs(losses[i]), abs(losses[j]), 1e-300)
            if abs(losses[i] - losses[j]) <= rel_tol_clone * scale
                # Decide which copy is the "keeper": lower cost, then older, then
                # lower index. If j is the keeper, i is redundant.
                j_keeps =
                    (costs[j] < costs[i]) || (
                        costs[j] == costs[i] && (
                            births[j] < births[i] ||
                            (births[j] == births[i] && j < i)
                        )
                    )
                if j_keeps
                    redundant[i] = true
                    break
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # ---- 4. bloat detection ---------------------------------------------------
    # i is bloated if a strictly smaller member already matches its loss within
    # a slack of 0.1%: extra nodes purchase (almost) no accuracy.
    rel_tol_bloat = 1e-3
    bloated = falses(n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        bad[i] && continue
        for j in 1:n
            bad[j] && continue
            if complexities[j] < complexities[i] &&
                losses[j] <= losses[i] * (1 + rel_tol_bloat) + 1e-300
                bloated[i] = true
                break
            end
        end
    end

    # ---- 5. crowding in complexity space -------------------------------------
    # Soft niche occupancy: how many members live within +/-1 complexity of i.
    crowd = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        cnt = 0
        for j in 1:n
            if abs(complexities[j] - complexities[i]) <= 1
                cnt += 1
            end
        end
        crowd[i] = (cnt - 1) / n  # fraction of *other* members sharing the niche
    end

    # ---- 6. Pareto (cost-complexity) elitism ---------------------------------
    nondominated = trues(n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        if bad[i]
            nondominated[i] = false
            continue
        end
        for j in 1:n
            (j == i) && continue
            bad[j] && continue
            if complexities[j] <= complexities[i] && costs[j] < costs[i]
                nondominated[i] = false
                break
            end
        end
    end
    # Global champion (best cost) gets the strongest protection.
    best_idx = 1
    best_cost = Inf
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        if !bad[i] && costs[i] < best_cost
            best_cost = costs[i]
            best_idx = i
        end
    end

    # ---- 7. age term (background age-regularized drift) ----------------------
    bmin = minimum(births)
    bmax = maximum(births)
    brange = bmax - bmin
    age_norm = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        # 1.0 for the oldest member, 0.0 for the newest.
        age_norm[i] = brange > 0 ? (bmax - births[i]) / brange : 0.0
    end

    # ---- 8. combine into a replacement priority and pick the argmax ----------
    excluded = falses(n)
    @inbounds for idx in exclude_indices
        if 1 <= idx <= n
            excluded[idx] = true
        end
    end

    priority = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        if excluded[i]
            priority[i] = -Inf
            continue
        end
        p = 0.0
        p += bad[i] ? 100.0 : 0.0            # broken members first
        p += redundant[i] ? 4.0 : 0.0        # exact clones next
        p += bloated[i] ? 1.5 : 0.0          # then complexity that buys nothing
        p += 1.0 * crowd[i]                  # thin out over-populated sizes
        p += 1.0 * age_norm[i]               # keep age-regularized turnover
        # Protection: unique, non-dominated stepping stones are kept.
        if nondominated[i] && !redundant[i]
            p -= 6.0
        end
        if i == best_idx && !redundant[i]
            p -= 20.0
        end
        priority[i] = p
    end

    # argmax over priority (== argmin over negated priority, using the fast util).
    neg = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        neg[i] = -priority[i]
    end
    chosen = argmin_fast(neg)

    # Safety net: if every index was excluded (priority all -Inf), return the
    # first legal index, or 1 as a last resort.
    @inbounds if excluded[chosen]
        for i in 1:n
            if !excluded[i]
                return i
            end
        end
        return 1
    end
    return chosen
end

saturated_profile_correlation_loss_gen19.name: saturated_profile_correlation_loss_gen19_1_gen19_4
saturated_profile_correlation_loss_gen19.code:
"""
    saturated_profile_correlation_loss_gen19_1_gen19_4(tree, dataset, options)

Affine-invariant *shape* loss: it compares the standardized prediction profile to
the standardized target profile through a smooth, odd, saturating map, and
reports `sqrt(1 - |r|)` where `r` is the correlation of the two saturated
profiles. Because standardization plus an odd map is equivariant under any
affine rescaling of either series (including sign flips), an expression that
matches the target up to `a*f + b` still receives exactly zero shape loss, so the
search can find *structure* before constants are tuned. A small bounded
normalized raw-error term then acts as a calibration tie-breaker that pushes the
correctly scaled/offset representative of each affine family to the front, and it
becomes the entire loss when the target is constant (shape is undefined there).

Steps:
 1. One fused pass accumulates origin-shifted power sums (shift by the first
    sample) for prediction and target, plus the raw squared-error sum.
 2. Means and centered second moments are recovered from those sums; harmless
    negative roundoff is clipped at zero.
 3. A second pass standardizes both series by their standard deviations and maps
    them through `s(z) = z / sqrt(1 + (z/c)^2)` with `c = 4`, accumulating the
    five sums needed for the correlation of the saturated profiles.
 4. Loss = `sqrt(1 - |r|) + (1/32) * nmse/(1 + nmse)`.

Changes vs. the parent:
 * Replaced the per-element Welford recursion (two divisions per sample) with a
   single shifted-power-sum pass; the shift by `prediction[1]`/`y[1]` keeps the
   cancellation error of `Σd² - (Σd)²/n` small while being much cheaper, and the
   raw-error sum is now folded into that same pass.
 * The shape term is now the correlation of *softly saturated* standardized
   profiles instead of raw standardized profiles. This keeps exactness and full
   affine/sign invariance, but a handful of extreme samples (very common in
   Feynman-style rational/exponential targets) can no longer dominate the shape
   signal, so partially-correct structures are ranked by how well they match the
   *bulk* of the profile rather than by a few outliers.
 * The saturated statistics are bounded (`|s| < 4`), so the second pass cannot
   overflow and no separate magnitude/overflow heuristics are needed; the
   correlation is clamped to `[-1, 1]` before the square root.
 * Same non-negative, size-agnostic contract as the parent: no complexity term.
"""
function saturated_profile_correlation_loss_gen19_1_gen19_4(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    y = dataset.y
    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # Origin shift: subtracting the first sample makes the power sums
    # well-conditioned without needing a running-mean recursion.
    p0 = L(prediction[1])
    y0 = L(y[1])
    if !(isfinite(p0) && isfinite(y0))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    sum_p = zero_l   # Σ (p_i - p0)
    sum_p2 = zero_l  # Σ (p_i - p0)^2
    sum_y = zero_l   # Σ (y_i - y0)
    sum_y2 = zero_l  # Σ (y_i - y0)^2
    raw_sum = zero_l # Σ (p_i - y_i)^2 (unnormalized)

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        t = L(y[i])
        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(t))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        dp = p - p0
        dt = t - y0
        sum_p += dp
        sum_p2 += dp * dp
        sum_y += dt
        sum_y2 += dt * dt

        # Overflow here is allowed: it maps to a saturated calibration term.
        if isfinite(raw_sum)
            res = p - t
            raw_sum += res * res
        end
    end

    if !(isfinite(sum_p) && isfinite(sum_p2) && isfinite(sum_y) && isfinite(sum_y2))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    mean_p = p0 + sum_p / n_l
    mean_y = y0 + sum_y / n_l

    # Centered second moments; clip tiny negative roundoff.
    m2_p = max(sum_p2 - (sum_p * sum_p) / n_l, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(sum_y2 - (sum_y * sum_y) / n_l, zero_l)

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) && isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    target_is_variable = m2_y > zero_l
    prediction_is_variable = m2_p > zero_l

    # Variable targets are calibrated against their own spread; constant targets
    # against their magnitude with a unit floor.
    target_scale = target_is_variable ? sqrt(m2_y / n_l) : max(one_l, abs(mean_y))
    if !(isfinite(target_scale) && target_scale > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Bounded normalized raw error (divide twice to dodge target_scale^2 overflow).
    bounded_raw = if isfinite(raw_sum)
        raw_nmse = max(((raw_sum / n_l) / target_scale) / target_scale, zero_l)
        isfinite(raw_nmse) ? raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse) : one_l
    else
        one_l
    end

    # Shape is undefined for a constant target: calibration is the whole loss.
    if !target_is_variable
        return L(bounded_raw)
    end

    # A constant prediction has no profile at all -> maximal shape loss.
    if !prediction_is_variable
        loss_flat = one_l + (one_l / L(32)) * bounded_raw
        return isfinite(loss_flat) ? L(loss_flat) : L(Inf)
    end

    sd_p = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)
    sd_y = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    if !(isfinite(sd_p) && isfinite(sd_y) && sd_p > zero_l && sd_y > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end
    inv_sd_p = one_l / sd_p
    inv_sd_y = one_l / sd_y

    # Saturation half-scale in standard-deviation units: near-linear inside the
    # bulk (|s(z) - z| < 3% at |z| = 1) and bounded by c for extreme samples.
    inv_c2 = one_l / L(16)  # c = 4

    su = zero_l
    sv = zero_l
    suu = zero_l
    svv = zero_l
    suv = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        zp = (L(prediction[i]) - mean_p) * inv_sd_p
        zt = (L(y[i]) - mean_y) * inv_sd_y

        # Smooth odd saturating map: preserves exact equality (hence r = ±1 at an
        # exact affine match) while limiting the leverage of extreme points.
        u = zp / sqrt(one_l + zp * zp * inv_c2)
        v = zt / sqrt(one_l + zt * zt * inv_c2)

        su += u
        sv += v
        suu += u * u
        svv += v * v
        suv += u * v
    end

    # Correlation of the saturated profiles (all sums are bounded by c^2 * n).
    cov_uv = suv - (su * sv) / n_l
    var_u = suu - (su * su) / n_l
    var_v = svv - (sv * sv) / n_l

    shape_term = if isfinite(cov_uv) && isfinite(var_u) && isfinite(var_v) &&
                    var_u > zero_l && var_v > zero_l
        denom = sqrt(var_u * var_v)
        r = denom > zero_l ? cov_uv / denom : zero_l
        # Sign-flip invariance: |r| == 1 for either orientation of an affine match.
        abs_r = clamp(isfinite(r) ? abs(r) : zero_l, zero_l, one_l)
        sqrt(max(one_l - abs_r, zero_l))
    else
        one_l
    end

    # Shape leads the search; the bounded raw term only breaks ties inside an
    # affine-equivalent family (favoring the correctly scaled/offset member).
    loss_value = shape_term + (one_l / L(32)) * bounded_raw
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

paired_motif_duplication_gen19_6.name: paired_motif_duplication_gen19_6
paired_motif_duplication_gen19_6.code:
"""
    paired_motif_duplication_gen19_6(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Duplicates one sampled subtree and combines the two copies with a random binary operator.
The second copy optionally receives a cyclic feature shift, allowing the mutation to create
both exact repetitions such as `f(x) * f(x)` and parallel forms such as `f(x₁) + f(x₂)`.

Steps:
1. Return unchanged when no binary operators are available.
2. Sample one subtree and make two independent copies.
3. Cyclically shift the variables in the second copy by a random offset.
4. Replace the sampled subtree with a binary combination of the two copies.

Compared with the parent, this merges the independent donor and target selections into one
motif selection and removes randomized operand ordering. The resulting mutation is smaller
and makes structural repetition explicit, while retaining exact duplication, powers, and
feature-symmetric motifs.
"""
function paired_motif_duplication_gen19_6(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # Apply one consistent cyclic feature mapping throughout a motif.
    function shift_features!(node, shift::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeatures)
            end
            return
        end

        for i in 1:node.degree
            shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift)
        end
    end

    # Pair a subtree directly with a transformed copy of itself.
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    original = copy(target)
    duplicate = copy(target)

    if nfeatures > 1
        shift_features!(duplicate, rand(rng, 0:(nfeatures - 1)))
    end

    replacement = constructorof(N)(;
        op=rand(rng, 1:options.nops[2]),
        children=(original, duplicate),
    )
    set_node!(target, replacement)

    return tree
end

pareto_crowding_rare_niche_tournament_se.name: pareto_crowding_rare_niche_tournament_selection_gen19_7
pareto_crowding_rare_niche_tournament_se.code:
"""
    pareto_crowding_rare_niche_tournament_selection_gen19_7(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Select an individual using a Pareto tournament that jointly preserves useful
complexity niches, young lineages, and distinct structural representatives.

The operator synthesizes crowding suppression with multi-objective niche selection:

1. Sample a tournament pool enlarged slightly beyond `tournament_selection_n`, so
   local redundancy and niche occupancy can be estimated reliably.
2. Compute the usual adaptive-parsimony-adjusted cost and each candidate's global
   complexity frequency.
3. Identify redundant candidates using equal complexity plus nearly equal loss as
   a cheap structural-clone proxy, with shared-parent siblings treated as partial
   duplicates. Only copies that are worse than an existing representative receive
   a multiplicative quality penalty, leaving the best representative untouched.
4. Construct a separate niche-congestion objective from global and pool-local
   complexity occupancy, age, sibling density, and near-clone density. Younger,
   uncommon, and lineage-distinct candidates therefore remain competitive without
   receiving an unconditional fitness bonus.
5. Perform full non-dominated sorting over `(crowding-adjusted cost, congestion)`.
   Within each Pareto front, use a scale-free rank compromise weighted toward
   quality, then apply the usual geometric tournament probability.
6. Occasionally select the rarest complexity among the first two Pareto fronts.
   This restores starved complexity bands while preventing arbitrarily poor rare
   candidates from bypassing all quality control.

The clone test deliberately avoids expression-tree hashing or allocation-heavy
structural comparisons. All diversity pressures are mild and tournament-local, so
the method approaches ordinary adaptive-parsimony selection when the sampled pool
is diverse and its complexity niches are balanced.
"""
function pareto_crowding_rare_niche_tournament_selection_gen19_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Mild tunables: quality remains the primary objective.
    pool_scale = 1.5
    clone_penalty = 1.30
    sibling_redundancy_weight = 0.35
    loss_rtol = 1e-6
    redundancy_cap = 4.0

    local_complexity_weight = 0.15
    age_weight = 0.15
    sibling_density_weight = 0.20
    clone_density_weight = 0.20
    quality_tradeoff = 0.72
    p_rare_niche = 0.08

    n_base = max(1, options.tournament_selection_n)
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    n <= 1 && return pool[1]

    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    frequencies = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    frequency_table = running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies
    scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    # Compute the standard exploitation objective before local crowding penalties.
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        frequency = if (
            0 < complexity <= options.maxsize &&
            complexity <= length(frequency_table)
        )
            Float64(frequency_table[complexity])
        else
            0.0
        end
        frequencies[i] = frequency

        adjusted_costs[i] = if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            member.cost * exp(scaling * L(frequency))
        else
            member.cost
        end
    end

    # Pool-relative age: zero is newest and one is oldest.
    birth_min = pool[1].birth
    birth_max = pool[1].birth
    for i in 2:n
        birth_min = min(birth_min, pool[i].birth)
        birth_max = max(birth_max, pool[i].birth)
    end
    birth_span = max(birth_max - birth_min, 1)

    local_complexity_counts = ones(Int, n)
    sibling_counts = ones(Int, n)
    clone_counts = zeros(Int, n)
    loss_tolerance = L(loss_rtol)

    # Symmetric density statistics are used by the congestion objective.
    for i in 1:(n - 1)
        for j in (i + 1):n
            if complexities[i] == complexities[j]
                local_complexity_counts[i] += 1
                local_complexity_counts[j] += 1

                li = pool[i].loss
                lj = pool[j].loss
                loss_scale = max(abs(li), abs(lj), eps(L))
                if abs(li - lj) <= loss_tolerance * loss_scale
                    clone_counts[i] += 1
                    clone_counts[j] += 1
                end
            end

            parent_i = pool[i].parent
            if parent_i != 0 && parent_i == pool[j].parent
                sibling_counts[i] += 1
                sibling_counts[j] += 1
            end
        end
    end

    # Accumulate redundancy only from better candidates. Thus each clone cluster
    # retains an unpenalized representative instead of suppressing the whole niche.
    adjusted_order = sortperm(adjusted_costs)
    redundancy = zeros(Float64, n)
    for position in 2:n
        i = adjusted_order[position]
        li = pool[i].loss
        weight = 0.0

        for better_position in 1:(position - 1)
            j = adjusted_order[better_position]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(abs(li), abs(lj), eps(L))
            same_solution_proxy = (
                complexities[i] == complexities[j] &&
                abs(li - lj) <= loss_tolerance * loss_scale
            )

            if same_solution_proxy
                weight += 1.0
            elseif pool[i].parent != 0 && pool[i].parent == pool[j].parent
                weight += sibling_redundancy_weight
            end
        end
        redundancy[i] = min(weight, redundancy_cap)
    end

    # Sign-safe worsening for the unusual case of a negative cost.
    worsen = function (cost::L, factor::Float64)
        typed_factor = L(factor)
        return cost >= zero(L) ? cost * typed_factor : cost / typed_factor
    end

    quality_scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    niche_scores = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    density_denominator = Float64(n - 1)

    for i in 1:n
        crowd_factor = clone_penalty^redundancy[i]
        quality_scores[i] = worsen(adjusted_costs[i], crowd_factor)

        local_complexity_density =
            Float64(local_complexity_counts[i] - 1) / density_denominator
        sibling_density =
            Float64(sibling_counts[i] - 1) / density_denominator
        clone_density = Float64(clone_counts[i]) / density_denominator
        normalized_age =
            Float64(birth_max - pool[i].birth) / Float64(birth_span)

        # Lower congestion is better. Age is kept out of the quality score so a
        # weak newcomer must still offer a meaningful Pareto diversity tradeoff.
        niche_scores[i] =
            frequencies[i] +
            local_complexity_weight * local_complexity_density +
            age_weight * normalized_age +
            sibling_density_weight * sibling_density +
            clone_density_weight * clone_density
    end

    # Build the Pareto dominance graph in O(n²).
    dominated_count = zeros(Int, n)
    dominates = [Int[] for _ in 1:n]

    for i in 1:(n - 1)
        for j in (i + 1):n
            i_dominates_j = (
                quality_scores[i] <= quality_scores[j] &&
                niche_scores[i] <= niche_scores[j] &&
                (
                    quality_scores[i] < quality_scores[j] ||
                    niche_scores[i] < niche_scores[j]
                )
            )
            j_dominates_i = (
                quality_scores[j] <= quality_scores[i] &&
                niche_scores[j] <= niche_scores[i] &&
                (
                    quality_scores[j] < quality_scores[i] ||
                    niche_scores[j] < niche_scores[i]
                )
            )

            if i_dominates_j
                push!(dominates[i], j)
                dominated_count[j] += 1
            elseif j_dominates_i
                push!(dominates[j], i)
                dominated_count[i] += 1
            end
        end
    end

    # Assign true non-dominated front numbers rather than using raw dominance count.
    front_rank = zeros(Int, n)
    remaining_dominators = copy(dominated_count)
    current_front = findall(==(0), remaining_dominators)
    front_number = 1

    while !isempty(current_front)
        next_front = Int[]
        for i in current_front
            front_rank[i] = front_number
            for j in dominates[i]
                remaining_dominators[j] -= 1
                if remaining_dominators[j] == 0
                    push!(next_front, j)
                end
            end
        end
        current_front = next_front
        front_number += 1
    end

    # Rare-niche exploration is restricted to high-quality Pareto fronts.
    if rand() < p_rare_niche
        best_idx = 0
        for i in 1:n
            front_rank[i] <= 2 || continue

            if best_idx == 0 ||
               frequencies[i] < frequencies[best_idx] ||
               (
                   frequencies[i] == frequencies[best_idx] &&
                   local_complexity_counts[i] <
                   local_complexity_counts[best_idx]
               ) ||
               (
                   frequencies[i] == frequencies[best_idx] &&
                   local_complexity_counts[i] ==
                   local_complexity_counts[best_idx] &&
                   niche_scores[i] < niche_scores[best_idx]
               ) ||
               (
                   frequencies[i] == frequencies[best_idx] &&
                   local_complexity_counts[i] ==
                   local_complexity_counts[best_idx] &&
                   niche_scores[i] == niche_scores[best_idx] &&
                   quality_scores[i] < quality_scores[best_idx]
               )
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        return pool[best_idx]
    end

    # Scale-free objective ranks provide a quality-biased compromise within each
    # Pareto front, allowing the niche objective to matter even when p == 1.
    quality_rank = zeros(Float64, n)
    niche_rank = zeros(Float64, n)
    quality_order = sortperm(quality_scores)
    niche_order = sortperm(niche_scores)

    for position in 1:n
        normalized_position = Float64(position - 1) / Float64(n - 1)
        quality_rank[quality_order[position]] = normalized_position
        niche_rank[niche_order[position]] = normalized_position
    end

    compromise_scores = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        compromise_scores[i] =
            quality_tradeoff * quality_rank[i] +
            (1.0 - quality_tradeoff) * niche_rank[i]
    end

    ranked_indices = collect(1:n)
    sort!(
        ranked_indices;
        by=i -> (
            front_rank[i],
            compromise_scores[i],
            quality_rank[i],
            niche_scores[i],
        ),
    )

    p = clamp(Float64(options.tournament_selection_p), eps(Float64), 1.0)
    chosen_rank = if p >= 1.0
        1
    else
        rank_offsets = collect(0:(n - 1))
        probabilities = p .* ((1.0 - p) .^ rank_offsets)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        StatsBase.sample(weights)
    end

    return pool[ranked_indices[chosen_rank]]
end

pareto_lineage_decongested_niche_tournam.name: pareto_lineage_decongested_niche_tournament_gen19_8
pareto_lineage_decongested_niche_tournam.code:
"""
    pareto_lineage_decongested_niche_tournament_gen19_8(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

A Pareto-aware, lineage-decongesting tournament selection operator designed to prevent
both **lineage monopolies** (population overrun by near-identical clone/sibling chains)
and **complexity-niche starvation** (extinction of intermediate building blocks) during
symbolic regression search.

### Core Idea & Mechanism:
1. **Enlarged Sample Pool**: Samples `~1.5 * tournament_selection_n` distinct members
   to provide sufficient sample density for Pareto ranking, lineage tracking, and niche estimation.
2. **Local Pareto-Front Identification & Parsimony Attenuation**: Computes raw loss and
   complexity to evaluate local Pareto dominance rank (how many pool members dominate member `i`).
   Non-dominated expressions (rank 0) represent empirical Pareto frontier anchors; their adaptive
   parsimony pressure is attenuated so that high-complexity, low-loss breakthroughs are not
   prematurely extinguished.
3. **Multi-Level Lineage & Clone De-congestion**:
   Ranks pool members by score and penalizes redundant copies of better solutions:
   - Identical complexity with matching loss (tolerance `loss_rtol`): weight 1.0 (clone)
   - Immediate parent-child relationship (`parent == ref`): weight 0.50 (direct lineage step)
   - Sibling relationship (`shared parent`): weight 0.35 (sibling branch)
   The best representative of each lineage/cluster is untouched; inferior replicas are geometrically demoted.
4. **Youth Turnover & Pareto Bonus**:
   - Newer expressions receive a mild recency discount (`youth_discount`), preventing stale
     champions from repeatedly winning tournament slots without structural progress.
   - Pareto-optimal solutions receive a modest quality bonus (`pareto_discount`).
5. **Quality-Guaranteed Rare Niche Pick**:
   With probability `p_rare_niche`, instead of picking a random or broken expression in a rare band,
   identifies the *niche champion* (fittest pool member) for each represented complexity and returns
   the champion belonging to the rarest complexity niche. Otherwise, executes the standard geometric
   tournament ladder (`tournament_selection_p`).

### Changes vs. Parent (`crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen10_4`):
- **Pareto-Dominance Rank Protection**: Actively protects non-dominated (Loss vs Complexity) individuals
  from parsimony over-penalization, preserving structural diversity along the Pareto front.
- **Direct Ancestor-Descendant Tracking**: Added detection for `parent == ref` links to suppress
  sequential mutation chains of the same lineage monopolizing the population.
- **Quality-Guaranteed Niche Selection**: The parent picked the lowest-frequency pool member
  unconditionally (often selecting degenerate/broken mutations). The improved operator identifies the
  best representative of each complexity band before picking the rarest, ensuring that exploration
  injects high-quality structural building blocks.
- **Sign-Consistent Generalized Inflation**: Ensures robust handling of zero, positive, and negative
  loss/cost values for both penalties (>1.0) and discounts (<1.0).
"""
function pareto_lineage_decongested_niche_tournament_gen19_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # ---------------- 0. Tunable Hyperparameters ---------------------------------
    pool_scale = 1.5              # sample size multiplier relative to tournament_selection_n
    clone_penalty = 1.35          # geometric cost inflation per redundancy unit
    parent_child_weight = 0.50    # redundancy weight for direct ancestor-descendant
    sibling_weight = 0.35         # redundancy weight for shared parent siblings
    loss_rtol = 1e-6              # relative tolerance for identical loss detection
    youth_discount = 0.05         # max relative score discount for freshest solutions
    pareto_discount = 0.12        # relative score bonus for non-dominated solutions
    p_rare_niche = 0.10           # probability of quality-guaranteed niche champion pick

    # Sign-safe multiplier for minimization: f > 1 makes score worse, f < 1 makes score better
    inflate = function (x::L, f::Float64)
        fl = L(f)
        if x > zero(L)
            return x * fl
        elseif x < zero(L)
            return x / fl
        else
            return x + (fl - L(1))
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 1. Sample Tournament Pool ----------------------------------
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)
    if n == 1
        return pool[1]
    end

    # ---------------- 2. Complexities and Local Pareto Dominance -----------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        complexities[i] = compute_complexity(pool[i], options)
    end

    # Compute Pareto dominance count within the tournament pool
    pareto_rank = zeros(Int, n)
    for i in 1:n
        ci = complexities[i]
        li = pool[i].loss
        for j in 1:n
            j == i && continue
            cj = complexities[j]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            # Member j dominates i if j is no worse in both objectives and strictly better in at least one
            if (cj <= ci && lj <= li) && (cj < ci || lj < li)
                pareto_rank[i] += 1
            end
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 3. Base Scores with Pareto-Attenuated Parsimony ------------
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        size = complexities[i]
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            # Attenuate parsimony pressure on Pareto-optimal solutions (rank 0 and 1)
            attenuation = pareto_rank[i] == 0 ? L(0.60) : (pareto_rank[i] == 1 ? L(0.80) : L(1.00))
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency * attenuation)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 4. Multi-level Lineage & Clone De-congestion ---------------
    order = sortperm(scores)
    redundancy = zeros(Float64, n)
    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        wi = 0.0
        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss

            # 1) Exact / near clone (same complexity and identical loss)
            same_loss = abs(li - lj) <= L(loss_rtol) * max(abs(li), abs(lj), eps(L))
            if complexities[i] == complexities[j] && same_loss
                wi += 1.0
            # 2) Direct ancestor-descendant chain (one is the immediate parent of the other)
            elseif (pool[i].parent != 0 && pool[i].parent == pool[j].ref) ||
                   (pool[j].parent != 0 && pool[j].parent == pool[i].ref)
                wi += parent_child_weight
            # 3) Siblings from the same parent
            elseif pool[i].parent != 0 && pool[i].parent == pool[j].parent
                wi += sibling_weight
            end
        end
        redundancy[i] = wi
    end

    # ---------------- 5. Youth Turnover & Pareto Bonus Application ---------------
    birth_min = pool[1].birth
    birth_max = pool[1].birth
    for i in 2:n
        b = pool[i].birth
        b < birth_min && (birth_min = b)
        b > birth_max && (birth_max = b)
    end
    birth_span = max(birth_max - birth_min, 1)

    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        recency = (pool[i].birth - birth_min) / birth_span # 0.0 (oldest) .. 1.0 (newest)
        youth_factor = 1.0 - youth_discount * recency
        pareto_factor = pareto_rank[i] == 0 ? (1.0 - pareto_discount) : (pareto_rank[i] == 1 ? (1.0 - 0.5 * pareto_discount) : 1.0)
        clone_factor = clone_penalty ^ redundancy[i]

        combined_factor = clone_factor * youth_factor * pareto_factor
        penalized[i] = inflate(scores[i], combined_factor)
    end

    # ---------------- 6a. Quality-Guaranteed Rare Niche Exploration --------------
    if rand() < p_rare_niche
        best_idx = 1
        best_freq = Inf
        best_score = penalized[1]

        # Scan for champions: best performer per unique complexity represented in the pool
        for i in 1:n
            ci = complexities[i]
            pi = penalized[i]
            is_niche_best = true
            for j in 1:n
                if j != i && complexities[j] == ci
                    pj = penalized[j]
                    if pj < pi || (pj == pi && j < i)
                        is_niche_best = false
                        break
                    end
                end
            end

            # Among niche champions, select the one in the rarest global complexity band
            if is_niche_best
                f = if (0 < ci <= options.maxsize)
                    Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[ci])
                else
                    0.0
                end
                if f < best_freq || (f == best_freq && pi < best_score)
                    best_freq = f
                    best_score = pi
                    best_idx = i
                end
            end
        end
        return pool[best_idx]
    end

    # ---------------- 6b. Standard Geometric Tournament Ladder ------------------
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        if tournament_winner == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, tournament_winner)[2][end]
        end
    end
    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

symmetry_motif_recombination_gen15_1_gen.name: symmetry_motif_recombination_gen15_1_gen19_9
symmetry_motif_recombination_gen15_1_gen.code:
"""
    symmetry_motif_recombination_gen15_1_gen19_9(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

A structural mutation operator that recycles an already-evolved subexpression *motif*: it clones a
donor subtree, re-indexes the clone's variables with one of several symmetry-preserving index maps,
optionally "dresses" it with a unary operator, and couples it back into the tree with a binary
operator biased toward the canonical accumulators `+` / `*`.

# Core Idea
Ground-truth laws are overwhelmingly assembled from *repeated functional forms* evaluated on
different variables or coordinates: `0.5*m*(vx^2 + vy^2)`, `(x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2`, `a*b + c*d`,
`x*sin(x)`. Rediscovering each copy independently through point mutations is exponentially unlikely,
so this operator reuses structure that evolution has already paid for.

# Synthesis of the two parents
* From parent 1 (`symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_6`): the lean, single-traversal feature remapping
  and a compact control flow — one coupling path, no homologous-grafting heuristics.
* From parent 2 (`symmetry_aware_motif_coupling_gen14_8`): a `maxsize`-derived size budget so the
  offspring is admissible, tiered donor sampling that prefers compound variable-bearing motifs (so the
  mutation does not degenerate into `insert_random_op`), targeted feature substitution alongside the
  cyclic shift, root-biased target selection, self-coupling degeneracy avoidance, and the `+`/`*` bias.
* New in this version:
  - **Pairwise feature transposition.** A dedicated remap mode that *swaps* two feature indices
    throughout the motif (`x1 ↔ x2`). This is exactly the exchange symmetry / antisymmetry that
    neither a global cyclic shift nor a one-way substitution can express, and it makes forms such as
    `f(x1,x2) + f(x2,x1)` or `(x1-x2) * (x2-x1)` reachable in a single mutation.
  - **Optional unary dressing of the clone.** With small probability (and only if the budget allows)
    the motif is wrapped in a random unary operator before coupling, producing the very common
    `u ⊕ g(u')` shapes (`x + sin(x)`, `r * exp(-r)`) that otherwise need two coordinated mutations.
  - **Unified cumulative mode selection** with weights conditioned on how many *distinct* features the
    motif carries (identity-only for constant motifs; shift-favoured for single-feature motifs;
    substitution/transposition up-weighted for multi-feature motifs).

# Steps
1. Bail out if there is no binary operator or no size headroom (`maxsize - size(tree) - 1 < 1`).
2. Sample a donor subtree fitting the budget, tiered: compound & variable-bearing → variable-bearing → any fit.
3. Deep-copy it into an independent motif.
4. Pick the target: the root with probability 0.32, otherwise a uniformly random node.
5. Remap the motif's features via cyclic shift / targeted substitution / pairwise transposition /
   identity, with weights adapted to the motif's feature content; if donor === target and identity was
   drawn, force a shift half the time to avoid the trivially simplifiable `u ⊕ u`.
6. Optionally wrap the motif in a unary operator (probability 0.15, budget permitting).
7. Replace the target with `motif ⊕ copy(target)`, operator biased toward `+`/`*`, operand order random.

# Assumptions
* Feature indices span `1:nfeatures`, so `mod1` shifts are always valid.
* The tree grows by exactly `size(motif) + 1` nodes (plus 1 if dressed), which the budget enforces.
"""
function symmetry_motif_recombination_gen15_1_gen19_9(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Guard: coupling a duplicated motif requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ size budget
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    # Result size == tree_size + size(motif) + 1 (target subtree is duplicated in place)
    budget = maxsize - tree_size - 1
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ helpers
    # Apply an arbitrary index map to every variable leaf of a subtree (single traversal)
    function _map_features!(node, fmap)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = fmap(node.feature)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _map_features!(get_child(node, i), fmap)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Distinct feature indices appearing in a subtree
    function _collect_features(node)
        acc = Int[]
        function _walk(n)
            if n.degree == 0
                if !n.constant && !(n.feature in acc)
                    push!(acc, n.feature)
                end
            else
                for i in 1:(n.degree)
                    _walk(get_child(n, i))
                end
            end
            return nothing
        end
        _walk(node)
        return acc
    end

    _fits(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget
    _has_var(t) = any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, t)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ Step 1: donor
    # Tier 1: compound, variable-bearing motifs — the genuine symmetry carriers.
    # (Falling back to bare leaves would just reproduce `insert_random_op`.)
    _tier1(t) = t.degree > 0 && _fits(t) && _has_var(t)
    _tier2(t) = _fits(t) && _has_var(t)

    donor = if count(_tier1, tree) > 0 && rand(rng) < 0.8
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_tier1))
    elseif count(_tier2, tree) > 0
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_tier2))
    elseif count(_fits, tree) > 0
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_fits))
    else
        return tree  # nothing fits within the complexity budget
    end

    motif = copy(donor)
    motif_size = count_nodes(motif)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ Step 2: target
    # Root-biased: symmetric accumulations (`f(x) + f(y)`) live near the top of real laws.
    target = if rand(rng) < 0.32
        tree
    else
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    end
    self_coupling = target === donor

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ Step 3: remap features
    if nfeatures > 1
        feats = _collect_features(motif)
        nf = length(feats)

        if nf == 0
            # Constant-only motif: no remapping is meaningful (identity map).
            nothing
        else
            # Adaptive cumulative weights over {shift, substitution, transposition, identity}.
            # Single-feature motifs: substitution and transposition coincide, so favour the
            # cheap global shift. Multi-feature motifs: swaps/substitutions are the only maps
            # that can express `(x1-x2) -> (y1-y2)` or `(x1,x2) -> (x2,x1)`.
            if nf == 1
                p_shift, p_subst, p_swap = 0.55, 0.22, 0.0
            else
                p_shift, p_subst, p_swap = 0.28, 0.30, 0.27
            end
            r = rand(rng)

            if r < p_shift
                # (a) cyclic shift: replicate the whole functional form on the next variable block
                shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
                _map_features!(motif, f -> mod1(f + shift, nfeatures))
            elseif r < p_shift + p_subst
                # (b) targeted substitution: replace exactly one feature everywhere; this can
                # import a variable that does not yet appear anywhere in the tree.
                src = feats[rand(rng, 1:nf)]
                dst = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
                dst >= src && (dst += 1)  # uniform over destinations != src
                _map_features!(motif, f -> (f == src ? dst : f))
            elseif r < p_shift + p_subst + p_swap
                # (c) pairwise transposition: swap two indices throughout the motif, giving
                # exchange (anti)symmetry `f(x1,x2) ↔ f(x2,x1)` in one step.
                a = feats[rand(rng, 1:nf)]
                b = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
                b >= a && (b += 1)
                _map_features!(motif, f -> (f == a ? b : (f == b ? a : f)))
            else
                # (d) identity: enables powers (`u*u`) and rational self-couplings (`u/u`).
                # If donor and target coincide, half the time force a shift so we do not
                # produce the trivially simplifiable `u ⊕ u`.
                if self_coupling && rand(rng, Bool)
                    shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
                    _map_features!(motif, f -> mod1(f + shift, nfeatures))
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ Step 4: optional unary dressing
    # `u ⊕ g(u')` forms (x + sin(x), r*exp(-r)) are very common; costs one extra node.
    if options.nops[1] > 0 && motif_size + 1 <= budget && rand(rng) < 0.15
        motif = constructorof(N)(; op=rand(rng, 1:(options.nops[1])), children=(motif,))
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ Step 5: couple
    # Bias toward `+` and `*`, the canonical symmetric accumulators of physical laws.
    binops = options.operators.binops
    pref = Int[]
    for i in 1:(options.nops[2])
        op = binops[i]
        (op === (+) || op === (*)) && push!(pref, i)
    end
    bin_op = if !isempty(pref) && rand(rng) < 0.7
        pref[rand(rng, 1:length(pref))]
    else
        rand(rng, 1:(options.nops[2]))
    end

    target_copy = copy(target)
    # Randomize operand ordering so non-commutative operators explore both arrangements
