    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2: operator lookup
    binops = options.operators.binops
    nbin = options.nops[2]
    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op === (+), binops)
    idx_mul = findfirst(op -> op === (*), binops)
    idx_div = findfirst(op -> op === (/), binops)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3: template + budget
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)

    # Rational template `target / (1 + motif)` needs `/`, `+` and 3 extra nodes
    use_rational =
        (idx_div !== nothing) &&
        (idx_add !== nothing) &&
        rand(rng) < 0.35 &&
        (maxsize - tree_size - 3) >= 1

    # The target subtree is duplicated in place, so the donor must fit what remains
    budget = maxsize - tree_size - (use_rational ? 3 : 1)
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- helpers
    # Apply an index map to every variable leaf of the motif (single compact traversal)
    function _map_features!(node, fmap)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = fmap(node.feature)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _map_features!(get_child(node, i), fmap)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    _fits(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget
    # Compound, variable-bearing motifs are the interesting symmetry carriers
    _good(t) = t.degree > 0 && _fits(t) && any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, t)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4: donor
    donor = if count(_good, tree) > 0
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_good))
    else
        # Leaves always satisfy `_fits` when budget >= 1, so this sampler is non-empty
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_fits))
    end
    motif = copy(donor)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- target
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    self_coupling = target === donor

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5: feature remap
    if nfeatures > 1
        # Shift half the time; also force a shift for degenerate plain self-couplings (`u ⊕ u`),
        # but never for the rational template, where `u/(1+u)` is precisely the goal.
        do_shift = rand(rng) < 0.5 || (self_coupling && !use_rational)
        if do_shift
            shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
            _map_features!(motif, f -> mod1(f + shift, nfeatures))
        end
    end

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 6: coupling
    target_copy = copy(target)

    new_node = if use_rational
        # Self-referential saturation / correction factor: target / (1 + motif)
        c = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
        den = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_add, children=(c, motif))
        constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(target_copy, den))
    else
        # Plain symmetric coupling, biased toward the canonical accumulators `+` and `*`
        bin_op = if (idx_add !== nothing || idx_mul !== nothing) && rand(rng) < 0.65
            if idx_add !== nothing && idx_mul !== nothing
                rand(rng, Bool) ? idx_add : idx_mul
            elseif idx_add !== nothing
                idx_add
            else
                idx_mul
            end
        else
            rand(rng, 1:nbin)
        end
        # Randomize operand order so non-commutative operators are usable too
        children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
        constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children)
    end

    set_node!(target, new_node)
    return tree
end

tail_balanced_affine_angular_profile_los.name: tail_balanced_affine_angular_profile_loss_gen21_2
tail_balanced_affine_angular_profile_los.code:
"""
    tail_balanced_affine_angular_profile_loss_gen21_2(tree, dataset, options)

Score functional shape after the best global affine calibration
`a * prediction + b`, while retaining a small bounded raw-error term that favors
the correctly calibrated representative. Stable Welford moments determine the
affine fit and scale-aware constant-data fallbacks. A second pass evaluates fitted
residuals directly and combines ordinary normalized RMSE with a bounded,
target-tail-weighted RMSE. The tail profile modestly emphasizes difficult extreme
responses, helping distinguish globally correlated approximations from expressions
that reproduce nonlinear behavior throughout the target range without allowing
individual outliers to dominate. Exact raw predictions attain zero, invalid
evaluations return `Inf`, and expression complexity is deliberately excluded.
"""
function tail_balanced_affine_angular_profile_loss_gen21_2(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # First pass: stable moments for the least-squares affine calibration.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Remove harmless negative roundoff from Welford sums.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    relative_tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))
    target_rms = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    prediction_rms = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)

    target_is_variable =
        target_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_y
    prediction_is_variable =
        prediction_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_p

    if !target_is_variable
        # Affine shape is undefined for a constant target.
        target_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_y)
        raw_sum = zero_l
        raw_compensation = zero_l

        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            residual = L(prediction[i]) - L(dataset.y[i])
            if !isfinite(residual)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            normalized_residual = residual / target_scale
            term = normalized_residual * normalized_residual
            if !isfinite(term)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            corrected = term - raw_compensation
            updated = raw_sum + corrected
            if !isfinite(updated)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            raw_compensation = (updated - raw_sum) - corrected
            raw_sum = updated
        end

        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum / n_l, zero_l)
        loss_value = log1p(raw_nmse)
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
    end

    target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)
    if !(isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if prediction_is_variable
        slope = cov_py / m2_p
        intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
        if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end

    # Second pass: directly accumulate global, tail-balanced, and raw errors.
    affine_sum = zero_l
    affine_compensation = zero_l
    tail_affine_sum = zero_l
    tail_affine_compensation = zero_l
    tail_target_sum = zero_l
    tail_target_compensation = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l
    raw_compensation = zero_l
    raw_overflowed = false
    all_raw_exact = true

    tail_strength = L(3)

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_residual = p - y
        if !isfinite(raw_residual)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        all_raw_exact &= raw_residual == zero_l

        if !raw_overflowed
            raw_normalized = raw_residual / target_norm
            raw_term = raw_normalized * raw_normalized

            if isfinite(raw_term)
                corrected = raw_term - raw_compensation
                updated = raw_sum + corrected
                if isfinite(updated)
                    raw_compensation = (updated - raw_sum) - corrected
                    raw_sum = updated
                else
                    raw_overflowed = true
                end
            else
                raw_overflowed = true
            end
        end

        fitted = prediction_is_variable ? muladd(slope, p, intercept) : mean_y
        affine_residual = fitted - y
        affine_normalized = affine_residual / target_norm
        affine_term = affine_normalized * affine_normalized

        centered_y = y - mean_y
        centered_normalized = centered_y / target_norm
        target_term = centered_normalized * centered_normalized

        if !(isfinite(fitted) && isfinite(affine_residual) &&
             isfinite(affine_normalized) && isfinite(affine_term) &&
             isfinite(centered_y) && isfinite(centered_normalized) &&
             isfinite(target_term))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # A bounded leverage score increases smoothly from 1 at the target
        # center to at most 4 in the tails.
        deviation = abs(centered_y)
        tail_fraction = if deviation == zero_l
            zero_l
        elseif deviation <= target_rms
            deviation / (target_rms + deviation)
        else
            one_l / (one_l + target_rms / deviation)
        end
        tail_weight = one_l + tail_strength * tail_fraction * tail_fraction

        weighted_affine_term = tail_weight * affine_term
        weighted_target_term = tail_weight * target_term
        if !(isfinite(tail_weight) && isfinite(weighted_affine_term) &&
             isfinite(weighted_target_term))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        corrected = affine_term - affine_compensation
        updated = affine_sum + corrected
        if !isfinite(updated)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        affine_compensation = (updated - affine_sum) - corrected
        affine_sum = updated

        corrected = weighted_affine_term - tail_affine_compensation
        updated = tail_affine_sum + corrected
        if !isfinite(updated)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        tail_affine_compensation =
            (updated - tail_affine_sum) - corrected
        tail_affine_sum = updated

        corrected = weighted_target_term - tail_target_compensation
        updated = tail_target_sum + corrected
        if !isfinite(updated)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        tail_target_compensation =
            (updated - tail_target_sum) - corrected
        tail_target_sum = updated
    end

    # Guarantee that the actual finite target predictions are the zero-loss case.
    if all_raw_exact
        return zero_l
    end

    if !(isfinite(tail_target_sum) && tail_target_sum > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    global_nmse = clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l)
    tail_nmse = clamp(
        max(tail_affine_sum, zero_l) / tail_target_sum,
        zero_l,
        one_l,
    )

    # Keep the global affine angle dominant while adding a modest tail profile.
    tail_mix = one_l / L(4)
    shape_term =
        (one_l - tail_mix) * sqrt(global_nmse) +
        tail_mix * sqrt(tail_nmse)

    # Saturation prevents poor initial constants from overwhelming shape search.
    bounded_raw = if raw_overflowed
        one_l
    else
        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum, zero_l)
        if raw_nmse <= one_l
            raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse)
        else
            one_l / (one_l + one_l / raw_nmse)
        end
    end

    calibration_weight = one_l / L(256)
    loss_value = shape_term + calibration_weight * bounded_raw

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

pareto_seeded_crowding_niche_tournament_.name: pareto_seeded_crowding_niche_tournament_gen11_1_gen21_3
pareto_seeded_crowding_niche_tournament_.code:
"""
    pareto_seeded_crowding_niche_tournament_gen11_1_gen21_3(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Tournament selection designed to fight three failure modes seen in long PySR runs:

 1. **Lineage monopoly** — one champion skeleton and its near-clones fill the
    population, so search degenerates into constant-tuning of a single structure.
 2. **Complexity-niche starvation** — whole complexity bands go extinct, so the
    mid-size building blocks needed to assemble the true expression disappear.
 3. **Bloat drift** (new focus) — once a "good enough but wrong" skeleton is found,
    selection keeps picking its ever-larger descendants that bolt tiny correction
    terms onto it (e.g. `... + (-7.8e-5 / (x1/x2))`), burning the whole budget on
    micro-improvements while the correct, *smaller* structure is never revisited.

Core idea: score a slightly enlarged tournament pool with the usual
frequency-adjusted cost, then apply three *mild, multiplicative* corrections and
occasionally replace the fittest pick with a deliberately exploratory pick.

Steps:
 1. Sample a pool of `~1.5 * tournament_selection_n` distinct members (a bit larger
    than the default tournament so redundancy/niche/Pareto information exists).
 2. Compute complexity, complexity-frequency and the default adaptive-parsimony
    adjusted cost (`cost * exp(scaling * normalized_frequency[complexity])`).
 3. Redundancy (crowding) suppression: walking the pool from best to worst, count
    how many *better* pool members are effectively the same solution — identical
    complexity with loss equal to machine precision (weight 1.0) or merely to
    ~0.1% (weight `near_clone_weight`) — plus siblings sharing a parent reference
    (weight `sibling_weight`). Inflate the score geometrically with that weight, so
    the best representative of a cluster is untouched and its twins are demoted.
 4. Bloat (epsilon-dominance) suppression: if some *simpler* pool member reaches a
    loss within `bloat_rtol` of member `i`, then `i`'s extra size buys nothing;
    inflate its score in proportion to the relative excess complexity (capped by
    `bloat_cap`). This directly discourages the "giant champion + noise terms"
    lineage from monopolising selection.
 5. Youth discount: rank-based (robust to birth-counter outliers) discount of up to
    `youth_discount`, keeping lineage turnover alive.
 6. Exploratory picks:
      * with probability `p_pareto`, return a uniformly random member of the pool's
        (complexity, loss) Pareto front — this guarantees compact, promising
        skeletons (which are exactly the ones that later grow into the ground truth)
        keep receiving mutation effort even while a bloated champion dominates loss;
      * else with probability `p_rare_niche`, return the *best-scoring* member among
        those whose complexity frequency is at or below the pool median — a soft
        niche pick that repopulates starved complexity bands without promoting junk;
      * otherwise run the standard geometric tournament ladder
        (`tournament_selection_p`) over the penalized scores.

Heuristics / assumptions:
 - Equal complexity plus (relatively) equal loss is a cheap, allocation-free proxy
   for "structurally the same expression"; false positives merely nudge selection
   toward a different, equally good member, which is harmless.
 - Costs may be non-positive for exotic losses; the `inflate` helper divides instead
   of multiplying in that case so "factor > 1" always means "worse".
 - All penalties are mild and multiplicative, so behaviour degrades gracefully to
   the default tournament when the pool is clean (no clones, no bloat).

Changed vs. parent (`crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen10_4`):
 - Added the bloat / epsilon-dominance penalty (step 4), the main new mechanism.
 - Added the Pareto-front exploratory pick (step 6a) which seeds mutation effort on
   compact non-dominated skeletons instead of only on the loss champion.
 - Clone detection is now two-tiered (exact + ~0.1% near-clone) so re-tuned copies
   of the same structure with slightly different constants are also suppressed.
 - The rare-niche pick is *soft*: best member below the median frequency instead of
   the single rarest member (which was often a low-quality outlier).
 - Youth discount is rank-based rather than raw-birth-span based, removing
   sensitivity to a single very old or very new pool member.
"""
function pareto_seeded_crowding_niche_tournament_gen11_1_gen21_3(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # ---------------- tunables (kept mild so we degrade to default behaviour) ----
    pool_scale = 1.5           # pool size relative to tournament_selection_n
    clone_penalty = 1.35       # score inflation per unit of redundancy weight
    near_clone_weight = 0.5    # same complexity, loss equal to ~clone_rtol_near
    clone_rtol_exact = 1e-8    # "identical" loss tolerance
    clone_rtol_near = 1e-3     # "re-tuned copy" loss tolerance
    sibling_weight = 0.4       # a shared parent counts as a partial twin
    youth_discount = 0.05      # max relative cost discount for the newest members
    bloat_rtol = 0.02          # simpler member within 2% loss => extra size is bloat
    bloat_strength = 0.9       # inflation per unit of relative excess complexity
    bloat_cap = 2.0            # never inflate more than 2x for bloat
    p_pareto = 0.10            # probability of the Pareto-front exploratory pick
    p_rare_niche = 0.07        # probability of the soft rare-complexity pick

    # Multiplicative penalty/bonus that is sign-safe (f > 1 always means worse).
    inflate = function (x::L, f::Float64)
        fl = L(f)
        return x > zero(L) ? x * fl : x / fl
    end

    # ---------------- 1. sample the pool -----------------------------------------
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)
    n == 1 && return pool[1]

    # ---------------- 2. base (frequency-adjusted) scores ------------------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    freqs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size
        losses[i] = member.loss
        # out-of-range complexities are treated as maximally rare (frequency 0)
        freqs[i] = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
            Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
        else
            0.0
        end
        scores[i] = if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * L(freqs[i]))
        else
            member.cost
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 3. redundancy (clone / sibling) suppression -----------------
    # Process from best to worst so the best representative of a cluster is free of
    # penalty and each of its twins gets progressively demoted.
    order = sortperm(scores)
    redundancy = zeros(Float64, n)
    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = losses[i]
        wi = 0.0
        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = losses[j]
            scale = max(abs(li), abs(lj), eps(L))
            dl = abs(li - lj)
            if complexities[i] == complexities[j] && dl <= L(clone_rtol_exact) * scale
                wi += 1.0                      # essentially the identical solution
            elseif complexities[i] == complexities[j] && dl <= L(clone_rtol_near) * scale
                wi += near_clone_weight        # same structure, re-tuned constants
            elseif pool[i].parent != 0 && pool[i].parent == pool[j].parent
                wi += sibling_weight           # siblings: partial redundancy
            end
        end
        redundancy[i] = wi
    end

    # ---------------- 4. bloat (epsilon-dominance) suppression --------------------
    # If a strictly simpler pool member already matches member i's loss (within
    # bloat_rtol), the extra nodes of i are decoration, not discovery.
    bloat_factor = ones(Float64, n)
    for i in 1:n
        ci = complexities[i]
        li = losses[i]
        tol = li + L(bloat_rtol) * abs(li)   # "as good as i, up to bloat_rtol"
        min_c = ci
        for j in 1:n
            if complexities[j] < min_c && losses[j] <= tol
                min_c = complexities[j]
            end
        end
        if min_c < ci
            excess = (ci - min_c) / max(ci, 1)      # relative wasted complexity
            bloat_factor[i] = min(bloat_cap, 1.0 + bloat_strength * excess)
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 5. rank-based youth discount --------------------------------
    births = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        births[i] = pool[i].birth
    end
    birth_order = sortperm(births)               # oldest first
    recency = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for r in 1:n
        recency[birth_order[r]] = (r - 1) / (n - 1)   # 0 (oldest) .. 1 (newest)
    end

    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        factor =
            (clone_penalty^redundancy[i]) *
            bloat_factor[i] *
            (1.0 - youth_discount * recency[i])
        penalized[i] = inflate(scores[i], factor)
    end

    # ---------------- 6a. Pareto-front exploratory pick ---------------------------
    if rand() < p_pareto
        # Non-dominated in (complexity, loss): nobody is both no-bigger and no-worse.
        front = Int[]
        for i in 1:n
            dominated = false
            for j in 1:n
                j == i && continue
                if complexities[j] <= complexities[i] &&
                    losses[j] <= losses[i] &&
                    (complexities[j] < complexities[i] || losses[j] < losses[i])
                    dominated = true
                    break
                end
            end
            dominated || push!(front, i)
        end
        if !isempty(front)
            # Uniform over the front: spreads mutation effort across complexities,
            # so compact promising skeletons are not starved by a bloated champion.
            return pool[front[rand(1:length(front))]]
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 6b. soft rare-complexity (niche) pick -----------------------
    if rand() < p_rare_niche
        sorted_freqs = sort(freqs)
        median_freq = sorted_freqs[cld(n, 2)]
        best_idx = 0
        best_score = zero(L)
        for i in 1:n
            freqs[i] <= median_freq || continue
            if best_idx == 0 || penalized[i] < best_score
                best_idx = i
                best_score = penalized[i]
            end
        end
        best_idx != 0 && return pool[best_idx]
    end

    # ---------------- 6c. standard geometric tournament ladder --------------------
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        if tournament_winner == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, tournament_winner)[2][end]
        end
    end
    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

multiview_asinh_pseudohuber_loss_gen21_5.name: multiview_asinh_pseudohuber_loss_gen21_5
multiview_asinh_pseudohuber_loss_gen21_5.code:
"""
    multiview_asinh_pseudohuber_loss_gen21_5(tree, dataset, options)

Measure prediction error in three complementary, dimensionless views: residuals
normalized by target variation, a zero-centered `asinh` view that behaves like
relative error for large magnitudes, and a mean-centered `asinh` view that also
handles shifted targets. Each view uses a pseudo-Huber penalty, remaining
quadratic near an exact solution while limiting domination by outliers or
high-amplitude regimes. Target scales are estimated with mean absolute
statistics and guarded against constant or numerically degenerate targets.
This loss assumes that balancing additive and multiplicative behavior helps
expose the shared structure of an expression; it does not penalize complexity.
"""
function multiview_asinh_pseudohuber_loss_gen21_5(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zeroL = zero(L)
    oneL = one(L)

    # Estimate the target center and its raw magnitude using stable online means.
    center = zeroL
    raw_scale = zeroL
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        yi = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !isfinite(yi)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        wi = oneL / L(i)
        center = (oneL - wi) * center + wi * yi
        raw_scale = (oneL - wi) * raw_scale + wi * abs(yi)
    end

    if !isfinite(center) || !isfinite(raw_scale)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Mean absolute deviation supplies a robust scale for additive variation.
    variation_scale = zeroL
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        deviation = abs(L(dataset.y[i]) - center)
        if !isfinite(deviation)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        wi = oneL / L(i)
        variation_scale =
            (oneL - wi) * variation_scale + wi * deviation
    end

    if !isfinite(variation_scale)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Give constant targets a meaningful scale and avoid precision-level collapse.
    if raw_scale == zeroL && variation_scale == zeroL
        raw_scale = oneL
        variation_scale = oneL
    elseif raw_scale == zeroL
        raw_scale = variation_scale
    elseif variation_scale == zeroL
        variation_scale = raw_scale
    else
        scale_floor = L(16) * eps(L) * raw_scale
        variation_scale = max(variation_scale, scale_floor)
    end

    # Stable form of 2*(sqrt(1 + z^2) - 1): quadratic near zero, linear far away.
    robust_square(z) = begin
        a = abs(z)
        hp = hypot(oneL, a)
        L(2) * (a / hp) * (a / (oneL + oneL / hp))
    end

    w_standard = L(0.40)
    w_raw_asinh = L(0.35)
    w_centered_asinh = L(0.25)
    total = zeroL

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        pi = L(prediction[i])
        yi = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !isfinite(pi)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        residual = pi - yi
        centered_prediction = pi - center
        centered_target = yi - center

        # These three coordinates emphasize absolute shape, multiplicative
        # structure, and shifted nonlinear structure, respectively.
        z_standard = residual / variation_scale
        p_raw = pi / raw_scale
        y_raw = yi / raw_scale
        p_centered = centered_prediction / variation_scale
        y_centered = centered_target / variation_scale

        if !isfinite(z_standard) ||
           !isfinite(p_raw) || !isfinite(y_raw) ||
           !isfinite(p_centered) || !isfinite(y_centered)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        z_raw_asinh = asinh(p_raw) - asinh(y_raw)
        z_centered_asinh = asinh(p_centered) - asinh(y_centered)

        sample_loss =
            w_standard * robust_square(z_standard) +
            w_raw_asinh * robust_square(z_raw_asinh) +
            w_centered_asinh * robust_square(z_centered_asinh)

        if !isfinite(sample_loss)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        total += sample_loss
    end

    loss = total / L(n)
    return isfinite(loss) && loss >= zeroL ? L(loss) : L(Inf)
end

age_quality_lineage_survival_gen21_6.name: age_quality_lineage_survival_gen21_6
age_quality_lineage_survival_gen21_6.code:
"""
    age_quality_lineage_survival_gen21_6(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[]) -> Int

Hybrid age-regularized survival with quality-aware turnover, lineage thinning,
and a weak anti-bloat safeguard.

Compared with `age_diversity_survival_hybrid_gen20_2`, this operator retains the
mixture of global and tournament age pressure but adds two targeted mechanisms
intended to prevent the population from collapsing onto one inaccurate motif:

1. Protect the lowest-cost legal member.  The elite is selected after applying
   `exclude_indices`, so a crossover's second survival call still protects the
   best member it is actually allowed to replace.
2. With probability 0.15, remove the globally oldest non-elite member, ensuring
   that stale material cannot survive indefinitely.
3. With probability 0.15, sample a lineage and remove its oldest non-elite
   sibling when multiple live members share the same parent reference.  This
   selectively thins prolific local families without penalizing isolated
   structural scaffolds.
4. Otherwise, run a small replacement tournament.  Most tournaments remove the
   oldest sampled member, some remove the worst-cost member to accelerate
   selection, and a small fraction target excessive complexity.  Complexity
   pressure is activated only above 60% of `options.maxsize`; below that soft
   limit it falls back to age, avoiding a blanket bias against expressions
   complex enough to represent the ground truth.
5. All branches shield the elite and respect exclusions.  A deterministic
   oldest-member scan handles missed samples and other degenerate cases.

Sampling is with replacement and uses no candidate arrays.  Cost and complexity
ties are broken by age, favoring turnover of the older equivalent member.
"""
function age_quality_lineage_survival_gen21_6(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)

    # Find the best member among slots that this call is actually allowed to
    # replace.  This matters on the second survival call during crossover.
    elite_idx = 0
    elite_cost = first(pop.members).cost
    elite_birth = first(pop.members).birth
    legal_count = 0

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        (i in exclude_indices) && continue
        legal_count += 1

        c = pop.members[i].cost
        b = pop.members[i].birth
        if elite_idx == 0 ||
           isless(c, elite_cost) ||
           (!isless(c, elite_cost) && !isless(elite_cost, c) && b > elite_birth)
            elite_idx = i
            elite_cost = c
            elite_birth = b
        end
    end

    legal_count == 0 &&
        throw(ArgumentError("survival requires at least one non-excluded population member"))

    # If only one slot is legal, elite protection must be relaxed.
    legal_count == 1 && return elite_idx

    branch = rand()

    # Periodic global purge guarantees eventual removal of truly stale members.
    if branch < 0.15
        oldest_idx = 0
        oldest_birth = typemax(BT)
        oldest_cost = elite_cost

        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            ((i in exclude_indices) || i == elite_idx) && continue
            b = pop.members[i].birth
            c = pop.members[i].cost

            # On equal birth counters, discard the worse-cost member.
            if oldest_idx == 0 ||
               b < oldest_birth ||
               (b == oldest_birth && isless(oldest_cost, c))
                oldest_idx = i
                oldest_birth = b
                oldest_cost = c
            end
        end

        return oldest_idx
    end

    # Occasionally thin a prolific immediate lineage.  A random starting slot
    # followed by a circular scan guarantees a usable non-elite seed.
    if branch < 0.30
        seed_idx = 0
        start = rand(1:n)

        @inbounds for offset in 0:(n - 1)
            i = mod1(start + offset, n)
            ((i in exclude_indices) || i == elite_idx) && continue
            seed_idx = i
            break
        end

        parent_ref = pop.members[seed_idx].parent
        if parent_ref > 0
            family_count = 0
            family_idx = 0
            family_birth = typemax(BT)
            family_cost = elite_cost

            @inbounds for i in 1:n
                ((i in exclude_indices) || i == elite_idx) && continue
                pop.members[i].parent == parent_ref || continue

                family_count += 1
                b = pop.members[i].birth
                c = pop.members[i].cost
                if family_idx == 0 ||
                   b < family_birth ||
                   (b == family_birth && isless(family_cost, c))
                    family_idx = i
                    family_birth = b
                    family_cost = c
                end
            end

            # A singleton is not crowded, so leave it for the ordinary
            # tournament rather than spending lineage pressure on it.
            family_count >= 2 && return family_idx
        end
    end

    nonelite_count = legal_count - 1
    n_sample = min(nonelite_count, max(2, options.tournament_selection_n))

    criterion_draw = rand()
    criterion = if criterion_draw < 0.70
        1  # Regularized evolution: oldest sampled member.
    elseif criterion_draw < 0.90
        2  # Selection pulse: worst-cost sampled member.
    else
        3  # Weak anti-bloat pulse: most complex sampled member.
    end

    chosen_idx = 0
    chosen_birth = typemax(BT)
    chosen_cost = elite_cost
    chosen_complexity = -1

    # Keep an age-based fallback from the same sample, particularly for the
    # complexity branch when every sampled expression is below the soft limit.
    sampled_oldest_idx = 0
    sampled_oldest_birth = typemax(BT)
    sampled_oldest_cost = elite_cost

    @inbounds for _ in 1:n_sample
        i = rand(1:n)
        ((i in exclude_indices) || i == elite_idx) && continue

        member = pop.members[i]
        b = member.birth
        c = member.cost

        if sampled_oldest_idx == 0 ||
           b < sampled_oldest_birth ||
           (b == sampled_oldest_birth && isless(sampled_oldest_cost, c))
            sampled_oldest_idx = i
            sampled_oldest_birth = b
            sampled_oldest_cost = c
        end

        if criterion == 1
            if chosen_idx == 0 ||
               b < chosen_birth ||
               (b == chosen_birth && isless(chosen_cost, c))
                chosen_idx = i
                chosen_birth = b
                chosen_cost = c
            end
        elseif criterion == 2
            # `isless` gives a total ordering for floating losses, placing NaN
            # after finite values and therefore treating it as maximally bad.
            if chosen_idx == 0 ||
               isless(chosen_cost, c) ||
               (!isless(c, chosen_cost) && !isless(chosen_cost, c) && b < chosen_birth)
                chosen_idx = i
                chosen_birth = b
                chosen_cost = c
            end
        else
            complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
            if chosen_idx == 0 ||
               complexity > chosen_complexity ||
               (complexity == chosen_complexity && b < chosen_birth)
                chosen_idx = i
                chosen_birth = b
                chosen_cost = c
                chosen_complexity = complexity
            end
        end
    end

    if criterion == 3 && chosen_idx != 0
        soft_complexity_limit = max(4, (3 * options.maxsize) ÷ 5)
        if chosen_complexity <= soft_complexity_limit
            chosen_idx = sampled_oldest_idx
        end
    end

    chosen_idx != 0 && return chosen_idx

    # Sampling with replacement can miss every legal non-elite slot when the
    # population is tiny or heavily excluded.  Fall back to a guaranteed scan.
    oldest_idx = 0
    oldest_birth = typemax(BT)
    oldest_cost = elite_cost

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        ((i in exclude_indices) || i == elite_idx) && continue
        b = pop.members[i].birth
        c = pop.members[i].cost
        if oldest_idx == 0 ||
           b < oldest_birth ||
           (b == oldest_birth && isless(oldest_cost, c))
            oldest_idx = i
            oldest_birth = b
            oldest_cost = c
        end
    end

    return oldest_idx
end

age_complexity_tournament_survival_gen12.name: age_complexity_tournament_survival_gen12_gen21_7
age_complexity_tournament_survival_gen12.code:
"""
    age_complexity_tournament_survival_gen12_gen21_7(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[]) -> Int

Age-regularized survival with a mild anti-bloat bias: like the parent, this
draws a small random sample of slots and prefers to replace the *oldest*
member within that sample, but the effective "age" used for comparison is
discounted for members with high complexity relative to `options.maxsize`.
This means a member that is both old *and* bloated is strongly preferred for
replacement, while a young-but-simple or old-but-simple member is more likely
to survive.

Steps:
1. Draw `n_sample = clamp(options.tournament_selection_n, 2, pop.n)` random
   slot indices (with replacement).
2. Skip any sampled slot listed in `exclude_indices`.
3. For each remaining candidate compute an *effective birth score*:
   `score = birth * (1 - min(0.5, 0.5 * complexity / maxsize))`. Higher
   complexity (relative to `maxsize`) shrinks the score, making the member
   look artificially older, so it is more likely to be the minimum (and thus
   selected for replacement).
4. Return the sampled, non-excluded candidate with the smallest score.
5. If every draw landed on an excluded slot, fall back to a full deterministic
   scan using the same scoring rule, guaranteeing a valid, non-excluded index.

Why this changes vs. the parent: the parent used *pure* birth order for the
in-sample comparison, meaning any old member — however small or large its
expression — was equally likely to be flagged for death, and equally likely
to survive if it happened to dodge the sample. In the traced run, the
population repeatedly converged onto a single bloated motif
(`log(square(x3))/sqrt(x1)`-style decorations) that kept growing in complexity
while pushing out smaller, structurally distinct candidates purely by
out-living them in the random sample. By discounting the effective birth of
complex individuals, this operator adds a soft, bounded (capped at 50%)
pressure toward culling bloated members first, which frees population slots
for smaller/alternative-structure lineages without abandoning the core
age-regularized-evolution philosophy: age (now complexity-adjusted) remains
the *only* explicit replacement criterion, exclusion handling stays inline,
and a deterministic fallback still guarantees termination and correctness.
"""
function age_complexity_tournament_survival_gen12_gen21_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n

    # Small random sample of slots; bounded by the population size.
    n_sample = min(n, max(2, options.tournament_selection_n))

    best_idx = 0
    best_score = Inf  # effective (complexity-discounted) birth score

    for _ in 1:n_sample
        i = rand(1:n)
        # Exclusion handled inline, same as parent.
        (i in exclude_indices) && continue

        member = pop.members[i]
        b = Float64(member.birth)
        c = Float64(compute_complexity(member, options))

        # Bloated members (high complexity relative to maxsize) are made to
        # look "older" by shrinking their score, capped at a 50% discount so
        # a very young bloated member can still, at worst, look as old as
        # the oldest slot — age remains the dominant signal.
        bloat_discount = c / max(1, options.maxsize)
        score = b * (1.0 - min(0.5, 0.5 * bloat_discount))

        if best_idx == 0 || score < best_score
            best_idx = i
            best_score = score
        end
    end

    if best_idx == 0
        # Degenerate case: all draws were excluded. Deterministic scan over
        # the whole population using the same complexity-adjusted scoring so
        # behavior stays consistent with the sampled branch.
        for i in 1:n
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue

            member = pop.members[i]
            b = Float64(member.birth)
            c = Float64(compute_complexity(member, options))
            bloat_discount = c / max(1, options.maxsize)
            score = b * (1.0 - min(0.5, 0.5 * bloat_discount))

            if best_idx == 0 || score < best_score
                best_idx = i
                best_score = score
            end
        end
    end

    return best_idx
end

clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen21_.name: clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen21_8
clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen21_.code:
"""
    clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen21_8(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Simplified descendant of `crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen10_4`.

Core idea (unchanged): the default tournament tends to be monopolised by a single
champion skeleton and its near-identical clones, and whole complexity bands can go
extinct. This operator therefore (a) draws a slightly *larger* pool than the
default tournament so that redundancy information is visible, (b) demotes pool
members that duplicate a better member of the same pool, and (c) occasionally
selects the pool member sitting in the rarest complexity niche instead of the
fittest one.

Steps:
 1. Sample a pool of `~1.5 * tournament_selection_n` distinct members.
 2. Score each member with the standard adaptive-parsimony-adjusted cost
    (`cost * exp(scaling * normalized_frequency[complexity])`).
 3. Clone suppression: walk the pool from best to worst; for each member count how
    many *better* pool members are effectively the same solution (identical
    complexity and loss equal within a relative tolerance) and inflate its score
    geometrically by `clone_penalty^count`. The best representative of a cluster is
    untouched; its twins get progressively demoted.
 4. With probability `p_rare_niche`, return the pool member whose complexity has the
    lowest normalized frequency (ties broken by penalized score). Otherwise run the
    usual geometric tournament ladder over the penalized scores.

Removed / merged relative to the parent (and why this is still sound):
 - The **sibling (shared-parent) partial redundancy** term is dropped: siblings of a
   good parent are usually structurally distinct mutations, so penalising them
   suppressed useful variation while the exact-clone test already catches the cases
   that actually matter (identical complexity *and* identical loss).
 - The **youth discount** is dropped: it was a tiny (<=5%) multiplicative nudge whose
   effect is dominated by the clone penalty, and it required an extra pass over the
   pool to compute the birth range.
 - The sign-safe `inflate` closure is folded inline into the single place it is used;
   penalties are still multiplicative and >= 1 so "worse" always means worse, and
   with a redundancy-free pool the operator reduces exactly to the default
   frequency-adjusted tournament on a slightly larger sample.
"""
function clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen21_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # ---------------- tunables (mild, so we degrade to default behaviour) --------
    pool_scale = 1.5      # pool size relative to tournament_selection_n
    clone_penalty = 1.35  # score inflation per detected better twin
    loss_rtol = 1e-6      # relative tolerance for "same loss"
    p_rare_niche = 0.10   # probability of the explicit rare-complexity pick

    # ---------------- 1. sample a slightly enlarged pool -------------------------
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # ---------------- 2. base (frequency-adjusted) scores ------------------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 3. clone suppression ---------------------------------------
    # Best-to-worst order: the first member of each duplicate cluster is unpenalized,
    # each subsequent twin is demoted by another factor of `clone_penalty`.
    order = sortperm(scores)
    penalized = copy(scores)
    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        clones = 0
        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            # identical complexity + (relatively) identical loss => same solution
            same_loss = abs(li - lj) <= L(loss_rtol) * max(abs(li), abs(lj), eps(L))
            if complexities[i] == complexities[j] && same_loss
                clones += 1
            end
        end
        if clones > 0
            f = L(clone_penalty^clones)  # always >= 1
            # sign-safe: multiply for positive costs, divide otherwise, so that a
            # larger factor always means a worse (larger) penalized score
            penalized[i] = scores[i] > zero(L) ? scores[i] * f : scores[i] / f
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 4a. occasional rare-complexity (niche) pick -----------------
    if rand() < p_rare_niche
        best_idx = 1
        best_freq = Inf
        best_score = penalized[1]
        for i in 1:n
            c = complexities[i]
            f = if (0 < c <= options.maxsize)
                Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
            else
                0.0  # out-of-range sizes count as maximally rare
            end
            if f < best_freq || (f == best_freq && penalized[i] < best_score)
                best_freq = f
                best_score = penalized[i]
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        return pool[best_idx]
    end

    # ---------------- 4b. standard geometric tournament ladder --------------------
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        if tournament_winner == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, tournament_winner)[2][end]
        end
    end
    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

homologous_scaffold_mutation_gen21_9.name: homologous_scaffold_mutation_gen21_9
homologous_scaffold_mutation_gen21_9.code:
"""
    homologous_scaffold_mutation_gen21_9(tree, options, nfeatures, rng)

A structural mutation operator that introduces quasi-neutral linear scaffolds and
homologous subtree duplications to accelerate symbolic regression discovery.

Standard genetic programming point mutations struggle with two major structural hurdles:
1. Constant Starvation: Subtrees often discover the correct functional form (e.g., `sin(x)`)
   but lack linear scale and offset parameters (`c1 * sin(x) + c2`). Standard mutations that
   insert random constants drastically alter numerical values, causing individuals to be
   eliminated by selection before constant optimization can tune them. This mutation inserts
   a quasi-neutral affine scaffold (`1.0 * u + 0.0`) around a chosen node, preserving the
   initial fitness while opening differentiable pathways for continuous constant optimizers.
2. Multivariable Symmetry & Homology: Physics and engineering equations frequently contain
   symmetric or repeated motifs across dimensions (e.g., `x1^2 + x2^2` or `f(x1) * f(x2)`).
   Constructing identical subtrees independently across features is exponentially improbable.
   This operator clones an evolved subexpression, cyclically transposes feature indices to
   other input variables, and binds them via an algebraic operator (`+`, `*`, `-`, `/`).
3. Nonlinear & Rational Kernels: Synthesizes common physical motifs (such as Michaelis-Menten
   saturation `u / (u + 1)` or kinetic energy / power interactions `u * u`) directly from
   existing subtrees.
"""
function homologous_scaffold_mutation_gen21_9(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Check available operator counts
    n_bin = options.nops[2]
    n_una = options.nops[1]

    # If no binary operators exist, fall back to unary wrapping if available
    if n_bin == 0
        if n_una > 0
            target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
            op_idx = rand(rng, 1:n_una)
            new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=op_idx, children=(copy(target),))
            set_node!(target, new_node)
        end
        return tree
    end

    # Detect presence and indices of standard algebraic operators
    binops = options.operators.binops
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), binops)
    mult_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (*), binops)
    div_idx  = findfirst(op -> op == (/), binops)
    sub_idx  = findfirst(op -> op == (-), binops)

    # Randomly select a node to mutate
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))

    # Stochastic selection among structural mutation strategies:
    # 1: Quasi-Neutral Affine Scaffold
    # 2: Homologous Subtree Duplication & Feature Transposition
    # 3: Rational / Power Harmonic Scaffold
    mode = rand(rng, 1:3)

    if mode == 1
        # --- Mode 1: Quasi-Neutral Affine Scaffold ---
        # Wraps the target subexpression in a linear envelope (c1 * target + c2).
        # Initializing c1 = 1.0 and c2 = 0.0 preserves output values at insertion,
        # providing immediate gradient handles for subsequent constant optimization.
        if mult_idx !== nothing && plus_idx !== nothing
            scale_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
            bias_leaf  = constructorof(N)(T; val=zero(T))
            scaled_sub = constructorof(N)(; op=mult_idx, children=(scale_leaf, copy(target)))
            affine_sub = constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(scaled_sub, bias_leaf))
            set_node!(target, affine_sub)
        elseif mult_idx !== nothing
            scale_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
            scaled_sub = constructorof(N)(; op=mult_idx, children=(scale_leaf, copy(target)))
            set_node!(target, scaled_sub)
        elseif plus_idx !== nothing
            bias_leaf  = constructorof(N)(T; val=zero(T))
            offset_sub = constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(copy(target), bias_leaf))
            set_node!(target, offset_sub)
        else
            # Generic binary wrap fallback with identity-like neutral constant
            op_idx = rand(rng, 1:n_bin)
            const_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
            new_sub = constructorof(N)(; op=op_idx, children=(copy(target), const_leaf))
            set_node!(target, new_sub)
        end

    elseif mode == 2
        # --- Mode 2: Homologous Subtree Duplication & Feature Transposition ---
        # Duplicates target subtree, transposes its variable features to different
        # feature dimensions, and connects both copies using a binary operator.
        dup = copy(target)

        # Transpose feature indices across dimensions if multiple features exist
        if nfeatures > 1
            shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
            # Recursive inner helper to cyclically shift all feature indices in the duplicate
            function shift_features!(node::AbstractExpressionNode)
                if node.degree == 0
                    if !node.constant
                        node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeatures)
                    end
                else
                    for i in 1:(node.degree)
                        shift_features!(get_child(node, i))
                    end
                end
                return node
            end
            shift_features!(dup)
        end

        # Select a joining operator (preferring standard algebraic combinations)
        r = rand(rng)
        join_op = if plus_idx !== nothing && r < 0.40
            plus_idx
        elseif mult_idx !== nothing && r < 0.70
            mult_idx
        elseif sub_idx !== nothing && r < 0.85
            sub_idx
        elseif div_idx !== nothing && r < 0.95
            div_idx
        else
            rand(rng, 1:n_bin)
        end

        combined = constructorof(N)(; op=join_op, children=(copy(target), dup))
        set_node!(target, combined)

    else
        # --- Mode 3: Rational, Saturation & Power Kernel Scaffold ---
        # Constructs non-linear structural kernels directly from the target subtree:
        # Saturation: u / (u + 1.0), Power / Interaction: u * u, Reciprocal: 1.0 / u.
        sub_mode = rand(rng, 1:3)
        if sub_mode == 1 && div_idx !== nothing && plus_idx !== nothing
            # Saturation / Michaelis-Menten motif: target / (target + 1.0)
            one_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
            denom = constructorof(N)(; op=plus_idx, children=(copy(target), one_leaf))
            rational_node = constructorof(N)(; op=div_idx, children=(copy(target), denom))
            set_node!(target, rational_node)
        elseif sub_mode == 2 && mult_idx !== nothing
            # Quadratic / Self-interaction motif: target * target
            squared_node = constructorof(N)(; op=mult_idx, children=(copy(target), copy(target)))
            set_node!(target, squared_node)
        elseif sub_mode == 3 && div_idx !== nothing
            # Reciprocal / Inverse-law motif: 1.0 / target
            one_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
            inv_node = constructorof(N)(; op=div_idx, children=(one_leaf, copy(target)))
            set_node!(target, inv_node)
        else
            # Fallback: simple addition or multiplication with a unit constant
            fallback_op = mult_idx !== nothing ? mult_idx : (plus_idx !== nothing ? plus_idx : rand(rng, 1:n_bin))
            unit_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
            fallback_node = constructorof(N)(; op=fallback_op, children=(copy(target), unit_leaf))
            set_node!(target, fallback_node)
        end
    end

    return tree
end

pareto_protective_age_regularized_surviv.name: pareto_protective_age_regularized_survival_gen22_8
pareto_protective_age_regularized_surviv.code:
"""
    pareto_protective_age_regularized_survival_gen22_8(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

Age-regularized survival (replace-the-oldest) refined with a *Pareto-protection*
and *clone-culling* layer.

Core idea
---------
The parent operator always removes the oldest population member. That keeps a
healthy turnover, but it happily deletes a member that is currently the *only*
representative of some region of the accuracy/complexity trade-off curve, while
leaving behind exact duplicates and strictly dominated individuals. This variant
keeps age as the dominant selection pressure, but breaks ties *within the oldest
slice of the population* in favour of removing genuinely redundant material.

Steps
-----
1. Build the candidate list (all indices not in `exclude_indices`) and sort it by
   `birth`, oldest first — age remains the primary driver.
2. Restrict attention to a window containing the oldest ~25% of candidates
   (at least 2). Anything outside the window is considered "too young to die",
   so the operator can never behave much less age-regularized than the parent.
3. Precompute `(complexity, loss)` for every member and classify each windowed
   candidate:
     * rank 0 — broken member (NaN/Inf loss): remove first, it carries no signal;
     * rank 1 — clone: some other member has the same complexity and (to 1e-10
       relative tolerance) the same loss, and is older / lower-indexed, so this
       copy is pure redundancy;
     * rank 2 — Pareto-dominated: another member is at least as simple *and* at
       least as accurate, with strict improvement somewhere;
     * rank 3 — non-dominated (on the population's Pareto front): protected;
     * rank 100 — the current best-cost member: elite, protected unless nothing
       else is available.
4. Return the lowest-rank candidate; because the window is ordered oldest-first,
   ties are resolved by age exactly as in the parent.

Heuristics / safety
-------------------
* If every windowed candidate is non-dominated (rank 3), the returned index is
  simply the oldest candidate, i.e. **identical behaviour to the parent** — the
  operator only deviates when there is something demonstrably redundant to cull.
* `exclude_indices` is honoured by construction (excluded indices never enter the
  candidate list); degenerate populations fall back gracefully.
* Complexity/loss bookkeeping is O(n) plus O(window * n) comparisons, negligible
  next to the loss evaluations performed for each offspring.

Changed vs. parent
------------------
Adds (a) an oldest-slice window instead of a single hard argmin over births,
(b) NaN/Inf-loss purging, (c) clone culling with relative tolerance,
(d) Pareto-front and elite protection, while preserving the parent's fallback.
"""
function pareto_protective_age_regularized_survival_gen22_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    members = pop.members

    # ---- candidate set: every index not excluded ---------------------------
    candidates = Int[]
    for i in 1:n
        if !(i in exclude_indices)
            push!(candidates, i)
        end
    end
    isempty(candidates) && return 1                # degenerate safety net
    length(candidates) == 1 && return candidates[1]

    # ---- age ordering: oldest first (primary pressure, as in the parent) ---
    sort!(candidates; by = i -> members[i].birth)

    # Only the oldest quarter of the candidates may be reasoned about; this
    # bounds how far we can drift away from pure age-regularized replacement.
    w = max(2, cld(length(candidates), 4))
    w = min(w, length(candidates))

    # ---- precompute complexity, loss and cost for all members --------------
    comps = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    elite_idx = 0
    elite_cost = Inf
    for i in 1:n
        comps[i] = compute_complexity(members[i], options)
        l = Float64(members[i].loss)
        losses[i] = isnan(l) ? Inf : l             # treat NaN as worst possible
        c = Float64(members[i].cost)
        c = isnan(c) ? Inf : c
        if c < elite_cost                          # current best-cost member
            elite_cost = c
            elite_idx = i
        end
    end

    best_idx = candidates[1]                       # parent's answer by default
    best_rank = typemax(Int)

    for k in 1:w
        i = candidates[k]
        li = losses[i]
        ci = comps[i]

        rank = 3                                   # assume Pareto-optimal
        if !isfinite(li)
            rank = 0                               # broken: cull immediately
        else
            dominated = false
            duplicate = false
            for j in 1:n
                j == i && continue
                lj = losses[j]
                isfinite(lj) || continue           # broken members dominate nothing
                cj = comps[j]
                if cj == ci && isapprox(li, lj; rtol=1e-10, atol=0.0)
                    # Same complexity and essentially the same loss: whichever
                    # copy is older (index as final tie-break) is the keeper.
                    if (members[j].birth, j) < (members[i].birth, i)
                        duplicate = true
                    end
                elseif cj <= ci && lj <= li && (cj < ci || lj < li)
                    dominated = true
                end
            end
            rank = duplicate ? 1 : (dominated ? 2 : 3)
        end

        # Elitism: never evict the best-cost member while alternatives exist.
        if i == elite_idx
            rank = 100
        end

        if rank < best_rank
            best_rank = rank
            best_idx = i
            best_rank == 0 && break                # cannot do better than this
        end
    end

    return best_idx
end

symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_7_gen22.name: symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_7_gen22_3
symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_7_gen22.code:
"""
    symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_7_gen22_3(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

A structural mutation that duplicates a subexpression motif, optionally cyclically shifts its
feature indices, couples it with a target (or a normalizing constant) via a binary operator,
and occasionally wraps the result in a unary operator.

# Core Idea
Physical laws often repeat functional motifs across variables (e.g. `vx^2 + vy^2`) *and* also
normalize such motifs through a surrounding unary function, frequently against unity
(e.g. `sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)`, `1/(1+exp(-x))`). The parent operator only ever couples the motif with
a copy of an existing tree node via a binary operator, which makes "constant-anchored" normalized
forms (motif vs. `1`) structurally hard to reach, and it never introduces the enclosing unary
wrapper (`sqrt`, `exp`, `log`, ...) that is characteristic of these physical relations.

# Steps
1. Return early if no binary operators are configured.
2. Sample a donor subtree and deep-copy it into an independent motif.
3. If `nfeatures > 1`, cyclically shift the motif's variable leaves by a random offset
   (0 preserves features, enabling self-coupling like `x^2 - x`).
4. Choose a coupling partner: with probability `p_const` use a constant leaf (usually `1.0`,
   biasing toward normalized forms), otherwise copy an existing target node from the tree.
5. Couple the motif and partner under a random binary operator with randomized operand order,
   and splice the result back in place of the target (or, if a constant partner was used, in
   place of the donor's original sibling context via the sampled target node).
6. With probability `p_wrap`, wrap the newly formed node in a random unary operator, directly
   enabling normalization patterns such as `sqrt(1 - motif)` or `exp(motif)`.

# Changes vs. Parent
- Added a constant-anchored coupling path (motif vs. a constant, usually `1.0`) to make
  normalized/relativistic-style expressions structurally reachable.
- Added optional unary-operator wrapping of the coupled node to directly synthesize the
  enclosing function (e.g. `sqrt`) that so often surrounds these motifs in real physics formulae.
- Kept the cyclic feature-shift mechanism and lightweight, unified code path from the parent.
"""
function symmetric_motif_duplication_gen9_7_gen22_3(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Guard: binary coupling requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # Helper: cyclically permute feature indices in the motif leaves
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int, num_features::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, num_features)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift, num_features)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Step 1: Sample a donor subtree motif and duplicate it
    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    motif = copy(donor)

    # Step 2: Apply cyclic feature transformation (shift == 0 preserves features for self-coupling)
    if nfeatures > 1
        shift = rand(rng, 0:(nfeatures - 1))
        if shift > 0
            _shift_features!(motif, shift, nfeatures)
        end
    end

    # Step 3: Select the target node to be replaced in the tree
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))

    # Step 4: Choose the coupling partner — either a normalizing constant or a copy of the target.
    # Constant-anchored coupling (bias toward 1.0) directly enables forms like `1 - motif`.
    p_const = 0.25
    if rand(rng) < p_const
        const_val = rand(rng, Bool) ? one(T) : randn(rng, T)
        partner = constructorof(N)(T; val=const_val)
    else
        partner = copy(target)
    end
    bin_op = rand(rng, 1:options.nops[2])

    # Randomize operand ordering to support non-commutative operators (e.g. `1 - motif` vs `motif - 1`)
    children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (partner, motif) : (motif, partner)
    new_node = constructorof(N)(;
        op=bin_op,
        children=children,
    )

    # Step 5: Optionally wrap the coupled node in a unary operator to synthesize the enclosing
    # normalization function (e.g. sqrt(1 - motif)) directly, rather than relying on later mutations.
    p_wrap = 0.3
    if options.nops[1] > 0 && rand(rng) < p_wrap
        una_op = rand(rng, 1:options.nops[1])
        new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=una_op, children=(new_node,))
    end

    # Step 6: Splice the new structure in place of the sampled target node
    set_node!(target, new_node)

    return tree
end

diversity_lineage_pareto_niche_tournamen.name: diversity_lineage_pareto_niche_tournament_gen22_2
diversity_lineage_pareto_niche_tournamen.code:
"""
    diversity_lineage_pareto_niche_tournament_gen22_2(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Synthesis of the two parent operators (both crowding-suppressed niche tournaments)
into a single, stronger *structural-diversity* tournament.  The parents already
attacked **lineage monopoly** (clone/sibling suppression + youth discount) and
**complexity-niche starvation** (rare-complexity pick).  The execution trace shows a
third, closely related failure mode that neither parent handles: **skeleton lock-in**.
On `feynman_test_8` the whole Pareto front from 300k evals onwards is one motif
(`log(x3/((x1+x2)*(x2+c))) * (x2 + x0/c - x3)`) that is merely re-tuned and bloated;
the same loss value reappears at many different complexities, and the structural
family needed by the ground truth (a reciprocal `1/(1 + ...cos(x3))`) is never
sampled.  Once that happens, "same complexity + same loss" clone detection is too
narrow, because the clones live at *different* complexities (bloated variants of the
same skeleton).

Core idea (new): treat *loss value* as a cheap structural fingerprint.  Redundancy is
therefore measured across a small complexity window rather than only at identical
complexity, so bloated re-tunings of the reigning skeleton are demoted.  In exchange,
members that are locally Pareto-optimal in `(complexity, loss)` get a small bonus
(stepping stones survive), and a small fraction of selections is spent on two explicit
exploration moves: the *rarest complexity band* (from the parents) and a new
*loss-novelty* pick that grabs the fitness-competitive member which is most isolated
in loss space, i.e. most likely to carry a different skeleton.

Steps:
 1. Sample a pool of `~1.6 * tournament_selection_n` distinct members (slightly
    enlarged so redundancy / niche / novelty information exists).
 2. Score with the default adaptive-parsimony cost
    (`cost * exp(scaling * normalized_frequency[complexity])`).
 3. Crowding suppression, processing best -> worst so the best representative of a
    cluster stays untouched.  A better pool member contributes redundancy weight
      * `1.0`  if same complexity and essentially the same loss (exact clone),
      * `near_clone_weight` if essentially the same loss within
        `±complexity_window` complexity (bloated / re-tuned same skeleton),
      * `sibling_weight` if it shares the same non-zero parent reference.
    Total weight is capped (`max_redundancy`) and inflates the score geometrically.
 4. Local Pareto bonus: members not dominated inside the pool in
    `(complexity, loss)` receive a mild multiplicative discount `pareto_bonus`,
    protecting small/mid-size stepping stones that are not the pool's best cost.
 5. Youth discount: the freshest members get up to `youth_discount` relative cost
    reduction, keeping lineage turnover going (from the parents).
 6. Exploration modes (mutually exclusive, small probabilities):
      * `p_rare_niche`: return the member in the rarest complexity band, restricted
        to the better `quality_quantile` fraction of the pool so we never hand a
        useless individual to the mutation step.
      * `p_novelty`: among members whose loss is within `novelty_loss_factor` of the
        pool's best loss, return the one whose nearest-neighbour relative loss
        distance is largest (most isolated => most likely a distinct skeleton).
    Otherwise run the standard geometric tournament ladder over penalized scores.

Assumptions / heuristics:
 - Loss equality (within a relative tolerance) is a cheap, allocation-free proxy for
   "same expression skeleton"; false positives only shift selection to an equally
   good but different member, which is harmless (and is exactly what we want).
 - All adjustments are mild and multiplicative, and the `inflate` helper divides
   instead of multiplying for non-positive costs, so "worse" always means "worse"
   and behaviour degrades gracefully to the default tournament when the pool is
   already diverse.
"""
function diversity_lineage_pareto_niche_tournament_gen22_2(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # ---------------- tunables (mild, so we degrade to the default tournament) ----
    pool_scale = 1.6           # pool size relative to tournament_selection_n
    clone_penalty = 1.4        # score inflation per unit redundancy weight
    near_clone_weight = 0.6    # same loss, nearby complexity => bloated same skeleton
    complexity_window = 2      # complexity slack for the "near clone" test
    sibling_weight = 0.35      # shared parent counts as partial redundancy
    max_redundancy = 3.0       # cap so a crowded pool cannot explode the scores
    loss_rtol = 1e-8           # relative tolerance for "exactly the same loss"
    near_loss_rtol = 1e-3      # relative tolerance for "same skeleton, re-tuned"
    youth_discount = 0.05      # max relative discount for the newest members
    pareto_bonus = 0.9         # discount for locally non-dominated members
    p_rare_niche = 0.08        # probability of the rare-complexity exploration pick
    p_novelty = 0.07           # probability of the loss-novelty exploration pick
    novelty_loss_factor = 4.0  # fitness cap for novelty candidates
    quality_quantile = 0.75    # fraction of the pool eligible for the niche pick

    # Sign-safe multiplicative modifier: f > 1 always means "worse".
    inflate = function (x::L, f::Float64)
        fl = L(f)
        return x > zero(L) ? x * fl : x / fl
    end

    # ---------------- 1. sample the pool -----------------------------------------
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # ---------------- 2. base (frequency-adjusted) scores ------------------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size
        losses[i] = Float64(member.loss)
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Relative-distance helper on losses (our structural fingerprint).
    reldist = function (a::Float64, b::Float64)
        scale = max(abs(a), abs(b), 1e-300)
        return abs(a - b) / scale
    end

    # ---------------- 3. crowding / lineage suppression --------------------------
    # Walk from best to worst adjusted cost: the best representative of every
    # cluster keeps its score, later duplicates are progressively demoted.
    order = sortperm(scores)
    redundancy = zeros(Float64, n)
    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        w = 0.0
        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            d = reldist(losses[i], losses[j])
            dc = abs(complexities[i] - complexities[j])
            if d <= loss_rtol && dc == 0
                # exact clone: same size, same loss
                w += 1.0
            elseif d <= near_loss_rtol && dc <= complexity_window
                # same skeleton, bloated or constant-retuned variant
                w += near_clone_weight
            elseif pool[i].parent != 0 && pool[i].parent == pool[j].parent
                # sibling from the same parent: partial redundancy
                w += sibling_weight
            end
        end
        redundancy[i] = min(w, max_redundancy)
    end

    # ---------------- 4. local Pareto (stepping-stone) bonus ---------------------
    nondominated = trues(n)
    for i in 1:n
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue
            # j dominates i if it is no worse in both complexity and loss,
            # and strictly better in at least one of them.
            if complexities[j] <= complexities[i] &&
                losses[j] <= losses[i] &&
                (complexities[j] < complexities[i] || losses[j] < losses[i])
                nondominated[i] = false
                break
            end
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 5. youth discount ------------------------------------------
    birth_min = pool[1].birth
    birth_max = pool[1].birth
    for i in 2:n
        b = pool[i].birth
        b < birth_min && (birth_min = b)
        b > birth_max && (birth_max = b)
    end
    birth_span = max(birth_max - birth_min, 1)

    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        recency = (pool[i].birth - birth_min) / birth_span  # 0 (oldest) .. 1 (newest)
        factor = (clone_penalty^redundancy[i]) * (1.0 - youth_discount * recency)
        nondominated[i] && (factor *= pareto_bonus)
        penalized[i] = inflate(scores[i], factor)
    end

    # ---------------- 6. exploration modes ---------------------------------------
    mode_draw = rand()

    if mode_draw < p_rare_niche
        # Restrict to the better fraction of the pool so exploration stays useful.
        k = max(1, ceil(Int, quality_quantile * n))
        eligible = falses(n)
        for idx in sortperm(penalized)[1:k]
            eligible[idx] = true
        end
        best_idx = 0
        best_freq = Inf
        best_score = zero(L)
        for i in 1:n
            eligible[i] || continue
            c = complexities[i]
            f = if (0 < c <= options.maxsize)
                Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
            else
                0.0  # out-of-range sizes count as maximally rare
            end
            if best_idx == 0 || f < best_freq || (f == best_freq && penalized[i] < best_score)
                best_freq = f
                best_score = penalized[i]
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        best_idx != 0 && return pool[best_idx]

    elseif mode_draw < p_rare_niche + p_novelty
        # Loss-novelty pick: among fitness-competitive members, take the one that is
        # most isolated in loss space (a proxy for "carries a different skeleton").
        best_loss = minimum(losses)
        cap = best_loss > 0.0 ? best_loss * novelty_loss_factor : Inf
        best_idx = 0
        best_iso = -1.0
        for i in 1:n
            losses[i] <= cap || continue
            iso = Inf
            for j in 1:n
                i == j && continue
                d = reldist(losses[i], losses[j])
                d < iso && (iso = d)
            end
            isfinite(iso) || (iso = 0.0)
            if iso > best_iso
                best_iso = iso
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        best_idx != 0 && return pool[best_idx]
    end

    # ---------------- 7. standard geometric tournament ladder --------------------
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        if tournament_winner == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, tournament_winner)[2][end]
        end
    end
    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

affine_shape_stratified_softtail_loss_ge.name: affine_shape_stratified_softtail_loss_gen22_0
affine_shape_stratified_softtail_loss_ge.code:
"""
    affine_shape_stratified_softtail_loss_gen22_0(tree, dataset, options)

Shape-first loss combining affine-calibrated profile matching with bounded,
region-balanced relative-error diagnostics.

The expression is evaluated once. Stable Welford moments determine the least-squares
affine calibration `a * prediction + b`, allowing structurally correct candidates to
survive while their constants are still poorly tuned. Direct fitted residuals are then
used to avoid cancellation near exact matches.

The loss combines:

  1. normalized affine RMSE as the primary global shape signal;
  2. bounded, scale-damped pointwise relative errors;
  3. an L4 soft-tail term, which detects localized surrogate error without the
     noise sensitivity of a single worst-sample maximum;
  4. a stratified relative RMSE that gives equal influence to four target regimes
     separated by the target mean and one standard deviation, preventing dense,
     easy regions from hiding systematic errors in sparse tails;
  5. a small saturating raw-error term selecting the correctly calibrated member
     among expressions with the same affine shape.
