All auxiliary residual terms use the affine-calibrated prediction. No expression
complexity penalty is included. Constant targets fall back to scale-normalized
log-MSE. Runtime is one tree evaluation and two linear passes over the samples.
"""
function affine_shape_stratified_softtail_loss_gen22_0(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # Stable moments for the affine least-squares calibration.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Welford accumulators may become microscopically negative from roundoff.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    relative_tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))
    target_rms = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    prediction_rms = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)

    target_is_variable =
        target_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_y
    prediction_is_variable =
        prediction_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_p

    if !target_is_variable
        # Affine shape is undefined for a constant target.
        target_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_y)
        raw_sum = zero_l
        raw_compensation = zero_l

        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            p = L(prediction[i])
            y = L(dataset.y[i])
            residual = p - y

            if !isfinite(residual)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            normalized = residual / target_scale
            term = normalized * normalized
            if !isfinite(term)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            corrected = term - raw_compensation
            updated = raw_sum + corrected
            if !isfinite(updated)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            raw_compensation = (updated - raw_sum) - corrected
            raw_sum = updated
        end

        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum / n_l, zero_l)
        loss_value = log1p(raw_nmse)
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
    end

    target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)
    if !(isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # A constant prediction is calibrated to the target mean.
    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if prediction_is_variable
        slope = cov_py / m2_p
        intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
        if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end

    # Relative-error damping prevents targets near zero from dominating.
    relative_floor = target_rms / L(8)
    if !(isfinite(relative_floor) && relative_floor > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    affine_sum = zero_l
    affine_compensation = zero_l

    raw_sum = zero_l
    raw_compensation = zero_l
    raw_overflowed = false

    # Global second and fourth moments of bounded relative error.
    relative_sq_sum = zero_l
    relative_sq_compensation = zero_l
    relative_fourth_sum = zero_l
    relative_fourth_compensation = zero_l

    # Four target regimes: lower tail, lower center, upper center, upper tail.
    regime_sum_1 = zero_l
    regime_sum_2 = zero_l
    regime_sum_3 = zero_l
    regime_sum_4 = zero_l
    regime_count_1 = 0
    regime_count_2 = 0
    regime_count_3 = 0
    regime_count_4 = 0

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_residual = p - y
        if !isfinite(raw_residual)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Raw error is only a bounded calibration tie-breaker.
        if !raw_overflowed
            raw_normalized = raw_residual / target_norm
            raw_term = raw_normalized * raw_normalized

            if isfinite(raw_term)
                corrected_raw = raw_term - raw_compensation
                updated_raw = raw_sum + corrected_raw
                if isfinite(updated_raw)
                    raw_compensation = (updated_raw - raw_sum) - corrected_raw
                    raw_sum = updated_raw
                else
                    raw_overflowed = true
                end
            else
                raw_overflowed = true
            end
        end

        fitted = prediction_is_variable ? muladd(slope, p, intercept) : mean_y
        affine_residual = fitted - y
        affine_normalized = affine_residual / target_norm
        affine_term = affine_normalized * affine_normalized

        if !(isfinite(fitted) && isfinite(affine_residual) &&
             isfinite(affine_normalized) && isfinite(affine_term))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        corrected_affine = affine_term - affine_compensation
        updated_affine = affine_sum + corrected_affine
        if !isfinite(updated_affine)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        affine_compensation =
            (updated_affine - affine_sum) - corrected_affine
        affine_sum = updated_affine

        relative_denominator = abs(y) + relative_floor
        absolute_error = abs(affine_residual)
        if !(isfinite(relative_denominator) && relative_denominator > zero_l &&
             isfinite(absolute_error))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Compute |e|/(|e|+denominator) without overflowing the addition.
        bounded_relative = if absolute_error <= relative_denominator
            ratio = absolute_error / relative_denominator
            ratio / (one_l + ratio)
        else
            inverse_ratio = relative_denominator / absolute_error
            one_l / (one_l + inverse_ratio)
        end

        relative_sq = bounded_relative * bounded_relative
        relative_fourth = relative_sq * relative_sq

        corrected_relative =
            relative_sq - relative_sq_compensation
        updated_relative =
            relative_sq_sum + corrected_relative
        relative_sq_compensation =
            (updated_relative - relative_sq_sum) - corrected_relative
        relative_sq_sum = updated_relative

        corrected_fourth =
            relative_fourth - relative_fourth_compensation
        updated_fourth =
            relative_fourth_sum + corrected_fourth
        relative_fourth_compensation =
            (updated_fourth - relative_fourth_sum) - corrected_fourth
        relative_fourth_sum = updated_fourth

        if !(isfinite(relative_sq_sum) && isfinite(relative_fourth_sum))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Equalized target regimes expose systematic errors in sparsely sampled
        # portions of the response range.
        centered_y = y - mean_y
        if !isfinite(centered_y)
            return L(Inf)
        elseif centered_y < -target_rms
            regime_sum_1 += relative_sq
            regime_count_1 += 1
        elseif centered_y < zero_l
            regime_sum_2 += relative_sq
            regime_count_2 += 1
        elseif centered_y <= target_rms
            regime_sum_3 += relative_sq
            regime_count_3 += 1
        else
            regime_sum_4 += relative_sq
            regime_count_4 += 1
        end
    end

    # The least-squares affine fit cannot be worse than predicting mean(y).
    affine_nmse = clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l)
    shape_term = sqrt(affine_nmse)

    mean_relative_term =
        sqrt(max(relative_sq_sum / n_l, zero_l))
    soft_tail_term =
        sqrt(sqrt(max(relative_fourth_sum / n_l, zero_l)))

    regime_average = zero_l
    populated_regimes = 0

    if regime_count_1 > 0
        regime_average += regime_sum_1 / L(regime_count_1)
        populated_regimes += 1
    end
    if regime_count_2 > 0
        regime_average += regime_sum_2 / L(regime_count_2)
        populated_regimes += 1
    end
    if regime_count_3 > 0
        regime_average += regime_sum_3 / L(regime_count_3)
        populated_regimes += 1
    end
    if regime_count_4 > 0
        regime_average += regime_sum_4 / L(regime_count_4)
        populated_regimes += 1
    end

    if populated_regimes <= 0
        return L(Inf)
    end

    regime_average /= L(populated_regimes)
    stratified_relative_term = sqrt(max(regime_average, zero_l))

    bounded_raw = if raw_overflowed
        one_l
    else
        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum, zero_l)
        raw_nmse <= one_l ?
            raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse) :
            one_l / (one_l + one_l / raw_nmse)
    end

    # Global shape dominates. Relative terms refine near-matches, while raw error
    # remains too small to eliminate structurally correct, miscalibrated candidates.
    mean_relative_weight = L(3) / L(16)
    stratified_weight = one_l / L(8)
    soft_tail_weight = one_l / L(16)
    calibration_weight = one_l / L(256)

    loss_value =
        shape_term +
        mean_relative_weight * mean_relative_term +
        stratified_weight * stratified_relative_term +
        soft_tail_weight * soft_tail_term +
        calibration_weight * bounded_raw

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

stable_affine_shape_rmse_loss_gen22_1.name: stable_affine_shape_rmse_loss_gen22_1
stable_affine_shape_rmse_loss_gen22_1.code:
"""
    stable_affine_shape_rmse_loss_gen22_1(tree, dataset, options)

Evaluate an expression by its invariant functional shape under optimal affine
recalibration `a * prediction + b`, with a small bounded raw-error tie-breaker to
prefer correctly calibrated constants.

This operator synthesizes:
1. **Numerically Stable Online Moments (from Parent 1)**: Computes means, variances,
   and covariance via Welford updates in Pass 1, preventing catastrophic cancellation
   when predictions or targets have large mean offsets. Scale-relative variability
   checks guard against division by near-zero variance.
2. **Unified Scale Floor and Streamlined Two-Pass Flow (from Parent 2)**: Replaces
   separate branches and heavy compensation buffers with a single unified normalization
   scale `scale = target_norm > 0 ? target_norm : sqrt(n) * max(1, max|y|)`. This
   naturally degenerates the affine shape error to zero on constant targets, allowing
   the bounded raw error to cleanly optimize candidate constants without extra branching.
3. **Direct Residual Evaluation (both parents)**: Measures residual normalized RMSE
   directly from the fitted values `muladd(a, p, b) - y` in Pass 2, avoiding numerical
   drift near perfect correlation, while preserving monotone bounded raw error.
"""
function stable_affine_shape_rmse_loss_gen22_1(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)
    eps_l = eps(L)

    # --- Pass 1: Welford online accumulation for stable least-squares coefficients ---
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Roundoff safeguard
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    # Scale-relative variance thresholds to prevent jitter around flat predictions
    prediction_is_variable = m2_p > eps_l * (max_abs_p * max_abs_p) * n_l
    target_is_variable = m2_y > eps_l * (max_abs_y * max_abs_y) * n_l

    # Compute optimal affine coefficients (slope a and intercept b for a*p + b)
    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if prediction_is_variable && target_is_variable
        slope = cov_py / m2_p
        intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
        if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
            slope = zero_l
            intercept = mean_y
        end
    end

    # Unified normalization scale: floored to handle zero-variance target gracefully
    target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)
    scale = target_is_variable ? target_norm : sqrt(n_l) * max(one_l, max_abs_y)
    if !(isfinite(scale) && scale > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # --- Pass 2: Direct evaluation of fitted shape residual and raw error ---
    affine_sum = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_norm = (p - y) / scale
        raw_sum += raw_norm * raw_norm

        fitted = muladd(slope, p, intercept)
        affine_norm = (fitted - y) / scale
        affine_sum += affine_norm * affine_norm
    end

    if !isfinite(affine_sum)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Shape term: normalized RMSE of the optimal affine recalibration in [0, 1]
    shape_term = sqrt(clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l))

    # Bounded calibration tie-breaker: strictly monotonic in [0, 1), overflow-safe
    bounded_raw = if isfinite(raw_sum) && raw_sum >= zero_l
        raw_sum <= one_l ?
            raw_sum / (one_l + raw_sum) :
            one_l / (one_l + one_l / raw_sum)
    else
        one_l
    end

    calibration_weight = one_l / L(256)
    loss_value = shape_term + calibration_weight * bounded_raw

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

pareto_niche_declone_selection_gen22_4.name: pareto_niche_declone_selection_gen22_4
pareto_niche_declone_selection_gen22_4.code:
"""
    pareto_niche_declone_selection_gen22_4(pop::Population{T,L,N}, running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics, options::AbstractOptions)::PopMember{T,L,N}

Pareto-niche selection with explicit clone/sibling de-crowding, synthesizing the
non-dominated (cost, niche) ranking of `adaptive_pareto_niche_selection_gen18_7`
with the redundancy-aware crowding detector and rare-niche exploration kick of
`crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen10_4`.

# Core Idea
Two failure modes are targeted simultaneously: (a) premature convergence onto a
single over-refined skeleton whose near-identical clones flood tournaments, and
(b) starvation of whole complexity bands that removes useful mid-size building
blocks. Rather than folding redundancy into a single scalar cost (as in parent 2)
or only counting crude same-parent siblings (as in parent 1), this operator
builds a continuous "niche congestion" score that merges: complexity-bin
saturation, relative age, sibling lineage crowding, *and* an explicit
near-duplicate-solution detector (same complexity + near-identical loss). This
congestion score is then treated as a second objective alongside the
frequency-adjusted cost, and candidates are ranked via 2D Pareto dominance
(parent 1's mechanism) before a geometric rank-based draw. A small-probability
explicit rare-complexity pick (parent 2) is retained as a cheap, direct
insurance against total extinction of sparse complexity bands.

# Steps
1. Sample an enlarged pool (~1.5x `tournament_selection_n`, capped at `pop.n`)
   so redundancy/niche structure is actually visible.
2. Compute per-candidate complexity and frequency-adjusted cost.
3. Detect near-duplicate solutions: for each candidate, count how many *better*
   (lower adjusted cost) pool members share its complexity and have
   relatively-equal loss (full weight), or share its parent reference (partial
   weight) — this is the redundancy weight.
4. Build a niche-congestion score = normalized complexity frequency
   + weighted normalized age (older = more congested, to favor fresh lineages)
   + a scaled redundancy weight (clones/siblings inflate congestion).
5. Rank the pool by 2D Pareto dominance over (adjusted_cost, niche_congestion);
   sort by (dominance count, adjusted cost) so non-dominated, cheap, novel
   candidates lead.
6. With small probability `p_rare_niche`, bypass ranking and directly return the
   candidate from the rarest-populated complexity bin (ties by adjusted cost),
   as an explicit safeguard against niche extinction.
7. Otherwise draw the winner via the standard geometric ladder
   (`tournament_selection_p`) over the Pareto-sorted candidates.

# Heuristics & Assumptions
- Equal complexity + near-equal loss is a cheap, allocation-light proxy for
  "structurally redundant"; false positives are harmless (just nudge selection
  toward an equally good sibling).
- Treating congestion (frequency + age + redundancy) as a single second
  objective lets Pareto dominance naturally trade off exploration vs.
  exploitation without hand-tuned multiplicative penalties.
- Pool sizes of ~1.5x tournament size keep O(k^2) dominance/redundancy
  computation cheap while giving enough samples for reliable redundancy
  detection.
"""
function pareto_niche_declone_selection_gen22_4(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # ---------------- tunables ----------------------------------------------
    pool_scale = 1.5           # enlarge pool relative to tournament_selection_n
    sibling_weight = 0.4       # partial redundancy credit for shared-parent members
    loss_rtol = 1e-6           # relative tolerance for "same loss"
    redundancy_scale = 0.15    # how much redundancy weight contributes to congestion
    age_weight = 0.2           # how much normalized age contributes to congestion
    p_rare_niche = 0.08        # probability of explicit rare-complexity override

    # ---------------- 1. sample the pool ------------------------------------
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    if pool_size <= 1
        return pop.members[1]
    end
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    # ---------------- 2. complexity + frequency-adjusted cost ---------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    freqs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size
        freq = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
            Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
        else
            0.0
        end
        freqs[i] = freq
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost * exp(scaling * L(freq))
        else
            adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 3. near-duplicate / sibling redundancy detection ------
    # Process from best (lowest adjusted cost) to worst so only weaker twins
    # accrue redundancy weight, leaving the best representative unpenalized.
    order = sortperm(adjusted_costs)
    redundancy = zeros(Float64, n)
    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        wi = 0.0
        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            same_loss = abs(li - lj) <= L(loss_rtol) * max(abs(li), abs(lj), eps(L))
            if complexities[i] == complexities[j] && same_loss
                wi += 1.0
            elseif pool[i].parent > 0 && pool[i].parent == pool[j].parent
                wi += sibling_weight
            end
        end
        redundancy[i] = wi
    end

    # ---------------- 4. niche-congestion score (second objective) ---------
    max_birth = pool[1].birth
    for i in 2:n
        pool[i].birth > max_birth && (max_birth = pool[i].birth)
    end
    niche_scores = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        rel_age = Float64(max_birth - pool[i].birth)
        norm_age = max_birth > 0 ? (rel_age / Float64(max_birth)) : 0.0
        niche_scores[i] = freqs[i] + age_weight * norm_age + redundancy_scale * redundancy[i]
    end

    # ---------------- 5a. occasional explicit rare-niche pick ---------------
    if rand() < p_rare_niche
        best_idx = 1
        best_freq = Inf
        best_cost = adjusted_costs[1]
        for i in 1:n
            f = freqs[i]
            if f < best_freq || (f == best_freq && adjusted_costs[i] < best_cost)
                best_freq = f
                best_cost = adjusted_costs[i]
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        return pool[best_idx]
    end

    # ---------------- 5b. 2D Pareto dominance ranking -----------------------
    dom_count = zeros(Int, n)
    for i in 1:n
        cost_i = adjusted_costs[i]
        niche_i = niche_scores[i]
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue
            cost_j = adjusted_costs[j]
            niche_j = niche_scores[j]
            # j dominates i if no worse in both objectives and strictly better in one
            if (cost_j <= cost_i && niche_j <= niche_i) && (cost_j < cost_i || niche_j < niche_i)
                dom_count[i] += 1
            end
        end
    end

    ranked_indices = collect(1:n)
    sort!(ranked_indices; by=i -> (dom_count[i], adjusted_costs[i]))

    # ---------------- 6. rank-based geometric selection ----------------------
    chosen_idx = if p >= 1.0f0
        ranked_indices[1]
    else
        k_indices = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p .* ((1.0f0 - p) .^ k_indices)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        ranked_indices[tournament_winner_rank]
    end

    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

residual_correlation_injection_gen22_5.name: residual_correlation_injection_gen22_5
residual_correlation_injection_gen22_5.code:
"""
    residual_correlation_injection_gen22_5(tree, dataset, options, nfeatures, rng)

A data-aware mutation that looks at the *residual* between the current tree's
predictions and the true targets, and tries to correct it by injecting a
linear correction term `a * x_i` (chosen via least squares) into the
expression. The steps are:

1. Evaluate `tree` on `dataset.X`. If evaluation fails (e.g. domain errors),
   bail out and return the tree unchanged.
2. Compute the residual `dataset.y .- y_pred`. If it contains non-finite
   values, bail out.
3. For each feature column, compute its Pearson correlation with the
   residual (skipping near-constant features to avoid `NaN` correlations).
   The absolute correlation magnitudes are used as sampling weights, so
   the mutation stochastically favors features that best explain the
   remaining error, while still allowing exploration of weaker
   candidates (via `rng`) rather than deterministically always picking the
   single best one.
4. Given the chosen feature `x_i`, fit a least-squares scalar coefficient
   `a = <residual, x_i> / <x_i, x_i>` that approximately minimizes the
   remaining residual when correcting along that feature (a simple linear
   regression against a single covariate).
5. Build a `+`-rooted new tree: `tree + a * x_i`, using the model's actual
   `+`/`*` operators if present in `options.operators.binops` (falling back
   to a no-op if either operator is unavailable in the operator set).

This heuristic assumes the search space includes `+` and `*` binary
operators, and that a locally linear correction is a reasonable way to
reduce residual error — a cheap surrogate for a full symbolic residual fit.
"""
function residual_correlation_injection_gen22_5(
    tree::N,
    dataset,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Need targets and at least one feature to do anything data-driven.
    if nfeatures < 1 || dataset.y === nothing
        return tree
    end

    # Need + and * operators available to build the correction term.
    mult_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (*), options.operators.binops)
    add_idx = findfirst(op -> op == (+), options.operators.binops)
    if mult_idx === nothing || add_idx === nothing
        return tree
    end

    # Evaluate the current tree on the training data.
    y_pred, ok = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options.operators)
    if !ok
        return tree  # evaluation failed (e.g. div-by-zero, domain error)
    end

    residual = dataset.y .- y_pred
    if any(!isfinite, residual)
        return tree  # residual is degenerate; nothing sensible to correlate
    end

    # Compute |correlation| of each feature with the residual, used as
    # sampling weights (0 for near-constant / invalid features).
    weights = zeros(T, nfeatures)
    for i in 1:nfeatures
        xi = view(dataset.X, i, :)
        if var(xi) > eps(T)
            c = cor(xi, residual)
            weights[i] = isnan(c) ? zero(T) : T(abs(c))
        end
    end

    total_weight = sum(weights)
    if total_weight <= zero(T)
        return tree  # no feature correlates with the residual at all
    end

    # Weighted random sample of a feature index, biased toward features
    # that best explain the residual, but still allowing exploration.
    r = rand(rng, T) * total_weight
    cum = zero(T)
    chosen_feature = 1
    for i in 1:nfeatures
        cum += weights[i]
        if r <= cum
            chosen_feature = i
            break
        end
    end

    # Fit a scalar least-squares coefficient for the chosen feature against
    # the residual: a = <residual, x> / <x, x>.
    xi = view(dataset.X, chosen_feature, :)
    denom = sum(xi .^ 2)
    a = denom > eps(T) ? T(sum(residual .* xi) / denom) : zero(T)
    if a == zero(T) || !isfinite(a)
        return tree  # degenerate fit; skip mutation
    end

    # Build the correction term: a * x_chosen_feature.
    coeff_node = constructorof(N)(T; val=a)
    leaf_feature = constructorof(N)(T; feature=chosen_feature)
    scaled_feature = constructorof(N)(; op=mult_idx, children=(coeff_node, leaf_feature))

    # Graft the correction onto the whole tree via addition, returning a new root.
    newroot = constructorof(N)(; op=add_idx, children=(tree, scaled_feature))
    return newroot
end

structure_shaped_mse_gen22_6.name: structure_shaped_mse_gen22_6
structure_shaped_mse_gen22_6.code:
"""
    structure_shaped_mse_gen22_6(tree, dataset, options)

**Core idea (correlation-shaped MSE).**  Ordinary MSE only asks "how close are the
numbers?", so a candidate that has already discovered the *right functional shape* but
carries a wrong overall gain/offset (e.g. `x1*x2` when the truth is `3.7*x1*x2 - 2`) is
scored no better than a candidate that is numerically close by accident but structurally
wrong.  Ground-truth recovery, however, is fundamentally a search over *shapes*: once the
shape is right, PySR's constant optimizer and the mutation operators can fix the scale
cheaply.  This loss therefore multiplies the usual MSE by a *shape factor* derived from the
fraction of target variance that the prediction leaves unexplained after the best possible
affine rescaling `a*p + b` (Keijzer-style linear scaling, expressed in closed form as
`1 - r²`).  Predictions whose shape already matches the target get their MSE discounted by
up to ~32x, giving them a strong survival/tournament advantage, while predictions that are
merely numerically small-error but structurally uncorrelated are scored essentially as
plain MSE.

**Steps.**
1. Evaluate the tree; bail out with `Inf` on failure or non-finite output.
2. In a *single* fused pass accumulate `Σp, Σy, Σp², Σy², Σpy, Σ(p-y)²`, i.e. everything
   needed for both the MSE and the Pearson correlation `r` between prediction and target.
3. `u = 1 - r²` is the residual variance fraction that survives the optimal affine
   rescaling of the prediction (`u = 1` if the prediction is constant, which correctly
   denies constant expressions any bonus).
4. Return `mse * sqrt((u + δ) / (1 + δ))` with a small floor `δ = 1e-3`.

**Heuristics / assumptions.**
* The floor `δ` is essential: without it a perfectly-correlated-but-misscaled expression
  would receive *zero* loss and be indistinguishable from an exact solution.  With it, the
  raw MSE still appears linearly in the loss, so constant optimization and further
  mutations retain a real gradient toward the exact fit, and an exactly-fitting expression
  always strictly dominates a misscaled sibling.
* The factor is normalized by `sqrt(1 + δ)` so it lies in `(0, 1]`; the loss is thus never
  larger than the MSE, keeping its magnitude (and PySR's baseline normalization and `:log`
  score scaling) on the familiar MSE scale.
* `sqrt` (exponent 1/2) is a deliberately moderate shaping strength: enough to reorder
  tournaments, small enough not to let wildly inaccurate expressions dominate the frontier.
* Cost is one memory-bound pass over the prediction and target vectors — the same
  asymptotics and roughly the same runtime as MSE.
* Assumes a single scalar target; degenerate cases (constant `y`, `n < 3`) gracefully fall
  back to plain MSE.
"""
function structure_shaped_mse_gen22_6(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    y = dataset.y
    n = length(prediction)
    if n == 0
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Too few points for a meaningful correlation: fall back to plain MSE.
    if n < 3
        s = zero(L)
        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            d = L(prediction[i]) - L(y[i])
            s += d * d
        end
        return isfinite(s) ? L(s / n) : L(Inf)
    end

    # --- single fused pass: moments for MSE *and* for Pearson correlation -------------
    sp = zero(L)   # Σ p
    sy = zero(L)   # Σ y
    spp = zero(L)  # Σ p²
    syy = zero(L)  # Σ y²
    spy = zero(L)  # Σ p·y
    sse = zero(L)  # Σ (p - y)²
    @inbounds @simd for i in 1:n
        pv = L(prediction[i])
        yv = L(y[i])
        sp += pv
        sy += yv
        spp += pv * pv
        syy += yv * yv
        spy += pv * yv
        d = pv - yv
        sse += d * d
    end

    # Any NaN/Inf anywhere in the prediction poisons these accumulators -> reject.
    if !(isfinite(sse) && isfinite(spp) && isfinite(spy) && isfinite(sp))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    invn = one(L) / L(n)
    mp = sp * invn
    my = sy * invn
    mse = sse * invn

    # Biased (1/n) central moments; clamped at 0 to absorb catastrophic-cancellation noise.
    var_p = max(spp * invn - mp * mp, zero(L))
    var_y = max(syy * invn - my * my, zero(L))
    cov = spy * invn - mp * my

    # u = 1 - r² : target-variance fraction left unexplained after the *best* affine
    # rescaling a*p + b of the prediction.  Constant prediction or constant target => u = 1
    # (no shape bonus), which keeps trivial constant expressions from being rewarded.
    u = one(L)
    if var_p > zero(L) && var_y > zero(L)
        r2 = (cov * cov) / (var_p * var_y)
        u = one(L) - clamp(r2, zero(L), one(L))
    end

    # Shape factor in (0, 1]: floored so a perfectly-shaped-but-misscaled tree keeps a
    # strictly positive loss proportional to its raw MSE (preserving the optimizer's signal).
    delta = L(1e-3)
    factor = sqrt((u + delta) / (one(L) + delta))

    loss = mse * factor
    return isfinite(loss) ? L(loss) : L(Inf)
end

clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple.name: clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple_gen22_7
clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple.code:
"""
    clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple_gen22_7(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Simplified crowding-/niche-aware tournament selection.

Core idea (kept from the parent): sample a slightly enlarged tournament pool,
score it with the usual frequency-adjusted (adaptive-parsimony) cost, demote
members that are *redundant duplicates* of a better pool member so a single
champion skeleton cannot monopolise the lineage, and occasionally pick the pool
member sitting in the rarest complexity niche so that starved complexity bands
get repopulated (this is what the trace suggests is missing: the search spends a
million evaluations elaborating one big skeleton instead of building fresh
mid-size structures such as `x0 / sqrt(1 - (x1/x2)^2)`).

Steps:
 1. Sample `~1.5 * tournament_selection_n` distinct members (a bit larger than the
    default tournament so redundancy/niche info exists).
 2. Compute complexity and the default adaptive-parsimony-adjusted cost.
 3. Clone suppression: walk the pool from best to worst adjusted cost and bucket
    members by `(complexity, loss rounded to 6 significant digits)`. The first
    (best) member of a bucket is untouched; the k-th duplicate gets its score
    inflated by `clone_penalty^(k-1)`.
 4. With probability `p_rare_niche`, return the pool member with the lowest
    `normalized_frequencies` at its complexity (ties broken by penalized score).
 5. Otherwise, run the standard geometric tournament ladder over penalized scores.

Simplifications relative to the parent:
 - Dropped the sibling (shared-parent) partial-redundancy term: it largely
   overlaps with the clone test (siblings of an unchanged parent have identical
   complexity+loss) while adding a tunable and extra bookkeeping.
 - Dropped the youth/recency discount: it was a very mild (<=5%) multiplicative
   nudge whose effect is dominated by the clone penalty and the niche pick.
 - Replaced the O(n^2) pairwise clone-tolerance scan with a single O(n) pass over
   a hash bucket keyed by rounded loss, which is cheaper and easier to reason
   about; the grouping semantics ("same complexity + same loss to ~6 digits")
   are equivalent in spirit.
With no duplicates in the pool and no niche draw, the operator degrades exactly
to the default tournament, so behaviour remains safe.
"""
function clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple_gen22_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # ---------------- tunables ----------------------------------------------------
    pool_scale = 1.5        # pool size relative to tournament_selection_n
    clone_penalty = 1.35    # score inflation per additional duplicate
    p_rare_niche = 0.10     # probability of the explicit rare-complexity pick

    # ---------------- 1. sample the pool -----------------------------------------
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # ---------------- 2. base (frequency-adjusted) scores ------------------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
            else
                L(0)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 3. clone suppression (single pass, best -> worst) -----------
    penalized = copy(scores)
    order = sortperm(scores)
    # bucket key: (complexity, loss rounded to ~6 significant digits)
    seen = Dict{Tuple{Int,Float64},Int}()
    for a in 1:n
        i = order[a]
        key = (complexities[i], round(Float64(pool[i].loss); sigdigits=6))
        k = get(seen, key, 0)          # number of strictly better duplicates
        seen[key] = k + 1
        if k > 0
            f = L(clone_penalty^k)
            # sign-safe inflation: a factor > 1 must always mean "worse"
            penalized[i] = scores[i] > zero(L) ? scores[i] * f : scores[i] / f
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 4. occasional rare-complexity (niche) pick ------------------
    if rand() < p_rare_niche
        best_idx = 1
        best_freq = Inf
        best_score = penalized[1]
        for i in 1:n
            c = complexities[i]
            f = if (0 < c <= options.maxsize)
                Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
            else
                0.0  # out-of-range sizes count as maximally rare
            end
            if f < best_freq || (f == best_freq && penalized[i] < best_score)
                best_freq = f
                best_score = penalized[i]
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        return pool[best_idx]
    end

    # ---------------- 5. standard geometric tournament ladder ---------------------
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        if tournament_winner == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, tournament_winner)[2][end]
        end
    end
    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

age_dominant_quality_protected_survival_.name: age_dominant_quality_protected_survival_gen22_9
age_dominant_quality_protected_survival_.code:
"""
    age_dominant_quality_protected_survival_gen22_9(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

Synthesizes parent 2's simple, age-dominant philosophy (oldest members are the
default eviction target, with cost breaking ties) with parent 1's
quality-awareness (redundancy detection and Pareto-frontier protection) so
that age remains the primary turnover signal but the search no longer evicts
rare, high-quality, or non-dominated structures purely because they are old,
nor does it let a mediocre-but-old duplicate linger just because a newer
identical clone exists.

Steps:
1. Compute complexity, loss, cost, birth, and validity (finite) for every
   member.
2. Build tie-aware age and cost ranks in `[0, 1]` (oldest -> 1, worst cost ->
   1), exactly as in parent 1, avoiding the arbitrary ordering imposed by a
   naive `sortperm`-based rank on tied values (parent 2's weakness).
3. Combine age and cost ranks with age dominant (weight 0.75, matching
   parent 2's tunable blend) to form the base score: the primary driver of
   eviction remains "oldest, worst" rather than pure fitness.
4. Detect exact-signature redundancy via `(complexity, rounded loss)`. Only
   the best (lowest loss/cost, newest) representative of each signature is
   protected; other members sharing that niche receive an extra penalty so
   that stale duplicates are pruned ahead of the unique representative
   they mimic.
5. Build a lightweight Pareto frontier over one representative per
   complexity value in `(complexity, loss)` space. Non-dominated members
   receive protection that decays with age, so genuinely novel low-loss
   discoveries are shielded when young but can still eventually be replaced
   once stale.
6. Softly protect the single best-cost and best-loss members (age-decayed),
   preventing the champion from becoming an immortal blocker while still
   giving it priority survival while young/fresh.
7. Non-finite members receive a dominant penalty and are never treated as
   elites. A tiny random jitter breaks exact ties. Excluded indices are
   masked; if all are excluded, index 1 is returned as a degenerate
   fallback.
"""
function age_dominant_quality_protected_survival_gen22_9(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    n <= 1 && return 1

    # Mask exclusions once.
    excluded = falses(n)
    for idx in exclude_indices
        if 1 <= idx <= n
            excluded[idx] = true
        end
    end
    all(excluded) && return 1

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1) Gather per-member statistics.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    comp = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    lossf = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costf = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    births = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    broken = falses(n)

    for i in 1:n
        m = pop.members[i]
        comp[i] = compute_complexity(m, options)

        raw_loss = Float64(m.loss)
        raw_cost = Float64(m.cost)
        broken[i] = !isfinite(raw_loss) || !isfinite(raw_cost)

        lossf[i] = isfinite(raw_loss) ? raw_loss : Inf
        costf[i] = isfinite(raw_cost) ? raw_cost : Inf
        births[i] = Float64(m.birth)
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2) Tie-aware age and cost ranks in [0, 1].
    #    Age: 1 is oldest (default eviction target), 0 is newest.
    #    Cost: 1 is worst, 0 is best.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    denom = Float64(max(1, n - 1))
    age_rank = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    cost_rank = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)

    age_order = sortperm(births)  # ascending birth -> first is oldest
    k = 1
    while k <= n
        j = k
        while j < n && births[age_order[j + 1]] == births[age_order[k]]
            j += 1
        end
        # Oldest group gets rank near 1.0; newest near 0.0.
        rank_value = 1.0 - ((k - 1) + (j - 1)) / (2.0 * denom)
        for pos in k:j
            age_rank[age_order[pos]] = rank_value
        end
        k = j + 1
    end

    cost_order = sortperm(costf)
    k = 1
    while k <= n
        j = k
        while j < n && costf[cost_order[j + 1]] == costf[cost_order[k]]
            j += 1
        end
        rank_value = ((k - 1) + (j - 1)) / (2.0 * denom)
        for pos in k:j
            cost_rank[cost_order[pos]] = rank_value
        end
        k = j + 1
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3) Exact-signature redundancy detection: (complexity, rounded loss).
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    sigs = Vector{Tuple{Int,Float64}}(undef, n)
    sig_counts = Dict{Tuple{Int,Float64},Int}()
    for i in 1:n
        rl = isfinite(lossf[i]) ? round(lossf[i]; sigdigits=8) : Inf
        sigs[i] = (comp[i], rl)
        sig_counts[sigs[i]] = get(sig_counts, sigs[i], 0) + 1
    end

    # Keep the lowest-loss, then lowest-cost, then newest representative.
    sig_rep = Dict{Tuple{Int,Float64},Int}()
    for i in 1:n
        s = sigs[i]
        old = get(sig_rep, s, 0)
        if old == 0 ||
           lossf[i] < lossf[old] ||
           (lossf[i] == lossf[old] && costf[i] < costf[old]) ||
           (lossf[i] == lossf[old] && costf[i] == costf[old] &&
            births[i] > births[old])
            sig_rep[s] = i
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4) Lightweight Pareto frontier over one representative per complexity.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    best_at_complexity = Dict{Int,Int}()
    for i in 1:n
        c = comp[i]
        old = get(best_at_complexity, c, 0)
        if old == 0 ||
           lossf[i] < lossf[old] ||
           (lossf[i] == lossf[old] && costf[i] < costf[old]) ||
           (lossf[i] == lossf[old] && costf[i] == costf[old] &&
            births[i] > births[old])
            best_at_complexity[c] = i
        end
    end

    frontier_order = collect(values(best_at_complexity))
    sort!(frontier_order; by=i -> comp[i])

    nondom = falses(n)
    best_loss_so_far = Inf
    for idx in frontier_order
        current_loss = lossf[idx]
        if isfinite(current_loss) && current_loss < best_loss_so_far
            nondom[idx] = true
            best_loss_so_far = current_loss
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5) Identify best-cost / best-loss elites (ties favor simpler, newer).
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    best_cost_idx = 0
    best_loss_idx = 0
    for i in 1:n
        broken[i] && continue

        if best_cost_idx == 0 ||
           costf[i] < costf[best_cost_idx] ||
           (costf[i] == costf[best_cost_idx] &&
            comp[i] < comp[best_cost_idx]) ||
           (costf[i] == costf[best_cost_idx] &&
            comp[i] == comp[best_cost_idx] &&
            births[i] > births[best_cost_idx])
            best_cost_idx = i
        end

        if best_loss_idx == 0 ||
           lossf[i] < lossf[best_loss_idx] ||
           (lossf[i] == lossf[best_loss_idx] &&
            comp[i] < comp[best_loss_idx]) ||
           (lossf[i] == lossf[best_loss_idx] &&
            comp[i] == comp[best_loss_idx] &&
            costf[i] < costf[best_loss_idx]) ||
           (lossf[i] == lossf[best_loss_idx] &&
            comp[i] == comp[best_loss_idx] &&
            costf[i] == costf[best_loss_idx] &&
            births[i] > births[best_loss_idx])
            best_loss_idx = i
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6) Score every allowed member; the largest score is most expendable.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    age_weight = 0.75  # Age remains the dominant survival signal.

    best_score = -Inf
    best_choice = 0

    for i in 1:n
        excluded[i] && continue

        # Base score: age-dominant blend, exactly parent 2's philosophy but
        # using tie-aware ranks from parent 1.
        score = age_weight * age_rank[i] + (1.0 - age_weight) * cost_rank[i]

        # Redundant duplicates (same complexity & near-identical loss) that
        # are not the best representative receive extra pressure, scaled by
        # how crowded that niche is.
        sc = sig_counts[sigs[i]]
        if sc > 1 && sig_rep[sigs[i]] != i
            duplicate_penalty = 0.55 + 0.35 * min(1.0, (sc - 2) / 3.0)
            score += duplicate_penalty
        end

        # Invalid members dominate ordinary deletion candidates.
        broken[i] && (score += 5.0)

        # Pareto-frontier protection decays with age, so no finite member is
        # permanently frozen, but young novel discoveries are shielded.
        if nondom[i]
            score -= 1.0 * (1.0 - 0.55 * age_rank[i])
        end

        # Soft, age-decayed protection for the single best-cost/best-loss
        # champions, replacing parent 1's fuller mechanism but keeping its
        # anti-immortality property.
        if i == best_cost_idx
            score -= 1.2 * (1.0 - 0.75 * age_rank[i])
        end
        if i == best_loss_idx
            score -= 0.7 * (1.0 - 0.65 * age_rank[i])
        end

        # Small jitter breaks exact ties without disturbing ordering.
        score += 0.01 * rand()

        if score > best_score
            best_score = score
            best_choice = i
        end
    end

    return best_choice == 0 ? 1 : best_choice
end

age_diversity_survival_pareto_shield_gen.name: age_diversity_survival_pareto_shield_gen23_3
age_diversity_survival_pareto_shield_gen.code:
"""
    age_diversity_survival_pareto_shield_gen23_3(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[]) -> Int

Hybrid age-based survival that generalizes the elite-protection idea from
`age_diversity_survival_hybrid_gen20_2` into a lightweight **Pareto shield**,
while keeping the cheap sampled/global age-pressure mixture from both parents.

Motivation from the trace: pure age-regularized survival (parent 1) and pure
sampled-age survival (parent 2) both let the frontier converge onto
elaborations of a *single* motif (e.g. repeatedly decorating one
`(x0 + sin(x0)) * ...` skeleton) because only the single best-cost individual
was ever protected — every other complexity level was fair game for random
age-death, including the small, structurally distinct scaffolds that
crossover/mutation need to escape a local motif. This operator instead
protects the *entire* cheap Pareto frontier (the best-cost member at each
distinct complexity value), not just the single global best, so multiple
independent building blocks of different sizes survive simultaneously and
remain available as recombination scaffolds — while unprotected (dominated,
redundant) members still turn over under age pressure exactly as before.

Steps:
1. One O(n) pass computes, for every complexity value present in the
   population, the index of its lowest-cost member (`best_at_complexity`).
   The union of these indices is the "shield" — the same handful of slots
   that would appear on a Pareto front plot of cost vs. complexity.
2. With probability `global_prob` (0.2), mimic parent 1: deterministically
   scan the whole population and delete the oldest member that is neither
   excluded nor shielded (guarantees regular, non-random turnover of stale
   dominated material).
3. Otherwise, mimic parent 2: draw `n_sample = clamp(tournament_selection_n,
   2, n)` uniform random slots and delete the oldest one that is neither
   excluded nor shielded (soft age pressure, cheap, allocation-free per draw).
4. Fallback chain guarantees a valid, non-shielded, non-excluded return when
   possible, then relaxes the shield if every legal slot is protected, and
   finally relaxes everything but `exclude_indices` as a last resort.

Assumptions: `birth` is monotonically increasing (smaller = older), `pop.n >=
1`, `exclude_indices` is tiny, and `compute_complexity` is cheap relative to
evaluating a new offspring (a `Dict` is used since complexity values are not
guaranteed to be densely packed or bounded by `maxsize` at all times).
"""
function age_diversity_survival_pareto_shield_gen23_3(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)

    # ---- Step 1: build the cheap Pareto shield (best cost per complexity). ----
    best_at_complexity = Dict{Int,Int}()
    best_cost_at_complexity = Dict{Int,L}()
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        c = compute_complexity(pop.members[i], options)
        cost = pop.members[i].cost
        prev = get(best_cost_at_complexity, c, nothing)
        if prev === nothing || cost < prev
            best_cost_at_complexity[c] = cost
            best_at_complexity[c] = i
        end
    end
    # Cheap membership test set: the shielded slot indices.
    shielded = Set{Int}(values(best_at_complexity))

    best_idx = 0
    best_birth = typemax(BT)

    # ---- Steps 2 & 3: mixture of global-oldest and sampled-oldest, respecting the shield. ----
    global_prob = 0.2
    if rand() < global_prob
        # Parent-1 style deterministic scan, skipping excluded and shielded slots.
        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue
            (i in shielded) && continue
            b = pop.members[i].birth
            if best_idx == 0 || b < best_birth
                best_idx = i
                best_birth = b
            end
        end
    else
        # Parent-2 style sampled scan, skipping excluded and shielded slots.
        n_sample = min(n, max(2, options.tournament_selection_n))
        @inbounds for _ in 1:n_sample
            i = rand(1:n)
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue
            (i in shielded) && continue
            b = pop.members[i].birth
            if best_idx == 0 || b < best_birth
                best_idx = i
                best_birth = b
            end
        end
    end

    # ---- Step 4a: sampling found nothing legal -> deterministic scan, shield still respected. ----
    if best_idx == 0
        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue
            (i in shielded) && continue
            b = pop.members[i].birth
            if best_idx == 0 || b < best_birth
                best_idx = i
                best_birth = b
            end
        end
    end

    # ---- Step 4b: every legal slot is shielded -> relax the shield, keep exclusion. ----
    if best_idx == 0
        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue
            b = pop.members[i].birth
            if best_idx == 0 || b < best_birth
                best_idx = i
                best_birth = b
            end
        end
    end

    # Guaranteed non-zero as long as at least one slot is not excluded.
    return best_idx
end

crowding_and_lineage_aware_quality_gated.name: crowding_and_lineage_aware_quality_gated_niche_tournament_gen23_0
crowding_and_lineage_aware_quality_gated.code:
"""
    crowding_and_lineage_aware_quality_gated_niche_tournament_gen23_0(
        pop, running_search_statistics, options
    )

Tournament selection that merges the simple, robust clone/sibling crowding
penalty of the "crowding_suppressed_niche_tournament" family with the sharper
phenotype/lineage distinction and adaptive, quality-gated niche exploration of
the "novelty_weighted_quality_gated_niche_tournament" family.

Core idea: build an enlarged tournament pool, penalize members that are
redundant copies (same complexity + essentially identical loss) much more
strongly than members that merely share ancestry (parent/child/sibling links)
but differ appreciably in phenotype, discount the cost of the freshest members
in proportion to how *uncrowded* they are (so fresh clones don't dodge
suppression while genuinely novel young structures get a turnover boost), and
adapt the probability of an explicit niche-repopulation move to how crowded the
sampled pool actually is. The niche move itself is quality-gated: it keeps the
best representative of each populated complexity band, restricts attention to
the better fraction of those representatives, and picks the rarest complexity
among them (falling back to a pool-wide rarest-frequency pick if no valid
representative exists), so an empty niche is filled with a *good* solution
rather than an arbitrarily bad one.

Steps:
 1. Sample a pool of size `~1.5 * tournament_selection_n` (bounded by
    population size) and compute the default frequency-adjusted cost per
    member.
 2. Sweep the pool from best to worst adjusted cost. For each member, compare
    against every better member:
      - Same complexity and near-identical loss (tight relative tolerance) ->
        strong "clone" weight (full unit).
      - Otherwise, if the pair is lineage-related (shared parent, or one is
        the other's recorded ref/parent) *and* their complexities differ by at
        most 1 and losses agree within a looser relative tolerance -> a
        fractional "lineage" weight. Shared ancestry alone, without phenotypic
        similarity, is not penalized.
    Sum these weights into a per-member `redundancy` score.
 3. Convert redundancy into a multiplicative, sign-safe cost inflation
    (`clone_penalty ^ redundancy`), and additionally give younger members a
    small cost discount that is *attenuated* by their own redundancy (so a
    brand-new clone is not rewarded for being new, while a brand-new distinct
    structure gets the full turnover incentive).
 4. Estimate pool crowding (fraction of members with nonzero redundancy) and
    use it to set an adaptive niche-exploration probability.
 5. With that probability, keep one best-penalized-score representative per
    populated complexity band, restrict to the better ~2/3 of those
    representatives by score, and return whichever of them sits in the
    rarest complexity niche (ties broken by score). If no valid representative
    exists (e.g. everything out of `[1, maxsize]`), fall back to the
    pool-wide rarest-frequency member.
 6. Otherwise, run the standard geometric tournament ladder over the
    penalized scores.

Heuristics/assumptions: equal complexity plus near-equal loss is a cheap proxy
for "same solution"; lineage relation alone is weak evidence of redundancy and
is only trusted when phenotype is also close; all adjustments are mild and
multiplicative so the operator degrades gracefully to the default tournament
when the pool shows no redundancy or niche starvation.
"""
function crowding_and_lineage_aware_quality_gated_niche_tournament_gen23_0(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # ---------------- tunables ----------------------------------------------
    pool_scale = 1.5             # pool size relative to tournament_selection_n
    clone_penalty = 1.35         # score inflation base per unit redundancy
    clone_loss_rtol = 1e-6       # tight tolerance for "same solution"
    lineage_weight = 0.3         # partial redundancy for related-but-different members
    lineage_loss_rtol = 1e-2     # loose tolerance for lineage relatedness
    youth_discount = 0.04        # max relative cost discount for freshest members
    niche_probability_base = 0.09
    niche_probability_boost = 0.10
    niche_probability_max = 0.18
    quality_fraction = 2 / 3     # fraction of niche champions eligible for the niche pick

    # ---------------- 1. sample the pool ------------------------------------
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        size = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = size
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if (0 < size <= options.maxsize)
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size])
            else
                zero(L)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 2. clone vs lineage crowding weights ------------------
    order = sortperm(scores)
    redundancy = zeros(Float64, n)
    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        scale_i = max(abs(li), eps(L))
        weight = 0.0
        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(scale_i, abs(lj))

            same_phenotype =
                complexities[i] == complexities[j] &&
                abs(li - lj) <= L(clone_loss_rtol) * loss_scale
            if same_phenotype
                # Near-identical solution: strong evidence of redundancy.
                weight += 1.0
                continue
            end

            parent_i = pool[i].parent
            parent_j = pool[j].parent
            related =
                (parent_i != 0 && parent_i == parent_j) ||
                (parent_i != 0 && parent_i == pool[j].ref) ||
                (parent_j != 0 && parent_j == pool[i].ref)

            # Shared ancestry only counts when the phenotype is also close.
            if related &&
                abs(complexities[i] - complexities[j]) <= 1 &&
                abs(li - lj) <= L(lineage_loss_rtol) * loss_scale
                weight += lineage_weight
            end
        end
        redundancy[i] = weight
    end

    # ---------------- 3. youth discount attenuated by novelty --------------
    birth_min = pool[1].birth
    birth_max = pool[1].birth
    for i in 2:n
        b = pool[i].birth
        b < birth_min && (birth_min = b)
        b > birth_max && (birth_max = b)
    end
    birth_span = max(birth_max - birth_min, 1)

    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    crowded_count = 0
    for i in 1:n
        r = redundancy[i]
        r > 0.0 && (crowded_count += 1)
        recency = (pool[i].birth - birth_min) / birth_span  # 0 old .. 1 new
        novelty_weight = 1.0 / (1.0 + r)  # fresh clones get little to no discount
        factor = (clone_penalty^r) * (1.0 - youth_discount * recency * novelty_weight)
        typed_factor = L(factor)
        # Sign-safe: factor > 1 always worsens score, factor < 1 always improves it.
        penalized[i] = if scores[i] > zero(L)
            scores[i] * typed_factor
        elseif scores[i] < zero(L)
            scores[i] / typed_factor
        else
            scores[i]
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 4. adaptive niche-exploration probability -------------
    crowded_fraction = crowded_count / n
    niche_probability = min(
        niche_probability_max,
        niche_probability_base + niche_probability_boost * crowded_fraction,
    )

    # ---------------- 5. quality-gated rare-niche pick -----------------------
    if rand() < niche_probability
        penalized_order = sortperm(penalized)
        seen_complexities = falses(options.maxsize)
        niche_champions = Int[]
        for i in penalized_order
            c = complexities[i]
            if 0 < c <= options.maxsize && !seen_complexities[c]
                seen_complexities[c] = true
                push!(niche_champions, i)
            end
        end

        if !isempty(niche_champions)
            # Restrict the niche search to the better fraction of representatives.
            quality_count = max(1, cld(length(niche_champions) * 2, 3))
            best_idx = niche_champions[1]
            best_freq = Float64(
                running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexities[best_idx]]
            )
            best_score = penalized[best_idx]
            for pos in 2:min(quality_count, length(niche_champions))
                i = niche_champions[pos]
                freq = Float64(
                    running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexities[i]]
                )
                if freq < best_freq || (freq == best_freq && penalized[i] < best_score)
                    best_idx = i
                    best_freq = freq
                    best_score = penalized[i]
                end
            end
            return pool[best_idx]
        else
            # Fallback: no valid complexity representative in range, so pick the
            # pool-wide rarest complexity, tie-broken by penalized score.
            best_idx = 1
            best_freq = Inf
            best_score = penalized[1]
            for i in 1:n
                c = complexities[i]
                f = if (0 < c <= options.maxsize)
                    Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
                else
                    0.0
                end
                if f < best_freq || (f == best_freq && penalized[i] < best_score)
                    best_freq = f
                    best_score = penalized[i]
                    best_idx = i
                end
            end
            return pool[best_idx]
        end
    end

    # ---------------- 6. standard geometric tournament ladder ---------------
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        k = collect(0:(n - 1))
        prob_each = p * ((1 - p) .^ k)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(prob_each, sum(prob_each))
        tournament_winner = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        if tournament_winner == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, tournament_winner)[2][end]
        end
    end
    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

algebraic_factor_distribute_mutation_gen.name: algebraic_factor_distribute_mutation_gen23_1
algebraic_factor_distribute_mutation_gen.code:
"""
    algebraic_factor_distribute_mutation_gen23_1(tree, options, nfeatures, rng)

A *semantics-preserving* structural rewrite that applies the distributive law in
either direction, plus two trivial like-term collapses.  The idea is that the
usual mutation set (point mutations, insert/delete op, rotate) changes the
*meaning* of the tree at almost every step, so the search can only cross fitness
plateaus by luck.  Algebraic refactoring instead moves the expression to a
different *syntactic representative of the same function*: the loss is unchanged
(so the move is always accepted-ish under the usual annealing criterion), but the
tree shape — and therefore the set of edits reachable by the next mutation —
changes completely.  Concretely, `a*b + a*c  <->  a*(b+c)` lets a shared
sub-expression be edited once (factored form) or specialised independently in the
two branches (distributed form), which is exactly the manoeuvre needed to grow
ground-truth expressions such as `x1*(x2 + sin(x3))` out of partially-correct
ancestors, and to *shrink* redundant duplicates so the parsimony pressure stops
killing otherwise-good candidates.

Steps: (1) locate the `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` operator indices (bail out if the
relevant ones are absent); (2) traverse the tree once, collecting two candidate
pools — *factoring* moves (`a*b ± a*c -> a*(b±c)` for any of the four operand
pairings found by exact structural matching, `a/d ± c/d -> (a±c)/d`,
`a - a -> 0`, `a + a -> 2*a`) and *distributing* moves (`a*(b±c) -> a*b ± a*c`,
`(b±c)/d -> b/d ± c/d`), where distribution is only proposed if the duplicated
factor keeps the tree within `options.maxsize`; (3) prefer a factoring move with
probability 0.75 when both pools are non-empty (factoring is a strict complexity
win, so we bias toward it), otherwise distribute; (4) rewrite the chosen node
in place with `set_node!`, using `copy` on every reused subtree so no aliasing or
cycles are introduced.

Assumptions: operators are identified by identity with the Julia functions `+`,
`-`, `*`, `/`; rewrites are exact over the reals except for the removable
singularity introduced/removed by common-denominator factoring, which the fitness
evaluation handles anyway.  If nothing matches, the tree is returned untouched.
"""
function algebraic_factor_distribute_mutation_gen23_1(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    tree.degree == 0 && return tree

    # --- locate the arithmetic operators we know how to rewrite -------------
    binops = options.operators.binops
    plus_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (+), binops)
    minus_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (-), binops)
    mul_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (*), binops)
    div_idx = findfirst(op -> op === (/), binops)

    # need at least one additive op and one multiplicative op
    (plus_idx === nothing && minus_idx === nothing) && return tree
    (mul_idx === nothing && div_idx === nothing) && return tree

    # --- exact structural equality of two subtrees --------------------------
    function nodes_equal(a::N, b::N)
        a.degree == b.degree || return false
        if a.degree == 0
            a.constant == b.constant || return false
            return a.constant ? (a.val == b.val) : (a.feature == b.feature)
        end
        a.op == b.op || return false
        for i in 1:(a.degree)
            nodes_equal(get_child(a, i), get_child(b, i)) || return false
        end
        return true
    end

    # `t.op == nothing` is simply `false`, so missing operators are safe here
    is_addsub(t) = t.degree == 2 && (t.op == plus_idx || t.op == minus_idx)

    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : 30
    total_size = count_nodes(tree)

    # Each move is (kind, node, aux1, aux2)
    factor_moves = Any[]
    dist_moves = Any[]

    # --- single traversal collecting all applicable rewrites ---------------
    any(tree) do t
        if is_addsub(t)
            c1 = get_child(t, 1)
            c2 = get_child(t, 2)

            # like terms:  a - a -> 0   and   a + a -> 2*a
            if nodes_equal(c1, c2)
                if t.op == minus_idx
                    push!(factor_moves, (:zero, t, 0, 0))
                elseif mul_idx !== nothing
                    push!(factor_moves, (:double, t, 0, 0))
                end
            end

            # a*b ± a*c -> a*(b±c); try all four operand pairings
            if mul_idx !== nothing &&
                c1.degree == 2 && c1.op == mul_idx &&
                c2.degree == 2 && c2.op == mul_idx
                for i in 1:2, j in 1:2
                    if nodes_equal(get_child(c1, i), get_child(c2, j))
                        push!(factor_moves, (:factor_mul, t, i, j))
                    end
                end
            end

            # b/d ± c/d -> (b±c)/d  (common denominator)
            if div_idx !== nothing &&
                c1.degree == 2 && c1.op == div_idx &&
                c2.degree == 2 && c2.op == div_idx &&
                nodes_equal(get_child(c1, 2), get_child(c2, 2))
                push!(factor_moves, (:factor_div, t, 0, 0))
            end
        end

        # a*(b±c) -> a*b ± a*c   (duplicates `a`, so respect maxsize)
        if t.degree == 2 && mul_idx !== nothing && t.op == mul_idx
            for k in 1:2
                s = get_child(t, k)
                a = get_child(t, 3 - k)
                if is_addsub(s) && total_size + count_nodes(a) + 1 <= maxsize
                    push!(dist_moves, (:dist_mul, t, k, 0))
                end
            end
        end

        # (b±c)/d -> b/d ± c/d   (duplicates the denominator)
        if t.degree == 2 && div_idx !== nothing && t.op == div_idx
            s = get_child(t, 1)
            d = get_child(t, 2)
            if is_addsub(s) && total_size + count_nodes(d) + 1 <= maxsize
                push!(dist_moves, (:dist_div, t, 0, 0))
            end
        end
        return false  # keep traversing the whole tree
    end

    (isempty(factor_moves) && isempty(dist_moves)) && return tree

    # Bias toward factoring: it never hurts the loss and reduces complexity.
    use_factor = !isempty(factor_moves) && (isempty(dist_moves) || rand(rng) < 0.75)
    kind, node, aux1, aux2 = use_factor ? rand(rng, factor_moves) : rand(rng, dist_moves)

    # --- apply the chosen rewrite in place --------------------------------
    if kind == :zero
        # a - a  ->  0
        set_node!(node, constructorof(N)(T; val=zero(T)))

    elseif kind == :double
        # a + a  ->  2 * a
        child = copy(get_child(node, 1))
        set_node!(
            node,
            constructorof(N)(;
                op=mul_idx, children=(constructorof(N)(T; val=T(2)), child)
            ),
        )

    elseif kind == :factor_mul
        # (…*shared…) ± (…*shared…)  ->  shared * (rest1 ± rest2)
        c1 = get_child(node, 1)
        c2 = get_child(node, 2)
        addsub_op = node.op
        shared = copy(get_child(c1, aux1))
        rest1 = copy(get_child(c1, 3 - aux1))
        rest2 = copy(get_child(c2, 3 - aux2))
        inner = constructorof(N)(; op=addsub_op, children=(rest1, rest2))
        set_node!(node, constructorof(N)(; op=mul_idx, children=(shared, inner)))

    elseif kind == :factor_div
        # b/d ± c/d  ->  (b ± c)/d
        c1 = get_child(node, 1)
        c2 = get_child(node, 2)
        addsub_op = node.op
        num1 = copy(get_child(c1, 1))
        num2 = copy(get_child(c2, 1))
        den = copy(get_child(c1, 2))
        inner = constructorof(N)(; op=addsub_op, children=(num1, num2))
        set_node!(node, constructorof(N)(; op=div_idx, children=(inner, den)))

    elseif kind == :dist_mul
        # a*(b±c) -> (a*b) ± (a*c), preserving the original operand ordering
        k = aux1
        s = get_child(node, k)
        a = get_child(node, 3 - k)
        inner_op = s.op
        b = copy(get_child(s, 1))
        c = copy(get_child(s, 2))
        if k == 2  # sum was on the right: a*(b±c)
            t1 = constructorof(N)(; op=mul_idx, children=(copy(a), b))
            t2 = constructorof(N)(; op=mul_idx, children=(copy(a), c))
        else       # sum was on the left: (b±c)*a
            t1 = constructorof(N)(; op=mul_idx, children=(b, copy(a)))
            t2 = constructorof(N)(; op=mul_idx, children=(c, copy(a)))
        end
        set_node!(node, constructorof(N)(; op=inner_op, children=(t1, t2)))

    else  # :dist_div
        # (b±c)/d -> (b/d) ± (c/d)
        s = get_child(node, 1)
        d = get_child(node, 2)
        inner_op = s.op
        b = copy(get_child(s, 1))
        c = copy(get_child(s, 2))
        t1 = constructorof(N)(; op=div_idx, children=(b, copy(d)))
        t2 = constructorof(N)(; op=div_idx, children=(c, copy(d)))
        set_node!(node, constructorof(N)(; op=inner_op, children=(t1, t2)))
    end

    # `set_node!` rewrites contents in place, so the root object is unchanged.
    return tree
end

pareto_crowding_age_regularized_survival.name: pareto_crowding_age_regularized_survival_gen23_gen23_2
pareto_crowding_age_regularized_survival.code:
"""
    pareto_crowding_age_regularized_survival_gen23_gen23_2(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

Synthesis of pure age-regularized replacement (parent 2) with Pareto/clone-aware
tie-breaking inside the oldest slice of the population (parent 1), plus a new
*global bloat-clone purge* and a *complexity-niche crowding* term.

Motivation from observed searches
--------------------------------
Pareto fronts in long runs (e.g. `feynman_II_13_23`) fill up with dozens of
structurally different but numerically near-identical expressions that differ
only by cosmetic bloat (`x/x` factors, `+0.003` constants, re-associated terms).
Those members consume population slots and tournament probability mass without
adding search information, and the useful, sparsely-populated complexity niches
(the low-complexity "skeletons" that could still be refined into the true
formula) get starved. Pure age replacement (parent 2) cannot see this; parent 1
can, but only inside the oldest 25% window, so a freshly-born exact copy of a
bloated incumbent survives for a long time.

Core idea
---------
Split the decision into two levels of confidence:

* **Level A (global, unconditional):** members that carry *no* information are
  removable anywhere in the population, regardless of age — broken members
  (NaN/Inf loss) and *bloat clones* (some other member attains the same loss to
  a relative tolerance of 1e-8 while being no more complex). Removing these can
  never lose front coverage, so age pressure is safely bypassed. Oldest such
  member wins (age is still the tie-break).
* **Level B (age-windowed, as in parent 1):** if nothing is redundant, restrict
  attention to the oldest ~25% of candidates and prefer, in order,
  Pareto-dominated members from *crowded* complexity niches, then dominated
  members that are the sole occupant of their niche, then non-dominated members.
  Within a rank, the more crowded complexity niche is culled first and ties go
  to the oldest candidate — so with a fully non-dominated, uncrowded window the
  operator reduces *exactly* to parent 2 (replace the oldest).

Steps
-----
1. Build candidate list honouring `exclude_indices`; sort oldest-first.
2. Precompute complexity, sanitized loss, and the current best-cost (elite)
   index; elite is protected unless it is the only available candidate.
3. Count occupancy of each complexity value (the "niche crowding" signal).
4. Level A scan over *all* candidates (oldest-first): return the first broken
   member; else the first bloat clone.
5. Level B scan over the oldest `max(2, ceil(len/4))` candidates: rank
   0 = dominated & crowded niche, 1 = dominated & unique niche,
   2 = non-dominated; tie-break by (−niche occupancy, age).
6. Fallback: the oldest candidate (parent-2 behaviour).

Heuristics / assumptions
------------------------
* Loss equality uses `rtol=1e-8` (with a tiny absolute floor) — tight enough
  that genuinely distinct fits are not confused, loose enough to catch
  constant-optimized re-parameterizations of the same function.
* "No more complex and same loss" implies redundancy; the keeper is the simpler
  member, or (at equal complexity) the older / lower-indexed one, which makes
  the relation antisymmetric so at least one copy always survives.
* Cost is O(n) plus O(n·n) cheap comparisons with n = population size (tens),
  negligible next to offspring loss evaluations.
"""
function pareto_crowding_age_regularized_survival_gen23_gen23_2(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    members = pop.members

    # ---- candidate set: every index not excluded ---------------------------
    candidates = Int[]
    for i in 1:n
        if !(i in exclude_indices)
            push!(candidates, i)
        end
    end
    isempty(candidates) && return 1                     # degenerate safety net
    length(candidates) == 1 && return candidates[1]

    # ---- age ordering: oldest first (age stays the tie-break everywhere) ---
    sort!(candidates; by = i -> (members[i].birth, i))

    # ---- precompute complexity / loss / elite ------------------------------
    comps = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    elite_idx = 0
    elite_cost = Inf
    for i in 1:n
        comps[i] = compute_complexity(members[i], options)
        l = Float64(members[i].loss)
        losses[i] = isnan(l) ? Inf : l                  # NaN treated as worst
        c = Float64(members[i].cost)
        c = isnan(c) ? Inf : c
        if c < elite_cost                               # best-cost member
            elite_cost = c
            elite_idx = i
        end
    end

    # ---- complexity-niche occupancy (crowding signal) ---------------------
    maxc = 0
    for i in 1:n
        maxc = max(maxc, comps[i])
    end
    niche = zeros(Int, maxc + 1)                        # index by comps[i] + 1
    for i in 1:n
        niche[comps[i] + 1] += 1
    end

    # Same loss (to relative tolerance) with no extra complexity => redundant.
    # Antisymmetric: keeper is the simpler member, else the older/lower index.
    is_bloat_clone = function (i::Int)
        li = losses[i]
        isfinite(li) || return false
        ci = comps[i]
        for j in 1:n
            j == i && continue
            lj = losses[j]
            isfinite(lj) || continue                    # broken members keep nothing alive
            comps[j] <= ci || continue
            if isapprox(li, lj; rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-14)
