    denom = varp * vary
    S = if denom > zero(L)
        # clamp guards against tiny negative values from catastrophic cancellation
        max(one(L) - (covpy * covpy) / denom, zero(L))
    else
        one(L)  # constant prediction (or constant target): no exploitable shape
    end

    loss = E * (one(L) + S)
    return isfinite(loss) ? loss : L(Inf)
end

pareto_progress_niche_selection_gen24_5.name: pareto_progress_niche_selection_gen24_5
pareto_progress_niche_selection_gen24_5.code:
"""
    pareto_progress_niche_selection_gen24_5(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Select a parent using a randomized mixture of three complementary search tempos:
cost exploitation, loss-complexity Pareto progress, and exploratory niche selection.
A bounded tournament is sampled, after which candidates are ranked by penalized cost,
raw loss, Pareto domination, improvement over simpler candidates, complexity-bin
occupancy, lineage crowding, and age. The exploratory tempo favors recent descendants
from uncommon lineages and underrepresented complexity sizes, while the frontier tempo
rewards expressions whose additional complexity produces measurable loss improvement.
Finally, geometric rank selection applies `tournament_selection_p`, retaining controlled
selection noise. The heuristic assumes productive ground-truth expressions usually lie
near a loss-complexity frontier, while occasional niche and youth protection prevents
premature concentration around a single complexity or lineage.
"""
function pareto_progress_niche_selection_gen24_5(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Population selection is undefined for an empty population; normal search
    # operation guarantees at least one member.
    available = min(pop.n, length(pop.members))
    tournament_size = min(max(1, options.tournament_selection_n), available)
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, tournament_size; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)

    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    occupancies = zeros(Float64, n)

    for i in 1:n
        raw_loss = Float64(sample[i].loss)
        raw_cost = Float64(sample[i].cost)

        # Invalid candidates remain selectable only if the tournament has no
        # finite alternatives.
        losses[i] = isfinite(raw_loss) ? raw_loss : Inf
        costs[i] = isfinite(raw_cost) ? raw_cost : Inf
        complexities[i] = compute_complexity(sample[i], options)

        size = complexities[i]
        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament &&
           1 <= size <= options.maxsize &&
           size <= length(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies)
            frequency = Float64(
                running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[size],
            )
            occupancies[i] = isfinite(frequency) ? max(0.0, frequency) : 0.0
        end
    end

    # Compare occupancy relatively within this tournament so the signal remains
    # useful even when global frequency magnitudes drift during the search.
    max_occupancy = maximum(occupancies)
    frequency_pressure = if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
        clamp(Float64(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling) / 20.0, 0.0, 2.0)
    else
        0.0
    end
    if max_occupancy > 0.0
        occupancies .*= frequency_pressure / max_occupancy
    else
        fill!(occupancies, 0.0)
    end

    denominator = Float64(max(n - 1, 1))
    cost_ranks = zeros(Float64, n)
    loss_ranks = zeros(Float64, n)
    domination = zeros(Float64, n)
    progress_penalty = zeros(Float64, n)
    lineage_crowding = zeros(Float64, n)
    age_penalty = zeros(Float64, n)

    for i in 1:n
        simpler_count = 0
        simpler_beaten = 0

        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue

            cost_ranks[i] += costs[j] < costs[i]
            loss_ranks[i] += losses[j] < losses[i]

            # Number of sampled candidates that Pareto-dominate this candidate
            # in the raw-loss/complexity plane.
            if complexities[j] <= complexities[i] &&
               losses[j] <= losses[i] &&
               (complexities[j] < complexities[i] || losses[j] < losses[i])
                domination[i] += 1.0
            end

            # Added complexity is justified when it improves upon simpler
            # expressions sampled in the same tournament.
            if complexities[j] < complexities[i]
                simpler_count += 1
                simpler_beaten += losses[i] < losses[j]
            end

            # Protect against a successful parent monopolizing reproduction.
            if sample[i].parent > 0 && sample[j].parent == sample[i].parent
                lineage_crowding[i] += 1.0
            end

            # Larger birth values are newer; old candidates receive a small
            # penalty only in the exploratory tempo.
            age_penalty[i] += sample[j].birth > sample[i].birth
        end

        cost_ranks[i] /= denominator
        loss_ranks[i] /= denominator
        domination[i] /= denominator
        lineage_crowding[i] /= denominator
        age_penalty[i] /= denominator

        progress_penalty[i] = if simpler_count == 0
            0.0
        else
            1.0 - Float64(simpler_beaten) / Float64(simpler_count)
        end
    end

    # Randomly alternate between exploitation, frontier advancement, and
    # diversity recovery rather than forcing one pressure throughout a run.
    mode = StatsBase.sample(StatsBase.Weights([0.55, 0.30, 0.15], 1.0))
    scores = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)

    for i in 1:n
        scores[i] = if mode == 1
            # Conventional exploitation, softened by Pareto and occupancy terms.
            0.55 * cost_ranks[i] +
            0.25 * loss_ranks[i] +
            0.15 * domination[i] +
            0.05 * occupancies[i]
        elseif mode == 2
            # Seek frontier expressions whose complexity pays for itself.
            0.35 * domination[i] +
            0.25 * progress_penalty[i] +
            0.20 * cost_ranks[i] +
            0.10 * loss_ranks[i] +
            0.10 * occupancies[i]
        else
            # Scout viable but underrepresented complexity and lineage niches,
            # with mild protection for newly created genetic material.
            0.30 * domination[i] +
            0.20 * loss_ranks[i] +
            0.25 * occupancies[i] +
            0.15 * lineage_crowding[i] +
            0.10 * age_penalty[i]
        end
    end

    # Respect PySR's tournament stochasticity using a truncated geometric rank
    # distribution over the composite scores.
    p_raw = Float64(options.tournament_selection_p)
    p = isfinite(p_raw) ? clamp(p_raw, 0.0, 1.0) : 1.0

    chosen_idx = if n == 1 || p >= 1.0
        argmin_fast(scores)
    elseif p <= 0.0
        rank = StatsBase.sample(StatsBase.Weights(fill(1.0, n), Float64(n)))
        bottomk_fast(scores, rank)[2][end]
    else
        rank_weights = [p * (1.0 - p)^(rank - 1) for rank in 1:n]
        rank = StatsBase.sample(
            StatsBase.Weights(rank_weights, sum(rank_weights)),
        )
        bottomk_fast(scores, rank)[2][end]
    end

    return sample[chosen_idx]
end

simplified_affine_relative_loss_gen24_7.name: simplified_affine_relative_loss_gen24_7
simplified_affine_relative_loss_gen24_7.code:
"""
    simplified_affine_relative_loss_gen24_7(tree, dataset, options)

A streamlined affine-shape loss that grades expressions by how well their optimal
linear calibration `a * prediction + b` matches the target under scale-damped relative
weighting, combined with a bounded raw-error tie-breaker.

Core Idea & Simplification Rationale
------------------------------------
The parent operator (`affine_shape_relative_uniformity_loss_gen12_5`) prioritized
functional shape while penalizing Padé-style rational surrogates on small targets by
combining four distinct metrics (absolute affine NMSE, damped relative affine MSE, peak
relative error, and raw NMSE) accumulated via multiple Kahan-compensated loops with
branching fallbacks.

This simplified operator preserves the same core search dynamics with lower complexity:
1. **Merged Shape & Relative Metrics**: Instead of tracking separate absolute affine RMSE
   and relative affine RMSE terms with multiple heuristic weights, this operator computes
   a single scale-damped relative RMSE of the affine-calibrated fit:
   `(a * prediction + b - y) / (|y| + damping)`.
   The damped denominator smoothly interpolates between absolute error (when `|y|` is small)
   and relative error (when `|y|` is large), capturing both overall profile alignment and
   uniform domain fidelity in a single term.
2. **Dropped Peak Error Heuristic**: Eliminates the noisy worst-case relative error tracking
   (`max_rel_sq`), reducing sensitivity to isolated boundary points and removing squashing logic.
3. **Removed Kahan Summation Overhead**: Standard accumulation provides ample precision for
   typical symbolic regression sample sizes while eliminating accumulator variables and
   branching overhead.
4. **Unified Control Flow**: Constant targets and constant predictions are handled via a
   single consistent mathematical path without duplicating residual loops.
"""
function simplified_affine_relative_loss_gen24_7(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    eps_l = eps(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Pass 1: Welford accumulation for means, variances, and covariance.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    target_std = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)

    # Determine affine calibration parameters (slope a, intercept b).
    # If prediction or target is constant, the fit safely falls back to mean(y).
    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if m2_p > eps_l && m2_y > eps_l
        slope = cov_py / m2_p
        intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
        if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
            slope = zero_l
            intercept = mean_y
        end
    end

    # Relative error damping floor prevents zero-division and balances small vs large targets.
    damping = max(target_std * L(0.1), sqrt(eps_l))

    # Scale for raw calibration error normalization.
    raw_scale = target_std > eps_l ? target_std : max(abs(mean_y), one_l)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Pass 2: Calibrated relative residual and raw residual sums of squares.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    sum_rel_sq = zero_l
    sum_raw_sq = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        fitted = muladd(slope, p, intercept)
        rel_residual = (fitted - y) / (abs(y) + damping)
        raw_residual = (p - y) / raw_scale

        sum_rel_sq += rel_residual * rel_residual
        sum_raw_sq += raw_residual * raw_residual
    end

    if !(isfinite(sum_rel_sq) && isfinite(sum_raw_sq))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Damped-relative affine RMSE captures both profile shape and uniform domain accuracy.
    rel_rmse = sqrt(max(sum_rel_sq / n_l, zero_l))

    # Bounded raw calibration error acts as a modest tie-breaker for properly tuned constants.
    raw_rmse = sqrt(max(sum_raw_sq / n_l, zero_l))
    bounded_raw = raw_rmse / (one_l + raw_rmse)

    # Primary signal is affine relative shape; small tie-breaker prefers correct scale/offset.
    loss_val = rel_rmse + L(0.005) * bounded_raw

    return isfinite(loss_val) ? L(max(loss_val, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

pareto_crowding_age_survival_gen24_8.name: pareto_crowding_age_survival_gen24_8
pareto_crowding_age_survival_gen24_8.code:
"""
    pareto_crowding_age_survival_gen24_8(pop::Population{T,L,N}, options::AbstractOptions; exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[])::Int where {T,L,N}

A multi-objective, niche-aware survival operator for symbolic regression that balances
age-based exploration (regularized evolution), Pareto optimality preservation, and
complexity-space diversity.

# Core Idea:
Standard age-regularized evolution replaces the oldest individual unconditionally,
which risks discarding critical Pareto-optimal expressions (or non-dominated trade-offs)
before they can be exploited. Conversely, purely fitness-based replacement leads to
premature convergence and complexity bloat clusters.

`pareto_crowding_age_survival_gen24_8` computes a composite **Replacement Priority Score** for each
candidate individual:
1. **Pareto Protection**: Individuals on the current empirical Pareto frontier (non-dominated
   in raw loss vs. expression complexity) receive a substantial survival shield to prevent
   accidental loss of frontier solutions.
2. **Niche Crowding Pressure**: Complexity niches with many redundant individuals suffer
   elevated replacement pressure, encouraging the population to disperse across diverse
   complexity levels and preventing bloat bottlenecks.
3. **Domination & Sub-optimality Penalty**: Individuals strictly dominated either within
   their complexity niche or by simpler expressions are prioritized for replacement.
4. **Age Regularization**: Normalized age provides the continuous baseline churn of
   regularized evolution. If the entire population is Pareto-optimal, the operator seamlessly
   degenerates to classical age-based FIFO replacement.

# Steps:
1. Filter out candidate indices specified in `exclude_indices`.
2. Extract the raw loss, complexity, and birth order for all valid population members.
3. Compute the empirical Pareto frontier across the (loss, complexity) trade-off surface.
4. Compute complexity niche counts to measure crowding density.
5. Calculate the replacement priority score for each valid member combining age, crowding,
   domination penalties, and Pareto immunity.
6. Return the index of the individual with the highest replacement score (breaking ties
   by oldest birth order).

# Heuristics & Assumptions:
- `member.loss` is the true objective to trade off against `compute_complexity(member, options)`.
- Non-finite losses (NaN/Inf) are assigned maximum replacement priority.
- Respects `exclude_indices` for multi-offspring replacements (e.g., crossover).
"""
function pareto_crowding_age_survival_gen24_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T,L,N}
    n = pop.n
    n == 0 && return 1

    # Identify eligible candidate indices
    valid_indices = Int[]
    sizehint!(valid_indices, n)
    for i in 1:n
        if !(i in exclude_indices)
            push!(valid_indices, i)
        end
    end

    # Fallback if all candidates are excluded
    if isempty(valid_indices)
        return (n in exclude_indices) ? 1 : n
    end

    # Fast path: single candidate
    length(valid_indices) == 1 && return valid_indices[1]

    # Pre-extract attributes for valid members
    num_valid = length(valid_indices)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, num_valid)
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, num_valid)
    births = Vector{Int}(undef, num_valid)
    is_valid_loss = Vector{Bool}(undef, num_valid)

    min_birth = typemax(Int)
    max_birth = typemin(Int)
    max_c = 0

    for (k, idx) in enumerate(valid_indices)
        m = pop.members[idx]
        c = compute_complexity(m, options)
        b = Int(m.birth)
        l_val = Float64(m.loss)

        complexities[k] = c
        births[k] = b
        max_c = max(max_c, c)

        min_birth = min(min_birth, b)
        max_birth = max(max_birth, b)

        if isnan(l_val) || isinf(l_val)
            losses[k] = Inf
            is_valid_loss[k] = false
        else
            losses[k] = l_val
            is_valid_loss[k] = true
        end
    end

    # Compute niche counts and minimum loss per complexity bin
    min_loss_at_c = fill(Inf, max_c + 1)
    count_at_c = zeros(Int, max_c + 1)

    for k in 1:num_valid
        c = complexities[k]
        count_at_c[c + 1] += 1
        if is_valid_loss[k] && losses[k] < min_loss_at_c[c + 1]
            min_loss_at_c[c + 1] = losses[k]
        end
    end

    # Compute Pareto prefix minimum loss: min loss achievable at complexity <= c
    pareto_prefix_min = fill(Inf, max_c + 1)
    current_min = Inf
    for c in 0:max_c
        if min_loss_at_c[c + 1] < current_min
            current_min = min_loss_at_c[c + 1]
        end
        pareto_prefix_min[c + 1] = current_min
    end

    # Evaluate Replacement Priority Score for each candidate
    # Higher score = higher priority to be culled / replaced
    best_replace_idx = valid_indices[1]
    highest_score = -Inf
    oldest_birth_for_tie = typemax(Int)

    birth_range = max(1, max_birth - min_birth)

    for (k, idx) in enumerate(valid_indices)
        # Immediate maximum replacement priority for invalid loss
        if !is_valid_loss[k]
            return idx
        end

        l = losses[k]
        c = complexities[k]
        b = births[k]

        # 1. Normalized Age component: older members receive higher score in [0.0, 1.0]
        norm_age = Float64(max_birth - b) / Float64(birth_range)

        # 2. Complexity Niche Crowding component: penalties for overpopulated bins
        # Ratio of extra members in this complexity bin relative to population size
        niche_excess = max(0, count_at_c[c + 1] - 1)
        crowding_score = Float64(niche_excess) / Float64(n)

        # 3. Pareto Optimality and Domination assessment
        is_niche_best = (l <= min_loss_at_c[c + 1])
        is_pareto_optimal = (l <= pareto_prefix_min[c + 1])

        domination_penalty = 0.0
        pareto_shield = 0.0

        if is_pareto_optimal
            # Strong survival protection for Pareto-optimal trade-offs
            pareto_shield = 2.0
        elseif is_niche_best
            # Best in its complexity class, but dominated by a simpler model
            domination_penalty = 0.4
        else
            # Dominated even within its own complexity class (redundant/inferior)
            domination_penalty = 0.9
        end

        # Composite Replacement Score
        score = (1.0 * norm_age) + (1.2 * crowding_score) + domination_penalty - pareto_shield

        # Find maximum score, breaking ties by oldest birth order
        if score > highest_score || (score == highest_score && b < oldest_birth_for_tie)
            highest_score = score
            oldest_birth_for_tie = b
            best_replace_idx = idx
        end
    end

    return best_replace_idx
end

affine_shape_logcalib_loss_gen9_gen24_9.name: affine_shape_logcalib_loss_gen9_gen24_9
affine_shape_logcalib_loss_gen9_gen24_9.code:
"""
    affine_shape_logcalib_loss_gen9_gen24_9(tree, dataset, options)

Two-pass, affine-invariant "shape first, calibration second" loss.

Core idea (kept from the parent):
  1. Pass 1 accumulates numerically stable Welford moments of the prediction `p`
     and target `y` (means, centered second moments, covariance) plus the maximum
     absolute magnitudes used for scale-relative variability tests.
  2. The best affine calibration `a*p + b` is obtained in closed form from those
     moments, and pass 2 evaluates the *fitted* residuals directly. Evaluating
     residuals rather than forming `var(y) - cov^2/var(p)` avoids catastrophic
     cancellation exactly where it matters most: when the candidate is a
     structural match up to scale/offset.
  3. The primary loss term is the affine-residual RMSE normalized by the target
     standard deviation (i.e. `sqrt(1 - R^2)`), which is invariant to badly tuned
     multiplicative/additive constants and therefore lets correct *structures*
     survive before their constants are optimized. A small bounded term built
     from the *raw* (uncalibrated) error is added so that, among affine-equivalent
     candidates, only the properly calibrated one reaches zero loss.

What changed versus the parent:
  * The calibration tie-breaker is now **log-compressed** before squashing:
    `t = log1p(raw_nmse)`, `calib = t / (1 + t)`. The parent's `x/(1+x)` map
    saturated almost immediately (raw NMSE 4 -> 0.80, 100 -> 0.99), so constant
    optimization received essentially no gradient once the constants were more
    than a little off. The log-compressed map spreads many orders of magnitude
    of raw error over the bounded range, giving a usable monotone signal for
    constant tuning while still remaining bounded (it can never dominate shape).
  * Both the affine NMSE and the raw NMSE are snapped to zero below an explicit
    `O(n * eps)` accumulation-noise floor, so genuinely exact structure attains a
    hard zero instead of comparing floating-point dust, and exact expressions are
    separated from near-misses only by real (above-noise) differences.
  * The constant-target fallback now uses the same bounded log map, keeping the
    returned loss in the same `[0, 1 + w]` range for every branch (helps PySR's
    `:log` score scaling behave uniformly).
  * Minor hardening: the raw accumulator overflow flag also covers non-finite
    Kahan corrections, the affine slope is only used when the prediction is
    genuinely variable, and all early exits return `L(Inf)`.

No expression-complexity term is included; parsimony is handled by PySR.
"""
function affine_shape_logcalib_loss_gen9_gen24_9(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Pass 1: stable moments for the affine least-squares coefficients.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        # Covariance update uses the freshly updated target mean (standard Welford).
        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Welford sums can be microscopically negative after roundoff.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    # Scale-relative variability tests (meaningful even for tiny datasets).
    relative_tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))
    target_rms = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    prediction_rms = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)
    target_is_variable = target_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_y
    prediction_is_variable = prediction_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_p

    # Accumulation-noise floor: normalized squared sums cannot be resolved below
    # roughly n * eps, so anything smaller is treated as exact.
    noise_floor = L(4) * n_l * eps(L)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Degenerate branch: constant target => affine shape is undefined.
    # Fall back on scale-normalized raw error, mapped through the same
    # bounded log squash so all branches share one output range.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    if !target_is_variable
        target_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_y)
        raw_sum = zero_l
        raw_compensation = zero_l

        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            p = L(prediction[i])
            y = L(dataset.y[i])
            residual = p - y
            if !isfinite(residual)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            # Divide before squaring so huge targets cannot overflow.
            normalized_residual = residual / target_scale
            term = normalized_residual * normalized_residual
            if !isfinite(term)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            corrected = term - raw_compensation
            updated = raw_sum + corrected
            if !isfinite(updated)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            raw_compensation = (updated - raw_sum) - corrected
            raw_sum = updated
        end

        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum / n_l, zero_l)
        raw_nmse = raw_nmse <= noise_floor ? zero_l : raw_nmse
        t = log1p(raw_nmse)
        loss_value = t / (one_l + t)
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
    end

    target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)
    if !(isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Closed-form affine calibration. A constant prediction can only fit the mean.
    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if prediction_is_variable
        slope = cov_py / m2_p
        intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
        if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Pass 2: evaluate fitted (affine) and raw residuals directly. Both sums
    # are normalized by the target's total centered norm, so they are the
    # standard NMSE-style quantities `sum(r^2) / sum((y - mean_y)^2)`.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    affine_sum = zero_l
    affine_compensation = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l
    raw_compensation = zero_l
    raw_overflowed = false

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_residual = p - y
        if !isfinite(raw_residual)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Raw error only acts as a bounded tie-breaker: overflow just saturates it.
        if !raw_overflowed
            raw_normalized = raw_residual / target_norm
            raw_term = raw_normalized * raw_normalized
            if isfinite(raw_term)
                corrected = raw_term - raw_compensation
                updated = raw_sum + corrected
                if isfinite(updated) && isfinite(corrected)
                    raw_compensation = (updated - raw_sum) - corrected
                    raw_sum = updated
                else
                    raw_overflowed = true
                end
            else
                raw_overflowed = true
            end
        end

        fitted = prediction_is_variable ? muladd(slope, p, intercept) : mean_y
        affine_residual = fitted - y
        affine_normalized = affine_residual / target_norm
        affine_term = affine_normalized * affine_normalized

        if !(isfinite(fitted) && isfinite(affine_residual) &&
             isfinite(affine_normalized) && isfinite(affine_term))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Kahan compensation matters here: near a structural match the affine
        # residuals are tiny and must not be swamped by summation error.
        corrected = affine_term - affine_compensation
        updated = affine_sum + corrected
        if !isfinite(updated)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        affine_compensation = (updated - affine_sum) - corrected
        affine_sum = updated
    end

    # The affine optimum can never be worse than predicting the target mean.
    affine_nmse = clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l)
    # Snap sub-noise values so exact structure gets a hard zero shape term.
    affine_nmse = affine_nmse <= noise_floor ? zero_l : affine_nmse
    shape_term = sqrt(affine_nmse)   # in [0, 1]; infinite slope at 0 pushes to exactness

    # Bounded, log-compressed calibration term in [0, 1). log1p keeps the map
    # ~identity for tiny errors (so exact predictions reach zero) while spreading
    # many orders of magnitude of raw error before saturating.
    bounded_calibration = if raw_overflowed
        one_l
    else
        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum, zero_l)
        raw_nmse = raw_nmse <= noise_floor ? zero_l : raw_nmse
        t = log1p(raw_nmse)
        isfinite(t) ? t / (one_l + t) : one_l
    end

    # Shape dominates; calibration only resolves affine-equivalent candidates.
    calibration_weight = one_l / L(256)
    loss_value = shape_term + calibration_weight * bounded_calibration

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

simplified_symmetric_motif_duplication_g.name: simplified_symmetric_motif_duplication_gen25_2
simplified_symmetric_motif_duplication_g.code:
"""
    simplified_symmetric_motif_duplication_gen25_2(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

A streamlined structural mutation operator that duplicates an existing subexpression motif,
optionally shifts its variable indices across dimensions, and couples it with a target node
using a binary operator (biased toward `+` and `*`).

# Core Idea
Symmetric structures and repeated functional motifs (e.g., `x1^2 + x2^2`, `a*b + c*d`, `u*u`)
are pervasive in physical and mathematical laws. Rather than rediscovering identical or shifted
subexpressions from scratch, this operator clones an existing subtree, applies a cyclic variable
shift to reflect coordinate/variable symmetry, and joins it into the tree via a binary operator.

# Steps
1. Compute the available node budget (`options.maxsize - count_nodes(tree) - 1`). If no binary
   operators exist or the budget is less than 1, return the tree unchanged.
2. Select a donor motif that fits the budget, prioritizing non-constant subtrees.
3. Sample a target node to couple with.
4. Clone the donor motif and uniformly apply a variable shift `shift ∈ 0:(nfeatures-1)`. When
   `shift == 0`, this performs an exact duplication (enabling self-interactions like `u*u`);
   when `shift > 0`, it rotates feature indices across dimensions.
5. Couple the target node and the transformed motif with a binary operator (biased toward `+` or `*`),
   randomizing child order to support non-commutative operators.

# Simplifications from Parent (`symmetric_motif_duplication_gen10_1_gen11_9`)
- **Unified Feature Remapping:** Replaced the three separate remapping modes (cyclic shift,
  targeted single-variable substitution with array allocations, and special-cased identity maps)
  with a single uniform shift `shift ∈ 0:(nfeatures-1)`. This covers both exact duplication
  (identity) and symmetry across dimensions in a single unified path without helper allocations.
- **Streamlined Donor Selection:** Removed the 3-tiered counting passes and multi-stage branch
  logic in favor of a single predicate filter that prioritizes meaningful (non-constant) subtrees
  fitting the size budget.
- **Concise Operator Selection:** Compacted the accumulator bias search for `+` and `*` into a
  concise lookup without manual buffer accumulation.
"""
function simplified_symmetric_motif_duplication_gen25_2(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Coupling requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # Enforce size budget to ensure the resulting tree fits within options.maxsize
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    budget = maxsize - tree_size - 1
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # Helper: cyclically shift variable indices in place
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int, nfeats::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeats)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift, nfeats)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Step 1: Select donor motif that fits budget, preferring non-constant subtrees
    valid_donor(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget
    meaningful_donor(t) = valid_donor(t) && (!t.constant || t.degree > 0)
    donor_filter = any(meaningful_donor, tree) ? meaningful_donor : valid_donor
    !any(donor_filter, tree) && return tree

    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=donor_filter))
    motif = copy(donor)

    # Step 2: Select target node to join with
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))

    # Step 3: Shift variable features (shift=0 keeps identity for powers/rational forms)
    if nfeatures > 1
        shift = rand(rng, 0:(nfeatures - 1))
        if shift > 0
            _shift_features!(motif, shift, nfeatures)
        end
    end

    # Step 4: Choose binary coupling operator (biased toward + and * if available)
    add_or_mul = findall(op -> op === (+) || op === (*), options.operators.binops)
    bin_op = if !isempty(add_or_mul) && rand(rng) < 0.7
        rand(rng, add_or_mul)
    else
        rand(rng, 1:(options.nops[2]))
    end

    # Step 5: Replace target with bin_op(target, motif) in randomized order
    target_copy = copy(target)
    children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
    new_node = constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children)
    set_node!(target, new_node)

    return tree
end

pareto_niche_crowding_survival_gen25_8.name: pareto_niche_crowding_survival_gen25_8
pareto_niche_crowding_survival_gen25_8.code:
"""
    pareto_niche_crowding_survival_gen25_8(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

Survival ("who dies") operator that generalizes age-regularized evolution into a
**Pareto-aware, niche-crowding** replacement rule.

Core idea
=========
Age-regularized evolution (the default) always kills the oldest member. This keeps
turnover high but is blind to *what* is being discarded: it happily deletes a
unique, non-dominated building block (e.g. the only simple, low-loss skeleton of the
ground-truth expression) while leaving behind dozens of redundant clones of the
current champion. Since ground-truth recovery usually proceeds by *growing* a
correct low-complexity skeleton, protecting the accuracy/complexity Pareto front and
deleting redundancy instead of age is expected to help exact-recovery rates.

This operator therefore assigns each member a *replacement priority* and removes the
member with the highest priority. Priority rewards:

  1. **Age** (`age_frac`): keeps the age-regularization pressure that prevents
     stagnation and lets bad-but-lucky members eventually leave.
  2. **Pareto dominatedness** (`dom_frac`): the number of members that are at least as
     simple *and* at least as accurate. Heavily dominated members contribute nothing
     to the front and are the cheapest to lose.
  3. **Niche crowding** (`crowd_frac`): occupancy of the member's exact-complexity
     bin. This spreads the population over the complexity axis, which is exactly the
     axis PySR must search to find the true expression size.
  4. **Redundancy / clones**: members sharing the same complexity *and* (numerically)
     the same loss are near-certain duplicates; all but one are free to delete.

and it *protects*:

  * members that are non-dominated **and** unique (the Pareto front is the search's memory),
  * the newest ~10% of members (a brand-new offspring gets at least one chance to be
    selected as a parent, otherwise mutation feedback is destroyed),
  * the current best-cost champion (near-absolute protection, i.e. elitism inside the
    population itself).

Steps
=====
1. Cache complexity, loss, birth and cost of every member (NaN losses/costs -> `Inf`).
2. Count Pareto dominators for each member (O(n^2), n is the population size, so this
   is negligible next to a single loss evaluation).
3. Detect clones (same complexity, relatively-equal loss) and complexity-niche counts.
4. Combine the normalized terms into a replacement priority with the protections above,
   add a tiny random jitter for tie-breaking (avoids systematically deleting the
   lowest-index member of a tied group), and return the argmax.
5. `exclude_indices` are never returned; if everything is excluded we fall back to the
   first admissible index (and to `1` in the degenerate case).

Assumptions / heuristics
========================
* Lower `loss` and lower complexity are both better; `cost` is the parsimony-adjusted
  objective already computed by SymbolicRegression.jl.
* Weights were chosen so that (a) a unique Pareto-front member essentially never dies,
  (b) among the remaining members, redundancy dominates age, and (c) age still breaks
  ties so the population cannot freeze.
* Uses `rand()` only for jitter, so behaviour is robust to the RNG stream.
"""
function pareto_niche_crowding_survival_gen25_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    n <= 1 && return 1

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- caches
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    births = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        member = pop.members[i]
        complexities[i] = compute_complexity(member, options)
        l = Float64(member.loss)
        losses[i] = isnan(l) ? Inf : l          # treat invalid losses as worst possible
        c = Float64(member.cost)
        costs[i] = isnan(c) ? Inf : c
        births[i] = Float64(member.birth)
    end

    # --------------------------------------- Pareto dominance counts (2D front)
    # n_dominators[i] = #{j : j is <= as complex AND <= as lossy, strictly better once}
    n_dominators = zeros(Int, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        ci = complexities[i]
        li = losses[i]
        for j in 1:n
            j == i && continue
            cj = complexities[j]
            lj = losses[j]
            if cj <= ci && lj <= li && (cj < ci || lj < li)
                n_dominators[i] += 1
            end
        end
    end
    max_dom = maximum(n_dominators)

    # ------------------------------------------------- clone / duplicate detection
    # Same complexity + (relatively) same loss => almost surely the same formula.
    clone_count = zeros(Int, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:(n - 1)
        for j in (i + 1):n
            if complexities[i] == complexities[j] && (
                losses[i] == losses[j] ||
                isapprox(losses[i], losses[j]; rtol=1e-9, atol=0.0)
            )
                clone_count[i] += 1
                clone_count[j] += 1
            end
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------- complexity-niche occupancy counts
    niche = Dict{Int,Int}()
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        niche[complexities[i]] = get(niche, complexities[i], 0) + 1
    end
    max_niche = maximum(values(niche))

    # --------------------------------------------------------- age normalization
    bmin = minimum(births)
    bmax = maximum(births)
    brange = bmax - bmin

    # Youth shield: protect the newest ~10% (at least 1) so fresh offspring survive
    # long enough to be sampled as parents at least once.
    n_shield = max(1, div(n, 10))
    sorted_births = sort(births; rev=true)
    shield_birth = sorted_births[min(n_shield, n)]

    # Champion (best parsimony-adjusted cost) receives near-absolute protection.
    champion_idx = argmin_fast(costs)

    # ------------------------------------------------- replacement priority search
    best_idx = 0
    best_priority = -Inf
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        (i in exclude_indices) && continue

        # older => closer to 1 (retains age-regularized turnover pressure)
        age_frac = brange > 0 ? (bmax - births[i]) / brange : 0.5
        # more dominated => closer to 1 (useless for the front)
        dom_frac = max_dom > 0 ? n_dominators[i] / max_dom : 0.0
        # more crowded complexity bin => closer to 1 (spread over the complexity axis)
        crowd_frac = max_niche > 1 ? (niche[complexities[i]] - 1) / (max_niche - 1) : 0.0

        priority = 1.0 * age_frac + 1.2 * dom_frac + 0.7 * crowd_frac

        # Pure redundancy: duplicates are the cheapest deletions available (saturating).
        priority += 1.5 * (min(clone_count[i], 3) / 3)

        # Protect unique, non-dominated members: they are the Pareto front / search memory.
        if n_dominators[i] == 0 && clone_count[i] == 0
            priority -= 4.0
        end

        # Do not immediately discard brand-new offspring.
        if births[i] >= shield_birth
            priority -= 2.5
        end

        # Population-level elitism for the current champion.
        if i == champion_idx
            priority -= 100.0
        end

        # Tiny jitter breaks exact ties without biasing toward low indices.
        priority += 0.05 * rand()

        if priority > best_priority
            best_priority = priority
            best_idx = i
        end
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ fallbacks
    if best_idx == 0
        # Everything was excluded (degenerate): return the first admissible index.
        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            (i in exclude_indices) || return i
        end
        return 1
    end

    return best_idx
end

adaptive_pareto_niche_survival_gen25_0.name: adaptive_pareto_niche_survival_gen25_0
adaptive_pareto_niche_survival_gen25_0.code:
"""
    adaptive_pareto_niche_survival_gen25_0(pop::Population{T,L,N}, options::AbstractOptions; exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[])::Int where {T,L,N}

Custom survival operator that balances age-regularization with Pareto frontier protection
and complexity-niche desaturation to select the optimal population member for replacement.

# Rationale & Heuristics:
1. **Immediate Purge of Non-Finite Individuals**:
   Members with `NaN` or `Inf` loss/cost provide zero evolutionary value and are prioritized
   for immediate replacement, freeing computational capacity.
2. **Pareto Frontier Protection**:
   Standard Age-Regularized Evolution (ARE) indiscriminately eliminates the oldest individuals,
   frequently destroying critical non-dominated Pareto stepping stones (best loss for a given
   complexity). This operator assigns a significant survival bonus (culling discount) to
   non-dominated individuals.
3. **Complexity-Niche Desaturation**:
   When multiple individuals share the same complexity bin, structural diversity decreases.
   A logarithmic congestion penalty is applied to overcrowded complexity bins to encourage
   exploration across diverse expression sizes.
4. **Age-Regularized Decay**:
   Older individuals receive higher base replacement priority, preserving the continuous
   population renewal and anti-bloat dynamics of regularized evolution.
"""
function adaptive_pareto_niche_survival_gen25_0(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T,L,N}
    n = pop.n
    if n == 0
        return 1
    end

    # Step 1: Pre-filter valid candidates not present in exclude_indices
    # Identify min and max birth timestamps across all members to normalize age
    min_birth = typemax(pop.members[1].birth)
    max_birth = typemin(pop.members[1].birth)

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        b = pop.members[i].birth
        if b < min_birth
            min_birth = b
        end
        if b > max_birth
            max_birth = b
        end
    end

    birth_range = Float64(max_birth - min_birth + 1)

    # Step 2: Compute complexities, check finiteness, and compute complexity histogram
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    is_finite_member = Vector{Bool}(undef, n)
    max_c = 0

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        c = compute_complexity(pop.members[i], options)
        complexities[i] = c
        if c > max_c
            max_c = c
        end
        loss_val = pop.members[i].loss
        cost_val = pop.members[i].cost
        is_finite_member[i] = isfinite(loss_val) && isfinite(cost_val)
    end

    # Count population density in each complexity niche
    niche_counts = zeros(Int, max_c)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        c = complexities[i]
        if c >= 1 && c <= max_c
            niche_counts[c] += 1
        end
    end

    # Step 3: Identify Pareto-dominated members
    # An individual is dominated if another finite individual has (<= complexity AND < loss)
    # or (< complexity AND <= loss).
    is_dominated = falses(n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        if !is_finite_member[i]
            is_dominated[i] = true
            continue
        end
        c_i = complexities[i]
        loss_i = pop.members[i].loss

        for j in 1:n
            if i == j || !is_finite_member[j]
                continue
            end
            c_j = complexities[j]
            loss_j = pop.members[j].loss

            if (c_j <= c_i && loss_j < loss_i) || (c_j < c_i && loss_j <= loss_i)
                is_dominated[i] = true
                break
            end
        end
    end

    # Step 4: Compute replacement score for each candidate
    # Higher replacement score = higher priority to be replaced (culled)
    best_candidate_idx = -1
    best_candidate_score = -Inf

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        # Skip indices marked for exclusion (e.g., during crossover pairs)
        if i in exclude_indices
            continue
        end

        # Non-finite candidates are culled with highest priority, broken by age
        if !is_finite_member[i]
            # Prioritize oldest non-finite individuals
            score = 1e9 + Float64(max_birth - pop.members[i].birth + 1)
        else
            # Age factor: linearly scales from ~0.0 (newest) to 1.0 (oldest)
            age_factor = Float64(max_birth - pop.members[i].birth + 1) / birth_range

            # Niche congestion factor: increases if complexity bin is crowded
            c_i = complexities[i]
            niche_count = (c_i >= 1 && c_i <= max_c) ? niche_counts[c_i] : 1
            congestion_factor = 1.0 + log(Float64(niche_count))

            # Pareto factor: non-dominated members receive a protective discount (0.2x),
            # while dominated members receive full/accelerated replacement pressure (1.5x)
            pareto_factor = is_dominated[i] ? 1.5 : 0.2

            score = age_factor * congestion_factor * pareto_factor
        end

        if score > best_candidate_score
            best_candidate_score = score
            best_candidate_idx = i
        end
    end

    # Fallback to first available index if no candidate met criteria
    if best_candidate_idx == -1
        for i in 1:n
            if !(i in exclude_indices)
                return i
            end
        end
        return 1
    end

    return best_candidate_idx
end

affine_shape_calibration_loss_simple_gen.name: affine_shape_calibration_loss_simple_gen25_1
affine_shape_calibration_loss_simple_gen.code:
"""
    affine_shape_calibration_loss_simple_gen25_1(tree, dataset, options)

Simplified affine-shape loss: rank expressions primarily by how well the *shape* of
their predictions matches the target after the best affine calibration
`a * prediction + b`, and break ties among affine-equivalent candidates with a small
bounded raw-error term so that only the correctly calibrated representative reaches
the minimum.

Steps:
1. One streaming Welford pass accumulates `mean_p`, `mean_y`, `m2_p`, `m2_y` and
   `cov_py`, rejecting any non-finite prediction/target immediately.
2. The least-squares slope/intercept are formed from those moments (slope is set to
   zero whenever the prediction has no variance, which makes the fit degenerate to
   the target mean automatically).
3. A second pass evaluates the *fitted* residuals directly (avoiding the catastrophic
   cancellation of `var(y) - cov^2/var(p)` near an exact structural match) together
   with the raw residuals, both normalized by `sqrt(m2_y)`.
4. The loss is `sqrt(affine_NMSE) + (1/256) * raw/(1+raw)`.

Simplifications relative to the parent:
* The separate constant-target branch (an entire extra loop) is folded into the
  common path: when `m2_y == 0` the normalizer becomes `max(1,|mean_y|)*sqrt(n)`,
  the affine fit reproduces the constant target exactly, so the shape term vanishes
  and the loss reduces to a monotone function of the normalized raw error — exactly
  the ordering the parent's special case produced (absolute scale is irrelevant
  because PySR normalizes losses by a baseline tree).
* Kahan compensation and the per-term overflow bookkeeping are removed; plain
  accumulation of already-normalized squared residuals is well scaled, and a single
  finiteness check at the end handles the rare overflow (bounded raw term saturates
  at 1, its supremum, and a non-finite shape term returns `Inf`).
* The scale-relative `max_abs`-based variability tests are replaced by simple
  positivity tests on the Welford second moments, since the subsequent code only
  needs to avoid dividing by zero.
"""
function affine_shape_calibration_loss_simple_gen25_1(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # ---- Pass 1: streaming (Welford) first and second moments ----
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y
        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k
        # covariance update uses the freshly updated target mean
        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # roundoff can make Welford sums microscopically negative
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    # Single normalizer for both residual streams. For a constant target we fall
    # back to a target-scale normalizer; the affine fit then matches y exactly, so
    # the shape term is 0 and only the (monotone) raw term orders the candidates.
    target_norm = m2_y > zero_l ? sqrt(m2_y) : max(one_l, abs(mean_y)) * sqrt(n_l)
    if !(isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # ---- Least-squares affine calibration from the moments ----
    slope = m2_p > zero_l ? cov_py / m2_p : zero_l
    intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
    if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # ---- Pass 2: fitted and raw residuals, evaluated directly ----
    affine_sum = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_normalized = (p - y) / target_norm
        raw_sum += raw_normalized * raw_normalized

        fitted = muladd(slope, p, intercept)
        affine_normalized = (fitted - y) / target_norm
        affine_sum += affine_normalized * affine_normalized
    end

    if !isfinite(affine_sum)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # The affine optimum can never be worse than predicting the target mean,
    # so the normalized affine error lies in [0, 1] up to roundoff.
    shape_term = sqrt(clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l))

    # Bounded, saturating raw-error tie-breaker: affine-equivalent structures with
    # bad constants stay competitive, but exact calibration is still preferred.
    bounded_raw = if isfinite(raw_sum) && raw_sum >= zero_l
        raw_sum / (one_l + raw_sum)
    else
        one_l  # supremum of x/(1+x): overflow saturates instead of poisoning the loss
    end

    loss_value = shape_term + bounded_raw / L(256)
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

affine_angular_profile_loss_2pass_gen9_1.name: affine_angular_profile_loss_2pass_gen9_1_gen25_3
affine_angular_profile_loss_2pass_gen9_1.code:
"""
    affine_angular_profile_loss_2pass_gen9_1_gen25_3(tree, dataset, options)

Measure functional shape with the residual angle of the best affine calibration
`a * prediction + b`, then use a bounded *calibration-defect* term to select the
correctly calibrated representative among shape-equivalent trees. The first pass
computes stable Welford moments and scale-aware variability tests. A second pass
evaluates both the raw (identity-calibrated) and affine-fitted residuals directly,
avoiding the cancellation in `var(y) - cov(p,y)^2 / var(p)` near an exact structural
match.

Compared with the parent (`..._gen8_1`), the tie-breaker no longer uses the raw
normalized error directly. Instead it uses `raw_nmse - affine_nmse`, i.e. the excess
normalized error the raw (uncalibrated, slope=1/intercept=0) prediction incurs over
the *best possible* affine recalibration of that same prediction. Since the affine
fit is a least-squares optimum, this excess is always non-negative and is exactly
zero when the tree's own constants already realize the optimal slope/intercept. This
cleanly isolates "how mis-calibrated is this specific representative" from "how good
is the functional shape" (the latter is already captured by `shape_term`), whereas
the parent's raw-error tie-breaker conflated the two, letting shape quality leak into
the supposedly-orthogonal calibration signal. As before, constant targets fall back
to normalized raw error and no expression-complexity penalty is included.
"""
function affine_angular_profile_loss_2pass_gen9_1_gen25_3(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # First pass: stable moments for the affine least-squares coefficients.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        # The covariance update uses the newly updated target mean.
        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Welford sums can be microscopically negative after roundoff.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    # Relative standard-deviation tests remain meaningful for very small data.
    relative_tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))
    target_rms = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    prediction_rms = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)
    target_is_variable =
        target_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_y
    prediction_is_variable =
        prediction_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_p

    if !target_is_variable
        # Affine shape is undefined for a constant target. Use scale-normalized
        # raw MSE, accumulated after division to avoid squaring large targets.
        target_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_y)
        raw_sum = zero_l
        raw_compensation = zero_l

        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            p = L(prediction[i])
            y = L(dataset.y[i])
            residual = p - y

            if !isfinite(residual)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            normalized_residual = residual / target_scale
            term = normalized_residual * normalized_residual
            if !isfinite(term)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            corrected = term - raw_compensation
            updated = raw_sum + corrected
            if !isfinite(updated)
                return L(Inf)
            end
            raw_compensation = (updated - raw_sum) - corrected
            raw_sum = updated
        end

        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum / n_l, zero_l)
        loss_value = log1p(raw_nmse)
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
    end

    target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)
    if !(isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if prediction_is_variable
        slope = cov_py / m2_p
        intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
        if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end

    # Second pass: directly evaluate both the raw (identity-calibrated) and the
    # affine-fitted residuals. Direct evaluation is more accurate near perfect
    # correlation than subtracting two almost-equal variances.
    affine_sum = zero_l
    affine_compensation = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l
    raw_compensation = zero_l
    raw_overflowed = false

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_residual = p - y
        if !isfinite(raw_residual)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        if !raw_overflowed
            raw_normalized = raw_residual / target_norm
            raw_term = raw_normalized * raw_normalized

            if isfinite(raw_term)
                corrected = raw_term - raw_compensation
                updated = raw_sum + corrected
                if isfinite(updated)
                    raw_compensation = (updated - raw_sum) - corrected
                    raw_sum = updated
                else
                    raw_overflowed = true
                end
            else
                raw_overflowed = true
            end
        end

        fitted = prediction_is_variable ? muladd(slope, p, intercept) : mean_y
        affine_residual = fitted - y
        affine_normalized = affine_residual / target_norm
        affine_term = affine_normalized * affine_normalized

        if !(isfinite(fitted) && isfinite(affine_residual) &&
             isfinite(affine_normalized) && isfinite(affine_term))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        corrected = affine_term - affine_compensation
        updated = affine_sum + corrected
        if !isfinite(updated)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        affine_compensation = (updated - affine_sum) - corrected
        affine_sum = updated
    end

    # The affine optimum cannot be worse than fitting the target mean.
    affine_nmse = clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l)
    shape_term = sqrt(affine_nmse)

    # Calibration defect: the excess normalized error of the raw (uncalibrated)
    # prediction over the best possible affine recalibration of itself. This is
    # always >= 0 (the affine fit is a least-squares optimum over slope/
    # intercept) and equals zero exactly when this representative's own
    # constants are already optimally calibrated, so it is a clean, shape-
    # independent tie-breaker among functionally equivalent trees.
    bounded_calibration = if raw_overflowed
        one_l
    else
        calibration_defect = max(raw_sum - affine_sum, zero_l)
        # Saturating map keeps the tie-breaker bounded and monotone.
        calibration_defect <= one_l ?
            calibration_defect / (one_l + calibration_defect) :
            one_l / (one_l + one_l / calibration_defect)
    end

    calibration_weight = one_l / L(256)
    loss_value = shape_term + calibration_weight * bounded_calibration

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

motif_duplication_with_modulated_rationa.name: motif_duplication_with_modulated_rational_coupling_gen12_gen20_6_gen25_4
motif_duplication_with_modulated_rationa.code:
"""
    motif_duplication_with_modulated_rational_coupling_gen12_gen20_6_gen25_4(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Structural mutation that **reuses evolved structure**: it clones a subexpression *motif*, optionally
re-indexes its variables, and couples the clone back into the tree either as a plain symmetric
accumulation (`target ⊕ motif`), inside a self-referential rational template
(`target / (1 ± motif)`), or — new in this version — inside a **modulated rational template**
(`target / (1 ± motif * f(x_k))`) where `f` is a saturating unary function (`cos`, `sin`, `exp`,
`tanh`, ...) applied to a *fresh* feature.

# Motivation for the change
The parent's rational coupling already lets a subexpression appear both in the numerator and
inside `1 ± (...)` in the denominator, which is the key structural trick behind relativistic /
Compton-scattering-like laws. But the search trace on
`x0/(1 + x0/(x1*x2^2)*(1-cos(x3)))` shows the population getting stuck: it can build
`x0/(1+motif)` but never the *product* `motif * (1 - cos(x3))` inside the denominator, because no
existing mutation multiplies a duplicated motif by a fresh angular/saturating factor of an
*unrelated* variable. Point mutations essentially never assemble this three-way coupling
(duplicate ⊗ new-variable ⊗ trig-wrap) by chance. This version adds that missing piece as a third,
minority coupling mode, directly targeting angular-correction / saturation forms
(Compton scattering, relativistic Doppler, Michaelis–Menten with cooperativity, radiative transfer,
drag with a modulating angle, etc.).

# Steps
1. Guard: need at least one binary operator.
2. Locate `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` operator indices once.
3. Decide the coupling template up front (since each costs a different number of extra nodes) and
   derive the donor size budget accordingly:
   * plain coupling: `size(motif) + 1` extra nodes,
   * rational coupling `target / (c ± motif)`: `size(motif) + 3` extra nodes,
   * modulated rational coupling `target / (c ± motif * f(x_k))`: `size(motif) + 6` extra nodes
     (mul, unary wrapper, fresh leaf, plus the 3 from plain rational). Requires `*` and at least
     one unary operator, and is only attempted a minority of the time even when rational coupling
     is chosen.
4. Tiered donor sampling (from parent 2): prefer compound, variable-bearing subtrees that fit the
   budget; fall back to any variable-bearing subtree, then to any subtree that fits.
5. Remap the motif's features with cyclic shift, targeted single-feature substitution, or identity,
   exactly as before (the modulator's feature is chosen independently, see step 6).
6. Couple:
   * modulated rational (new): build a fresh unary term `f(x_k)`, biased toward saturating
     functions (`cos`, `sin`, `exp`, `tanh`) if present, with `x_k` preferentially chosen to be a
     feature *not already present in the motif* (so the modulator carries genuinely new
     information, mirroring `theta` being independent of the `E_n/(m c^2)` ratio it modulates);
     splice as `target / (c ± motif * f(x_k))`.
   * plain rational (as before): `target / (c ± motif)`.
   * plain symmetric coupling (as before): `target ⊕ motif`, biased toward `+`/`*`.

# Assumptions / heuristics
- `c = 1` is the canonical scale; PySR's constant optimizer refines it.
- The modulator feature is drawn preferentially from features absent in the motif to encourage
  compositional novelty rather than re-using the same variable twice.
- Modulated rational coupling is a minority sub-mode of an already-minority rational mode, so the
  operator stays primarily a symmetry duplicator with only occasional forays into richer templates.
"""
function motif_duplication_with_modulated_rational_coupling_gen12_gen20_6_gen25_4(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 1: guard
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2: operator lookup
    binops = options.operators.binops
    nbin = options.nops[2]
    function _op_index(f)
        for i in 1:nbin
            binops[i] === f && return i
        end
        return nothing
    end
    idx_add = _op_index(+)
    idx_sub = _op_index(-)
    idx_mul = _op_index(*)
    idx_div = _op_index(/)

    nuna = options.nops[1]
    unaops = nuna > 0 ? options.operators.unaops : ()
    function _una_index(f)
        for i in 1:nuna
            unaops[i] === f && return i
        end
        return nothing
    end

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3: template + size budget
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)

    rational_ok = (idx_div !== nothing) && (idx_add !== nothing || idx_sub !== nothing)
    want_rational = rational_ok && rand(rng) < 0.35
    # Modulated sub-mode needs `*` and at least one unary op, plus room for 6 extra nodes.
    modulated_ok = want_rational && (idx_mul !== nothing) && (nuna > 0)
    use_modulated = modulated_ok && rand(rng) < 0.4 && (maxsize - tree_size - 6) >= 1
    use_rational = want_rational && (maxsize - tree_size - 3) >= 1

    extra_nodes = if use_modulated
        6
    elseif use_rational
        3
    else
        1
    end
    budget = maxsize - tree_size - extra_nodes
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- helpers
    # Distinct feature indices in a subtree
    function _collect_features!(acc::Vector{Int}, node)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant && !(node.feature in acc)
                push!(acc, node.feature)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _collect_features!(acc, get_child(node, i))
            end
        end
        return acc
    end

    # Apply an arbitrary index map to every variable leaf (single compact traversal)
    function _map_features!(node, fmap)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = fmap(node.feature)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _map_features!(get_child(node, i), fmap)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    _fits(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget
    _has_var(t) = any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, t)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4: donor (tiered)
    n_tier1 = count(t -> t.degree > 0 && _fits(t) && _has_var(t), tree)
    n_tier2 = count(t -> _fits(t) && _has_var(t), tree)
    n_tier3 = count(_fits, tree)

    donor = if n_tier1 > 0 && rand(rng) < 0.8
        # Compound, variable-bearing motifs: the interesting symmetry carriers
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> t.degree > 0 && _fits(t) && _has_var(t)))
    elseif n_tier2 > 0
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> _fits(t) && _has_var(t)))
    elseif n_tier3 > 0
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_fits))
    else
        return tree  # nothing fits the budget
    end
    motif = copy(donor)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- target
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    self_coupling = target === donor

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5: feature remapping
    if nfeatures > 1
        r = rand(rng)
        if r < 0.40
            # (a) cyclic shift: replicate the functional form across a block of variables
            shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
            _map_features!(motif, f -> mod1(f + shift, nfeatures))
        elseif r < 0.72
            # (b) targeted substitution: replace exactly one feature of the motif everywhere
            feats = _collect_features!(Int[], motif)
            if !isempty(feats)
                src = feats[rand(rng, 1:length(feats))]
                dst = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
                dst >= src && (dst += 1)  # uniform over destinations != src
                _map_features!(motif, f -> (f == src ? dst : f))
            end
        else
            # (c) identity: powers (u*u), rational self-couplings (u/(1+u)), ratios (u/u')
            # Only force a shift for degenerate *plain* self-couplings; for the rational
            # template `u/(1+u)` (and the modulated variant) the identity map is exactly what we want.
            if self_coupling && !use_rational && rand(rng, Bool)
                shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
                _map_features!(motif, f -> mod1(f + shift, nfeatures))
            end
        end
    end

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 6: coupling
    target_copy = copy(target)

    new_node = if use_modulated
        # Modulated self-referential saturation: target / (1 ± motif * f(x_k))
        c = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
        den_op = if idx_add !== nothing && idx_sub !== nothing
            rand(rng, Bool) ? idx_add : idx_sub
        elseif idx_add !== nothing
            idx_add
        else
            idx_sub
        end
        # Bias the modulator toward classic saturating/angular functions when available
        pref_una = Int[]
        for fn in (cos, sin, exp, tanh)
            i = _una_index(fn)
            i !== nothing && push!(pref_una, i)
        end
        una_op = if !isempty(pref_una) && rand(rng) < 0.7
            pref_una[rand(rng, 1:length(pref_una))]
        else
            rand(rng, 1:nuna)
        end
        # Prefer a feature *not* already present in the motif, so the modulator adds
        # genuinely new information (e.g. an independent angle theta) rather than
        # re-using a variable the motif already depends on.
        motif_feats = _collect_features!(Int[], motif)
        mod_feat = if nfeatures > 1 && !isempty(motif_feats) && rand(rng) < 0.7
            others = filter(f -> !(f in motif_feats), 1:nfeatures)
            isempty(others) ? rand(rng, 1:nfeatures) : rand(rng, others)
        else
            rand(rng, 1:nfeatures)
        end
        modulator = constructorof(N)(; op=una_op, children=(constructorof(N)(T; feature=mod_feat),))
        prod_node = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_mul, children=(motif, modulator))
        den = constructorof(N)(; op=den_op, children=(c, prod_node))
        constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(target_copy, den))
    elseif use_rational
        # Plain self-referential saturation / correction factor: target / (1 ± motif)
        c = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
        den_op = if idx_add !== nothing && idx_sub !== nothing
            rand(rng, Bool) ? idx_add : idx_sub
        elseif idx_add !== nothing
            idx_add
        else
            idx_sub
        end
        den = constructorof(N)(; op=den_op, children=(c, motif))
        constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(target_copy, den))
    else
        # Plain symmetric coupling, biased toward the canonical accumulators `+` and `*`
        pref = Int[]
        idx_add !== nothing && push!(pref, idx_add)
        idx_mul !== nothing && push!(pref, idx_mul)
        bin_op = if !isempty(pref) && rand(rng) < 0.65
            pref[rand(rng, 1:length(pref))]
        else
            rand(rng, 1:nbin)
        end
        # Randomize operand order to support non-commutative operators
        children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
        constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children)
    end

    set_node!(target, new_node)
    return tree
end

pareto_niche_lineage_tournament_gen25_5.name: pareto_niche_lineage_tournament_gen25_5
pareto_niche_lineage_tournament_gen25_5.code:
"""
    pareto_niche_lineage_tournament_gen25_5(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Selection operator that replaces the single scalar tournament criterion of the default
operator with a *composite rank* built from four complementary pressures, all computed
locally inside the sampled tournament (so cost stays O(n^2) in the tournament size, which
is tiny, and no global population statistics beyond the ones already provided are needed).

Core idea
=========
Ground-truth recovery in symbolic regression usually fails not because the search cannot
optimize loss, but because the population collapses onto a single high-accuracy lineage at
one complexity level, destroying the intermediate "stepping stone" structures that the
true expression needs. This operator therefore rewards a candidate for being:

1. **Cheap** — its frequency-adjusted cost rank inside the tournament (this reproduces the
   default behaviour, including `use_frequency_in_tournament` and
   `adaptive_parsimony_scaling`, and is the dominant term).
2. **Non-dominated** — its number of local (loss, complexity) Pareto dominators. A member
   that lies on the local Pareto front is preferred even if its scalar cost is mediocre,
   which protects short, slightly-worse expressions that are frequently the true
   stepping stones toward the exact formula. The dominator count is capped so that a
   badly dominated member is not penalized without bound.
3. **In a rare complexity niche** — its rank in `normalized_frequencies` at its own
   complexity, so under-explored sizes get a mild boost. This actively fills gaps in the
   complexity spectrum instead of only exponentially penalizing crowded sizes.
4. **From an under-represented lineage** — a penalty equal to the number of *other*
   sampled members sharing the same `parent` reference. This breaks up sibling floods
   produced when one parent happens to be mutated many times in a generation, and is a
   cheap proxy for genotypic diversity when no distance metric is available.

Steps
=====
1. Sample `tournament_selection_n` distinct members (without replacement).
2. Compute complexity, raw loss, frequency-adjusted cost, and complexity frequency for each.
3. Convert adjusted costs and frequencies into ordinal ranks inside the tournament
   (ranks, not raw values, so the composite score is scale-free and robust to losses
   spanning many orders of magnitude, `Inf`, or `NaN`).
4. Count local Pareto dominators and same-parent siblings.
5. Combine into `score = cost_rank + 2*min(dominators,4) + 0.35*(rarity_rank-1) + 0.5*siblings`.
6. With small probability (`P_EXPLORE`) return the rarest-niche member of the local Pareto
   front instead (pure stepping-stone exploration); otherwise draw from the score ordering
   with the usual geometric `tournament_selection_p` distribution, so the user-facing
   knob keeps its meaning.

Assumptions / heuristics
========================
* Lower `loss` and lower complexity are both desirable (standard SR setting).
* `member.parent` may be `<= 0` for members with no recorded parent; those are not
  treated as siblings of each other.
* Non-finite costs/losses are pushed to the worst ranks rather than crashing the sort.
* The weights (2.0, 0.35, 0.5) are deliberately small relative to `cost_rank`, so the
  operator behaves like the default tournament in the common case and only re-orders
  near-ties — the regime where diversity decisions actually matter.
"""
function pareto_niche_lineage_tournament_gen25_5(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T,L,N}
    members = pop.members
    n_pop = length(members)
    n_sample = min(options.tournament_selection_n, n_pop)

    # --- Step 1: sample the tournament (indices, to avoid copying members) ---
    sample_idx = StatsBase.sample(1:n_pop, n_sample; replace=false)

    # --- Step 2: gather per-candidate quantities ---
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n_sample)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_sample)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_sample)
    freqs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_sample)
    scaling = Float64(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n_sample
        member = members[sample_idx[i]]
        c = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = c

        # frequency of this complexity size (0 if out of the tracked range)
        f = if 0 < c <= options.maxsize
            Float64(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
        else
            0.0
        end
        freqs[i] = f

        raw_loss = Float64(member.loss)
        losses[i] = isfinite(raw_loss) ? raw_loss : Inf

        raw_cost = Float64(member.cost)
        adjusted_costs[i] = if !isfinite(raw_cost)
            Inf  # never let NaN/Inf poison the sort
        elseif options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            # identical to the default adaptive-parsimony adjustment
            raw_cost * exp(scaling * f)
        else
            raw_cost
        end
    end

    # --- Step 3: ordinal ranks (1 = best) for cost and for niche rarity ---
    cost_rank = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_sample)
    for (r, i) in enumerate(sortperm(adjusted_costs))
        cost_rank[i] = Float64(r)
    end

    rarity_rank = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_sample)
    for (r, i) in enumerate(sortperm(freqs))  # ascending frequency => rarest gets rank 1
        rarity_rank[i] = Float64(r)
    end

    # --- Step 4a: local Pareto dominance count on (loss, complexity) ---
    dom_count = zeros(Int, n_sample)
    for i in 1:n_sample
        li = losses[i]
        ci = complexities[i]
        for j in 1:n_sample
            j == i && continue
            lj = losses[j]
            cj = complexities[j]
            # j dominates i if it is no worse in both objectives and strictly better in one
            if lj <= li && cj <= ci && (lj < li || cj < ci)
                dom_count[i] += 1
            end
        end
    end
