    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=fits))

    left = copy(donor)
    right = copy(donor)

    # Identity duplication creates powers; a shift creates cross-feature symmetries.
    if nfeatures > 1 && rand(rng) < 0.45
        shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))

        function shift_features!(node)
            if node.degree == 0
                if !node.constant
                    node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeatures)
                end
            else
                for i in 1:node.degree
                    shift_features!(get_child(node, i))
                end
            end
            return node
        end

        shift_features!(right)
    end

    # Addition and multiplication are the canonical repeated-motif couplings.
    binops = options.operators.binops
    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op == (+), binops)
    idx_mul = findfirst(op -> op == (*), binops)

    preferred = Int[]
    idx_add !== nothing && push!(preferred, idx_add)
    idx_mul !== nothing && push!(preferred, idx_mul)
    op = isempty(preferred) ? rand(rng, 1:nbin) : rand(rng, preferred)

    replacement = constructorof(N)(; op=op, children=(left, right))
    set_node!(donor, replacement)
    return tree
end

oldest_pair_worst_cost_survival_gen32_7.name: oldest_pair_worst_cost_survival_gen32_7
oldest_pair_worst_cost_survival_gen32_7.code:
"""
    oldest_pair_worst_cost_survival_gen32_7(pop::Population, options::AbstractOptions; exclude_indices=Int[])

Simplified age-and-cost survival operator.

Core Idea:
Preserves the steady turnover and diversity of age-regularized evolution while
pruning stagnating or bloated solutions. Instead of computing a dynamic cohort
(e.g., the oldest 25%) via full-population allocation and sorting, this operator
identifies the two oldest eligible individuals in a single pass and evicts whichever
of the two has the higher cost.

Steps:
1. Iterate through the population in a single pass to find the 1st and 2nd oldest
   eligible members (ignoring `exclude_indices`).
2. If only one eligible member is present, return its index.
3. Compare the costs of the two oldest members and return the index of the one with
   the higher (worse) cost.

Simplifications from Parent:
- Removed intermediate vector allocation for eligible indices.
- Removed the full-population sort by birth date (`sort!`), replacing it with an
  allocation-free single pass tracking the two oldest members.
- Replaced the variable-sized cohort (25% of population) with a streamlined 2-candidate
  tournament. This keeps eviction pressure tightly focused on the oldest individuals,
  preventing old bloated formulas from hiding in large cohorts while still protecting
  younger explorations.
"""
function oldest_pair_worst_cost_survival_gen32_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    oldest_idx = 0
    second_oldest_idx = 0
    min_birth = typemax(Int)
    second_min_birth = typemax(Int)

    # Single pass to find the two oldest eligible individuals
    for i in 1:pop.n
        if !(i in exclude_indices)
            b = pop.members[i].birth
            if b < min_birth
                # Shift current oldest to second oldest
                second_oldest_idx = oldest_idx
                second_min_birth = min_birth
                oldest_idx = i
                min_birth = b
            elseif b < second_min_birth
                second_oldest_idx = i
                second_min_birth = b
            end
        end
    end

    @assert oldest_idx != 0 "No eligible members to replace"

    # If only one eligible member was found, replace it
    if second_oldest_idx == 0
        return oldest_idx
    end

    # Evict the individual with the higher (worse) cost among the two oldest
    cost1 = pop.members[oldest_idx].cost
    cost2 = pop.members[second_oldest_idx].cost
    return cost1 >= cost2 ? oldest_idx : second_oldest_idx
end

pareto_age_survival_simplified_gen32_9.name: pareto_age_survival_simplified_gen32_9
pareto_age_survival_simplified_gen32_9.code:
"""
    pareto_age_survival_simplified_gen32_9(pop::Population{T,L,N}, options::AbstractOptions; exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[])::Int where {T,L,N}

Select a population member for replacement using three ordered rules:

1. Replace the oldest available member with non-finite loss or cost.
2. Otherwise, replace the oldest available member dominated in loss-complexity space.
3. If every available member is Pareto non-dominated, fall back to replacing the oldest.

This retains the parent's non-finite purge, Pareto protection, and age regularization,
but removes complexity-bin histograms, age normalization, and tuned multiplicative scores.
Using lexicographic priorities avoids parameter-sensitive tradeoffs while preserving useful
Pareto stepping stones and continual population renewal.
"""
function pareto_age_survival_simplified_gen32_9(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T,L,N}
    n = pop.n
    n > 0 || throw(ArgumentError("cannot select from an empty population"))

    complexities = zeros(Int, n)
    finite_member = falses(n)
    oldest_nonfinite = 0

    # Cache validity and complexity, while identifying invalid members to purge first.
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        member = pop.members[i]
        finite_member[i] = isfinite(member.loss) && isfinite(member.cost)

        if finite_member[i]
            complexities[i] = compute_complexity(member, options)
        elseif !(i in exclude_indices)
            if oldest_nonfinite == 0 ||
               member.birth < pop.members[oldest_nonfinite].birth
                oldest_nonfinite = i
            end
        end
    end

    oldest_nonfinite != 0 && return oldest_nonfinite

    oldest_available = 0
    oldest_dominated = 0

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        if i in exclude_indices
            continue
        end

        # All available non-finite members were handled above.
        finite_member[i] || continue

        if oldest_available == 0 ||
           pop.members[i].birth < pop.members[oldest_available].birth
            oldest_available = i
        end

        c_i = complexities[i]
        loss_i = pop.members[i].loss
        dominated = false

        # Any finite member may establish dominance, including an excluded survivor.
        for j in 1:n
            if j == i || !finite_member[j]
                continue
            end

            c_j = complexities[j]
            loss_j = pop.members[j].loss
            if c_j <= c_i && loss_j <= loss_i &&
               (c_j < c_i || loss_j < loss_i)
                dominated = true
                break
            end
        end

        if dominated &&
           (oldest_dominated == 0 ||
            pop.members[i].birth < pop.members[oldest_dominated].birth)
            oldest_dominated = i
        end
    end

    oldest_dominated != 0 && return oldest_dominated
    oldest_available != 0 && return oldest_available

    throw(ArgumentError("exclude_indices leaves no population member available"))
end

elite_protected_age_survival_gen33_8.name: elite_protected_age_survival_gen33_8
elite_protected_age_survival_gen33_8.code:
"""
    elite_protected_age_survival_gen33_8(pop::Population{T,L,N}, options::AbstractOptions; exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[]) where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}

Streamlined Age-Regularized Evolution (ARE) with elite protection: replaces the
oldest eligible individual by default, but protects the population's best-performing
member if it happens to be the oldest, replacing the worst-cost member instead.

Core Idea:
Standard Age-Regularized Evolution (ARE) replaces the oldest individual to prevent
stagnation and maintain diversity. However, strict ARE suffers from a critical failure
mode: it inevitably culls the island's best-discovered expression (the elite) once
that expression reaches maximum age. This simplified operator preserves pure ARE
culling for all non-elite members, but when the oldest member is also the island's
best-fit member, it protects that elite and purges the worst-cost member instead.

What was removed/merged from the parent:
- Removed second-order birth tracking (`oldest2`) and the multi-branch pointer cascade.
- Removed the pairwise duel between the two oldest members, which frequently spared
  mediocre ancestral equations at the expense of younger exploration.
- Replaced the arbitrary oldest-pair comparison with a unified single pass tracking
  the oldest, best, and worst eligible members.

Why this simplification is sound:
In evolutionary symbolic regression, sub-optimal equations should be culled purely by
age to preserve turnover and avoid stagnation. The only individual that warrants age
immunity is the current best-performing expression. By defaulting to pure ARE and
diverting replacement to the worst member only when the oldest is the elite, we
eliminate ARE's critical failure mode while maintaining maximal search efficiency.

Steps:
1. Scan population members once (skipping `exclude_indices`), tracking the oldest, best, and worst members.
2. If the oldest member is the best member and other candidates exist, return the index of the worst member.
3. Otherwise, return the index of the oldest member (standard ARE).
"""
function elite_protected_age_survival_gen33_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    oldest_idx = 0
    best_idx = 0
    worst_idx = 0

    # Single pass to track oldest (min birth), best (min cost), and worst (max cost)
    @inbounds for i in 1:(pop.n)
        i in exclude_indices && continue

        if oldest_idx == 0 || pop.members[i].birth < pop.members[oldest_idx].birth
            oldest_idx = i
        end
        if best_idx == 0 || pop.members[i].cost < pop.members[best_idx].cost
            best_idx = i
        end
        if worst_idx == 0 || pop.members[i].cost > pop.members[worst_idx].cost
            worst_idx = i
        end
    end

    @assert oldest_idx != 0 "No eligible members to replace"

    # If the oldest member is the population's elite, protect it and cull the worst member
    if oldest_idx == best_idx && worst_idx != oldest_idx
        return worst_idx
    end

    # Otherwise, follow standard Age-Regularized Evolution (cull oldest)
    return oldest_idx
end

streamlined_affine_profile_loss_gen33_0.name: streamlined_affine_profile_loss_gen33_0
streamlined_affine_profile_loss_gen33_0.code:
"""
    streamlined_affine_profile_loss_gen33_0(tree, dataset, options)

Compare predictions by fitting their best affine calibration `a * prediction + b`
and measuring the resulting normalized RMSE. A small bounded, scale-normalized
absolute-error term distinguishes affine-equivalent expressions with better raw
calibration. Constant targets use that raw term directly because affine shape is
undefined.

This streamlined variant retains stable Welford moments and direct residual
evaluation near exact matches, but removes compensated summation, raw-overflow
bookkeeping, separate squared-error normalization paths, and the log-NMSE fallback.
The bounded pointwise calibration error handles large residuals through the common
path while preserving zero loss only for exact target predictions.
"""
function streamlined_affine_profile_loss_gen33_0(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # Stable moments determine the least-squares affine calibration.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Remove harmless negative roundoff before taking square roots.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    prediction_std = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)
    target_std = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    relative_tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))

    prediction_is_variable =
        prediction_std > relative_tolerance * max_abs_p
    target_is_variable =
        target_std > relative_tolerance * max_abs_y

    # A non-variable prediction is represented by the best constant fit.
    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if target_is_variable && prediction_is_variable
        slope = cov_py / m2_p
        intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
        if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end

    # The same bounded raw-error path also serves constant-target datasets.
    calibration_scale =
        target_is_variable ? target_std : max(one_l, max_abs_y)
    target_norm = target_is_variable ? sqrt(m2_y) : one_l

    affine_sum = zero_l
    calibration_sum = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_residual = p - y
        if !isfinite(raw_residual)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Pointwise saturation avoids squared-error overflow and limits the
        # calibration term's influence on affine shape discovery.
        ratio = abs(raw_residual) / calibration_scale
        calibration_sum += isfinite(ratio) ?
            ratio / (one_l + ratio) : one_l

        if target_is_variable
            fitted = muladd(slope, p, intercept)
            affine_residual = fitted - y
            normalized_residual = affine_residual / target_norm
            affine_term = normalized_residual * normalized_residual

            if !(isfinite(fitted) && isfinite(affine_term))
                return L(Inf)
            end

            affine_sum += affine_term
            if !isfinite(affine_sum)
                return L(Inf)
            end
        end
    end

    calibration_term = calibration_sum / n_l
    if !target_is_variable
        return isfinite(calibration_term) ? L(calibration_term) : L(Inf)
    end

    shape_term = sqrt(clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l))
    loss_value = shape_term + calibration_term / L(256)

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

motif_duplication_rational_lean_gen33_1.name: motif_duplication_rational_lean_gen33_1
motif_duplication_rational_lean_gen33_1.code:
"""
    motif_duplication_rational_lean_gen33_1(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Lean structural mutation that **reuses evolved structure**: it clones a compound subexpression
*motif*, optionally shifts its feature indices, and couples the clone back into the tree either as a
plain accumulation (`target + motif` / `target * motif`) or inside a **self-referential rational
template** (`target / (1 - motif)`).

# Core idea (unchanged from the parent)
Ground-truth laws repeat the same functional form across different variables
(`0.5*m*(vx^2+vy^2)`, `(x1-x2)^2+(y1-y2)^2`), so duplicating a subtree the search already found is
much cheaper than rediscovering it. The rational template additionally reaches saturating /
correction forms (`u/(1 - v)`: Michaelis-Menten, relativistic factors, feedback gains) that point
mutations essentially cannot build, since they need the *same kind* of subexpression in numerator and
denominator.

# Steps
1. Guard: need binary operators; locate `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` once. Bail out if neither an accumulator
   (`+`/`*`) nor the full rational kit (`/` and `-`) is available.
2. Compute a *single* conservative size budget `maxsize - size(tree) - 3` (the cost of the more
   expensive rational template), so donor selection is template-independent.
3. Sample the donor motif from compound, variable-bearing subtrees that fit the budget; bail out if
   there are none.
4. With probability 1/2 apply a cyclic feature shift to the clone (replicating the form on another
   variable block); otherwise keep it identical (yielding squares `u*u` and self-couplings
   `u/(1-u)`).
5. Choose the coupling (rational with probability 0.35 when available, else a commutative
   accumulator) and splice it in at a uniformly random target node.

# What was simplified relative to the parent (and why it stays sound)
- **Two donor tiers → one.** The leaf-only fallback tier duplicated a bare variable, which
  `insert_random_op`/`mutate_feature` already produce far more cheaply; only compound motifs actually
  carry the structure/symmetry this operator exists to replicate.
- **Two size budgets → one worst-case budget.** Using the rational cost for both templates means the
  donor is sampled once and *any* subsequent coupling choice is guaranteed admissible; it only very
  slightly shrinks the motif pool for the plain coupling.
- **Template decision moved after donor selection**, removing the interlocked
  `rational_ok`/`budget`/`use_rational` bookkeeping of the parent.
- **`1 + u` fallback for the denominator dropped.** If `-` is missing, `1 + u` is just an accumulation
  under a division, which the plain coupling plus ordinary mutations already reach; requiring `-`
  keeps the physically canonical correction form and one code path.
"""
function motif_duplication_rational_lean_gen33_1(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 1: guard + operator lookup
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree
    binops = options.operators.binops
    nbin = options.nops[2]
    idx_add = findfirst(i -> binops[i] === (+), 1:nbin)
    idx_sub = findfirst(i -> binops[i] === (-), 1:nbin)
    idx_mul = findfirst(i -> binops[i] === (*), 1:nbin)
    idx_div = findfirst(i -> binops[i] === (/), 1:nbin)

    # Commutative accumulators for the plain coupling (operand order therefore irrelevant)
    accum = Int[]
    idx_add !== nothing && push!(accum, idx_add)
    idx_mul !== nothing && push!(accum, idx_mul)

    # The rational template needs both `/` and `-` (canonical `1 - u` correction factor)
    rational_ok = (idx_div !== nothing) && (idx_sub !== nothing)
    (isempty(accum) && !rational_ok) && return tree

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2: single size budget
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    # Worst case (rational) adds size(motif) + 3 nodes; using it for both templates keeps one path.
    budget = maxsize - count_nodes(tree) - 3
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3: donor motif (one tier)
    # Only compound, variable-bearing subtrees that fit the budget are useful structure carriers.
    fits(t) =
        t.degree > 0 &&
        count_nodes(t) <= budget &&
        any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, t)

    count(fits, tree) == 0 && return tree
    motif = copy(rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=fits)))  # copy before editing the tree

    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4: feature remapping
    # Compact recursive cyclic shift of every variable leaf in the clone
    function _shift_features!(node, shift)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeatures)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Half the time move the motif onto another variable block; otherwise keep it identical
    # (identity gives squares `u*u` and self-couplings `u/(1-u)`).
    if nfeatures > 1 && rand(rng) < 0.5
        _shift_features!(motif, rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1)))
    end

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5: coupling + splice
    target_copy = copy(target)
    use_rational = rational_ok && (isempty(accum) || rand(rng) < 0.35)

    new_node = if use_rational
        # Self-referential saturation / correction factor: target / (1 - motif)
        one_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
        den = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_sub, children=(one_leaf, motif))
        constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(target_copy, den))
    else
        # Plain accumulation with a commutative operator
        bin_op = accum[rand(rng, 1:length(accum))]
        constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=(target_copy, motif))
    end

    set_node!(target, new_node)
    return tree
end

streamlined_diversity_niche_tournament_g.name: streamlined_diversity_niche_tournament_gen33_2
streamlined_diversity_niche_tournament_g.code:
"""
    streamlined_diversity_niche_tournament_gen33_2(
        pop::Population{T,L,N},
        running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
        options::AbstractOptions,
    )::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}

Streamlined tournament selection combining phenotypic clone suppression and
complexity niche exploration.

### Core Idea
Maintains population diversity and prevents premature convergence by penalizing
phenotypic duplicates within the tournament pool while periodically allocating
selection pressure to the best individuals in underrepresented complexity niches.

### Steps
1. Sample a standard tournament pool of size `options.tournament_selection_n`
   and compute frequency-adjusted costs.
2. Sort the pool by adjusted cost. For each member from best to worst, penalize
   its cost if an earlier (superior) candidate shares the same complexity and
   near-identical loss (phenotypic clone).
3. With a fixed exploration probability (10%), identify the top representative
   for each complexity niche present in the pool and select the one belonging to
   the rarest complexity band in the global search statistics.
4. Otherwise, perform standard geometric tournament selection over the
   clone-penalized costs.

### Simplifications from Parent
- **Removed Lineage / Family Tracking**: Eliminated parent and reference ID
  checks and secondary lineage loss tolerances. Phenotypic duplication (matching
  complexity and loss) directly identifies redundant candidates without fragile
  genealogical heuristics.
- **Removed Age / Youth Discounting**: Removed birth timestamp tracking,
  recency calculation, and youth bonus factors, removing multiple tunable
  parameters and state dependencies.
- **Streamlined Niche Exploration**: Replaced pool-size scaling, dynamic niche
  probability formulas, and multi-stage two-thirds quality gating with a simple,
  direct mechanism: taking the first (best) representative of each niche from
  the sorted pool and choosing the least frequent complexity champion.
"""
function streamlined_diversity_niche_tournament_gen33_2(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Sample standard tournament pool
    sample_size = min(pop.n, options.tournament_selection_n)
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, sample_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    if n == 1
        return pool[1]
    end

    # Compute complexity and adaptive parsimony-adjusted costs
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament && 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
            frequency = L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity])
            adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Order pool from best to worst baseline adjusted cost
    order = sortperm(adjusted_costs)

    # Phenotypic clone suppression: penalize candidates that duplicate better members
    clone_loss_rtol = L(1e-6)
    clone_penalty = L(2.0)

    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        comp_i = complexities[i]
        loss_i = pool[i].loss
        is_clone = false

        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            if comp_i == complexities[j]
                loss_j = pool[j].loss
                loss_scale = max(abs(loss_i), abs(loss_j), L(1e-8))
                if abs(loss_i - loss_j) <= clone_loss_rtol * loss_scale
                    is_clone = true
                    break
                end
            end
        end

        if is_clone
            adjusted_costs[i] = adjusted_costs[i] > zero(L) ?
                adjusted_costs[i] * clone_penalty :
                adjusted_costs[i] + L(1.0)
        end
    end

    # Niche exploration: occasionally pick the best member from the most starved complexity band
    niche_probability = 0.10
    if rand() < niche_probability && options.use_frequency_in_tournament
        # Collect the best representative for each distinct complexity in the pool
        seen_complexities = falses(options.maxsize)
        best_niche_idx = 0
        min_frequency = Inf

        for idx in order
            c = complexities[idx]
            if 0 < c <= options.maxsize && !seen_complexities[c]
                seen_complexities[c] = true
                freq = running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c]
                if freq < min_frequency
                    min_frequency = freq
                    best_niche_idx = idx
                end
            end
        end

        if best_niche_idx > 0
            return pool[best_niche_idx]
        end
    end

    # Standard geometric tournament selection over diversity-adjusted costs
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(adjusted_costs)
    else
        ranks = collect(0:(n - 1))
        probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        selected_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)

        if selected_rank == 1
            argmin_fast(adjusted_costs)
        else
            bottomk_fast(adjusted_costs, selected_rank)[2][end]
        end
    end

    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen33_.name: clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen33_3
clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen33_.code:
"""
    clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen33_3(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Simplified crowding-aware tournament selection.

Core idea (kept from the parent): sample a slightly enlarged tournament pool, penalize
members that look like phenotypic duplicates of a *better* pool member, and occasionally
make an explicit "niche move" that selects the best representative of the rarest
complexity band so that starved complexity levels get repopulated.

Steps:

 1. Sample `1.5 * tournament_selection_n` members and compute the standard
    adaptive-parsimony-adjusted costs.
 2. For each member, count how many strictly better members share its complexity and
    have essentially the same loss. This count is a cheap proxy for redundancy
    (clones / phenotypic duplicates).
 3. Multiply the adjusted cost by `crowding_penalty^count` in a sign-safe way, so
    duplicates fall down the tournament ladder.
 4. With a small fixed probability, do a niche move: keep the best representative of
    each complexity, restrict to the better half of those representatives (quality
    gate), and return the one whose complexity is rarest per
    `normalized_frequencies`.
 5. Otherwise run the usual geometric tournament ladder on the adjusted scores.

Removed / merged relative to the parent:

  * Lineage (parent/sibling) suppression was dropped. It required extra similarity
    conditions and only contributed a fractional weight, so nearly all of its effect
    is already captured by the clone test; shared ancestry alone does not imply
    redundancy.
  * The youth/recency discount was dropped. It was a small multiplicative nudge
    (<=3%) that rarely changed tournament ranks, and it needed a full pass to compute
    the birth range.
  * The crowding-adaptive niche probability was folded into a single fixed
    probability, and the quality gate was simplified from two-thirds to one-half of
    the niche champions.

The result keeps the two mechanisms that actually break monopolies -- duplicate
suppression and quality-gated complexity-niche exploration -- at a fraction of the
bookkeeping cost.
"""
function clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_gen33_3(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Tunables: only two remain after simplification.
    pool_scale = 1.5
    crowding_penalty = 1.35
    clone_loss_rtol = 1e-6
    niche_probability = 0.10

    # Slightly enlarged pool so duplicates and niche occupancy are observable.
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # Standard adaptive-parsimony-adjusted costs plus cached complexities.
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity])
            else
                zero(L)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Duplicate counting: walk best-to-worst so only better members set the baseline.
    order = sortperm(scores)
    duplicate_count = zeros(Int, n)

    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        count = 0
        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(max(abs(li), abs(lj)), eps(L))
            # Equal complexity + (nearly) equal loss is our phenotype-duplication proxy.
            if complexities[i] == complexities[j] &&
                abs(li - lj) <= L(clone_loss_rtol) * loss_scale
                count += 1
            end
        end
        duplicate_count[i] = count
    end

    # Sign-safe multiplicative penalty: factor > 1 always worsens the score.
    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        factor = L(crowding_penalty^duplicate_count[i])
        penalized[i] = if scores[i] > zero(L)
            scores[i] * factor
        elseif scores[i] < zero(L)
            scores[i] / factor
        else
            scores[i]
        end
    end

    # Occasional niche move: repopulate the rarest complexity band with a decent member.
    if rand() < niche_probability
        penalized_order = sortperm(penalized)
        seen = falses(options.maxsize)
        champions = Int[]

        # Best representative of each valid complexity, in quality order.
        for i in penalized_order
            complexity = complexities[i]
            if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize && !seen[complexity]
                seen[complexity] = true
                push!(champions, i)
            end
        end

        if !isempty(champions)
            # Quality gate: only consider the better half of the champions.
            gate = max(1, cld(length(champions), 2))
            best_idx = champions[1]
            best_frequency = Float64(
                running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexities[best_idx]]
            )

            for position in 2:gate
                i = champions[position]
                frequency = Float64(
                    running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexities[i]]
                )
                # Champions are already sorted by quality, so ties keep the better member.
                if frequency < best_frequency
                    best_idx = i
                    best_frequency = frequency
                end
            end

            return pool[best_idx]
        end
    end

    # Standard geometric tournament ladder over the duplicate-adjusted scores.
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        ranks = collect(0:(n - 1))
        probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        selected_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)

        if selected_rank == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, selected_rank)[2][end]
        end
    end

    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

age_diversity_survival_pareto_shield_sim.name: age_diversity_survival_pareto_shield_simple_gen26_1_gen33_4
age_diversity_survival_pareto_shield_sim.code:
"""
    age_diversity_survival_pareto_shield_simple_gen26_1_gen33_4(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[]) -> Int

Further-simplified Pareto-shielded age-based survival.

Core idea (kept from the parent): protect the cheap Pareto frontier — the
lowest-cost member(s) at each distinct complexity value — from random age-death,
so structurally distinct scaffolds of several sizes survive as recombination
material, while everything else still turns over under age pressure.

Steps:
1. Two flat O(n) passes build the shield instead of the parent's single pass
   with index-tracking/unshield bookkeeping: pass one records, per complexity,
   the minimum cost seen (`Dict{Int,L}`, no index bookkeeping); pass two flags
   `shielded[i] = true` whenever member `i`'s cost equals its complexity's
   minimum. This removes the branchy "new champion found, unshield the old
   one" logic entirely, at the (irrelevant) cost of a second cheap pass — and
   as a side effect it protects *all* co-cheapest members at a complexity, not
   just the last one seen, which changes results on tied inputs.
2. Draw `n_sample = clamp(tournament_selection_n, 2, n)` uniform random slots
   and return the oldest one that is neither excluded nor shielded — the same
   allocation-free soft age pressure as the parent.
3. Single fallback: if no legal slot was sampled, scan the whole population
   once and return the oldest non-excluded member, ignoring the shield.

Removed/merged relative to the parent:
* The single-pass "track current champion index, unshield the previous
  champion when beaten" logic is replaced by two straightforward passes with
  no conditional unshielding — fewer branches, easier to reason about, and it
  now shields cost-ties together rather than only the most-recently-seen one.
* The parent's already-collapsed single fallback scan is kept as-is (it was
  already the minimal sound fallback), so no further merging was needed there.
"""
function age_diversity_survival_pareto_shield_simple_gen26_1_gen33_4(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    BT = typeof(first(pop.members).birth)

    # ---- Step 1a: cheapest cost seen per complexity (no index bookkeeping). ----
    min_cost_at_c = Dict{Int,L}()
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        c = compute_complexity(pop.members[i], options)
        complexities[i] = c
        prev = get(min_cost_at_c, c, nothing)
        if prev === nothing || pop.members[i].cost < prev
            min_cost_at_c[c] = pop.members[i].cost
        end
    end

    # ---- Step 1b: shield every member matching its complexity's minimum. ----
    shielded = fill(false, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        shielded[i] = pop.members[i].cost <= min_cost_at_c[complexities[i]]
    end

    best_idx = 0
    best_birth = typemax(BT)

    # ---- Step 2: sampled age pressure over unprotected slots only. ----
    n_sample = min(n, max(2, options.tournament_selection_n))
    @inbounds for _ in 1:n_sample
        i = rand(1:n)
        shielded[i] && continue
        (i in exclude_indices) && continue
        b = pop.members[i].birth
        if best_idx == 0 || b < best_birth
            best_idx = i
            best_birth = b
        end
    end

    # ---- Step 3: single fallback — oldest non-excluded member, shield relaxed. ----
    if best_idx == 0
        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue
            b = pop.members[i].birth
            if best_idx == 0 || b < best_birth
                best_idx = i
                best_birth = b
            end
        end
    end

    return best_idx
end

motif_duplication_accumulator_gen33_5.name: motif_duplication_accumulator_gen33_5
motif_duplication_accumulator_gen33_5.code:
"""
    motif_duplication_accumulator_gen33_5(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Duplicate a variable-bearing subtree and attach the clone to a random target using `+` or `*`.
This preserves the central motif-reuse idea: evolved forms can be repeated on the same variables
(to create squares and repeated terms) or shifted to another feature block.

Steps:
1. Find the available commutative accumulation operators (`+` and `*`) and compute the remaining
   size budget.
2. Sample any variable-bearing subtree that fits the budget and clone it.
3. Optionally shift every feature in the clone by one random cyclic offset.
4. Replace a random target with `target + motif` or `target * motif`.

Compared with the parent, this removes the rational wrapping template, its constant and denominator
construction, and the compound-versus-leaf donor tiers. A single donor filter and coupling path are
used instead. This remains sound because additive repetition, products, squares, and cross-feature
symmetries are broadly useful across symbolic-regression tasks, while rational forms can still be
assembled by ordinary operator mutations without making every duplication substantially larger.
"""
function motif_duplication_accumulator_gen33_5(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Restrict coupling to stable, commutative motif accumulators.
    binops = options.operators.binops
    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op === (+), binops)
    idx_mul = findfirst(op -> op === (*), binops)

    accumulators = Int[]
    idx_add !== nothing && push!(accumulators, idx_add)
    idx_mul !== nothing && push!(accumulators, idx_mul)
    isempty(accumulators) && return tree

    # Wrapping a target adds one operator plus the complete donor clone.
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    budget = maxsize - count_nodes(tree) - 1
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # Use one broad donor pool: the motif must fit and contain a variable.
    fits(t) =
        count_nodes(t) <= budget &&
        any(node -> node.degree == 0 && !node.constant, t)

    any(fits, tree) || return tree
    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=fits))
    motif = copy(donor)

    # Either preserve the variables or replicate the same form on another cyclic block.
    if nfeatures > 1 && rand(rng, Bool)
        shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))

        function shift_features!(node)
            if node.degree == 0
                if !node.constant
                    node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeatures)
                end
            else
                for i in 1:(node.degree)
                    shift_features!(get_child(node, i))
                end
            end
            return node
        end

        shift_features!(motif)
    end

    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    op = rand(rng, accumulators)
    replacement = constructorof(N)(;
        op=op,
        children=(copy(target), motif),
    )

    set_node!(target, replacement)
    return tree
end

streamlined_motif_duplication_gen33_6.name: streamlined_motif_duplication_gen33_6
streamlined_motif_duplication_gen33_6.code:
"""
    streamlined_motif_duplication_gen33_6(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Streamlined structural mutation that reuses evolved subexpressions (motifs). It clones a
donor subtree, optionally shifts its feature indices to exploit symmetry across variables,
and couples it with a target node either as an algebraic combination (`target ⊕ motif`)
or inside a self-referential rational saturation template (`target / (1 + motif)`).

# Core Idea
Evolution often discovers useful functional building blocks (e.g., `x1*x2^2`, `x-y`, or coordinate
distances) in one part of an expression. Duplicating these motifs—either translated to other
variables or coupled into saturation denominators—allows the search to quickly build complex
symmetric and rational physical laws (e.g., Compton scattering, Michaelis–Menten) without
needing to independently re-evolve identical structure.

# Steps
1. Guard: Ensure at least one binary operator exists.
2. Locate binary operators (`+`, `*`, `/`) using standard lookup.
3. Determine coupling mode (rational template `target / (1 + motif)` vs plain binary coupling `target ⊕ motif`).
4. Sample target and donor subtrees, ensuring the resulting tree fits within `options.maxsize`.
5. Shift features: With 60% probability, apply a cyclic feature shift `f → (f + k) mod n` to replicate
   the functional motif across other variables; otherwise preserve identity for powers and self-couplings.
6. Couple the motif into the target node and return the modified tree.

# Simplifications from Parent
- **Removed 3-pass tiered donor filtering**: Eliminated multi-pass `count(...)` filtering and fallback
  cascades in favor of direct node sampling with an exact, non-allocating size budget check.
- **Unified feature remapping**: Dropped the dedicated targeted feature substitution branch and feature
  vector allocations, collapsing variable transformation into a single recursive cyclic shift.
- **Streamlined operator lookup and coupling**: Replaced custom loops and preference array allocations
  with idiomatic `findfirst` and a canonical `1 + motif` denominator structure.
"""
function streamlined_motif_duplication_gen33_6(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Guard: requires at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # Locate common binary operators
    binops = options.operators.binops
    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op == (+), binops)
    idx_mul = findfirst(op -> op == (*), binops)
    idx_div = findfirst(op -> op == (/), binops)

    # Decide whether to build a rational saturation template: target / (1 + motif)
    use_rational = (idx_div !== nothing) && (idx_add !== nothing) && (rand(rng) < 0.35)
    extra_nodes = use_rational ? 3 : 1  # div + add + 1.0 vs single binary op

    # Select target to replace and donor subtree to clone
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))

    # Admissibility check against max complexity budget
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    motif_size = count_nodes(donor)
    if tree_size + motif_size + extra_nodes > maxsize
        return tree
    end

    motif = copy(donor)

    # In-place helper for shifting feature indices
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeatures)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Remap features: shift variables across coordinates or retain identity for self-couplings
    if nfeatures > 1 && rand(rng) < 0.60
        shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
        _shift_features!(motif, shift)
    end

    target_copy = copy(target)

    # Couple the motif into the tree
    new_node = if use_rational
        # Self-referential rational template: target / (1 + motif)
        c = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
        den = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_add, children=(c, motif))
        constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(target_copy, den))
    else
        # Plain algebraic coupling biased toward + and *
        bin_op = if idx_add !== nothing && idx_mul !== nothing
            rand(rng, Bool) ? idx_add : idx_mul
        elseif idx_add !== nothing
            idx_add
        elseif idx_mul !== nothing
            idx_mul
        else
            rand(rng, 1:options.nops[2])
        end
        children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
        constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children)
    end

    set_node!(target, new_node)
    return tree
end

age_cost_cohort_survival_gen33_7.name: age_cost_cohort_survival_gen33_7
age_cost_cohort_survival_gen33_7.code:
"""
    age_cost_cohort_survival_gen33_7(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

A streamlined survival operator combining age regularization with cost-aware pruning.
Rather than computing full dual ranking vectors across the entire population and blending
them with floating-point weights, this operator simplifies the process into two clear steps:
1. Sort eligible members by birth order to identify the oldest cohort (the top candidates
   for replacement under age-regularized evolution).
2. Evict the member within this oldest cohort that has the worst (highest) cost.

Modifications & Simplifications from Parent:
- Removed global cost-ranking, normalized rank vectors, and floating-point weight blending (0.75 / 0.25).
- Replaced the continuous multi-criteria score with a discrete two-stage selection: oldest cohort
  filtering followed by maximum-cost selection.

Why this simplification is sound:
Age regularization's core benefit is protecting newly minted offspring from premature elimination.
By restricting fitness-based eviction strictly to the oldest cohort, young individuals remain fully
protected, while stale, poorly performing, or bloated individuals within the senior population are
preferentially discarded over high-performing veterans.
"""
function age_cost_cohort_survival_gen33_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Filter out excluded indices
    eligible = [i for i in 1:(pop.n) if !(i in exclude_indices)]
    @assert !isempty(eligible) "No eligible members to replace"

    # Sort eligible indices by birth ascending (oldest members first)
    sort!(eligible, by=i -> pop.members[i].birth)

    # Restrict candidate pool to the oldest cohort (top ~25% oldest, at least 2 when possible)
    k = min(length(eligible), max(2, div(length(eligible), 4)))
    oldest_cohort = @view eligible[1:k]

    # Return the index of the oldest cohort member with the highest (worst) cost
    return argmax(i -> pop.members[i].cost, oldest_cohort)
end

scaled_affine_correlation_loss_gen33_9.name: scaled_affine_correlation_loss_gen33_9
scaled_affine_correlation_loss_gen33_9.code:
"""
    scaled_affine_correlation_loss_gen33_9(tree, dataset, options)

Compare prediction and target shape through the sine of their centered correlation
angle, which is equivalent to the normalized residual of the best affine fit.
A first pass validates values and finds safe scales; a second pass computes scaled
Welford moments together with raw error. A small bounded raw-NRMSE term then favors
the correctly calibrated representative among affine-equivalent expressions.
Constant targets fall back to scale-normalized raw error.

This simplifies the parent by avoiding explicit slope/intercept fitting and a
separate fitted-residual accumulation. It also removes compensated summation and
relative variability heuristics, and collapses raw-error overflow handling to simple
saturation. The correlation identity retains the affine-profile objective while the
scaled moments provide inexpensive numerical stability.
"""
function scaled_affine_correlation_loss_gen33_9(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    # Validate the evaluated data and obtain scales before computing moments.
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end
        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))
    end

    p_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_p)
    y_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_y)

    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l
    raw_overflowed = false

    # Scaling bounds the values used by Welford's online moment updates.
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        ps = p / p_scale
        ys = y / y_scale

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = ps - mean_p
        delta_y = ys - mean_y
        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        m2_p += delta_p * (ps - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (ys - mean_y)
        cov_py += delta_p * (ys - mean_y)

        # Raw error uses the target scale so it can be compared with target spread.
        if !raw_overflowed
            raw_residual = p / y_scale - ys
            raw_term = raw_residual * raw_residual
            updated = raw_sum + raw_term
            if isfinite(raw_term) && isfinite(updated)
                raw_sum = updated
            else
                raw_overflowed = true
            end
        end
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Remove harmless negative roundoff from sums of squares.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    if m2_y == zero_l
        # Affine shape is undefined for a constant target.
        if raw_overflowed
            return L(Inf)
        end
        raw_mse = max(raw_sum / L(n), zero_l)
        loss_value = log1p(raw_mse)
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
    end

    # The residual sine sqrt(1 - ρ²) profiles out both affine slope and offset.
    shape_term = one_l
    if m2_p > zero_l
        denominator = sqrt(m2_p) * sqrt(m2_y)
        if !(isfinite(denominator) && denominator > zero_l)
            return L(Inf)
        end
        abs_correlation = clamp(abs(cov_py) / denominator, zero_l, one_l)
        shape_term = sqrt(max(one_l - abs_correlation * abs_correlation, zero_l))
    end

    # Saturated raw NRMSE breaks ties without overwhelming the shape objective.
    bounded_raw = if raw_overflowed
        one_l
    else
        raw_norm = sqrt(max(raw_sum, zero_l))
        target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)
        raw_norm / (raw_norm + target_norm)
    end

    loss_value = shape_term + bounded_raw / L(256)
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

clone_suppressed_quality_niche_tournamen.name: clone_suppressed_quality_niche_tournament_gen34_6
clone_suppressed_quality_niche_tournamen.code:
"""
    clone_suppressed_quality_niche_tournament_gen34_6(
        pop, running_search_statistics, options
    )

Simplified diversity-aware tournament selection retaining the parent's two strongest
ideas: direct clone suppression and quality-gated complexity-niche exploration.

The operator:

1. Samples a modestly enlarged tournament pool and computes the standard
   adaptive-parsimony-adjusted costs.
2. Processes candidates from best to worst and applies one fixed penalty to later
   members with the same complexity and nearly identical loss.
3. With a small fixed probability, selects the rarest complexity among the better
   two-thirds of complexity champions; otherwise it uses the usual geometric
   tournament ranking.

Lineage penalties, birth-based discounts, accumulated crowding weights, and
crowding-dependent niche probabilities are removed. These signals add tuning and
can suppress useful descendants despite structural differences. Direct phenotype
duplication remains the clearest inexpensive redundancy signal, while the
quality-gated niche step preserves controlled exploration of underrepresented
complexities.
"""
function clone_suppressed_quality_niche_tournament_gen34_6(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    pool_scale = 1.5
    clone_loss_rtol = L(1e-6)
    clone_penalty = L(1.35)
    niche_probability = 0.10

    # A slightly larger pool makes local duplication and complexity coverage visible.
    base_size = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(base_size, round(Int, pool_scale * base_size)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    adjusted_scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity])
            else
                zero(L)
            end
            adjusted_scores[i] =
                member.cost * exp(parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            adjusted_scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Penalize each later near-duplicate once rather than accumulating several
    # ancestry and crowding terms.
    base_order = sortperm(adjusted_scores)
    for position in 2:n
        i = base_order[position]
        loss_i = pool[i].loss
        is_duplicate = false

        for earlier_position in 1:(position - 1)
            j = base_order[earlier_position]
            complexities[i] == complexities[j] || continue

            loss_j = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(abs(loss_i), abs(loss_j), eps(L))
            if abs(loss_i - loss_j) <= clone_loss_rtol * loss_scale
                is_duplicate = true
                break
            end
        end

        if is_duplicate
            # Keep the penalty sign-safe: it always makes the score less favorable.
            if adjusted_scores[i] > zero(L)
                adjusted_scores[i] *= clone_penalty
            elseif adjusted_scores[i] < zero(L)
                adjusted_scores[i] /= clone_penalty
            end
        end
    end

    ranked_indices = sortperm(adjusted_scores)

    if rand() < niche_probability
        # Keep only the best adjusted-score representative of each complexity.
        seen_complexities = falses(options.maxsize)
        niche_champions = Int[]

        for i in ranked_indices
            complexity = complexities[i]
            if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize &&
                !seen_complexities[complexity]
                seen_complexities[complexity] = true
                push!(niche_champions, i)
            end
        end

        if !isempty(niche_champions)
            # Restrict rarity-based exploration to reasonably competitive niches.
            quality_count = max(1, cld(2 * length(niche_champions), 3))
            selected_idx = niche_champions[1]
            selected_frequency = Float64(
                running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[
                    complexities[selected_idx]
                ],
            )

            for position in 2:quality_count
                i = niche_champions[position]
                frequency = Float64(
                    running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[
                        complexities[i]
                    ],
                )

                if frequency < selected_frequency ||
                    (frequency == selected_frequency &&
                     adjusted_scores[i] < adjusted_scores[selected_idx])
                    selected_idx = i
                    selected_frequency = frequency
                end
            end

            return pool[selected_idx]
        end
    end

    # Select directly from the sorted ranking using the standard geometric ladder.
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    selected_rank = if p == 1.0
        1
    else
        ranks = collect(0:(n - 1))
        probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        StatsBase.sample(weights)
    end

    return pool[ranked_indices[selected_rank]]
end

clone_gated_niche_tournament_gen19_gen34.name: clone_gated_niche_tournament_gen19_gen34_4
clone_gated_niche_tournament_gen19_gen34.code:
"""
    clone_gated_niche_tournament_gen19_gen34_4(
        pop, running_search_statistics, options
    )

Simplified crowding-aware tournament selection that keeps only the two most
impactful ideas from the parent operator: clone suppression and adaptive
complexity-niche exploration. Lineage/family-based partial suppression and the
crowding-attenuated youth discount are removed, since clone detection alone
captures most of the redundancy signal, and a flat youth nudge is simpler and
nearly as effective without the extra attenuation term.

Steps:
 1. Sample an enlarged tournament pool and compute the usual
    adaptive-parsimony-adjusted scores.
 2. For each member, count how many *better* members in the pool are
    near-duplicates (same complexity, nearly identical loss). This is the only
    crowding signal used (lineage-based partial penalties are dropped as a
    minor, redundant heuristic).
 3. Apply a multiplicative penalty proportional to clone count, plus a small
    flat youth discount for newer members (no attenuation by crowding weight,
    since clones are already penalized directly).
 4. With probability that grows with observed clone crowding, perform a niche
    move: keep the best representative of each complexity, then pick whichever
    of those representatives has the rarest complexity (dropping the parent's
    extra "best two-thirds" quality gate, since the representatives are already
    the best-in-niche and thus reasonably safe).
 5. Otherwise, run the standard geometric tournament ladder on the adjusted
    scores.
"""
function clone_gated_niche_tournament_gen19_gen34_4(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Mild tunables: clone evidence dominates, youth is a small nudge.
    pool_scale = 1.5
    crowding_penalty = 1.35
    clone_loss_rtol = 1e-6
    youth_discount = 0.03
    niche_probability_base = 0.08
    niche_probability_boost = 0.10
    niche_probability_max = 0.18

    # Sample a larger pool so local crowding and niche occupancy are observable.
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # Compute complexity and the default adaptive-parsimony-adjusted score.
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity])
            else
                zero(L)
            end
            scores[i] =
                member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Clone-only crowding: count better members that are near-duplicates.
    order = sortperm(scores)
    crowding = zeros(Float64, n)

    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        scale_i = max(abs(li), eps(L))
        weight = 0.0

        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(scale_i, abs(lj))

            same_phenotype =
                complexities[i] == complexities[j] &&
                abs(li - lj) <= L(clone_loss_rtol) * loss_scale

            if same_phenotype
                weight += 1.0
            end
        end

        crowding[i] = weight
    end

    # Find the age range once; recency is used only as a mild novelty preference.
    birth_min = pool[1].birth
    birth_max = pool[1].birth
    for i in 2:n
        birth = pool[i].birth
        birth < birth_min && (birth_min = birth)
        birth > birth_max && (birth_max = birth)
    end
    birth_span = max(birth_max - birth_min, 1)

    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    crowded_count = 0

    for i in 1:n
        redundancy = crowding[i]
        redundancy > 0.0 && (crowded_count += 1)

        recency = (pool[i].birth - birth_min) / birth_span

        # Clone penalty dominates; youth is a flat, unattenuated nudge.
        factor = crowding_penalty^redundancy * (1.0 - youth_discount * recency)
        typed_factor = L(factor)

        # Sign-safe adjustment: larger factors always make the score less fit.
        penalized[i] = if scores[i] > zero(L)
            scores[i] * typed_factor
        elseif scores[i] < zero(L)
            scores[i] / typed_factor
        else
            scores[i]
        end
    end

    # Increase explicit niche exploration when the sampled pool shows monopoly.
    crowded_fraction = crowded_count / n
    niche_probability = min(
        niche_probability_max,
        niche_probability_base + niche_probability_boost * crowded_fraction,
    )

    if rand() < niche_probability
        # Keep one best representative per valid complexity niche.
        penalized_order = sortperm(penalized)
        seen_complexities = falses(options.maxsize)
        niche_champions = Int[]

        for i in penalized_order
            complexity = complexities[i]
            if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize && !seen_complexities[complexity]
                seen_complexities[complexity] = true
                push!(niche_champions, i)
            end
        end

        if !isempty(niche_champions)
            # Pick whichever representative belongs to the rarest complexity.
            best_idx = niche_champions[1]
            best_frequency = Float64(
                running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexities[best_idx]]
            )

            for position in 2:length(niche_champions)
                i = niche_champions[position]
                frequency = Float64(
                    running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexities[i]]
                )

                if frequency < best_frequency
                    best_idx = i
                    best_frequency = frequency
                end
            end

            return pool[best_idx]
        end
    end

    # Standard geometric tournament ladder over diversity-adjusted scores.
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        ranks = collect(0:(n - 1))
        probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        selected_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)

        if selected_rank == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, selected_rank)[2][end]
        end
    end

    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

oldest_dominated_survival_gen34_8.name: oldest_dominated_survival_gen34_8
oldest_dominated_survival_gen34_8.code:
"""
    oldest_dominated_survival_gen34_8(pop::Population{T,L,N}, options::AbstractOptions; exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[])::Int where {T,L,N}

Selects an individual for replacement using a simplified combination of Pareto protection
and age-regularized turnover.

The operator first removes the oldest eligible member with non-finite loss or cost. Otherwise,
it replaces the oldest member weakly dominated in `(complexity, loss)` space, falling back to
the oldest eligible member when the entire eligible population is non-dominated. Objective
ties are considered dominated when another equivalent member exists, providing a lightweight
form of niche desaturation without a complexity histogram.

Compared with the parent, this removes age normalization, congestion scores, logarithmic
penalties, and tuned Pareto multipliers. Using age only as a tie-breaker between dominated
members preserves Pareto stepping stones while retaining steady population renewal.
"""
function oldest_dominated_survival_gen34_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T,L,N}
    n = pop.n
    n == 0 && return 1

    BT = typeof(pop.members[1].birth)
    oldest_idx = 0
    oldest_birth = typemax(BT)
    invalid_idx = 0
    invalid_birth = typemax(BT)

    # Find the oldest legal candidate and prioritize invalid individuals.
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        i in exclude_indices && continue

        member = pop.members[i]
        if member.birth < oldest_birth
            oldest_birth = member.birth
            oldest_idx = i
        end

        if (!isfinite(member.loss) || !isfinite(member.cost)) &&
           member.birth < invalid_birth
            invalid_birth = member.birth
            invalid_idx = i
        end
    end

    oldest_idx == 0 && throw(ArgumentError("exclude_indices contains every population index"))
    invalid_idx != 0 && return invalid_idx

    # Only finite members can define or dominate the loss-complexity frontier.
    finite_member = Vector{Bool}(undef, n)
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        member = pop.members[i]
        finite_member[i] = isfinite(member.loss) && isfinite(member.cost)
        complexities[i] = finite_member[i] ? compute_complexity(member, options) : 0
    end

    dominated_idx = 0
    dominated_birth = typemax(BT)

    # Replace the oldest weakly dominated candidate. Including exact objective
    # ties makes redundant copies replaceable without an explicit niche count.
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        (i in exclude_indices || !finite_member[i]) && continue

        c_i = complexities[i]
        loss_i = pop.members[i].loss
        dominated = false

        for j in 1:n
            (j == i || !finite_member[j]) && continue

            if complexities[j] <= c_i && pop.members[j].loss <= loss_i
                dominated = true
                break
            end
        end

        if dominated && pop.members[i].birth < dominated_birth
            dominated_birth = pop.members[i].birth
            dominated_idx = i
        end
    end

    return dominated_idx == 0 ? oldest_idx : dominated_idx
end

simplified_affine_profile_loss_gen34_7.name: simplified_affine_profile_loss_gen34_7
simplified_affine_profile_loss_gen34_7.code:
"""
    simplified_affine_profile_loss_gen34_7(tree, dataset, options)

Score predictions by the residual of their best affine calibration, preserving the
parent operator's preference for expressions with the correct functional shape.
The loss computes sample means, fits a least-squares slope from centered moments,
and directly evaluates the calibrated residual. A small bounded raw-NRMSE term
then favors expressions whose constants are already correctly calibrated.

This streamlined version removes compensated summation, scale-aware prediction
variability heuristics, the separate constant-target loss, and the raw-overflow
state machine. Constant targets are handled through a shared regularized target
norm, while exactly constant predictions simply use a zero slope. The bounded
raw term uses NRMSE rather than NMSE, making this operator functionally distinct
while retaining zero loss only for exact target predictions.
"""
function simplified_affine_profile_loss_gen34_7(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # First pass: online means avoid overflow-prone raw sums.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        k = L(i)
        mean_p += (p - mean_p) / k
        mean_y += (y - mean_y) / k
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Second pass: centered moments for the affine least-squares slope.
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        dp = L(prediction[i]) - mean_p
        dy = L(dataset.y[i]) - mean_y
        m2_p += dp * dp
        m2_y += dy * dy
        cov_py += dp * dy
    end

    if !(isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # A small scale-relative floor handles constant and nearly constant targets
    # without a separate loss branch.
    target_scale = max(one_l, abs(mean_y))
    target_floor = sqrt(eps(L)) * sqrt(n_l) * target_scale
    target_norm = max(sqrt(max(m2_y, zero_l)), target_floor)
    if !(isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Exactly constant predictions cannot supply a meaningful affine direction.
    slope = m2_p > zero_l ? cov_py / m2_p : zero_l
    if !isfinite(slope)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Third pass: direct residual evaluation remains accurate near an exact fit.
    affine_sum = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        fitted = mean_y + slope * (p - mean_p)
        affine_residual = (fitted - y) / target_norm
        affine_term = affine_residual * affine_residual

        if !(isfinite(fitted) && isfinite(affine_term))
            return L(Inf)
        end
        affine_sum += affine_term
        if !isfinite(affine_sum)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        raw_residual = p - y
        if !isfinite(raw_residual)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Raw overflow is harmless because this component is intentionally bounded.
        raw_normalized = raw_residual / target_norm
        raw_sum += raw_normalized * raw_normalized
    end

    shape_term = sqrt(clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l))

    bounded_raw = if isfinite(raw_sum)
        raw_nrmse = sqrt(max(raw_sum, zero_l))
        raw_nrmse / (one_l + raw_nrmse)
    else
        one_l
    end

    loss_value = shape_term + bounded_raw / L(256)
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

motif_duplication_rational_lean_gen34_0.name: motif_duplication_rational_lean_gen34_0
motif_duplication_rational_lean_gen34_0.code:
"""
    motif_duplication_rational_lean_gen34_0(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Lean structural mutation that **reuses evolved structure**: it clones a *compound* subexpression
(a "motif"), optionally shifts its feature indices, and couples the clone back into the tree either
as a plain accumulation (`target + motif` / `target * motif`) or inside a self-referential rational
template (`target / (1 - motif)`).

# Core idea
Ground-truth laws repeat the same functional form across different variables
(`0.5*m*(vx^2+vy^2)`, `(x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2`), so duplicating a subtree the search already found is
much cheaper than rediscovering it. The rational template additionally reaches saturating /
correction forms (`u/(1-v)`: Michaelis-Menten, relativistic factors, feedback gains) that point
mutations cannot construct, because they need the *same kind* of subexpression in numerator and
denominator.

# Steps
1. Guard on the existence of binary operators and look up `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` once.
2. Compute a single conservative size budget for the donor motif: `maxsize - size(tree) - 3`
   (3 extra nodes is the worst case, i.e. the rational template).
3. Flip a coin between the two coupling templates (rational only if `/` and `-` exist, plain only if
   `+` or `*` exists).
4. Sample a donor motif uniformly among *compound* (degree > 0), variable-bearing subtrees that fit
   the budget; if there is none, return the tree unchanged.
5. With probability 1/2 cyclically shift all feature indices of the clone (replicating the form on a
   different variable block); otherwise keep it identical (yielding squares `u*u` and self-couplings
   `u/(1-u)`).
6. Splice at a uniformly random target node.

# What was simplified relative to the parent (and why it is sound)
- **Two donor tiers → one.** The fallback tier that accepted bare variable leaves is dropped: a
  single-leaf motif produces `target + x` / `target * x` / `target/(1-x)`, which ordinary
  insert/point mutations already generate cheaply. The compound tier carries all the structural
  information this operator exists for.
- **Two size budgets → one uniform budget.** Instead of tracking `size+1` for the plain coupling and
  `size+3` for the rational one, the worst-case budget (`-3`) is used for both. This only makes the
  plain coupling marginally more conservative near `maxsize`, while removing a branch and the
  template/budget coupling entirely.
- **Template probability 0.35 → fair coin flip.** One fewer magic constant; the rational template is
  the mode that unlocks otherwise-unreachable forms, so giving it equal weight is at least as good.
- **Feasibility bookkeeping folded in.** `rational_ok` no longer re-derives a template-specific size
  test, since the single budget already guarantees admissibility for both templates.
"""
function motif_duplication_rational_lean_gen34_0(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # ------------------------------------------------ Step 1: guard + one-shot operator lookup
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree
    binops = options.operators.binops
    nbin = options.nops[2]
    find_op(f) = findfirst(i -> binops[i] === f, 1:nbin)
    idx_add = find_op(+)
    idx_sub = find_op(-)
    idx_mul = find_op(*)
    idx_div = find_op(/)

    # Canonical (commutative) accumulator for the plain coupling; `nothing` if neither exists
    accum = if idx_add !== nothing && idx_mul !== nothing
        rand(rng, Bool) ? idx_add : idx_mul
    elseif idx_add !== nothing
        idx_add
    else
        idx_mul
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------ Step 2: single conservative size budget
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    # Worst case (rational template) adds 3 nodes on top of the motif
    budget = maxsize - count_nodes(tree) - 3
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # ------------------------------------------------ Step 3: coupling template (fair coin)
    rational_ok = (idx_div !== nothing) && (idx_sub !== nothing)
    use_rational = rational_ok && (accum === nothing || rand(rng, Bool))
    (!use_rational && accum === nothing) && return tree

    # ------------------------------------------------ Step 4: donor motif (single tier)
    # Only compound, variable-bearing subtrees that fit the budget carry useful structure
    usable(t) =
        t.degree > 0 &&
        count_nodes(t) <= budget &&
        any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, t)

    count(usable, tree) == 0 && return tree
    motif = copy(rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=usable)))  # copy before editing the tree

    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))

    # ------------------------------------------------ Step 5: optional cyclic feature shift
    function shift_features!(node, shift)
        if node.degree == 0
            node.constant || (node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeatures))
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    if nfeatures > 1 && rand(rng, Bool)
        shift_features!(motif, rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1)))
    end

    # ------------------------------------------------ Step 6: splice the clone back in
    target_copy = copy(target)
    new_node = if use_rational
        # Saturation / correction factor: target / (1 - motif)
        one_leaf = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
        den = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_sub, children=(one_leaf, motif))
        constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(target_copy, den))
    else
        # Plain accumulation with a commutative operator: operand order is irrelevant
        constructorof(N)(; op=accum, children=(target_copy, motif))
    end

    set_node!(target, new_node)
    return tree
end

streamlined_motif_duplication_gen34_1.name: streamlined_motif_duplication_gen34_1
streamlined_motif_duplication_gen34_1.code:
"""
    streamlined_motif_duplication_gen34_1(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Streamlined structural mutation that clones an evolved subexpression motif, optionally shifts
its feature indices to exploit variable symmetries, and splices it into the tree via either a
rational correction template (`target / (1 - motif)`) or a plain algebraic coupling (`target ⊕ motif`).

# Core Idea
Physical laws frequently repeat functional patterns across variables (e.g., kinetic energy `0.5*m*(vx^2 + vy^2)`,
Euclidean distances `(x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2`) or incorporate relativistic/saturation correction factors
