    pool_scale = 1.5
    clone_loss_rtol = 1e-6
    clone_penalty = L(1.35)
    niche_probability = 0.10

    # A slightly larger pool makes local duplication and niche coverage visible.
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    # Start from the default frequency-adjusted tournament objective.
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity])
            else
                zero(L)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Retain the best representative of each near-identical phenotype and apply
    # only one penalty to every redundant alternative.
    base_order = sortperm(scores)
    is_clone = falses(n)

    for position in 2:n
        i = base_order[position]
        li = pool[i].loss

        for earlier_position in 1:(position - 1)
            j = base_order[earlier_position]
            complexities[i] == complexities[j] || continue

            lj = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(abs(li), abs(lj), eps(L))
            if abs(li - lj) <= L(clone_loss_rtol) * loss_scale
                is_clone[i] = true
                break
            end
        end
    end

    adjusted_scores = copy(scores)
    for i in 1:n
        is_clone[i] || continue

        # Ensure the penalty worsens both positive and negative scores.
        if adjusted_scores[i] > zero(L)
            adjusted_scores[i] *= clone_penalty
        elseif adjusted_scores[i] < zero(L)
            adjusted_scores[i] /= clone_penalty
        end
    end

    ranking = sortperm(adjusted_scores)

    if rand() < niche_probability
        # Extract the best adjusted-score representative of each valid complexity.
        seen_complexities = falses(options.maxsize)
        niche_champions = Int[]

        for i in ranking
            complexity = complexities[i]
            if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize &&
                !seen_complexities[complexity]
                seen_complexities[complexity] = true
                push!(niche_champions, i)
            end
        end

        if !isempty(niche_champions)
            # Restrict rarity-based exploration to reasonably competitive niches.
            quality_count = max(1, cld(2 * length(niche_champions), 3))
            best_idx = niche_champions[1]
            best_frequency = running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[
                complexities[best_idx]
            ]

            for position in 2:quality_count
                i = niche_champions[position]
                frequency = running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[
                    complexities[i]
                ]

                if frequency < best_frequency ||
                    (frequency == best_frequency &&
                     adjusted_scores[i] < adjusted_scores[best_idx])
                    best_idx = i
                    best_frequency = frequency
                end
            end

            return pool[best_idx]
        end
    end

    # Standard geometric tournament selection over the adjusted ranking.
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    selected_rank = if p == 1.0
        1
    else
        ranks = 0:(n - 1)
        probabilities = p .* ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        StatsBase.sample(weights)
    end

    return pool[ranking[selected_rank]]
end

simplified_affine_profile_loss_gen36_5.name: simplified_affine_profile_loss_gen36_5
simplified_affine_profile_loss_gen36_5.code:
"""
    simplified_affine_profile_loss_gen36_5(tree, dataset, options)

Compare predictions with the target after fitting the least-squares affine calibration
`a * prediction + b`. Stable Welford moments determine the calibration, and a second
pass directly accumulates the normalized fitted-residual RMSE so near-exact structural
matches are not lost through variance subtraction. A small bounded raw NRMSE term
breaks ties in favor of expressions that already have the correct scale and offset.
Constant targets fall back to scale-normalized raw MSE.

This streamlined variant removes extrema tracking, compensated summation, and the
parent's separate overflow algebra. Mean-relative variability tests and ordinary
finite-checked accumulation retain the essential numerical safeguards at lower cost.
The raw tie-breaker uses bounded NRMSE rather than bounded NMSE, giving calibration a
clearer but still secondary role. No expression-complexity penalty is included.
"""
function simplified_affine_profile_loss_gen36_5(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # One-pass centered moments for the affine least-squares fit.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])
        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Remove harmless negative roundoff from centered sums of squares.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))
    std_p = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)
    std_y = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)

    prediction_scale = max(abs(mean_p), std_p)
    target_scale = max(abs(mean_y), std_y)
    prediction_is_variable = std_p > tolerance * prediction_scale
    target_is_variable = std_y > tolerance * target_scale

    if !target_is_variable
        # Affine shape contains no information for a constant target.
        normalization = max(one_l, abs(mean_y))
        raw_sum = zero_l

        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            residual = (L(prediction[i]) - L(dataset.y[i])) / normalization
            term = residual * residual
            raw_sum += term

            if !(isfinite(term) && isfinite(raw_sum))
                return L(Inf)
            end
        end

        loss_value = log1p(max(raw_sum / n_l, zero_l))
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
    end

    target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)
    if !(isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # A non-variable prediction is equivalent to fitting the target mean.
    slope = zero_l
    intercept = mean_y
    if prediction_is_variable
        slope = cov_py / m2_p
        intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_p
        if !(isfinite(slope) && isfinite(intercept))
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end

    affine_sum = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        raw_residual = p - y
        if !isfinite(raw_residual)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        # Raw overflow only saturates the bounded calibration term.
        raw_normalized = raw_residual / target_norm
        raw_sum += raw_normalized * raw_normalized

        fitted = muladd(slope, p, intercept)
        affine_normalized = (fitted - y) / target_norm
        affine_term = affine_normalized * affine_normalized
        affine_sum += affine_term

        if !(isfinite(fitted) && isfinite(affine_term) && isfinite(affine_sum))
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end

    # The fitted affine residual is normalized by the target's centered energy.
    shape_term = sqrt(clamp(affine_sum, zero_l, one_l))

    # A bounded raw NRMSE favors the correctly calibrated representative without
    # overwhelming the affine-invariant structural signal.
    raw_nrmse = isfinite(raw_sum) ? sqrt(max(raw_sum, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
    bounded_raw = isfinite(raw_nrmse) ?
        raw_nrmse / (one_l + raw_nrmse) :
        one_l

    calibration_weight = one_l / L(64)
    loss_value = shape_term + calibration_weight * bounded_raw

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

simple_budget_only_self_saturation_gen36.name: simple_budget_only_self_saturation_gen36_6
simple_budget_only_self_saturation_gen36.code:
"""
    simple_budget_only_self_saturation_gen36_6(tree, options, nfeatures, rng)

Duplicate a subtree `u` and replace it in place with the rational saturation scaffold
`u / (1 + u)`. The two copies are independent, so later point mutations can specialize
them into forms such as `u / (1 + u*v)` or `x0 / (1 + x0/(x1*x2^2))` — structures that
are essentially unreachable through single point mutations, but which dominate the
ground truth of many physics benchmarks (see the trace, where the search had to grope
its way towards exactly this rational shape).

Steps:
1. Require both `+` and `/` to exist among the binary operators.
2. Compute the remaining size budget (duplicating a subtree of size `s` costs `s + 3`).
3. Sample uniformly among nodes that fit the budget and are *not* a bare constant leaf.
4. Replace the sampled node with `u / (1 + u)` (independent copies).

Simplifications relative to the parent:
- The separate `has_variable` pre-scan over the whole tree is removed; feasibility is
  now decided by a single `count` over the eligibility predicate, which subsumes both
  the "something exists" and "something fits the budget" questions.
- The parent's eligibility predicate ran an `any(...)` traversal per candidate node to
  demand a variable somewhere inside the subtree. That is replaced by the O(1) local
  test "not a bare constant leaf". This is cheaper and slightly more permissive: a
  subtree such as `sin(c)` or `c1*c2` may now be saturated as well. That is sound —
  the scaffold is still a meaningful rational reparametrization, and only truly
  degenerate targets (a lone constant, where `c/(1+c)` is just another constant) are
  excluded, so no mutation budget is wasted on no-ops.
"""
function simple_budget_only_self_saturation_gen36_6(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    binops = options.operators.binops
    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op === (+), binops)
    idx_div = findfirst(op -> op === (/), binops)

    # The mutation only builds the rational saturation template, so both ops are needed.
    (idx_add === nothing || idx_div === nothing) && return tree

    # Replacing a subtree of size s by u/(1+u) adds s (the copy) + 3 (one, +, /) nodes.
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    budget = maxsize - count_nodes(tree) - 3
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # Single cheap predicate: fits the budget and is not a lone constant leaf
    # (saturating a bare constant would just be a constant reparametrization).
    _eligible(t) = !(t.degree == 0 && t.constant) && count_nodes(t) <= budget

    # One guard replaces the parent's two separate feasibility checks.
    count(_eligible, tree) == 0 && return tree

    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_eligible))

    # Copies are deliberately independent so later mutations can differentiate
    # numerator and denominator (e.g. u / (1 + u*v)).
    numerator = copy(target)
    motif = copy(target)
    one_node = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
    denominator = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_add, children=(one_node, motif))
    replacement = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(numerator, denominator))

    set_node!(target, replacement)
    return tree
end

simple_self_product_duplication_gen36_7.name: simple_self_product_duplication_gen36_7
simple_self_product_duplication_gen36_7.code:
"""
    simple_self_product_duplication_gen36_7(tree, options, nfeatures, rng)

Duplicate one variable-containing subtree `u` and replace it with `u * u`.

Steps:
1. Require multiplication.
2. Compute the remaining size budget.
3. Sample a variable-containing subtree whose duplicate fits.
4. Replace it with two independent copies joined by `*`.

This retains the parent's central subtree-duplication idea while removing the rational
scaffold, its constant node, and the need for both `+` and `/`. Self-products directly
introduce common squares and interaction terms; later mutations may independently
specialize either copy. `nfeatures` is retained for mutation-interface compatibility.
"""
function simple_self_product_duplication_gen36_7(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    binops = options.operators.binops
    idx_mul = findfirst(op -> op === (*), binops)
    idx_mul === nothing && return tree

    # Replacing a size-s subtree by u*u increases the tree size by s + 1.
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    budget = maxsize - count_nodes(tree) - 1
    budget < 1 && return tree

    has_variable = any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, tree)
    has_variable || return tree

    eligible(t) =
        count_nodes(t) <= budget &&
        any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, t)

    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=eligible))

    # Independent copies can later diverge into related but distinct factors.
    replacement = constructorof(N)(;
        op=idx_mul,
        children=(copy(target), copy(target)),
    )
    set_node!(target, replacement)
    return tree
end

motif_duplication_simple_rational_gen27_.name: motif_duplication_simple_rational_gen27_10_gen36_8
motif_duplication_simple_rational_gen27_.code:
"""
    motif_duplication_simple_rational_gen27_10_gen36_8(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Further simplified structural mutation: clone a variable-bearing subtree ("motif"), optionally shift
its feature indices, and splice the clone back either as a plain accumulation (`target + motif` /
`target * motif`) or inside a self-referential rational template (`target / (1 - motif)`).

# Core idea (unchanged from parent)
Reusing already-evolved substructure is cheaper than rediscovering it from scratch, and the
`u/(1-v)` template reaches saturating/correction forms (Michaelis-Menten, relativistic factors,
feedback gains) that ordinary point mutations essentially cannot build because they require the
*same* subexpression to appear in numerator and denominator.

# Steps
1. Guard: need at least one binary operator; locate `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`.
2. Decide plain vs. rational coupling first (rational costs 3 extra nodes, plain costs 1), derive a
   donor-size budget from `options.maxsize`.
3. Sample a single donor motif tier: any subtree that fits the budget and contains a variable
   (no separate "prefer compound" tier — this is the main simplification).
4. With probability 1/2, cyclically shift the clone's feature indices (replicates the form across a
   variable block); otherwise keep it identical (gives `u*u` squares and `u/(1-u)` self-couplings).
5. Splice: `target / (1 - motif)` for rational, else `target ⊕ motif` with `⊕ ∈ {+, *}`.

# What was simplified relative to the parent
- **Two donor tiers (compound-preferred, then any) → one tier.** Sampling any variable-bearing
  subtree that fits the budget already covers both squares and larger structural motifs; the
  compound-preference pass only reweighted the same pool and is dropped for simplicity.
- **Donor filtering closures merged/streamlined.** A single `fits_var` predicate is used directly in
  one `NodeSampler` call instead of branching on `count(...)` twice with different filters.
- Everything else (rational-vs-plain decision, budget derivation, feature shift, splicing) is kept
  since it is the load-bearing mechanism for reaching self-referential rational forms.
"""
function motif_duplication_simple_rational_gen27_10_gen36_8(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 1: guard + operator lookup
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree
    binops = options.operators.binops
    nbin = options.nops[2]
    _op(f) = findfirst(i -> binops[i] === f, 1:nbin)
    idx_add = _op(+)
    idx_sub = _op(-)
    idx_mul = _op(*)
    idx_div = _op(/)

    # Canonical accumulators for the plain coupling mode
    accum = Int[]
    idx_add !== nothing && push!(accum, idx_add)
    idx_mul !== nothing && push!(accum, idx_mul)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2: template + size budget
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)

    # `1 - u` is the canonical correction form; fall back to `1 + u` if `-` is unavailable
    den_op = idx_sub !== nothing ? idx_sub : idx_add
    rational_ok = (idx_div !== nothing) && (den_op !== nothing) && (maxsize - tree_size - 3) >= 1

    # Rational is the minority mode (35%), unless it is the only feasible coupling
    use_rational = rational_ok && (isempty(accum) || rand(rng) < 0.35)
    (!use_rational && isempty(accum)) && return tree

    budget = use_rational ? (maxsize - tree_size - 3) : (maxsize - tree_size - 1)
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3: donor motif (single tier)
    # Candidate motifs must fit the budget and carry at least one variable
    fits_var(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget && any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, t)

    count(fits_var, tree) == 0 && return tree  # nothing usable fits the budget
    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=fits_var))
    motif = copy(donor)  # copy before any in-place edits to the tree

    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4: feature remapping
    # Single compact traversal that shifts every variable leaf index
    function _shift_features!(node, shift)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeatures)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Half the time replicate the form on a different variable block; otherwise keep it identical
    # (identity yields squares `u*u` and self-couplings `u/(1-u)`).
    if nfeatures > 1 && rand(rng) < 0.5
        _shift_features!(motif, rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1)))
    end

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5: coupling
    target_copy = copy(target)
    new_node = if use_rational
        # Self-referential saturation / correction factor: target / (1 - motif)
        c = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
        den = constructorof(N)(; op=den_op, children=(c, motif))
        constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(target_copy, den))
    else
        # Plain accumulation with a commutative operator, so operand order does not matter
        bin_op = accum[rand(rng, 1:length(accum))]
        constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=(target_copy, motif))
    end

    set_node!(target, new_node)
    return tree
end

clone_filtered_quality_niche_tournament_.name: clone_filtered_quality_niche_tournament_gen36_9
clone_filtered_quality_niche_tournament_.code:
"""
    clone_filtered_quality_niche_tournament_gen36_9(
        pop::Population{T,L,N},
        running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
        options::AbstractOptions,
    )::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}

Streamlined clone-filtered niche tournament selection that combines phenotype deduplication
and rare-complexity exploration into a single clean pipeline.

### Core Idea:
1. Samples a standard tournament pool and computes frequency-adjusted parsimony scores.
2. Filters out inferior phenotypic clones (same complexity and near-identical loss)
   in a single quality-ordered pass.
3. With a small exploration probability (10%), selects the candidate from the rarest complexity
   niche among the top unique candidates; otherwise returns the winner via standard tournament ranking.

### Simplifications from Parent:
- Replaced the two-pass sorting and score-penalty multiplier arithmetic with direct first-win
  phenotype deduplication.
- Removed custom pool oversampling factors to use standard tournament configuration directly.
- Merged separate complexity-champion tracking directly into the deduplicated quality ranking,
  simplifying niche exploration to a single scan over top candidates.
"""
function clone_filtered_quality_niche_tournament_gen36_9(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Sample standard tournament pool
    sample_size = min(pop.n, options.tournament_selection_n)
    sample = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, sample_size; replace=false)
    n = length(sample)

    # Compute complexity and parsimony-adjusted scores
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    adjusted_scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = sample[i]
        c = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = c

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament && 0 < c <= options.maxsize
            freq = L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c])
            adjusted_scores[i] = member.cost * exp(parsimony_scaling * freq)
        else
            adjusted_scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Sort candidates by quality (lower adjusted score is better)
    sorted_indices = sortperm(adjusted_scores)

    # Single-pass clone filtering: keep only the best representative for each (complexity, loss) phenotype
    unique_indices = Int[]
    for idx in sorted_indices
        c_i = complexities[idx]
        loss_i = sample[idx].loss
        is_clone = false

        for u_idx in unique_indices
            if complexities[u_idx] == c_i
                loss_u = sample[u_idx].loss
                loss_scale = max(abs(loss_i), abs(loss_u), eps(L))
                if abs(loss_i - loss_u) <= L(1e-6) * loss_scale
                    is_clone = true
                    break
                end
            end
        end

        if !is_clone
            push!(unique_indices, idx)
        end
    end

    n_unique = length(unique_indices)

    # Exploration branch: pick the rarest complexity niche among top-performing candidates
    if rand() < 0.10
        top_k = max(1, cld(2 * n_unique, 3))
        best_niche_idx = unique_indices[1]
        c_best = complexities[best_niche_idx]
        min_freq = if 0 < c_best <= options.maxsize
            running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c_best]
        else
            0.0
        end

        for k in 2:top_k
            cand_idx = unique_indices[k]
            c = complexities[cand_idx]
            freq = if 0 < c <= options.maxsize
                running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c]
            else
                0.0
            end

            if freq < min_freq
                min_freq = freq
                best_niche_idx = cand_idx
            end
        end

        return sample[best_niche_idx]
    end

    # Standard tournament selection over deduplicated candidates
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    if p == 1.0 || n_unique == 1
        return sample[unique_indices[1]]
    else
        ranks = collect(0:(n_unique - 1))
        probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        selected_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        return sample[unique_indices[selected_rank]]
    end
end

simple_self_saturation_reject_gen33_gen3.name: simple_self_saturation_reject_gen33_gen37_9
simple_self_saturation_reject_gen33_gen3.code:
"""
    simple_self_saturation_reject_gen33_gen37_9(tree, options, nfeatures, rng)

Rational-saturation duplication, simplified. The core idea is unchanged: pick a
variable-containing subtree `u` and replace it with the scaffold `u / (1 + u)`, where the
two copies of `u` are independent so later mutations can specialize numerator and
denominator into forms like `u / (1 + u*v)` or `u / (v - w)` — shapes that are very hard to
assemble with point mutations alone (see the search trace, where progress hinged on finding
`x0 / (square(x2/x1) + c)`).

Steps:
1. Require both `+` and `/` among the binary operators.
2. Compute the remaining size budget (duplication of a size-`s` subtree costs `s + 3`).
3. Sample *any* variable-containing subtree, then reject the mutation if it does not fit the
   budget.
4. Otherwise splice in `u / (1 + u)`.

Simplified relative to the parent: the parent's eligibility filter combined *two* conditions
(contains a variable AND `count_nodes(t) <= budget`), which forces a `count_nodes` call for
every candidate node — an O(n^2) scan — plus a redundant precomputed `has_variable` flag.
Here the size test is folded out of the filter into a single post-hoc rejection on the one
sampled node, and the redundant flag is merged into the sampler guard. This is sound because
the size limit is still enforced exactly (never exceeding `maxsize`); the only behavioural
change is that occasionally an over-large subtree is drawn and the mutation is a no-op,
which the surrounding mutation loop already handles like any other failed proposal.
"""
function simple_self_saturation_reject_gen33_gen37_9(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    binops = options.operators.binops
    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op === (+), binops)
    idx_div = findfirst(op -> op === (/), binops)

    # The scaffold needs both `+` (for `1 + u`) and `/`.
    (idx_add === nothing || idx_div === nothing) && return tree

    # Replacing a subtree of size s with u/(1+u) costs s (the extra copy) + 3 (/, +, 1).
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    budget = maxsize - count_nodes(tree) - 3
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # Only variable-containing motifs are worth duplicating (constants would collapse).
    _has_var(t) = any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, t)
    _has_var(tree) || return tree

    # Cheap sampler: structural condition only, no per-node size computation.
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_has_var))

    # Post-hoc size rejection replaces the parent's size-aware filter.
    count_nodes(target) <= budget || return tree

    # Independent copies so later mutations can differentiate numerator/denominator.
    numerator = copy(target)
    motif = copy(target)
    one_node = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
    denominator = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_add, children=(one_node, motif))
    replacement = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(numerator, denominator))

    set_node!(target, replacement)
    return tree
end

simplified_clone_penalized_niche_tournam.name: simplified_clone_penalized_niche_tournament_gen37_7
simplified_clone_penalized_niche_tournam.code:
"""
    simplified_clone_penalized_niche_tournament_gen37_7(
        pop, running_search_statistics, options
    )

Streamlined crowding-aware tournament selection combining direct phenotypic clone
suppression and complexity-niche exploration.

### Core Idea
Maintains population diversity and structural exploration by:
1. Sampling an expanded tournament pool to expose duplicate expressions.
2. Computing parsimony-adjusted fitness scores.
3. Penalizing inferior duplicates that share identical complexity and loss with a better
   competitor in the tournament pool.
4. With a fixed probability (10%), selecting the champion of the rarest complexity niche
   present in the pool.
5. Otherwise selecting via standard geometric tournament selection on penalized scores.

### Simplifications from Parent
- **Removed Lineage Tracking**: Dropped parent reference matching and lineage loss
  tolerances. Phenotypic identity (same complexity and loss) captures genuine redundancy
  directly without ancestry graph heuristics.
- **Removed Age/Recency Heuristic**: Dropped birth-order discounting, avoiding fitness
  distortions and age-vs-quality trade-off hyperparameters.
- **Removed Dynamic Niche Probability & Multi-Stage Quality Gate**: Replaced the crowding-
  adapted niche probability formula and 2/3 fractional gate with a single, fast pass that
  selects the rarest complexity champion in the pool.
"""
function simplified_clone_penalized_niche_tournament_gen37_7(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Configuration parameters
    pool_scale = 1.5
    clone_penalty = 1.4
    clone_loss_rtol = 1e-6
    niche_exploration_prob = 0.10

    # 1. Sample an enlarged pool to expose local crowding
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # 2. Compute complexities and parsimony-adjusted base scores
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        c = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = c

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            freq = (0 < c <= options.maxsize) ? L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c]) : zero(L)
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * freq)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # 3. Penalize phenotypic duplicates: candidates preceded by identical phenotype
    order = sortperm(scores)
    penalized = copy(scores)
    rtol = L(clone_loss_rtol)

    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        ci = complexities[i]
        scale_i = max(abs(li), eps(L))
        clones_ahead = 0

        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            if ci == complexities[j]
                lj = pool[j].loss
                if abs(li - lj) <= rtol * max(scale_i, abs(lj))
                    clones_ahead += 1
                end
            end
        end

        if clones_ahead > 0
            factor = L(clone_penalty^clones_ahead)
            penalized[i] = if scores[i] > zero(L)
                scores[i] * factor
            elseif scores[i] < zero(L)
                scores[i] / factor
            else
                scores[i]
            end
        end
    end

    # 4. Complexity-niche exploration: champion of rarest complexity present
    if rand() < niche_exploration_prob
        penalized_order = sortperm(penalized)
        seen_complexities = falses(options.maxsize)
        best_idx = 0
        min_freq = Inf
        best_score = typemax(L)

        for idx in penalized_order
            c = complexities[idx]
            if 0 < c <= options.maxsize && !seen_complexities[c]
                seen_complexities[c] = true
                freq = running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[c]
                score = penalized[idx]
                if freq < min_freq || (freq == min_freq && score < best_score)
                    min_freq = freq
                    best_score = score
                    best_idx = idx
                end
            end
        end

        if best_idx != 0
            return pool[best_idx]
        end
    end

    # 5. Standard geometric tournament selection over penalized scores
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        ranks = collect(0:(n - 1))
        probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        selected_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)

        if selected_rank == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, selected_rank)[2][end]
        end
    end

    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

oldest_replaceable_survival_gen37_0.name: oldest_replaceable_survival_gen37_0
oldest_replaceable_survival_gen37_0.code:
"""
    oldest_replaceable_survival_gen37_0(pop::Population{T,L,N}, options::AbstractOptions; exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[])::Int where {T,L,N}

Simplified Pareto-protecting, age-regularized survival operator.

Core idea: a member is *replaceable* if it contributes nothing new to the
`(complexity, loss)` frontier — either its objectives are non-finite, or some
other member is at least as simple and at least as accurate (weak domination,
so exact duplicates count as replaceable). Among all replaceable eligible
members the oldest is removed; if every eligible member is non-dominated, the
oldest eligible member is removed, exactly like default age-regularized
evolution.

Steps:
1. One pass over the population records complexities, finiteness, and the
   oldest eligible index.
2. One `O(n^2)` pass marks each eligible finite member as weakly dominated.
3. Return the oldest replaceable member, else the oldest eligible member.

Simplifications relative to the parent: the dedicated "oldest invalid member"
pre-pass and its separate return path are folded into the single replaceability
test (non-finite members are inherently dominated, so they are removed first
unless a strictly older dominated member exists), and the separate
finiteness/complexity precomputation loop is merged into the main scan. This
keeps the two behaviours that matter — never discarding a Pareto stepping stone
and steady turnover of stale/redundant individuals — with a single decision rule.
"""
function oldest_replaceable_survival_gen37_0(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T,L,N}
    n = pop.n
    n == 0 && return 1

    BT = typeof(pop.members[1].birth)
    finite_member = Vector{Bool}(undef, n)
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)

    oldest_idx = 0
    oldest_birth = typemax(BT)

    # Single scan: cache finiteness/complexity and track the oldest eligible member.
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        member = pop.members[i]
        finite_member[i] = isfinite(member.loss) && isfinite(member.cost)
        complexities[i] = finite_member[i] ? compute_complexity(member, options) : 0

        if !(i in exclude_indices) && member.birth < oldest_birth
            oldest_birth = member.birth
            oldest_idx = i
        end
    end

    oldest_idx == 0 && throw(ArgumentError("exclude_indices contains every population index"))

    replaceable_idx = 0
    replaceable_birth = typemax(BT)

    # Oldest replaceable member: non-finite objectives, or weakly dominated
    # (a tie in both complexity and loss makes redundant copies replaceable).
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        i in exclude_indices && continue

        replaceable = !finite_member[i]
        if !replaceable
            c_i = complexities[i]
            loss_i = pop.members[i].loss
            for j in 1:n
                (j == i || !finite_member[j]) && continue
                if complexities[j] <= c_i && pop.members[j].loss <= loss_i
                    replaceable = true
                    break
                end
            end
        end

        if replaceable && pop.members[i].birth < replaceable_birth
            replaceable_birth = pop.members[i].birth
            replaceable_idx = i
        end
    end

    # Fall back to plain age-regularized replacement when nothing is replaceable.
    return replaceable_idx == 0 ? oldest_idx : replaceable_idx
end

clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple.name: clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple_gen37_1
clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple.code:
"""
    clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple_gen37_1(
        pop, running_search_statistics, options
    )

Simplified crowding-aware tournament selection.

Core idea (kept from the parent): sample a slightly enlarged tournament pool, penalize
members that look like phenotypic duplicates of better members already in the pool, and
occasionally make an explicit "niche" move toward a starved complexity band instead of
running the usual tournament ladder.

Steps:

 1. Sample a pool of `1.5 * tournament_selection_n` members and compute the standard
    adaptive-parsimony-adjusted costs.
 2. For each member, count how many *better* members share its complexity and have a
    nearly identical loss (a cheap proxy for being the same phenotype). Multiply the
    score by `crowding_penalty^count` in a sign-safe way, so duplicates are demoted.
 3. With a small fixed probability, do a niche move: keep the best representative of
    each occupied complexity, restrict attention to the better half of those
    representatives (quality gate), and return the one whose complexity is rarest
    according to `normalized_frequencies`.
 4. Otherwise, run the usual geometric tournament ladder on the adjusted scores.

Removed/merged relative to the parent:

  - Lineage (parent/child/sibling) suppression: it required phenotypic similarity
    anyway, so the clone test already captures nearly all of its effect, at a fraction
    of the bookkeeping.
  - The youth/recency discount and its crowding attenuation: it was a ~3% nudge that
    interacted subtly with the clone penalty; dropping it leaves the penalty factor
    always >= 1 and much easier to reason about.
  - The crowding-adaptive niche probability: replaced by a single fixed probability in
    the middle of the parent's range, since the clone penalty already reacts to
    crowding continuously.
  - The two-thirds quality gate is folded into a simpler "better half" cut, and the
    frequency comparison is a single rarest-complexity scan.

This remains sound because the dominant mechanism (suppressing exact phenotypic clones
of already-better members) and the complexity-niche escape hatch are both retained.
"""
function clone_suppressed_niche_tournament_simple_gen37_1(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Tunables: clone evidence is the only diversity signal; niche move is rare.
    pool_scale = 1.5
    crowding_penalty = 1.35
    clone_loss_rtol = 1e-6
    niche_probability = 0.12

    # Enlarged pool so that duplicates and empty complexity niches are observable.
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # Standard adaptive-parsimony-adjusted costs, plus cached complexities.
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity])
            else
                zero(L)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Walk from best to worst; each member is compared only against better ones,
    # so the better representative of a duplicate pair is never penalized.
    order = sortperm(scores)
    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)

    for a in 1:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        clone_count = 0

        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(max(abs(li), abs(lj)), eps(L))

            # Equal complexity + nearly equal loss ~ same phenotype.
            if complexities[i] == complexities[j] &&
                abs(li - lj) <= L(clone_loss_rtol) * loss_scale
                clone_count += 1
            end
        end

        # Factor is always >= 1; sign-safe so it always worsens the score.
        factor = L(crowding_penalty^clone_count)
        penalized[i] = if scores[i] > zero(L)
            scores[i] * factor
        elseif scores[i] < zero(L)
            scores[i] / factor
        else
            scores[i]
        end
    end

    if rand() < niche_probability
        # Best representative of each occupied complexity, in score order.
        penalized_order = sortperm(penalized)
        seen = falses(options.maxsize)
        champions = Int[]

        for i in penalized_order
            complexity = complexities[i]
            if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize && !seen[complexity]
                seen[complexity] = true
                push!(champions, i)
            end
        end

        if !isempty(champions)
            # Quality gate: only the better half of the champions are eligible.
            eligible = max(1, cld(length(champions), 2))
            best_idx = champions[1]
            best_frequency = Float64(
                running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexities[best_idx]]
            )

            # Pick the rarest complexity; ties break toward the better score,
            # which is automatic since champions are already score-sorted.
            for position in 2:eligible
                i = champions[position]
                frequency = Float64(
                    running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexities[i]]
                )
                if frequency < best_frequency
                    best_idx = i
                    best_frequency = frequency
                end
            end

            return pool[best_idx]
        end
    end

    # Usual geometric tournament ladder over the clone-adjusted scores.
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        ranks = collect(0:(n - 1))
        probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        selected_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)

        if selected_rank == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, selected_rank)[2][end]
        end
    end

    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

streamlined_affine_correlation_loss_gen3.name: streamlined_affine_correlation_loss_gen37_2
streamlined_affine_correlation_loss_gen3.code:
"""
    streamlined_affine_correlation_loss_gen37_2(tree, dataset, options)

Streamlined affine-invariant shape loss with a small calibration tie-breaker.

Steps:
 1. Evaluate the expression and collect stable means, variances, covariance,
    scale estimates, and raw squared error in one pass.
 2. Measure shape mismatch as `sqrt(1 - r^2)`, making the main objective
    invariant to affine rescaling of nonconstant predictions.
 3. Add a bounded raw-error term with weight `1/256` to prefer expressions with
    the correct scale and offset.
 4. For effectively constant targets, replace correlation with scale-normalized
    `log1p` MSE because affine shape is undefined.

Compared with the parent, this removes the precision-trigger heuristic, fitted
residual pass, compensated summation, and associated fallback branches. Exact
predictions still receive zero loss, while ordinary candidates require only one
statistics pass. Expression complexity is intentionally not penalized here.
"""
function streamlined_affine_correlation_loss_gen37_2(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)
    if !isfinite(n_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Online moments avoid materializing residual or centered-data arrays.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l

    raw_sum = zero_l
    raw_saturated = false
    exact_match = true

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))
        exact_match &= (p == y)

        # Raw error is only a bounded tie-breaker, so overflow means saturation.
        if !raw_saturated
            residual = p - y
            term = residual * residual
            updated = raw_sum + term

            if isfinite(residual) && isfinite(term) && isfinite(updated)
                raw_sum = updated
            else
                raw_saturated = true
            end
        end

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Roundoff can make theoretically nonnegative moments slightly negative.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    if exact_match
        return zero_l
    end

    relative_tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))
    target_rms = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    prediction_rms = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)

    target_is_variable =
        target_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_y
    prediction_is_variable =
        prediction_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_p

    if !target_is_variable
        # Correlation is undefined for constant targets, so use normalized MSE.
        target_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_y)
        normalized_sum = zero_l

        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            p = L(prediction[i])
            y = L(dataset.y[i])

            # Divide first to avoid overflow in p - y when both are very large.
            normalized_residual = p / target_scale - y / target_scale
            term = normalized_residual * normalized_residual
            updated = normalized_sum + term

            if !(isfinite(normalized_residual) &&
                 isfinite(term) &&
                 isfinite(updated))
                return L(Inf)
            end

            normalized_sum = updated
        end

        normalized_mse = max(normalized_sum / n_l, zero_l)
        loss_value = log1p(normalized_mse)
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
    end

    # A constant prediction has no recoverable affine shape.
    affine_nmse = one_l
    if prediction_is_variable
        prediction_norm = sqrt(m2_p)
        target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)

        if !(isfinite(prediction_norm) && prediction_norm > zero_l &&
             isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        correlation = (cov_py / prediction_norm) / target_norm
        correlation = clamp(correlation, -one_l, one_l)
        affine_nmse = clamp(
            one_l - correlation * correlation,
            zero_l,
            one_l,
        )
    end

    shape_term = sqrt(affine_nmse)

    # Compute raw_sum / (m2_y + raw_sum) without overflowing the denominator.
    bounded_raw = if raw_saturated
        one_l
    elseif raw_sum <= m2_y
        ratio = raw_sum / m2_y
        ratio / (one_l + ratio)
    else
        inverse_ratio = m2_y / raw_sum
        one_l / (one_l + inverse_ratio)
    end

    loss_value = shape_term + bounded_raw / L(256)
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

streamlined_motif_duplication_gen37_3.name: streamlined_motif_duplication_gen37_3
streamlined_motif_duplication_gen37_3.code:
"""
    streamlined_motif_duplication_gen37_3(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Streamlined structural mutation that clones an evolved subexpression (motif) and integrates
it into the expression tree either via symmetric accumulation (`target ⊕ motif`) or as a
self-referential rational correction (`target / (1 + motif)`).

# Core Idea
Evolutionary symbolic regression frequently discovers reusable functional blocks (e.g.,
coordinate symmetries, kinetic terms, or nonlinear response forms). Duplicating these
discovered motifs across variables or embedding a subexpression into a rational denominator
`u / (1 + u)` enables rapid discovery of symmetric and saturating physical laws without
requiring dozens of coordinated point mutations.

# Steps
1. Guard & Operator Lookup: Check that binary operators exist and identify indices for `+`,
   `*`, and `/` using standard search.
2. Template & Budget: Decide upfront whether to apply the rational template `target / (1 + motif)`
   or a plain binary coupling `target ⊕ motif`, and compute the motif size budget from `options.maxsize`.
3. Donor Sampling: Sample any subtree from the current tree that fits the size budget.
4. Feature Remapping: With 50% probability (when `nfeatures > 1`), cyclically shift all variable
   indices across the motif (`x_i → x_{(i+k) % D}`) to replicate structure across variable blocks;
   otherwise keep features unchanged for exact self-coupling / rational saturation.
5. Splicing: Splice the motif into a randomly chosen target node in-place using either the
   rational saturation template or a binary accumulator (biased toward `+` and `*`).

# Simplifications from Parent
- **Removed 3-tier donor sampling**: Eliminated multi-pass counting and conditional tier logic
  in favor of a single budget-filtered node sampler.
- **Unified feature remapping**: Replaced the feature collection and single-variable substitution
  machinery with a simple binary choice: cyclic shift (for cross-feature symmetry) versus identity
  (for rational self-couplings and powers).
- **Streamlined rational & operator lookup**: Simplified operator discovery using `findfirst` and
  standardized the rational denominator to the canonical `1 + motif` form, trimming branching
  while preserving the essential physics-motivated saturation mode.
"""
function streamlined_motif_duplication_gen37_3(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # -------------------------------------------------- Step 1: Guard & Operator Lookup
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    binops = options.operators.binops
    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op == (+), binops)
    idx_div = findfirst(op -> op == (/), binops)
    idx_mul = findfirst(op -> op == (*), binops)

    # -------------------------------------------------- Step 2: Template & Budget
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)

    # Rational template target / (1 + motif) requires div, add, and constant 1 (3 extra nodes)
    can_rational = (idx_div !== nothing) && (idx_add !== nothing)
    use_rational = can_rational && (rand(rng) < 0.30) && (maxsize - tree_size >= 4)

    budget = maxsize - tree_size - (use_rational ? 3 : 1)
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # -------------------------------------------------- Step 3: Donor Sampling
    fits_budget(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget
    count(fits_budget, tree) == 0 && return tree
    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=fits_budget))
    motif = copy(donor)

    # -------------------------------------------------- Step 4: Feature Remapping
    # Either cyclically shift variables (symmetry) or keep identity (self-coupling/powers)
    if nfeatures > 1 && rand(rng, Bool)
        shift = rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1))
        function _shift_features!(node)
            if node.degree == 0
                if !node.constant
                    node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeatures)
                end
            else
                for i in 1:(node.degree)
                    _shift_features!(get_child(node, i))
                end
            end
            return node
        end
        _shift_features!(motif)
    end

    # -------------------------------------------------- Step 5: Coupling into Target
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    target_copy = copy(target)

    new_node = if use_rational
        # Construct saturating rational form: target / (1 + motif)
        one_const = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
        den = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_add, children=(one_const, motif))
        constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(target_copy, den))
    else
        # Symmetric accumulation: bias toward + or * if available
        preferred = filter(!isnothing, [idx_add, idx_mul])
        op = (!isempty(preferred) && rand(rng) < 0.70) ?
            rand(rng, preferred) :
            rand(rng, 1:options.nops[2])
        # Randomize operand order to allow non-commutative combinations
        children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
        constructorof(N)(; op=op, children=children)
    end

    set_node!(target, new_node)
    return tree
end

streamlined_affine_shape_precision_loss_.name: streamlined_affine_shape_precision_loss_gen37_4
streamlined_affine_shape_precision_loss_.code:
"""
    streamlined_affine_shape_precision_loss_gen37_4(tree, dataset, options)

Simplified affine-invariant shape loss with a weak calibration preference.

Steps:
 1. Evaluate the expression and collect stable prediction/target moments plus raw
    squared error in one Welford pass.
 2. For variable targets, score affine shape using `sqrt(1 - r^2)`.
 3. Recompute the fitted residual only for strong near-matches, using one fixed
    threshold to preserve precision around the optimum.
 4. Add a small bounded raw-error term; for effectively constant targets, use
    scale-normalized `log1p` MSE instead.

Compared with the parent, this removes the adaptive precision threshold,
compensated summation, and detailed raw-overflow bookkeeping. Raw-error overflow
simply saturates its bounded tie-breaker, while the core affine-shape and
near-match precision mechanisms are retained.
"""
function streamlined_affine_shape_precision_loss_gen37_4(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)
    if !isfinite(n_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Stable online moments and a simple raw squared-error accumulator.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l
    exact_match = true

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))
        exact_match = exact_match && p == y

        # Overflow only saturates the later bounded calibration term.
        residual = p - y
        term = residual * residual
        if isfinite(raw_sum) && isfinite(term)
            updated = raw_sum + term
            raw_sum = isfinite(updated) ? updated : L(Inf)
        else
            raw_sum = L(Inf)
        end

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y
        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) &&
         isfinite(m2_p) && isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Welford moments can acquire tiny negative values from roundoff.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    if exact_match
        return zero_l
    end

    relative_tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))
    target_rms = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    prediction_rms = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)

    target_is_variable =
        target_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_y
    prediction_is_variable =
        prediction_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_p

    if !target_is_variable
        # Correlation has no useful meaning for a constant target.
        target_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_y)
        sqrt_n = sqrt(n_l)
        normalized_mse = zero_l

        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            p = L(prediction[i])
            y = L(dataset.y[i])

            # Divide before subtraction and squaring to reduce overflow risk.
            normalized_residual =
                (p / target_scale - y / target_scale) / sqrt_n
            term = normalized_residual * normalized_residual

            if !isfinite(term)
                return L(Inf)
            end

            normalized_mse += term
            if !isfinite(normalized_mse)
                return L(Inf)
            end
        end

        loss_value = log1p(max(normalized_mse, zero_l))
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
    end

    target_norm = sqrt(m2_y)
    if !(isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # A numerically constant prediction has no affine shape information.
    affine_nmse = one_l

    if prediction_is_variable
        prediction_norm = sqrt(m2_p)
        if !(isfinite(prediction_norm) && prediction_norm > zero_l)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        correlation = (cov_py / prediction_norm) / target_norm
        if !isfinite(correlation)
            return L(Inf)
        end

        correlation = clamp(correlation, -one_l, one_l)
        affine_nmse = clamp(
            one_l - correlation * correlation,
            zero_l,
            one_l,
        )

        # A fixed trigger replaces the parent's adaptive threshold.
        if affine_nmse <= one_l / L(256)
            slope = cov_py / m2_p

            if isfinite(slope)
                direct_sum = zero_l
                direct_ok = true

                @inbounds for i in 1:n
                    p = L(prediction[i])
                    y = L(dataset.y[i])

                    fitted = muladd(slope, p - mean_p, mean_y)
                    normalized_residual = (fitted - y) / target_norm
                    term = normalized_residual * normalized_residual

                    if !(isfinite(fitted) && isfinite(term))
                        direct_ok = false
                        break
                    end

                    direct_sum += term
                    if !isfinite(direct_sum)
                        direct_ok = false
                        break
                    end
                end

                if direct_ok
                    affine_nmse = clamp(direct_sum, zero_l, one_l)
                end
            end
        end
    end

    shape_term = sqrt(affine_nmse)

    # Calibration is only a bounded tie-breaker, so overflow maps to saturation.
    bounded_raw = if isfinite(raw_sum)
        raw_nmse = raw_sum / m2_y
        if isfinite(raw_nmse)
            raw_nmse = max(raw_nmse, zero_l)
            raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse)
        else
            one_l
        end
    else
        one_l
    end

    loss_value = shape_term + bounded_raw / L(256)
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

crowding_niche_tournament_simplified_gen.name: crowding_niche_tournament_simplified_gen37_5
crowding_niche_tournament_simplified_gen.code:
"""
    crowding_niche_tournament_simplified_gen37_5(
        pop, running_search_statistics, options
    )

Simplified crowding-aware tournament selection that keeps only the two most
important ideas from the parent operator: penalizing exact phenotype clones
(same complexity, near-identical loss) and occasionally forcing exploration
of the rarest complexity niche when the sampled pool looks crowded.

Steps:
 1. Sample an enlarged pool and compute the usual adaptive-parsimony-adjusted
    scores (same as `default_selection`).
 2. For each member, count how many *better* members in the pool are
    near-duplicates (same complexity, loss within a relative tolerance) and
    apply a multiplicative penalty proportional to that count. This is the
    core crowding signal; the parent's extra lineage/parent-child fractional
    penalty and youth/recency discount are dropped since clone detection
    alone captures most of the redundancy signal, and removing the extras
    reduces variance and cost.
 3. If the pool shows a high fraction of crowded members, occasionally skip
    the tournament and directly return the best member of the rarest
    populated complexity niche (using `normalized_frequencies`), which
    repopulates starved complexity bands. The parent's two-step "quality
    gate over best two-thirds of niche champions" is simplified to a single
    direct choice of the globally rarest niche's best representative, since
    that already avoids picking degenerate members (we still use the best
    scorer within that niche).
 4. Otherwise, apply the standard geometric tournament ladder to the
    penalized scores.
"""
function crowding_niche_tournament_simplified_gen37_5(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Tunables: fewer knobs than the parent, keeping only the essentials.
    pool_scale = 1.5
    crowding_penalty = 1.35
    clone_loss_rtol = 1e-6
    niche_probability_base = 0.08
    niche_probability_boost = 0.10
    niche_probability_max = 0.18

    # Sample a larger pool so local crowding and niche occupancy are observable.
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, round(Int, pool_scale * n_base)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    # Compute complexity and the default adaptive-parsimony-adjusted score.
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity])
            else
                zero(L)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Process from best to worst; count clone-like duplicates among better members.
    order = sortperm(scores)
    redundancy = zeros(Float64, n)

    for a in 2:n
        i = order[a]
        li = pool[i].loss
        scale_i = max(abs(li), eps(L))
        count = 0.0

        for b in 1:(a - 1)
            j = order[b]
            lj = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(scale_i, abs(lj))

            same_phenotype =
                complexities[i] == complexities[j] &&
                abs(li - lj) <= L(clone_loss_rtol) * loss_scale

            same_phenotype && (count += 1.0)
        end

        redundancy[i] = count
    end

    # Apply a sign-safe multiplicative penalty proportional to redundancy count.
    penalized = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    crowded_count = 0
    for i in 1:n
        redundancy[i] > 0.0 && (crowded_count += 1)
        typed_factor = L(crowding_penalty^redundancy[i])
        penalized[i] = if scores[i] > zero(L)
            scores[i] * typed_factor
        elseif scores[i] < zero(L)
            scores[i] / typed_factor
        else
            scores[i]
        end
    end

    # Increase explicit niche exploration when the sampled pool shows monopoly.
    crowded_fraction = crowded_count / n
    niche_probability = min(
        niche_probability_max,
        niche_probability_base + niche_probability_boost * crowded_fraction,
    )

    if rand() < niche_probability
        # Find the rarest populated complexity present in the pool, and
        # return its best (lowest-penalized-score) representative.
        best_complexity = -1
        best_frequency = Inf
        for i in 1:n
            complexity = complexities[i]
            if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
                frequency = Float64(
                    running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity]
                )
                if frequency < best_frequency
                    best_frequency = frequency
                    best_complexity = complexity
                end
            end
        end

        if best_complexity != -1
            best_idx = -1
            best_score = typemax(L)
            for i in 1:n
                if complexities[i] == best_complexity && penalized[i] < best_score
                    best_score = penalized[i]
                    best_idx = i
                end
            end
            best_idx != -1 && return pool[best_idx]
        end
    end

    # Standard geometric tournament ladder over diversity-adjusted scores.
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        argmin_fast(penalized)
    else
        ranks = collect(0:(n - 1))
        probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        selected_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)

        if selected_rank == 1
            argmin_fast(penalized)
        else
            bottomk_fast(penalized, selected_rank)[2][end]
        end
    end

    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

simplified_variable_saturation_gen37_6.name: simplified_variable_saturation_gen37_6
simplified_variable_saturation_gen37_6.code:
"""
    simplified_variable_saturation_gen37_6(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Transform a randomly selected variable leaf `x` into the rational saturation template
`x / (1 + x)` (Michaelis-Menten / Langmuir scaffold). This directly injects foundational
saturating non-linearities that standard point mutations struggle to construct from scratch.

Steps:
1. Verify availability of both addition (`+`) and division (`/`) in binary operators.
2. Check that adding 4 nodes (1 leaf replaced by 5 nodes) respects `options.maxsize`.
3. Check for at least one variable leaf in the tree.
4. Uniformly sample a variable leaf `x`.
5. Replace `x` in-place with `x / (1 + x)`.

Simplifications from Parent:
- Replaced general subtree filtering (which required evaluating subtree sizes and variable
  containment predicates over all nodes) with direct sampling of variable leaves.
- Eliminated deep copying and per-candidate size budget calculations; the node increase
  is fixed at +4.
- This soundly retains the primary evolutionary advantage—injecting non-linear saturation
  scaffolds—while drastically reducing computational overhead and algorithmic complexity.
"""
function simplified_variable_saturation_gen37_6(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Require both addition and division operators to build rational saturation.
    binops = options.operators.binops
    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op === (+), binops)
    idx_div = findfirst(op -> op === (/), binops)
    (idx_add === nothing || idx_div === nothing) && return tree

    # Expanding a leaf into x / (1 + x) replaces 1 node with 5, adding exactly 4 nodes.
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    count_nodes(tree) + 4 > maxsize && return tree

    # Ensure at least one variable leaf exists in the tree.
    any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, tree) || return tree

    # Sample a variable leaf uniformly at random.
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=t -> t.degree == 0 && !t.constant))

    # Construct the saturation scaffold x / (1 + x) with independent leaf nodes.
    feat = target.feature
    x_num = constructorof(N)(T; feature=feat)
    x_den = constructorof(N)(T; feature=feat)
    one_node = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
    denom = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_add, children=(one_node, x_den))
    replacement = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(x_num, denom))

    # Replace the target variable leaf in-place.
    set_node!(target, replacement)
    return tree
end

oldest_dominated_survival_simple_gen37_8.name: oldest_dominated_survival_simple_gen37_8
oldest_dominated_survival_simple_gen37_8.code:
"""
    oldest_dominated_survival_simple_gen37_8(pop::Population{T,L,N}, options::AbstractOptions; exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[])::Int where {T,L,N}

Age-regularized replacement restricted to Pareto-dominated members.

Core idea (unchanged from the parent): never throw away a member that is currently the sole
occupant of a point on the `(complexity, loss)` frontier, because such members are the
stepping stones the search needs; among everything else, remove the oldest so the population
keeps turning over.

Steps:
1. One pass computes, for every member, its complexity and an "effective loss" where any
   non-finite loss/cost is mapped to `typemax(L)` and the complexity to `maxsize + 1`.
   The same pass records the oldest eligible index.
2. One pass marks a member as weakly dominated if some other member has both complexity
   and effective loss less than or equal to its own (exact ties count as dominated, so
   duplicate expressions remain replaceable without any explicit niche counting).
3. Return the oldest weakly dominated eligible member, or the oldest eligible member if the
   whole eligible population is non-dominated.

Simplifications relative to the parent: the dedicated "invalid individuals first" scan and the
`finite_member` bookkeeping array are gone. Invalid members are folded into the ordinary
dominance test by giving them the worst possible objective values, which makes them dominated
by every finite member (and by each other) so they are still preferentially recycled, just
ranked by age like any other dominated member. This keeps the operator's two essential
behaviours -- frontier protection and age-based turnover -- with a single uniform code path.
"""
function oldest_dominated_survival_simple_gen37_8(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T,L,N}
    n = pop.n
    n == 0 && return 1

    BT = typeof(pop.members[1].birth)
    oldest_idx = 0
    oldest_birth = typemax(BT)

    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    bad_complexity = options.maxsize + 1

    # Single pass: objectives (with invalid members pushed to the worst corner) + oldest eligible.
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        member = pop.members[i]
        if isfinite(member.loss) && isfinite(member.cost)
            complexities[i] = compute_complexity(member, options)
            losses[i] = member.loss
        else
            # Invalid members get the worst objectives, so every finite member dominates them.
            complexities[i] = bad_complexity
            losses[i] = typemax(L)
        end

        if !(i in exclude_indices) && member.birth < oldest_birth
            oldest_birth = member.birth
            oldest_idx = i
        end
    end

    oldest_idx == 0 && throw(ArgumentError("exclude_indices contains every population index"))

    dominated_idx = 0
    dominated_birth = typemax(BT)

    # Second pass: oldest weakly dominated eligible member.
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        i in exclude_indices && continue

        birth_i = pop.members[i].birth
        # Only a younger-than-current-best candidate could change the answer.
        birth_i < dominated_birth || continue

        c_i = complexities[i]
        loss_i = losses[i]

        for j in 1:n
            j == i && continue
            if complexities[j] <= c_i && losses[j] <= loss_i
                dominated_birth = birth_i
                dominated_idx = i
                break
            end
        end
    end

    # Fall back to plain age-regularized removal when nothing is dominated.
    return dominated_idx == 0 ? oldest_idx : dominated_idx
end

age_survival_pareto_front_shield_gen27_0.name: age_survival_pareto_front_shield_gen27_0_gen38_1
age_survival_pareto_front_shield_gen27_0.code:
"""
    age_survival_pareto_front_shield_gen27_0_gen38_1(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[]) -> Int

Age-based survival with a *Pareto-front* shield (simplified from the parent's
"best-at-each-complexity" shield).

Core idea (kept): protect the cheap, structurally useful frontier of the
population from random age-death so that a spread of scaffold sizes survives as
recombination material, while everything dominated/redundant still turns over
under age pressure.

Steps:
1. One O(n) pass fills two small fixed-size arrays (indexed by complexity):
   the lowest cost seen at each complexity and the index achieving it. No `Dict`,
   no "unshield the previous champion" bookkeeping.
2. One ascending sweep over complexities keeps a running minimum cost and shields
   a complexity's champion only if it strictly improves on every *simpler*
   complexity — i.e. the shield is exactly the cost/complexity Pareto front.
3. Draw `n_sample = clamp(tournament_selection_n, 2, n)` uniform slots and return
   the oldest one that is neither shielded nor excluded (cheap, allocation-free
   age pressure).
4. Single fallback: if the sample hit only shielded/excluded slots, scan the whole
   population and return the oldest non-excluded member (shield relaxed).

Removed/merged relative to the parent:
* The `Dict{Int,Int}` champion map plus its shield/unshield toggling is replaced
  by two flat arrays and a single monotone sweep — fewer branches, no hashing.
* The shield itself is *shrunk*: only non-dominated champions are protected
  instead of the champion of every complexity value. A champion that is worse
  than some simpler expression is not useful recombination material, so removing
  its protection simply restores healthy age turnover, which is the main driver
  of exploration in age-regularized evolution.
* Only one fallback scan remains (shield-relaxed, exclusion-respecting), so the
  function can never return an excluded index while staying a single code path.
"""
function age_survival_pareto_front_shield_gen27_0_gen38_1(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n
    members = pop.members
    BT = typeof(first(members).birth)

    # ---- Step 1: per-complexity champion (lowest cost) via flat arrays. ----
    cmax = max(1, options.maxsize + 1)
    best_cost = fill(typemax(L), cmax)
    champ = zeros(Int, cmax)
    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        c = clamp(compute_complexity(members[i], options), 1, cmax)
        if members[i].cost < best_cost[c]
            best_cost[c] = members[i].cost
            champ[c] = i
        end
    end

    # ---- Step 2: shield only the Pareto front (champions that beat all simpler ones). ----
    shielded = fill(false, n)
    running_min = typemax(L)
    @inbounds for c in 1:cmax
        i = champ[c]
        i == 0 && continue
        if best_cost[c] < running_min
            shielded[i] = true          # non-dominated: worth keeping alive
            running_min = best_cost[c]
        end
    end

    victim = 0
    victim_birth = typemax(BT)

    # ---- Step 3: sampled age pressure over unprotected slots only. ----
    n_sample = min(n, max(2, options.tournament_selection_n))
    @inbounds for _ in 1:n_sample
        i = rand(1:n)
        shielded[i] && continue
        (i in exclude_indices) && continue
        b = members[i].birth
        if victim == 0 || b < victim_birth
            victim = i
            victim_birth = b
        end
    end

    # ---- Step 4: single fallback — oldest non-excluded member, shield relaxed. ----
    if victim == 0
        @inbounds for i in 1:n
            (i in exclude_indices) && continue
            b = members[i].birth
            if victim == 0 || b < victim_birth
                victim = i
                victim_birth = b
            end
        end
    end

    return victim
end

correlation_affine_shape_loss_simple_gen.name: correlation_affine_shape_loss_simple_gen38_0
correlation_affine_shape_loss_simple_gen.code:
"""
    correlation_affine_shape_loss_simple_gen38_0(tree, dataset, options)

Simplified single-pass affine-invariant shape loss.

Core idea (kept from the parent): rank candidates primarily by how well their
*shape* matches the target up to an arbitrary affine calibration
(`sqrt(1 - r^2)`, where `r` is the Pearson correlation), and break ties with a
small, saturating raw-error term so that correctly scaled/offset expressions are
preferred among structurally equivalent shapes. This lets partially-correct
structures (e.g. the `x0 * f(x1,x2,x3)` skeletons seen in the trace) surface on
the Pareto front before their constants are tuned.

Steps:
 1. One pass over the data accumulating Welford moments (`mean`, `M2` for
    prediction and target, and the covariance) together with the plain
    sum of squared residuals.
 2. Shape term: `sqrt(1 - clamp(r,-1,1)^2)`, computed with sequential divisions
    to avoid forming `cov^2` or `M2_p * M2_y`.
 3. Tie-breaker: normalize the raw squared-error sum by the target's centered
    sum of squares plus a tiny scale floor, then map it through
    `x / (1 + x)` so it is bounded in `[0, 1)` and can never outrank a genuine
    shape improvement; it enters with weight `1/256`.

Removed / merged relative to the parent (and why this stays sound):
 * The selective *second* data pass that re-fitted the affine calibration with
   compensated summation for high-correlation candidates is dropped. It only
   refined already-near-perfect candidates; the ordering of such candidates is
   still resolved by the bounded raw-error tie-breaker, and dropping it removes
