                if frequency < best_frequency ||
                    (frequency == best_frequency &&
                     adjusted_scores[i] < adjusted_scores[best_idx])
                    best_idx = i
                    best_frequency = frequency
                end
            end

            return pool[best_idx]
        end
    end

    # Apply the usual geometric tournament ladder to the adjusted ranking.
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    if p == 1.0
        return pool[selection_order[1]]
    end

    ranks = collect(0:(n - 1))
    probabilities = p * ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
    weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
    selected_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)

    return pool[selection_order[selected_rank]]
end

clone_suppressed_quality_niche_tournamen.name: clone_suppressed_quality_niche_tournament_gen45_9
clone_suppressed_quality_niche_tournamen.code:
"""
    clone_suppressed_quality_niche_tournament_gen45_9(
        pop, running_search_statistics, options
    )

Simplified crowding-aware tournament selection built around the parent's two most
reliable diversity signals: near-duplicate suppression and quality-gated complexity
exploration.

The operator:

 1. Samples a standard-sized tournament and computes adaptive-parsimony-adjusted costs.
 2. Processes candidates by quality and applies one fixed penalty to later members
    with the same complexity and nearly identical loss.
 3. With a small fixed probability, selects the globally rarest complexity among
    the better half of the pool's best complexity representatives.
 4. Otherwise uses the usual geometric tournament ranking.

Compared with the parent, this removes the enlarged pool, lineage heuristics, age
discounts, accumulated crowding weights, and crowding-dependent exploration rate.
Ancestry and recency are noisy proxies for structural novelty, while a single clone
penalty preserves the robust anti-monopoly effect. The fixed, quality-gated niche
move retains useful exploration without promoting arbitrarily poor rare candidates.
"""
function clone_suppressed_quality_niche_tournament_gen45_9(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    clone_loss_rtol = L(1e-6)
    clone_penalty = L(1.35)
    niche_probability = 0.10

    # Use the standard tournament size to avoid changing selection pressure.
    pool_size = min(pop.n, options.tournament_selection_n)
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    scores = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    adaptive_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    # Start from the default adaptive-parsimony score.
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity])
            else
                zero(L)
            end
            scores[i] = member.cost * exp(adaptive_scaling * frequency)
        else
            scores[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Retain the best member of each near-duplicate phenotype and penalize later
    # copies once, rather than accumulating lineage and crowding penalties.
    base_order = sortperm(scores)
    penalized = copy(scores)

    for rank in 2:n
        i = base_order[rank]
        loss_i = pool[i].loss
        is_clone = false

        for prior_rank in 1:(rank - 1)
            j = base_order[prior_rank]
            loss_j = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(abs(loss_i), abs(loss_j), eps(L))

            if complexities[i] == complexities[j] &&
                abs(loss_i - loss_j) <= clone_loss_rtol * loss_scale
                is_clone = true
                break
            end
        end

        if is_clone
            # Sign-safe: the penalty always moves a score in the worse direction.
            if penalized[i] > zero(L)
                penalized[i] *= clone_penalty
            elseif penalized[i] < zero(L)
                penalized[i] /= clone_penalty
            end
        end
    end

    ranked = sortperm(penalized)

    if rand() < niche_probability
        # Record the best adjusted-score representative of each valid complexity.
        seen = falses(options.maxsize)
        niche_champions = Int[]

        for i in ranked
            complexity = complexities[i]
            if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize && !seen[complexity]
                seen[complexity] = true
                push!(niche_champions, i)
            end
        end

        if !isempty(niche_champions)
            # Restrict rarity-based exploration to the better half of champions.
            quality_count = max(1, cld(length(niche_champions), 2))
            chosen_idx = niche_champions[1]
            chosen_frequency = Inf

            for position in 1:quality_count
                i = niche_champions[position]
                frequency =
                    running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexities[i]]

                # Champions are already quality-ordered, so ties retain the better one.
                if frequency < chosen_frequency
                    chosen_idx = i
                    chosen_frequency = frequency
                end
            end

            return pool[chosen_idx]
        end
    end

    # Apply the standard geometric tournament ladder to the adjusted ranking.
    p = options.tournament_selection_p
    chosen_idx = if p == 1.0
        ranked[1]
    else
        ranks = 0:(n - 1)
        probabilities = p .* ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        weights = StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities))
        selected_rank = StatsBase.sample(weights)
        ranked[selected_rank]
    end

    return pool[chosen_idx]
end

oldest_only_survival_gen45_3.name: oldest_only_survival_gen45_3
oldest_only_survival_gen45_3.code:
"""
Pure age-first survival.

Scans eligible population members once and replaces the individual with the
smallest birth value. Birth ties are resolved by population order. This removes
the parent's cost tie-break, preserving age-regularized turnover while avoiding
an additional quality heuristic that could reduce diversity among same-age
individuals.
"""
function oldest_only_survival_gen45_3(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    oldest_idx = 0

    # Keep the first eligible member encountered at the minimum birth value.
    for i in 1:pop.n
        i in exclude_indices && continue

        if oldest_idx == 0 || pop.members[i].birth < pop.members[oldest_idx].birth
            oldest_idx = i
        end
    end

    @assert oldest_idx != 0 "No eligible members to replace"
    return oldest_idx
end

affine_angular_profile_loss_1pass_simpli.name: affine_angular_profile_loss_1pass_simplified_gen45_0
affine_angular_profile_loss_1pass_simpli.code:
"""
    affine_angular_profile_loss_1pass_simplified_gen45_0(tree, dataset, options)

Simplified single-pass variant of the parent's two-pass affine-angular-profile loss.
Core idea kept: measure functional shape via how well an affine recalibration
`a*prediction + b` matches the target (angular/shape residual), using a small
bounded raw-error term as a calibration tie-breaker so exact predictions still
score strictly best.

What was removed/merged relative to the parent:
- The second evaluation pass (which recomputed fitted residuals directly to avoid
  cancellation) is dropped. Instead the shape term is computed directly from the
  Welford moments via `1 - r^2` (squared correlation), clamped to `[0,1]` for
  numerical safety. This is algebraically equivalent to the affine-NMSE but needs
  only one pass over the data.
- Kahan/compensated summation and the raw-error overflow bookkeeping are dropped;
  a plain running sum is used since this is not the bottleneck the parent worried
  about (extreme precision near a perfect fit matters most for the correlation
  term, which is handled via the moment-based `r^2` formula rather than summation).
- The constant-target fallback and scale-relative variability tests are kept,
  since they are cheap and important for robustness.

Steps:
1. Evaluate the tree; bail out to `Inf` on failure.
2. Single pass: accumulate Welford means/variances/covariance of `(p, y)` and a
   plain running sum of squared raw residuals `(p-y)^2`.
3. If the target is (numerically) constant, fall back to normalized raw MSE.
4. Otherwise compute `r^2 = cov^2 / (var_p * var_y)` (0 if prediction is
   constant), turn it into a shape term `sqrt(1 - r^2)`, and add a small bounded
   raw-error tie-breaker so poorly calibrated but structurally-correct trees still
   rank below correctly calibrated ones.
"""
function affine_angular_profile_loss_1pass_simplified_gen45_0(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # Single pass: Welford moments for the affine fit, plus a plain running sum
    # of squared raw residuals for the calibration tie-breaker.
    mean_p = zero_l
    mean_y = zero_l
    m2_p = zero_l
    m2_y = zero_l
    cov_py = zero_l
    max_abs_p = zero_l
    max_abs_y = zero_l
    raw_sum = zero_l

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        p = L(prediction[i])
        y = L(dataset.y[i])

        if !(isfinite(p) && isfinite(y))
            return L(Inf)
        end

        max_abs_p = max(max_abs_p, abs(p))
        max_abs_y = max(max_abs_y, abs(y))

        k = L(i)
        delta_p = p - mean_p
        delta_y = y - mean_y

        mean_p += delta_p / k
        mean_y += delta_y / k

        cov_py += delta_p * (y - mean_y)
        m2_p += delta_p * (p - mean_p)
        m2_y += delta_y * (y - mean_y)

        residual = p - y
        raw_sum += residual * residual
    end

    if !(isfinite(mean_p) && isfinite(mean_y) && isfinite(m2_p) &&
         isfinite(m2_y) && isfinite(cov_py) && isfinite(raw_sum))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Guard against microscopic negative roundoff.
    m2_p = max(m2_p, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(m2_y, zero_l)

    relative_tolerance = sqrt(eps(L))
    target_rms = sqrt(m2_y / n_l)
    prediction_rms = sqrt(m2_p / n_l)
    target_is_variable = target_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_y
    prediction_is_variable = prediction_rms > relative_tolerance * max_abs_p

    if !target_is_variable
        # Affine shape is undefined for a constant target: fall back to
        # scale-normalized raw MSE.
        target_scale = max(one_l, max_abs_y)
        raw_nmse = max(raw_sum / (n_l * target_scale * target_scale), zero_l)
        loss_value = log1p(raw_nmse)
        return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(loss_value) : L(Inf)
    end

    # Squared correlation, computed directly from moments (0 if prediction is
    # essentially constant, since no affine fit can then track the target).
    r2 = zero_l
    if prediction_is_variable
        r2 = (cov_py * cov_py) / (m2_p * m2_y)
        if !isfinite(r2)
            return L(Inf)
        end
    end
    r2 = clamp(r2, zero_l, one_l)

    shape_term = sqrt(one_l - r2)

    # Bounded raw-error tie-breaker, normalized by target variance so it stays
    # scale-free and saturates instead of dominating the shape term.
    raw_nmse = max(raw_sum / m2_y, zero_l)
    bounded_raw = raw_nmse / (one_l + raw_nmse)

    calibration_weight = one_l / L(256)
    loss_value = shape_term + calibration_weight * bounded_raw

    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

simplified_motif_duplication_gen45_2.name: simplified_motif_duplication_gen45_2
simplified_motif_duplication_gen45_2.code:
"""
    simplified_motif_duplication_gen45_2(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}

Streamlined structural mutation that clones an evolved subexpression *motif* and couples it
back into the expression tree either via an algebraic accumulator (`target ⊕ motif`) or inside
a self-referential rational form (`target / (1 + motif)`).

# Core Idea
Discovered mathematical and physical laws frequently feature repeated subexpressions across
variables (e.g. kinetic energy terms, distance metrics) or self-saturating rational fractions
(e.g., Compton scattering, Michaelis–Menten kinetics). Reusing existing evolved subtrees
avoids re-discovering the same structure from scratch.

# Steps
1. **Operator lookup & budget check**: Identify available operators (`+`, `*`, `/`) and allocate
   complexity budget for rational (`+3` nodes) or standard binary coupling (`+1` node).
2. **Donor sampling**: Select a motif subtree within budget, prioritizing compound expressions
   (`degree > 0`) over single leaves.
3. **Unified feature shift**: Re-index the motif's variables via a single cyclic offset
   `shift ∈ 0:(nfeatures - 1)`. When `shift == 0`, the identity mapping is preserved (power/saturation
   couplings); when `shift > 0`, the motif is replicated across other feature channels.
4. **Coupling**: With 35% probability (if `/` and `+` are available), wrap into `target / (1 + motif)`.
   Otherwise, couple with an accumulator biased toward `+` or `*`.

# Simplifications from Parent
- **Consolidated feature remapping**: Merged the parent's three separate remapping paths
  (cyclic shift, targeted pairwise substitution, and identity with conditional fallback) into a single
  compact cyclic shift `shift ∈ 0:(nfeatures - 1)`. This removes `_collect_features!` and all nested
  branching while still providing identity and feature rotation.
- **Streamlined donor selection**: Replaced 3 complex counting passes with a direct 2-stage fallback
  (compound subtrees if present, else any subtree).
- **Simplified operator indexing**: Replaced custom search loops and dynamic array allocations with
  direct `findfirst` lookups and static tuple filtering.
- **Canonical denominator**: Rational coupling directly uses `target / (1 + motif)` without branching
  on minus operators, allowing PySR's constant optimization to tune signs and scales.
"""
function simplified_motif_duplication_gen45_2(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    # Guard: need at least one binary operator
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    # Lookup canonical binary operators
    binops = options.operators.binops
    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op == (+), binops)
    idx_mul = findfirst(op -> op == (*), binops)
    idx_div = findfirst(op -> op == (/), binops)

    # Complexity budget check
    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)

    # Decide whether to attempt rational coupling: target / (1 + motif)
    can_rational = (idx_div !== nothing) && (idx_add !== nothing)
    use_rational = can_rational && (rand(rng) < 0.35) && (tree_size + 4 <= maxsize)

    extra_cost = use_rational ? 3 : 1
    budget = maxsize - tree_size - extra_cost
    budget < 1 && return tree

    # Donor selection: prefer compound subtrees that fit budget, fallback to any valid subtree
    filter_compound(t) = (t.degree > 0) && (count_nodes(t) <= budget)
    filter_any(t) = count_nodes(t) <= budget

    donor = if any(filter_compound, tree)
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=filter_compound))
    elseif any(filter_any, tree)
        rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=filter_any))
    else
        return tree
    end
    motif = copy(donor)

    # In-place helper to shift feature indices across variables
    function _shift_features!(node, shift::Int, nfeats::Int)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeats)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift, nfeats)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    # Unified feature remapping: shift == 0 retains identity, shift > 0 rotates variables
    if nfeatures > 1
        shift = rand(rng, 0:(nfeatures - 1))
        if shift > 0
            _shift_features!(motif, shift, nfeatures)
        end
    end

    # Target selection and splicing
    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    target_copy = copy(target)

    new_node = if use_rational
        # Spliced as target / (1 + motif)
        one_node = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
        den = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_add, children=(one_node, motif))
        constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(target_copy, den))
    else
        # Spliced via binary accumulator, biased toward + and *
        op_pool = filter(!isnothing, (idx_add, idx_mul))
        bin_op = (!isempty(op_pool) && rand(rng) < 0.70) ? rand(rng, op_pool) : rand(rng, 1:options.nops[2])
        children = rand(rng, Bool) ? (target_copy, motif) : (motif, target_copy)
        constructorof(N)(; op=bin_op, children=children)
    end

    set_node!(target, new_node)
    return tree
end

two_oldest_cost_survival_gen45_4.name: two_oldest_cost_survival_gen45_4
two_oldest_cost_survival_gen45_4.code:
"""
Two-oldest cost tournament survival operator.

Tracks the two oldest eligible individuals (smallest birth counters) in a single pass
and selects the one with the higher cost for replacement. If only one eligible member
exists, it is replaced directly.

Key improvements and simplifications over the parent:
- Replaces the parent's rigid single-oldest lexicographic scan with a 2-candidate tournament
  at the age boundary.
- Resolves the parent's limitation where cost tie-breaks are never activated due to strictly
  unique birth timestamps in PySR populations.
- Preserves regularized age-turnover while preventing high-fitness, Pareto-optimal backbones
  from being discarded unconditionally on age alone.
- Maintains zero memory allocations and O(N) single-pass computational efficiency.
"""
function two_oldest_cost_survival_gen45_4(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    oldest_idx = 0
    second_oldest_idx = 0

    # Single pass to identify the two oldest eligible population members
    for i in 1:pop.n
        i in exclude_indices && continue

        if oldest_idx == 0 || pop.members[i].birth < pop.members[oldest_idx].birth
            second_oldest_idx = oldest_idx
            oldest_idx = i
        elseif second_oldest_idx == 0 || pop.members[i].birth < pop.members[second_oldest_idx].birth
            second_oldest_idx = i
        end
    end

    @assert oldest_idx != 0 "No eligible members to replace"

    # If only one candidate is eligible, replace it directly
    if second_oldest_idx == 0
        return oldest_idx
    end

    # Replace the candidate with the worse (higher) cost among the two oldest
    if pop.members[oldest_idx].cost >= pop.members[second_oldest_idx].cost
        return oldest_idx
    else
        return second_oldest_idx
    end
end

simple_leaf_saturation_gen33_1_gen45_5.name: simple_leaf_saturation_gen33_1_gen45_5
simple_leaf_saturation_gen33_1_gen45_5.code:
"""
    simple_leaf_saturation_gen33_1_gen45_5(tree, options, nfeatures, rng)

Replace a randomly chosen *variable leaf* `x` with the rational saturation scaffold
`x / (1 + x)`. The two `x` copies are independent nodes, so later mutations can
specialize them into forms such as `x / (1 + y)` or `x / (1 + c*x)`.

Steps:
1. Require both `+` and `/` among the binary operators.
2. Check that the fixed size increase of this rewrite (+4 nodes) fits in `maxsize`.
3. Sample a variable leaf uniformly.
4. Overwrite it in place with `x / (1 + x)`.

Simplified from the parent by restricting the duplicated motif to a single variable
*leaf* instead of any variable-containing subtree. That removes: the per-candidate
`count_nodes` eligibility filter, the separate `has_variable` pre-scan (subsumed by
the leaf sampler's own filter), and the variable-size budget arithmetic (the size
delta is now the constant 4). This is sound because the saturation template is the
valuable structural leap; a leaf-level insertion is the cheapest way to introduce it,
costs a fixed and small amount of size budget, and larger saturated motifs can still
be grown afterwards by ordinary mutations acting inside the new numerator/denominator.
`nfeatures` is kept for mutation-interface compatibility.
"""
function simple_leaf_saturation_gen33_1_gen45_5(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    binops = options.operators.binops
    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op === (+), binops)
    idx_div = findfirst(op -> op === (/), binops)

    # Both operators are needed to build the u/(1+u) template.
    (idx_add === nothing || idx_div === nothing) && return tree

    # A leaf becomes a 5-node subtree, so the size grows by exactly 4.
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    count_nodes(tree) + 4 > maxsize && return tree

    # Only variable leaves are eligible targets; bail out if there are none.
    _is_var_leaf(t) = t.degree == 0 && !t.constant
    any(_is_var_leaf, tree) || return tree

    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_is_var_leaf))

    # Independent copies: later mutations can differentiate numerator/denominator.
    numerator = copy(target)
    motif = copy(target)
    one_node = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
    denominator = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_add, children=(one_node, motif))
    replacement = constructorof(N)(; op=idx_div, children=(numerator, denominator))

    set_node!(target, replacement)
    return tree
end

clone_pruned_parsimony_tournament_gen45_.name: clone_pruned_parsimony_tournament_gen45_6
clone_pruned_parsimony_tournament_gen45_.code:
"""
    clone_pruned_parsimony_tournament_gen45_6(pop, running_search_statistics, options)

Simplified diversity-aware tournament selection.

Core idea (kept from the parent): sample a moderately enlarged pool, rank it by the
standard adaptive-parsimony cost, and make sure near-duplicate individuals do not
crowd out the tournament ladder. Two members are treated as near-duplicates when
they share the same complexity and have (relatively) indistinguishable losses,
which is a cheap proxy for "same phenotype".

Steps:
 1. Sample `1.5 * tournament_selection_n` members (capped by the population size).
 2. Compute the usual frequency-adjusted cost for every candidate.
 3. Sort by that cost and walk the list from best to worst, keeping a candidate
    only if no already-kept candidate has the same complexity and an essentially
    identical loss. The best representative of each duplicate cluster survives.
 4. Run the usual geometric tournament ladder over the deduplicated, already
    sorted list of survivors.

What was removed / merged relative to the parent:
 - The whole quality-gated "rare complexity niche" branch (its own sort, its own
   champion scan, and the 10% probability) is gone; complexity exploration is
   still driven by the adaptive-parsimony frequency term that is part of the cost.
 - The multiplicative clone penalty (magnitude constant plus the sign-safe
   positive/negative/zero cases) is replaced by simply *pruning* clones from the
   pool. This is monotone in the ranking, needs no tuning constant, and cannot be
   inverted by negative custom objectives, so it is strictly more robust while
   being simpler.
 - Because the survivors are collected in ascending cost order, the tournament
   winner of rank `k` is just the `k`-th survivor, so `argmin_fast`/`bottomk_fast`
   and the second sort are no longer needed.
The best member of the pool is always kept, so the operator degrades gracefully to
plain adaptive-parsimony tournament selection when there are no duplicates.
"""
function clone_pruned_parsimony_tournament_gen45_6(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    running_search_statistics::RunningSearchStatistics,
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::PopMember{T,L,N} where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    # Slightly enlarged pool so that duplicate clusters are actually visible.
    n_base = options.tournament_selection_n
    pool_size = min(pop.n, max(n_base, cld(3 * n_base, 2)))
    pool = StatsBase.sample(pop.members, pool_size; replace=false)
    n = length(pool)

    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    adjusted_costs = Vector{L}(undef, n)
    parsimony_scaling = L(options.adaptive_parsimony_scaling)

    # Standard adaptive-parsimony score, identical to the default selector.
    for i in 1:n
        member = pool[i]
        complexity = compute_complexity(member, options)
        complexities[i] = complexity

        if options.use_frequency_in_tournament
            frequency = if 0 < complexity <= options.maxsize
                L(running_search_statistics.normalized_frequencies[complexity])
            else
                zero(L)
            end
            adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost * exp(parsimony_scaling * frequency)
        else
            adjusted_costs[i] = member.cost
        end
    end

    # Walk best-to-worst and keep only the first representative of each
    # (complexity, loss) cluster: duplicates are dropped instead of penalized.
    order = sortperm(adjusted_costs)
    clone_tolerance = L(1e-6)
    survivors = Int[]

    for i in order
        is_clone = false
        loss_i = pool[i].loss
        for j in survivors
            complexities[i] == complexities[j] || continue
            loss_j = pool[j].loss
            loss_scale = max(abs(loss_i), abs(loss_j), eps(L))
            if abs(loss_i - loss_j) <= clone_tolerance * loss_scale
                is_clone = true
                break
            end
        end
        is_clone || push!(survivors, i)
    end

    # `survivors` is non-empty (the pool best is always kept) and sorted by cost.
    m = length(survivors)
    p = options.tournament_selection_p

    selected_rank = if p == 1.0
        1
    else
        ranks = 0:(m - 1)
        probabilities = p .* ((1 - p) .^ ranks)
        StatsBase.sample(StatsBase.Weights(probabilities, sum(probabilities)))
    end

    # Ascending cost order means rank k is simply the k-th survivor.
    return pool[survivors[min(selected_rank, m)]]
end

duplicate_motif_with_normalized_correcti.name: duplicate_motif_with_normalized_correction_gen45_7
duplicate_motif_with_normalized_correcti.code:
"""
    duplicate_motif_with_normalized_correction_gen45_7(tree::N, options, nfeatures::Int, rng::AbstractRNG)

Simplified motif-reuse mutation. It copies one variable-bearing subtree, optionally shifts all
of its feature indices together, and attaches it to a random target using one of two focused forms:

1. A common symmetric accumulation, `target + motif` or `target * motif`.
2. When the required operators exist, a normalized correction
   `target / sqrt(1 ± motif * motif)`.

The second form directly assembles common Lorentz, geometric-normalization, and saturation laws such
as `x0 / sqrt(1 - (x1 / x2)^2)` from motifs already present in the tree.

Compared with the parent, this version removes donor-quality tiers, targeted single-feature
substitution, arbitrary rational denominators, operand-order randomization, and broad operator
biasing. Donors are selected through one size-and-variable filter, feature remapping is either a
single cyclic shift or identity, and plain coupling is restricted to `+` and `*` when available.
These reductions retain the central advantage—reusing evolved structure—while concentrating the
more complex branch on a high-value template suggested by the search trace.
"""
function duplicate_motif_with_normalized_correction_gen45_7(
    tree::N,
    options,
    nfeatures::Int,
    rng::AbstractRNG,
) where {T,N<:AbstractExpressionNode{T}}
    options.nops[2] == 0 && return tree

    binops = options.operators.binops
    unaops = options.operators.unaops
    nbin = options.nops[2]

    idx_add = findfirst(op -> op === (+), binops)
    idx_sub = findfirst(op -> op === (-), binops)
    idx_mul = findfirst(op -> op === (*), binops)
    idx_div = findfirst(op -> op === (/), binops)
    idx_sqrt = findfirst(op -> op === sqrt, unaops)

    tree_size = count_nodes(tree)
    maxsize = hasproperty(options, :maxsize) ? options.maxsize : typemax(Int)
    space = maxsize - tree_size
    space < 2 && return tree

    # This template adds two motif copies plus five structural nodes:
    # division, square multiplication, denominator operator, constant, and sqrt.
    normalized_available =
        idx_mul !== nothing &&
        idx_div !== nothing &&
        idx_sqrt !== nothing &&
        (idx_add !== nothing || idx_sub !== nothing)

    use_normalized =
        normalized_available &&
        space >= 7 &&
        rand(rng) < 0.40

    donor_budget = use_normalized ? (space - 5) ÷ 2 : space - 1
    donor_budget < 1 && return tree

    _has_variable(node) =
        any(n -> n.degree == 0 && !n.constant, node)
    _eligible_donor(node) =
        count_nodes(node) <= donor_budget && _has_variable(node)

    any(_eligible_donor, tree) || return tree

    donor = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree, filter=_eligible_donor))
    motif = copy(donor)

    # A global cyclic shift preserves relationships within a motif while allowing
    # the same functional form to be reused on another feature block.
    function _shift_features!(node, shift)
        if node.degree == 0
            if !node.constant
                node.feature = mod1(node.feature + shift, nfeatures)
            end
        else
            for i in 1:(node.degree)
                _shift_features!(get_child(node, i), shift)
            end
        end
        return node
    end

    if nfeatures > 1 && rand(rng) < 0.40
        _shift_features!(motif, rand(rng, 1:(nfeatures - 1)))
    end

    target = rand(rng, NodeSampler(; tree))
    target_copy = copy(target)

    replacement = if use_normalized
        # Duplicate the motif exactly to form motif² without requiring a square operator.
        motif_squared = constructorof(N)(;
            op=idx_mul,
            children=(motif, copy(motif)),
        )

        den_op = if idx_add !== nothing && idx_sub !== nothing
            rand(rng, Bool) ? idx_add : idx_sub
        elseif idx_add !== nothing
            idx_add
        else
            idx_sub
        end

        one_node = constructorof(N)(T; val=one(T))
        denominator_base = constructorof(N)(;
            op=den_op,
            children=(one_node, motif_squared),
        )
        denominator = constructorof(N)(;
            op=idx_sqrt,
            children=(denominator_base,),
        )

        constructorof(N)(;
            op=idx_div,
            children=(target_copy, denominator),
        )
    else
        # Prefer the two broadly useful symmetry couplings; use any binary
        # operator only when neither is configured.
        preferred = Int[]
        idx_add !== nothing && push!(preferred, idx_add)
        idx_mul !== nothing && push!(preferred, idx_mul)
        coupling_op = isempty(preferred) ? rand(rng, 1:nbin) : rand(rng, preferred)

        constructorof(N)(;
            op=coupling_op,
            children=(target_copy, motif),
        )
    end

    set_node!(target, replacement)
    return tree
end

one_pass_affine_profile_loss_gen45_8.name: one_pass_affine_profile_loss_gen45_8
one_pass_affine_profile_loss_gen45_8.code:
"""
    one_pass_affine_profile_loss_gen45_8(tree, dataset, options)

Shape-first loss: measure how well the prediction matches the target *up to the best
affine recalibration* `a * p + b`, with a small clipped raw-error tie-breaker that
still rewards expressions whose constants are already correct.

Steps:
 1. Evaluate the tree once.
 2. In a **single** pass, accumulate first and second moments of the prediction and
    target (shifted by the first sample for numerical stability) together with the
    raw sum of squared errors.
 3. Convert the shifted sums into centered second moments and use the least-squares
    identity `SSE_affine = Var(y) - Cov(p,y)^2 / Var(p)` to get the affine residual
    in closed form.
 4. Normalize by the target's standard deviation (with a tiny floor for constant
    targets) to obtain a scale-free shape term in [0, 1], and add a clipped raw
    NRMSE term with weight 1/256.

Simplifications relative to the parent:
 * The parent's two data passes (online means, then centered moments) are merged into
   **one** pass over the data. Stability is retained by shifting all values by the
   first sample, so the accumulated sums are already nearly centered.
 * The per-element `isfinite` guard inside the hot loop is removed; any non-finite
   prediction or target propagates into the accumulators, so a single finiteness
   check on the final moments is sufficient.
 * The `min(shape, 1)` clamp is dropped because the profiled residual can never
   exceed `Var(y)`, making the clamp mathematically inactive.

These changes keep the core idea (affine-invariant shape error plus a weak
calibration tie-break) while halving the data traffic of the parent.
"""
function one_pass_affine_profile_loss_gen45_8(
    tree::Union{AbstractExpression{T},AbstractExpressionNode{T}},
    dataset::Dataset{T,L},
    options::AbstractOptions,
)::L where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE}
    prediction, completed = eval_tree_array(tree, dataset.X, options)
    if !completed || isnothing(prediction)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    n = dataset.n
    if n <= 0 || length(prediction) != n || length(dataset.y) != n
        return L(Inf)
    end

    zero_l = zero(L)
    one_l = one(L)
    n_l = L(n)

    # Shift by the first sample: sums stay small even for large-offset data,
    # which is what made the parent's separate mean pass unnecessary.
    @inbounds p0 = L(prediction[1])
    @inbounds y0 = L(dataset.y[1])
    if !(isfinite(p0) && isfinite(y0))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    sp = zero_l      # sum of (p - p0)
    sy = zero_l      # sum of (y - y0)
    spp = zero_l     # sum of (p - p0)^2
    syy = zero_l     # sum of (y - y0)^2
    spy = zero_l     # sum of (p - p0)(y - y0)
    raw_ss = zero_l  # sum of (p - y)^2

    @inbounds for i in 1:n
        dp = L(prediction[i]) - p0
        dy = L(dataset.y[i]) - y0

        sp += dp
        sy += dy
        spp += dp * dp
        syy += dy * dy
        spy += dp * dy

        r = dp - dy + (p0 - y0)  # == p - y
        raw_ss += r * r
    end

    # Single finiteness gate: any bad sample poisons these accumulators.
    if !(isfinite(sp) && isfinite(sy) && isfinite(spp) && isfinite(syy) && isfinite(spy))
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # De-shift into centered second moments and the target mean.
    mean_y = y0 + sy / n_l
    m2_p = max(spp - sp * sp / n_l, zero_l)
    m2_y = max(syy - sy * sy / n_l, zero_l)
    cov_py = spy - sp * sy / n_l

    # Floor keeps the normalization usable when the target is (nearly) constant.
    target_norm = max(sqrt(m2_y), sqrt(eps(L)) * sqrt(n_l) * max(one_l, abs(mean_y)))
    if !(isfinite(target_norm) && target_norm > zero_l)
        return L(Inf)
    end

    # Least-squares identity for the optimal affine fit: no extra data pass needed.
    profile_ss = m2_y
    if m2_p > zero_l
        explained = cov_py * cov_py / m2_p
        isfinite(explained) || return L(Inf)
        profile_ss = max(m2_y - explained, zero_l)
    end

    # profile_ss <= m2_y <= target_norm^2, so this is automatically within [0, 1].
    shape_term = sqrt(profile_ss) / target_norm

    # Weak, bounded calibration pressure toward already-correct constants.
    bounded_raw = isfinite(raw_ss) ? min(sqrt(raw_ss) / target_norm, one_l) : one_l

    loss_value = shape_term + bounded_raw / L(256)
    return isfinite(loss_value) ? L(max(loss_value, zero_l)) : L(Inf)
end

pareto_niche_crowding_survival_init_3.name: pareto_niche_crowding_survival_init_3
pareto_niche_crowding_survival_init_3.code:
"""
    pareto_niche_crowding_survival_init_3(pop, options; exclude_indices=Int[])

Survival (replacement) operator that combines **age-regularization** with
**Pareto-front protection** and **complexity-niche crowding pressure**.

Core idea
---------
The default operator always kills the oldest member. That maintains turnover, but it
happily destroys the *only* accurate expression at some complexity level, which is
exactly the kind of stepping stone symbolic regression needs to reach a ground-truth
formula. Conversely, purely greedy replacement (kill the worst) collapses diversity.

This operator instead ranks every member by an *expendability score* built from four
signals, and replaces the most expendable one:

1. **Dominance count** — how many members are at least as simple *and* at least as
   accurate. A heavily dominated member carries no information the population does not
   already have, so it is the prime candidate for replacement.
2. **Structural-clone count** — members with identical complexity and (numerically)
   identical loss are duplicates; all but the oldest representative are pure waste.
   These are penalized hardest because clones are the main driver of premature
   convergence in tournament-based SR.
3. **Niche crowding** — how many other members occupy the same complexity level.
   Replacement pressure is concentrated on over-populated complexity bins, which keeps
   the population spread across the whole complexity axis (a proxy for the Pareto
   "hall of fame" that PySR ultimately reports).
4. **Age** — older members get a mild bonus to expendability, preserving the
   exploration benefits of age-regularized evolution.

Protections
-----------
* Non-dominated, non-duplicated members (the population's own Pareto front) receive a
  large score discount, so they are only replaced when nothing else is available.
* The single best-cost member is effectively never replaced (elitism).
* Members with non-finite loss/cost are treated as maximally expendable.

Stochastic age branch
---------------------
With probability `p_age` the operator falls back to pure oldest-first replacement
(restricted to unprotected members). This guarantees that no member can survive
forever by sitting in a sparse niche, avoiding the stagnation that fully
deterministic greedy/crowding schemes suffer from.

Assumptions / heuristics
------------------------
* `(complexity, loss)` is used for dominance (rather than `cost`) so that the operator's
  notion of "redundant" is independent of the adaptive parsimony term, which fluctuates.
* Complexity bins are exact integer complexities; this is a natural niche definition
  because SR complexity is already a small integer.
* Small random noise breaks score ties uniformly, so symmetric duplicates do not always
  lose the same slot.
* `exclude_indices` entries are given score `-Inf` and can therefore never be returned.
"""
function pareto_niche_crowding_survival_init_3(
    pop::Population{T,L,N},
    options::AbstractOptions;
    exclude_indices::Vector{Int}=Int[],
)::Int where {T<:DATA_TYPE,L<:LOSS_TYPE,N}
    n = pop.n

    # Trivial case: single-member population.
    n == 1 && return 1

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Gather per-member statistics once (complexity, loss, cost, birth).
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    complexities = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    losses = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    costs = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    births = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        m = pop.members[i]
        complexities[i] = compute_complexity(m, options)
        l = Float64(m.loss)
        # Non-finite (NaN/Inf) losses are mapped to +Inf: worst possible, fully dominated.
        losses[i] = isfinite(l) ? l : Inf
        c = Float64(m.cost)
        costs[i] = isfinite(c) ? c : Inf
        births[i] = Float64(m.birth)
    end

    min_birth, max_birth = extrema(births)
    birth_range = max(max_birth - min_birth, 1.0)  # guard against all-equal births

    # Elite (best cost) member: protected from replacement.
    best_cost_idx = 1
    for i in 2:n
        if costs[i] < costs[best_cost_idx]
            best_cost_idx = i
        end
    end

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Pairwise pass: dominance counts, clone counts, niche occupancy.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    n_dom = zeros(Int, n)            # number of members dominating i in (complexity, loss)
    n_clone = zeros(Int, n)          # number of older/earlier exact duplicates of i
    n_niche = ones(Int, n)           # members sharing i's complexity (including i itself)

    for i in 1:n
        ci = complexities[i]
        li = losses[i]
        bi = births[i]
        for j in 1:n
            j == i && continue
            cj = complexities[j]
            lj = losses[j]

            # Pareto dominance: simpler-or-equal and better-or-equal, strict in one.
            if (cj <= ci && lj < li) || (cj < ci && lj <= li)
                n_dom[i] += 1
            end

            if cj == ci
                n_niche[i] += 1
                # Numerically identical loss at identical complexity => structural clone.
                same_loss =
                    (isinf(li) && isinf(lj)) || abs(lj - li) <= 1e-10 * (1.0 + abs(li))
                if same_loss
                    # Keep the earliest-born representative; count only *earlier* twins,
                    # so exactly one member of a clone cluster ends up unpenalized.
                    if bj_is_earlier(births[j], bi, j, i)
                        n_clone[i] += 1
                    end
                end
            end
        end
    end

    # A member is "protected" if it sits on the population's Pareto front and is
    # not a redundant copy of an equally good, equally complex member.
    protected = [(n_dom[i] == 0 && n_clone[i] == 0) for i in 1:n]

    excluded = Set(exclude_indices)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Stochastic pure-age branch (age-regularized evolution fallback).
    #    Keeps turnover alive so nothing survives indefinitely.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    p_age = 0.2
    if rand() < p_age
        best_idx = 0
        best_birth = Inf
        # First try unprotected, non-elite members only.
        for i in 1:n
            (i in excluded) && continue
            i == best_cost_idx && continue
            protected[i] && continue
            if births[i] < best_birth
                best_birth = births[i]
                best_idx = i
            end
        end
        best_idx != 0 && return best_idx
        # Otherwise fall through to the scoring path (which relaxes protections).
    end

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Expendability score: higher == more deserving of replacement.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    scores = Vector{Float64}(undef, n)
    for i in 1:n
        if i in excluded
            scores[i] = -Inf   # never returnable
            continue
        end

        s = 0.0

        # (a) Redundancy in the accuracy/complexity trade-off.
        s += 3.0 * log1p(n_dom[i])

        # (b) Exact duplicates: strongest signal, they add zero diversity.
        s += 4.0 * n_clone[i]

        # (c) Crowding within the member's complexity niche.
        s += 1.5 * log1p(max(n_niche[i] - 1, 0))

        # (d) Age bonus: oldest member of the population gets ~1.0, newest ~0.0.
        s += 1.0 * (1.0 - (births[i] - min_birth) / birth_range)

        # (e) Broken/degenerate members are always fair game.
        if !isfinite(losses[i]) || !isfinite(costs[i])
            s += 10.0
        end

        # (f) Oversized expressions beyond the allowed maxsize should not linger.
        if complexities[i] > options.maxsize
            s += 5.0
        end

        # Protections (applied as large discounts so they still lose to -Inf exclusions).
        if protected[i]
            s -= 50.0
        end
        if i == best_cost_idx
            s -= 1.0e6  # elitism: effectively never replace the best-cost member
        end

        # Random tie-break jitter, small relative to the structural terms.
        s += 0.05 * rand()

        scores[i] = s
    end

    # argmax over scores (equivalently argmin over negated scores).
    return argmin_fast([-scores[i] for i in 1:n])
end

"""
    bj_is_earlier(bj, bi, j, i)

Tie-break helper for clone detection: returns `true` when member `j` should be
considered the *earlier* (surviving) representative of a clone cluster, using birth
order first and index as a deterministic fallback for simultaneous births.
"""
function bj_is_earlier(bj::Float64, bi::Float64, j::Int, i::Int)
    return bj < bi || (bj == bi && j < i)
end
